Porro Seneca in suis ait Proverbiis : Locutum me aliquando pœnituit; tacuisse, nunquam.
paras.en: [[3:5|A time to scatter stones|Tempus spargendi lapides]]: for at times hard men must be scattered this way and that, and their wicked fellowship and league broken up; and hard thoughts too, and the linking together of wanton imaginations, must be broken apart. [[3:5|and a time to gather|Et tempus colligendi]]: since one must labour that those who are divided in body be reunited by charity. Wicked and abject thoughts must also be called back to memory, so as to be disclosed in confession. [[3:5|A time to embrace|Tempus amplexandi]] the heavenly Bridegroom with the arms of charity, through the exercises of the contemplative life; [[3:5|and a time to be far from embraces|et tempus longe fieri ab amplexibus]], by giving oneself to the sorrow of penance, to the exercises of the active life, and to the needs of the body. [[3:6|A time to get|Tempus acquirendi]] grace and virtues, and spiritual progress, and the blessed life; [[3:6|and a time to lose|et tempus perdendi]] temporal things for the sake of things spiritual and eternal, nay, to lose oneself by mortification and the denial of oneself, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Matt 10:39|he that shall lose his life for me, shall find it|Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, inveniet eam]]. [[3:6|A time to keep|Tempus custodiendi]] oneself from sin, according to that saying: [[Prov 4:23|With all watchfulness keep thy heart|Omni custodia custodi cor tuum]]; [[3:6|and a time to cast away|et tempus abjiciendi]] such keeping, when a man shall be confirmed in good and safe from every danger: which will be in the fatherland. [[3:7|A time to rend|Tempus scindendi]] the hardness of the heart, that it may be opened to the word of God and softened to penance, according to that saying of Joel: [[Joel 2:13|rend your hearts, and not your garments|Scindite corda vestra, et non vestimenta vestra]]; [[3:7|and a time to sew|et tempus consuendi]], that is, to put together a sermon from the authorities of the Scriptures and of the doctors. [[3:7|A time to keep silence, and a time to speak|Tempus tacendi, et tempus loquendi]]. On this account Jerome says: After a long time, let us become masters from disciples. And Seneca says in his Proverbs: I have sometimes repented of having spoken; of having kept silent, never.

paras.t: Tempus dilectionis Dei et proximorum; et tempus odii vitiorum et eorum qui nobis in via Dei obsistunt, secundum quod tales : juxta quod scriptum est, Perfecto odio oderam illos. Unde et Christus : Si quis (inquit) venit ad me, et non odit patrem suum et matrem, non potest meus esse discipulus. Rursus, tempus odii sui ipsius, sicut subjunxit : Adhuc autem et animam suam. Ideo et in Evangelio Joannis loquitur, dicens : Qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam æternam custodit eam. Hoc odium est, iniquitatem odire, pravam inclinationem reprimere, debitam pro peccatis castigationem assumere. Tempus belli, contra invisibiles hostes ac aciem vitiorum. Ideo hortatur Apostolus : Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die mala, et in omnibus perfecti stare. Nempe, ut sanctus Job fassus est, Militia est vita hominis super terram. Christus quoque in Evangelio : Regnum, inquit, cœlorum vim patitur, et violenti rapiunt illud. Hinc Seneca loquitur : Pacem habeto cum hominibus, bellum cum vitiis. Et tempus pacis internæ cum Deo, pacis quoque temporalis cum proximis, sicut ad Romanos legitur : Si fieri potest, quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes. Quod si alii noluerint concordes et pacifici esse nobiscum, nos tamen tranquillitatem servemus in Deo. Hinc Seneca docet : Id age, ne quis merito tuo te oderit.
paras.en: [[3:8|A time of love|Tempus dilectionis]] of God and of our neighbours; [[3:8|and a time of hatred|et tempus odii]] of vices, and of those who stand against us in the way of God, in so far as they are such: according to what is written: [[Ps 138:22|I have hated them with a perfect hatred|Perfecto odio oderam illos]]. Whence Christ too: [[Luke 14:26|If any man|Si quis]] (he says) [[Luke 14:26|come to me, and hate not his father and mother|venit ad me, et non odit patrem suum et matrem]], [[Luke 14:26|he cannot be my disciple|non potest meus esse discipulus]]. Again, a time of hatred of oneself, as he added: [[Luke 14:26|yea and his own life also|Adhuc autem et animam suam]]. Therefore he also speaks in the Gospel of John, saying: [[John 12:25|he that hateth his life in this world keepeth it unto life eternal|Qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam æternam custodit eam]]. This hatred is to hate iniquity, to check evil inclination, to take on the chastisement due for sins. [[3:8|A time of war|Tempus belli]], against the invisible enemies and the battle line of the vices. Therefore the Apostle exhorts: [[Eph 6:13|take unto you the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day and to stand in all things perfect|Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die mala, et in omnibus perfecti stare]]. For indeed, as holy Job confessed, [[Job 7:1|The life of man upon earth is a warfare|Militia est vita hominis super terram]]. Christ too in the Gospel: [[Matt 11:12|the kingdom of heaven|Regnum, inquit, cœlorum]], he says, [[Matt 11:12|suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away|vim patitur, et violenti rapiunt illud]]. Hence Seneca says: Have peace with men, war with vices. [[3:8|And a time of peace|Et tempus pacis]], inward peace with God, and temporal peace too with our neighbours, as we read in the Epistle to the Romans: [[Rom 12:18|If it be possible, as much as is in you, have peace with all men.|Si fieri potest, quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes]] But if others will not be of one mind and peaceable with us, let us nonetheless keep our tranquillity in God. Hence Seneca teaches: See to it that no one hate you by your own desert.

paras.t: Quid habet amplius homo de labore suo, nisi aliquid prædictorum? quasi dicat : Stabilitatem non habet, neque salutem in vita præsenti. Vidi afflictionem, id est laboriosam exercitationem circa studium litterarium, quam dedit Deus permissive aut effective, filiis hominum, ut distendantur, id est, diversimode extendantur et occupentur, in ea : quatenus per hanc etiam a gravioribus vitiis et nimiis carnalitatibus retrahantur, periculosisque otiis careant, quamvis in ea ad salutem parum aut nihil proficiant.
paras.en: [[3:9|What hath man more of his labour|Quid habet amplius homo de labore suo]], other than some one of the things just named? As if to say: he has no stability, nor salvation, in the present life. [[3:10|I have seen the trouble|Vidi afflictionem]], that is, the toilsome exercise about the study of letters, [[3:10|which God hath given|quam dedit Deus]], by permitting it or by effecting it, [[3:10|the sons of men to be exercised|filiis hominum, ut distendantur]], that is, to be stretched out and busied in various ways, [[3:10|in it|in ea]]: so that by it they may also be drawn back from graver vices and from excessive carnality, and be free of dangerous idleness, although in it they make little or no progress toward salvation.

paras.t: Cuncta fecit Deus bona in tempore suo, id est, dum ea produxit, sive in principio mundi, seu postea. Unde in Genesi sæpe dicitur : Vidit Deus quod esset bonum. Omne enim creatum, aliquid increatæ bonitatis participat. Ideo ad Timotheum dicit Apostolus : Omnis creatura Dei bona. Vel ideo ait, In tempore suo, quoniam quamvis quædam nociva sint homini, eis importune utenti, tamen si tempore suo, id est opportuno, eis utatur, bona sunt ei. Et mundum tradidit disputationi eorum : id est, creaturas et ordinem universi exposuit Creator considerationi disputationique hominum; ut non inveniat homo opus, quod operatus est Deus, id est, nullam creaturam possit perfecte et plene cognoscere, sicut dictum est supra : Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone. Et quod ait, Ut non inveniat homo, intelligendum videtur concomitanter potius quam causaliter, sicut in Psalmo, Tibi soli peccavi, ut justificeris, etc. Potest tamen causaliter accipi, quoniam ideo voluit Deus homines sic deficere in cognitione creaturarum, quatenus ex hoc attendant incomprehensibilitatem et excellentiam Creatoris, imbecillitatemque proprii intellectus. Quod autem subjungitur, ab initio usque ad finem, referri potest ad verbum illud, Quod operatus est, ut sit sensus, quod nullam creaturam, ab exordio mundi usque ad finem ejus factam sive fiendam, possit homo plene cognoscere; vel ad illud, Ut non inveniat homo, scilicet ab initio vitæ suæ usque ad mortem.
paras.en: [[3:11|He hath made all things good in their time|Cuncta fecit Deus bona in tempore suo]], that is, when he brought them forth, whether in the beginning of the world or afterwards. Whence it is often said in Genesis: [[Gen 1:10|And God saw that it was good|Vidit Deus quod esset bonum]][[Gen 1:12||]][[Gen 1:18||]][[Gen 1:21||]][[Gen 1:25||]]. For every created thing shares in something of the uncreated goodness. Therefore the Apostle says to Timothy: [[1 Tim 4:4|every creature of God is good|Omnis creatura Dei bona]]. Or else he says *in their time* because, though some things are harmful to a man who uses them out of season, yet if he uses them in their time, that is, at the fitting time, they are good for him. [[3:11|and hath delivered the world to their consideration|Et mundum tradidit disputationi eorum]] [*disputatio*: discussion, inquiry]: that is, the Creator has set out the creatures and the order of the universe for the consideration and inquiry of men; [[3:11|so that man cannot find out the work which God hath made|ut non inveniat homo opus, quod operatus est Deus]], that is, so that he cannot know any creature perfectly and fully, as was said above: [[Eccles 1:8|All things are hard: man cannot explain them by word|Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone]]. And his saying *so that man cannot find out* seems to be understood as of what goes along with it rather than of a cause [that is, "so that" states a consequence, not a purpose], as in the Psalm: [[Ps 50:6|To thee only have I sinned|Tibi soli peccavi]], [[Ps 50:6|that thou mayst be justified|ut justificeris]], etc. Yet it can be taken as of a cause, since God willed that men should thus fall short in the knowledge of creatures in order that from this they might attend to the incomprehensibility and excellence of the Creator, and to the weakness of their own understanding. And what is added, [[3:11|from the beginning to the end|ab initio usque ad finem]], can be referred to the words *which God hath made*, so that the sense is that man cannot fully know any creature made, or to be made, from the beginning of the world to its end; or to the words *so that man cannot find out*, namely from the beginning of his life until death.

paras.t: Et cognovi quod non esset melius, nisi lætari in actibus bonis, et in Deo, seclusa curiosa, immoderata, et anxia exercitatione studendi; et facere bona opera in vita sua, per quæ mereatur ad plenitudinem scientiæ in futuro pertingere. Omnis enim homo qui comedit et bibit moderanter cibum et potum, non solum corporalem, sed etiam spiritualem, et videt bonum de labore suo, id est, ex laboribus suis et rebus laboriose acquisitis experitur fructum, atque consequitur commodum; hoc donum Dei est : quia ex gratia et auxilio ejus procedit. Videre autem, in Scripturis frequenter pro Gustare seu Experiri accipitur, ut in Psalmo : Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem ; et in Actibus Apostolorum : David appositus est ad patres suos, et vidit corruptionem.
paras.en: [[3:12|And I have known that there was no better thing than to rejoice|Et cognovi quod non esset melius, nisi lætari]] in good acts, and in God, setting aside a curious, immoderate and anxious exercise of study; [[3:12|and to do well|et facere bona opera]] [Denis: "to do good works"] [[3:12|in this life|in vita sua]], by which he may merit to attain to the fulness of knowledge in the life to come. [[3:13|For every man that eateth and drinketh|Omnis enim homo qui comedit et bibit]] food and drink in moderation, not only bodily but also spiritual, [[3:13|and seeth good of his labour|et videt bonum de labore suo]], that is, experiences the fruit of his labours and of the things got by labour, and obtains their benefit, [[3:13|this is the gift of God|hoc donum Dei est]]: for it proceeds from his grace and help. Now *to see* is often taken in the Scriptures for *to taste* or *to experience*, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 15:10|nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption|Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem]]; and in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 13:36|David|David]] [[Acts 13:36|was laid unto his fathers and saw corruption|appositus est ad patres suos, et vidit corruptionem]].

paras.t: Didici quod omnia opera, id est cuncta creata, quæ fecit Deus, perseverent in æternum. Supra jam dixit : Vidi nihil permanere sub sole. Quomodo ergo nunc ait, quod omnia opera Dei perseverent in æternum? Et respondendum, quod omnia permanent in æternum, vel in esse individuali ac proprio, quantum ad incorruptibilia, ut sunt corpora cœlestia, angeli et animæ rationales, et elementa, quoad se tota; vel in esse suæ speciei, et successione similium sibi usque ad finem mundi : sic enim tempus, motus, dies, nox, æstus et frigus dicuntur jugiter permanere. Nil autem sub sole permanet, uniformiter se habens. Non possumus eis quidquam addere, nec auferre : id est, nullam speciem possumus ordini universi apponere, neque abstrahere, quoniam decor et ordo mundi in specierum connexione ac integritate consistit. Certum est autem, quod individua innumerabilia quotidie auferantur, occidantur, seu corrumpantur. Homines quoque et bruta generant quotidie sibi similia. Quæ fecit Deus, ut timeatur. Omnia enim supergloriosus, omnipotens, sapientissimusque Creator instituit et produxit, quatenus ex consideratione eorum, ad Creatoris admirationem timoremque filialem, amorem et venerationem excitemur. Unde scriptum est : Universa propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus. Qui ait per Jeremiam : Me non timebitis, qui posui arenam terminum mari? Quod factum est, ipsum permanet, vel in se, vel in simili sibi. Quæ futura sunt, jam fuerunt in similibus sibi in specie, sicut expositum est in primo articulo; et Deus instaurat quod abiit, id est, restituit in simili sibi quod desiit esse.
paras.en: [[3:14|I have learned that all the works|Didici quod omnia opera]], that is, all created things, [[3:14|which God hath made, continue for ever|quæ fecit Deus, perseverent in æternum]]. He has already said above: I saw that [[Eccles 2:11|nothing was lasting under the sun|nihil permanere sub sole]]. How then does he now say that all the works of God continue for ever? The answer is that all things endure for ever, either in their individual and proper being, as regards the incorruptible things, such as the heavenly bodies, the angels and rational souls, and the elements taken as wholes; or in the being of their species, and in the succession of things like them until the end of the world: for so time, motion, day, night, heat and cold are said to endure continually. But nothing under the sun endures holding itself always the same. [[3:14|we cannot add any thing, nor take away|Non possumus eis quidquam addere, nec auferre]]: that is, we can add no species to the order of the universe, nor take one away, since the beauty and order of the world consists in the linking together and the completeness of the species. It is certain, however, that countless individuals are taken away, slain or corrupted every day; and men and brutes too beget their like every day. [[3:14|those things which God hath made that he may be feared|Quæ fecit Deus, ut timeatur]]. For the supremely glorious, almighty and most wise Creator founded and brought forth all things so that from the consideration of them we may be stirred to wonder at the Creator, and to filial fear, love and veneration. Whence it is written: [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself|Universa propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus]]. He it is who says through Jeremias: [[Jer 5:22|Will not you then fear me|Me non timebitis]], [[Jer 5:22|I have set the sand a bound for the sea|qui posui arenam terminum mari]]? [[3:15|That which hath been made, the same continueth|Quod factum est, ipsum permanet]], either in itself or in something like it. [[3:15|the things that shall be, have already been|Quæ futura sunt, jam fuerunt]] in things like them in species, as was explained in the first article[[Eccles 1:9||]]; [[3:15|and God restoreth that which is past|et Deus instaurat quod abiit]], that is, he restores in something like it what has ceased to be.

paras.t: Vidi sub sole in loco judicii impietatem : id est, in soliis judicialibus seu tribunalibus, vidi sedere impios judices ; et in loco justitiæ, iniquitatem : id est, eos qui resident ad conservandam justitiam inter alios, vidi esse injustos; vel qui primo fuerunt justi, vidi in injustitiam lapsos. Et dixi in corde meo : Justum et impium judicabit Dominus : id est, ex hoc quod in hoc mundo est tanta inordinatio ac injustitia in judicando, conclusi et perpendi, quod Deus essentialiter justus ac sapiens, qui nullum malum dimittit impunitum, nullumque bonum relinquit impræmiatum, universaque inordinata per culpam, reducit ad ordinem per pœnarum inflictionem : conclusi, inquam, quod ipse universos justissime judicabit, non solum in morte singulorum, sed et in die novissimo : et tempus omnis rei tunc erit : id est, tunc quælibet res recipiet et habebit quod ei debetur seu congruit ; tuncque erit consummatio temporis unicuique enti, quia deinceps tempus non erit, motu cæli cessante, juxta illud in Apocalypsi : Juravit per viventem in sæcula sæculorum : Quia tempus ultra non erit. Dicitur autem tempus rei esse, quum ei contingit aliquid speciale et arduum. Unde in Evangelio Joannis loquitur Christus : Tempus meum nondum advenit ; et alibi, Nondum venit hora mea.
paras.en: [[3:16|I saw under the sun in the place of judgment wickedness|Vidi sub sole in loco judicii impietatem]]: that is, on the seats of judgment or tribunals I saw wicked judges sitting; [[3:16|and in the place of justice iniquity|et in loco justitiæ, iniquitatem]]: that is, I saw that those who sit to preserve justice among others were unjust; or that those who were at first just had fallen into injustice. [[3:17|And I said in my heart: God shall judge both the just and the wicked|Et dixi in corde meo : Justum et impium judicabit Dominus]]: that is, from the fact that there is so much disorder and injustice in judging in this world, I concluded and weighed that God, who is just and wise by his very essence, who lets no evil go unpunished and leaves no good unrewarded, and brings back to order by the infliction of punishments all things put out of order by sin: I concluded, I say, that he will judge all men most justly, not only at the death of each, but also on the last day: [[3:17|and then shall be the time of every thing|et tempus omnis rei tunc erit]]: that is, then each thing will receive and have what is owed to it or befits it; and then will be the consummation of time for every being, for thereafter there will be no time, the motion of the heavens ceasing, according to that saying in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 10:6|And he swore by him that liveth for ever and ever|Juravit per viventem in sæcula sæculorum]]: [[Apoc 10:6|That time shall be no longer|Quia tempus ultra non erit]]. Now a thing's time is said to be when something special and weighty befalls it. Whence Christ says in the Gospel of John: [[John 7:6|My time is not yet come|Tempus meum nondum advenit]]; and elsewhere: [[John 2:4|My hour is not yet come|Nondum venit hora mea]].

paras.t: Dixi in corde meo de filiis hominum, ut probaret eos Deus : id est, hoc cogitavi atque appetii, ut Deus per suos effectus seu diversos eventus, perscrutaretur hominum qualitatem et proprietatem, non ut ipse agnosceret, sed ut eas nobis manifestaret : sicut dicitur in Scripturis homines tentare et probare, juxta illud Job : Probavit me Dominus quasi aurum quod per ignem transiit ; et in Psalmo : Quoniam probasti nos, Deus ; igne nos examinasti. Hinc subditur : et ostenderet similes esse bestiis. Istud loquitur Salomon in persona imperitorum, opinantium non esse vitam futuram, et cupientium hoc ipsum aliis demonstrari : quales fuerunt Sadducæi, sicut in actibus fertur Apostolorum : qui dixerunt non esse resurrectionem mortuorum, nec angelum, neque spiritum. Idcirco unus in specie, id est consimilis, interitus est hominis et jumentorum, id est similis mors hominum ac brutorum, ita quod anima hominis perit cum corpore ; et æqua utriusque conditio : sicut moritur homo, sic et illa moriuntur ; similiter spirant omnia, scilicet homines et jumenta, et nihil habet homo jumento amplius, id est, in nullo excedit dignitatem brutorum.
paras.en: [[3:18|I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God would prove them|Dixi in corde meo de filiis hominum, ut probaret eos Deus]]: that is, I thought of this and desired it, that God by his effects or by divers events should search out the quality and the properties of men, not so that he himself might know them, but so that he might make them plain to us: in the way that God is said in the Scriptures to try and to prove men, according to that saying of Job: The Lord [[Job 23:10|has tried me as gold that passeth through the fire|Probavit me Dominus quasi aurum quod per ignem transiit]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 65:10|For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us by fire|Quoniam probasti nos, Deus ; igne nos examinasti]]. Hence there is added: [[3:18|and shew them to be like beasts|et ostenderet similes esse bestiis]]. Solomon says this in the person of the ignorant, who think there is no life to come and desire this very thing to be shown to others: such as were the Sadducees, as is told in the Acts of the Apostles, who said [[Acts 23:8|that there is no resurrection|non esse resurrectionem]] of the dead, [[Acts 23:8|neither angel, nor spirit|nec angelum, neque spiritum]]. [[3:19|Therefore the death of man, and of beasts is one|Idcirco unus in specie, id est consimilis, interitus est hominis et jumentorum]] (*one in kind*, that is, alike), that is, the death of men and of brutes is alike, so that the soul of man perishes with the body; [[3:19|and the condition of them both is equal: as man dieth, so they also die: all things breathe alike|et æqua utriusque conditio : sicut moritur homo, sic et illa moriuntur ; similiter spirant omnia]], namely men and beasts, [[3:19|and man hath nothing more than beast|et nihil habet homo jumento amplius]], that is, in nothing does he exceed the dignity of the brutes.

paras.t: Ista est stultorum ac rudium hominum argumentatio, quod quia homines et jumenta in multis conveniunt, ideo homines in nullo jumenta transcendant, et instar brutorum deficiant, quum tamen in ratione et intellectu, ac libera voluntate illis præminent. Propter quod sanctus ille Job inquit : Deus docet nos super jumenta terræ, et super volucres cœli erudit nos.
paras.en: This is the reasoning of foolish and untaught men: that because men and beasts agree in many things, therefore men surpass beasts in nothing and come to an end like the brutes; whereas in reason and understanding and free will they stand above them. For which reason that holy man Job says: God [[Job 35:11|teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and instructeth us more than the fowls of the air|docet nos super jumenta terræ, et super volucres cœli erudit nos]] [the margin gives only "11"; the words are Job 35:11, spoken by Eliu].

paras.t: Cuncta subjacent vanitati, id est mutabilitati (ut supra magis expositum est), et omnia inferiora corruptibilia pergunt ad unum locum communem, id est, tendunt ad mortem, per quam revertuntur in terram. Hinc subditur : De terra facta sunt, quantum ad corpus in quo (quantum ad materiam) elementum terræ prædominatur. In aliquibus tamen proprietas aquæ prædominatur. Unde in Genesi legitur : Dixit Deus : Producant aquæ reptile animæ viventis, et volatile. Et in terram pariter, id est consimiliter, revertuntur, quantum ad corpus, quod in pulverem cineremque resolvitur, juxta illud in Genesi : Pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris. Verumtamen, sicut mixta ex elementis composita sunt, sic resolvuntur in ea. Sed resolutio in terram evidentior est, ideo magis exprimitur.
paras.en: [[3:19|all things are subject to vanity|Cuncta subjacent vanitati]], that is, to changeableness (as was explained more fully above), [[3:20|And all things|et omnia]], all the lower corruptible things, [[3:20|go to one place|pergunt ad unum locum]], a common place, that is, they tend toward death, through which they return to the earth. Hence there is added: [[3:20|of earth they were made|De terra facta sunt]], as regards the body, in which (as regards matter) the element of earth predominates. In some, however, the property of water predominates. Whence we read in Genesis: God said: [[Gen 1:20|let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having life, and the fowl|Producant aquæ reptile animæ viventis, et volatile]]. [[3:20|and into earth they return together|Et in terram pariter, id est consimiliter, revertuntur]] (*together*, that is, in like manner), as regards the body, which is dissolved into dust and ashes, according to that saying in Genesis: [[Gen 3:19|dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return|Pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris]]. Yet just as mixed bodies are composed of the elements, so they are dissolved into them; but the dissolving into earth is more evident, and so it is the one expressed.

paras.t: Quis novit, si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat sursum, id est, an animæ hominum morientium deducantur ad Dei judicium, seu ad loca cœlestia? et si spiritus, id est animæ irrationales, jumentorum descendat deorsum, id est, in potentiam materiæ redigatur, et de esse, cadat in non esse ac in nihileitatis abyssum, potius quam animæ hominum, sicque animæ hominum per immortalitatem præstantiores sint animabus brutorum? quasi dicat : Istud nemini constat. Sed (ut tactum est) Salomon loquitur ista, in persona carnalium et penitus bestialium hominum. De quibus etiam alibi habetur : Dixerunt impii : Non est refrigerium in fine hominis, et non est qui agnitus sit reversus ab inferis ; et post hæc erimus tanquam non fuerimus.
paras.en: [[3:21|Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend upward|Quis novit, si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat sursum]], that is, whether the souls of men who die are led to the judgment of God, or to the heavenly places? [[3:21|and if the spirit|et si spiritus]], that is, the irrational souls, [[3:21|of the beasts descend downward|jumentorum descendat deorsum]], that is, is brought back into the potency of matter, and falls from being into not-being and into the abyss of nothingness, rather than the souls of men, and so the souls of men are more excellent than the souls of brutes by their immortality? As if to say: this is certain to no one. But (as was touched on) Solomon says these things in the person of carnal and wholly beastlike men, of whom it is also said elsewhere: the wicked said: [[Wis 2:1|in the end of a man there is no remedy, and no man hath been known to have returned from hell|Non est refrigerium in fine hominis, et non est qui agnitus sit reversus ab inferis]]; [[Wis 2:2|after this we shall be as if we had not been|et post hæc erimus tanquam non fuerimus]].

paras.t: Stultissimi isti putaverunt, omnes eis similes esse in insipientia ista ; sed erraverunt gravissime : quia non solum ab initio mundi, providentia Dei et ejus judicium, ac immortalitas rationalium animarum, innotuerunt sanctis Patriarchis ac Prophetis, et eorum sequacibus, sed præcipuis quoque philosophis. Siquidem Plato in secundo Timæi disseruit : Passiones si frenarent ac subjugarent animæ, justam his levemque vitam fore voluit opifex Deus ; si vincerentur, injustam et laboriosam : et victricibus animabus, ad comparis stellæ contubernium ac sideream mansionem reditum patere, acturis deinceps vitam beatam ; victas vero, mutare sexum. In Phædone quoque testatur : Quicumque non lustratus et inexpiatus in Avernum abierit, in cœno jacebit ; demum expiatus atque lustratus illinc migrans, habitabit cum diis. Et rursus ibidem : In deorum, inquit, genus philosophanti et pure hinc emigranti, fas est meare. Itemque : Quoties abeunt defuncti in locum quo dæmon unumquemque portaverit, primum quidem in causam deportantur, utrum bene et sancte degerint, an minime. Et quicumque videbuntur mediocriter vitam transegisse, transeuntes in Acheronta, perveniunt in locum ubi habitabunt ; atque ab injustitiis expiati, dantes pœnas, absolvuntur. Sane quicumque videbuntur incurabiliter se habere, ob magnitudines piaculorum, hos Deus in competens jacit barathrum.
paras.en: These most foolish men thought that all were like them in this folly; but they erred most gravely: for from the beginning of the world the providence of God and his judgment, and the immortality of rational souls, were known not only to the holy Patriarchs and Prophets and their followers, but also to the chief philosophers. For Plato taught in the second part of the Timaeus: God the maker willed that if souls bridled and subdued the passions, their life should be just and light; if they were overcome, unjust and toilsome; and that for the victorious souls a return lies open to the companionship of their kindred star and to a starry dwelling, there to lead a blessed life thenceforth; but that the vanquished change their sex. In the Phaedo too he testifies: Whoever has gone down to Avernus unpurified and unexpiated will lie in the mire; but at length, expiated and purified, passing from there, he will dwell with the gods. And again in the same place: Into the race of the gods, he says, it is lawful for him to pass who has given himself to philosophy and departs hence pure. And again: Whenever the dead go away into the place to which his daemon [that is, the guardian spirit of each man, in Plato's account] has carried each one, they are first brought to judgment, whether they have lived well and holily or not. And those who are found to have lived their life indifferently pass into Acheron and come to the place where they will dwell; and, expiated of their injustices by paying the penalty, they are released. But those who are found to be in an incurable state because of the greatness of their crimes, God casts into the fitting pit.

paras.t: Insuper Aristoteles clarissime docet, intellectum esse immaterialem et immortalem, tam tertio de Anima, quam libro de Animalibus. Proclus quoque Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica subtilissime immortalitatem animæ probat, eo quod omne conversivum ad se ipsum, et reditivum ac reflexivum super proprium actum, necesse sit incorporeum et incorruptibile esse. Hinc theoremate 168 fatetur : Omnis intellectus, in æternitate substantiam habet, et potentiam, et operationem ; et postea, Omnis, inquit, anima, incorporea substantia est, et separabilis a corpore, impertibilis quoque et incorruptibilis.
paras.en: Moreover, Aristotle teaches most clearly that the intellect is immaterial and immortal, both in the third book On the Soul and in the book On Animals. Proclus the Platonist too, in his Elements of Theology, proves most subtly the immortality of the soul, on the ground that whatever is able to turn back upon itself, and to return and reflect upon its own act, must be incorporeal and incorruptible. Hence in theorem 168 he declares: Every intellect has its substance, its power and its operation in eternity; and afterwards: Every soul, he says, is an incorporeal substance, separable from the body, indivisible too, and incorruptible.

paras.t: Et deprehendi nil melius esse, quam lætari hominem in opere suo, et hanc esse partem illius. Istud dupliciter potest exponi. Primo, ut Salomon in carnalium persona loquens, eliciat ex præinducto errore, non esse melius, quam ut homo det se ad deliciandum in rebus carnalibus et terrenis, idque reputet felicitatem suam consistere. Secundo, ut introducat hæc verba ex sententia propria, ad reprobandum implicite errorem præfatum, ut sit sensus : Et deprehendi, ex ratione et illuminatione divina, nihil melius esse, quam lætari in opere suo, id est in actibus virtuosis, ex ratione ac deliberatione manantibus : qui proprie appellantur actus humani, quia per rationem differt homo a brutis, et speciem a rationali perfectione sortitur. Quis enim eum adducet, id est, quis perducet hominem viatorem ad hoc, ut post se futura cognoscat, id est, ut certitudinaliter prænoscat, quales post mortem suam filii et heredes ejus consistent, et qualiter vivent, ac bona sua consument? quasi dicat : Hoc communiter non revelatur hominibus, nec poterit revelari nisi a Deo, mediate vel immediate. Ideo expedit, sollicitudinem immoderatam et congregationem terrenorum avaram, prorsus abjicere, concessisque rebus moderate atque hilariter uti, ac indigentibus impertiri : et hanc esse partem illius, id est bonum præcipuum, et occupationem salubrem, ut in præsenti vita id agat, post quam amplius promereri non potest.
paras.en: [[3:22|And I have found that nothing is better than for a man to rejoice in his work, and that this is his portion|Et deprehendi nil melius esse, quam lætari hominem in opere suo, et hanc esse partem illius]]. This can be expounded in two ways. First, so that Solomon, speaking in the person of the carnal, draws from the error stated before that there is nothing better than for a man to give himself to taking his pleasure in carnal and earthly things, and to reckon that his happiness consists in this. Secondly, so that he brings in these words as his own judgment, to reprove implicitly the error already mentioned, so that the sense is: [[3:22|And I have found|Et deprehendi]], by reason and divine illumination, [[3:22|that nothing is better than|nihil melius esse, quam]] [[3:22|to rejoice in his work|lætari in opere suo]], that is, in virtuous acts flowing from reason and deliberation, which are properly called human acts, because it is by reason that man differs from the brutes and receives his species from the perfection of reason. [[3:22|For who shall bring him|Quis enim eum adducet]], that is, who will lead man the wayfarer to this, [[3:22|to know the things that shall be after him|ut post se futura cognoscat]], that is, to know beforehand with certainty what his sons and heirs will be after his death, and how they will live and spend his goods? As if to say: this is not commonly revealed to men, nor could it be revealed except by God, mediately or immediately. Therefore it is expedient to cast away altogether immoderate care and the greedy heaping up of earthly things, and to use the things granted us moderately and cheerfully, and to share them with the needy: [[3:22|and that this is his portion|et hanc esse partem illius]], that is, his chief good and wholesome occupation, that he do this in the present life, after which he can merit no more.

4.title: Elucidatio capituli quarti : Verti me ad alia.
4.title_en: Explanation of the fourth chapter: I turned myself to other things.

paras.t: Adhuc in isto capitulo introducit mirabilem ac miserabilem vanitatem, instabilitatem, ac impietatem rerum humanarum in statu præsenti. Propter quod in vita hac non est ponenda ultimata hominis salus.
paras.en: Further, in this chapter he brings in the wonderful and wretched vanity, instability and impiety of human things in the present state. For this reason man's final well-being is not to be placed in this life.

paras.t: Verti me ad alia, id est, mentem converti ad alia consideranda : juxta illud in Job, Cogitationes meæ variæ succedunt sibi, et mens in diversa rapitur. Et vidi calumnias, id est injuriationes et oppressiones iniquas, quæ sub sole geruntur, id est, in terra ab hominibus sibi invicem inferuntur, et lacrimas innocentium, et consolatorem neminem, id est, rarum aut nullum esse consolatorem eorum qui calumnias patiuntur, juxta illud Isaiæ: Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, quia non est qui intelligat. Unde in Psalmo ait Salvator: Sustinui qui simul contristaretur, et non fuit; et qui consolaretur, et non inveni; ac rursus in Isaia, Circumspexi, et non erat auxiliator. Nec posse resistere eorum violentiæ cunctorum auxilio destitutos, id est, innocentes et egenos oppressos, humana subsidia non habentes, non posse potentiorum ac iniquorum potestati tyrannidique resistere. Hinc in Habacuc legitur : Quare non respicis, Domine, contemptores, et taces conculcante impio justiorem se? Propter hoc lacerata est lex, quia impius prævalet adversus justum; propter hoc egreditur judicium perversum.
paras.en: [[4:1|I turned myself to other things|Verti me ad alia]], that is, I turned my mind to consider other things, according to that saying in Job: [[Job 20:2|various thoughts succeed one another in me, and my mind is hurried away to different things|Cogitationes meæ variæ succedunt sibi, et mens in diversa rapitur]]. [[4:1|and I saw the oppressions|Et vidi calumnias]], that is, wrongs and unjust oppressions, [[4:1|that are done under the sun|quæ sub sole geruntur]], that is, which men inflict on one another on earth, [[4:1|and the tears of the innocent|et lacrimas innocentium]], [[4:1|and they had no comforter|et consolatorem neminem]]: that is, that there is little or no comforter of those who suffer oppressions, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart, and men of mercy are taken away, because there is none that understandeth|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, quia non est qui intelligat]]. Hence in the Psalm the Saviour says: [[Ps 68:21|And I looked for one that would grieve together with me, but there was none: and for one that would comfort me, and I found none|Sustinui qui simul contristaretur, et non fuit; et qui consolaretur, et non inveni]]; and again in Isaias: [[Is 63:5|I looked about, and there was none to help|Circumspexi, et non erat auxiliator]]. [[4:1|and they were not able to resist their violence, being destitute of help from any|Nec posse resistere eorum violentiæ cunctorum auxilio destitutos]]: that is, that the innocent and needy who are oppressed, having no human aid, cannot resist the power and tyranny of the mightier and of the wicked. Hence we read in Habacuc: Why dost thou not look, O Lord, upon the despisers, [[Hab 1:13|and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|et taces conculcante impio justiorem se?]][[Hab 1:3||]] [the margin gives Habac. i, 13, 3, 4; in v. 13 Denis's wording differs from the Vulgate, which has *Quare respicis super iniqua agentes* and *devorante*, and v. 3 is a like complaint, not quoted] [[Hab 1:4|Therefore the law is torn in pieces|Propter hoc lacerata est lex]], [[Hab 1:4|because the wicked prevaileth against the just|quia impius prævalet adversus justum]]; [[Hab 1:4|therefore wrong judgment goeth forth|propter hoc egreditur judicium perversum]].

paras.t: Et laudavi magis mortuos, quam viventes : id est, tanto tædio inde afflictus sum, quod defunctos, qui talia mala nec agunt, nec sustinent, reputavi feliciores, quam viventes talia facientes aut patientes. Et verum est quod melius, id est minus malum sit mortuum esse, aut non esse, quam impie agere. Absolute tamen loquendo, non est melius mortuum esse, aut non esse, quam pati injurias atque adversa. Imo, si æquanimiter tolerentur, beatum est, sicut ait Salvator : Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam. Si vero non esset futura vita, aliquo modo sic esset. Salomon vero multa hic loquitur in infirmorum persona. Nam subdit :
paras.en: [[4:2|And I praised the dead rather than the living|Et laudavi magis mortuos, quam viventes]]: that is, I was so wearied and afflicted by this that I reckoned the departed, who neither do nor suffer such evils, happier than the living who do or suffer such things. And it is true that it is better, that is, a lesser evil, to be dead or not to be than to act wickedly. Yet speaking absolutely, it is not better to be dead or not to be than to suffer wrongs and adversities. Nay, if they are borne with an even mind, it is a blessed thing, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]]. But if there were no life to come, it would in some way be so. Solomon, however, says many things here in the person of the weak. For he adds:

paras.t: Et feliciorem utroque judicavi qui necdum natus est, nec vidit mala quæ sub sole fiunt. Per Necdum natum, possunt intelligi abortivi, seu fetus adhuc exsistentes in utero, vel qui erunt, et adhuc penitus non sunt. Vel [loquitur] secundum quorumdam hæresim seu errorem, qui putant animas esse ac vivere antequam descendant in corpora. Hos igitur reputavit feliciores, aut minus miseros jam natis et vivis, atque defunctis : quia mala pœnæ et culpæ hujus vitæ experti non sunt. Quod tamen absolute ita non est, nisi intelligatur de solis vitiosis vivis ac mortuis. Siquidem mala culpæ sunt maxima mala, et summe abominabilia. Propter quod Seneca in suis testatur Proverbiis : Tolerabilior est qui mori jubet, quam qui male vivere præcipit; itemque, Tolerabilior pœna est, vivere non posse, quam nescire, id est non scire vivere bene. Plato etiam in Phædone : Si anima, inquit, moreretur in corpore, lucrum inventum esset iniquis morientibus simul liberari a corpore atque malitia. Hinc in Politicis Aristoteles contestatur, quod homo impius decies millies pejor viliorque consistat, quam bestia. Unde et de proditore locutus est Christus : Bonum ei erat, si natus non esset homo ille.
paras.en: [[4:3|And I judged him happier than them both, that is not yet born, nor hath seen the evils that are done under the sun|Et feliciorem utroque judicavi qui necdum natus est, nec vidit mala quæ sub sole fiunt]]. By [[4:3|not yet born|Necdum natum]] may be understood those born untimely, or children still in the womb, or those who will be and as yet are not at all. Or he speaks according to the heresy or error of some who think that souls exist and live before they come down into bodies. These, then, he reckoned happier, or less wretched, than those already born and living, and than the dead, because they have not experienced the evils of punishment and of guilt of this life. Yet absolutely this is not so, unless it be understood only of the vicious, living and dead. For the evils of guilt are the greatest evils and supremely abominable. Wherefore Seneca testifies in his Proverbs: He is more bearable who bids us die than he who bids us live wickedly; and again: It is a more bearable punishment to be unable to live than not to know how, that is, not to know how to live well. Plato too in the Phaedo: If the soul, he says, died in the body, the wicked would have found a gain in dying, to be freed from the body and from their wickedness at once. Hence Aristotle in the Politics testifies that a wicked man is ten thousand times worse and viler than a beast. And so Christ said of the betrayer: [[Matt 26:24|It were better for him, if that man had not been born|Bonum ei erat, si natus non esset homo ille]][[Mark 14:21||]] [the margin gives Matt. xxvi, 24 and Mark xiv, 21; Denis's wording lies between the two].

paras.t: At vero circa istud, Feliciorem utroque judicavi qui nondum natus est, scribit quidam : Id est abortivum, qui nondum habet experientiam aliquam mali pœnæ aut mali culpæ actualis, et sic non sustinet aliquam pœnam sensibilem, sed habet vitam magis delectabilem, quam possit haberi in vita præsenti, secundum omnes doctores qui loquuntur de morientibus in solo peccato originali. Circa hoc dico, quod quamvis doctores communiter dicant illos non habere pœnam sensibilem, non tamen omnes hoc dicunt. Similiter hi qui dicunt illos non habere pœnam sensibilem, diversificantur; nec omnes dicunt eos habere vitam magis delectabilem, quam possit in hac vita haberi. Augustinus namque super Joannem, et Gregorius super illud Job, Multiplicabit vulnera mea, etiam sine causa, manifeste dicunt, infantulos illos in solo originali decedentes, non dumtaxat pœnam damni, sed et pœnam sensus habere, et torqueri ab igne, quamvis dicant illam pœnam esse mitissimam, comparatione eorum qui in mortali defuncti sunt. Quam opinionem sequitur Ubertinus in libro suo de Vita Salvatoris. Porro Bonaventura super quartum Sententiarum dicit, illos sic mortuos, esse in quodam medio inter gaudium et mœrorem, ita quod nec contristantur, nec delectantur, sed manent quasi in æquilibra quadam : dum ex una parte non contristantur, eo quod damnationem evaserunt; et ex alia parte non gaudent, quia beatitudinem amiserunt. Verumtamen in utroque hoc dicto, communi doctorum sententiæ magis consentio.
paras.en: But on these words, [[4:3|I judged him happier than them both, that is not yet born|Feliciorem utroque judicavi qui nondum natus est]], a certain writer says: That is, the untimely born, who has as yet no experience of any evil of punishment or of actual guilt, and so suffers no sensible punishment, but has a life more delightful than can be had in the present life, according to all the doctors who speak of those dying in original sin alone. On this I say that although the doctors commonly say that these have no sensible punishment, yet not all say so. Likewise those who say that they have no sensible punishment differ among themselves; nor do all say that they have a life more delightful than can be had in this life. For Augustine on John, and Gregory on that saying of Job, [[Job 9:17|multiply my wounds even without cause|Multiplicabit vulnera mea, etiam sine causa]], say plainly that those little ones who die in original sin alone have not only the punishment of loss but also the punishment of sense [that is, not only the loss of the sight of God but also positive pain], and are tormented by fire, though they say that this punishment is very mild in comparison with that of those who died in mortal sin. This opinion Ubertinus follows in his book on the Life of the Saviour. Bonaventure, on the other hand, on the fourth book of the Sentences, says that those who die thus are in a kind of mean between joy and sorrow, so that they are neither saddened nor delighted, but remain as it were in a kind of balance: since on the one hand they are not saddened, because they have escaped damnation, and on the other they do not rejoice, because they have lost beatitude. Yet on both these points I hold rather with the common opinion of the doctors.

paras.t: Rursus contemplatus sum omnes labores hominum, id est quosdam de omnibus, seu omnes in genere; et industrias, per quas intendunt ac enituntur ad divitias, voluptates, seu honores pertingere, animadverti patere invidiæ proximi : id est, consideravi quod industriose agentes ad obtinendum prospera mundi, expositi sint perversorum rancori, et invidias atque insidias patiantur : quia invidia est dolor de prosperitate alterius. Hinc sola miseria dicitur carere invidia. Nec soli mali, sed et boni patent invidiæ proximorum. Ideo Seneca dixit : Nondum felix es, si nondum te turba deridet : nam etsi nullos inimicos tibi faciat injuria, multos tamen facit invidia. Denique periculosum est invidentes habere : quia (ut Aristoteles Tulliusque fatentur) sicut ira quærit aperte nocere, ita invidia occulte. Hinc denuo Seneca loquitur : Maximo periculo custoditur, quod multis placet. Et in hoc ergo vanitas, scilicet in invidentia tali, et cura superflua est. Invidi namque sollicite quærunt, qualiter alios sua privent prosperitate ac gratia : quod superfluum est, miserrimum et iniquum. Quocirca scribit Albinus : Quid vanius quam homines proprias non deflere miserias, nec sua lugere peccata, et alios judicare, oblivisci se ipsos, melioribus invidere, et aliorum benefactis torqueri? Ideo rursus Seneca dicit : Utinam invidi oculos haberent in civitatibus cunctis, ut de omnium prosperitatibus et felicitatibus torquerentur. Nam quanta felicium gaudia, tanti gemitus invidorum. De talibus ait Gregorius : Dum electi et virtuosi præficiuntur, reprobi et iniqui ad furorem atque invidiam excitantur : quia boni mala nascentia, quæ imitari renuunt, persequuntur.
paras.en: [[4:4|Again I considered all the labours of men|Rursus contemplatus sum omnes labores hominum]], that is, some of all, or all in general; [[4:4|and I remarked that their industries|et industrias]], by which they aim and strive to attain riches, pleasures or honours, [[4:4|are exposed to the envy of their neighbour|animadverti patere invidiæ proximi]]: that is, I considered that those who busily strive to obtain the prosperity of the world are exposed to the rancour of the perverse, and suffer envy and plots: for envy is sorrow at another's prosperity. Hence misery alone is said to be free of envy. And not only the wicked but the good too are exposed to the envy of their neighbours. Therefore Seneca said: You are not yet happy if the crowd does not yet mock you; for though wrongdoing makes you no enemies, envy makes you many. Again, it is dangerous to have people envy you, because (as Aristotle and Tully say) as anger seeks to harm openly, so envy seeks to harm in secret. Hence Seneca says again: What pleases many is kept at the greatest peril. [[4:4|so in this also there is vanity|Et in hoc ergo vanitas]], namely in such envying, [[4:4|and fruitless care|et cura superflua est]]. For the envious anxiously seek how they may deprive others of their prosperity and favour: which is fruitless, most wretched and wicked. Wherefore Albinus [that is, Alcuin] writes: What is more vain than for men not to weep for their own miseries nor mourn their own sins, but to judge others, to forget themselves, to envy their betters, and to be tormented by the good deeds of others? Therefore Seneca says again: Would that the envious had eyes in every city, that they might be tormented at the prosperity and happiness of all. For as great as the joys of the happy are, so great are the groans of the envious. Of such Gregory says: When the elect and virtuous are set over others, the reprobate and wicked are stirred to fury and envy: because the good pursue the evils that spring up, which they refuse to imitate.

paras.t: Stultus complicat manus suas, id est, simul plicat eas a laboribus abstinendo, et comedit carnes suas, id est, se ipsum consumit inopia ac macilentia, quia pro necessariis refugit laborare. Spirituali quoque egestate tabescit, quia virtutum operibus renuit insudare. Dicens : Melior est pugillus, id est modicum quid, cum requie, id est corporali repausatione, quam plena utraque manus, id est multum seu abundantia, cum labore et afflictione animi, id est cum labore sollicito, et laboriosa occupatione, ac cura pro obtinendis in copia victui necessariis. Hoc modo excusat se piger ac negligens, et verba quæ in se veram possunt habere sententiam, applicat abusive ad excusandum suam ignaviam. Vere etenim melior est pugillus cum requie spirituali, et mentis tranquillitate inquietudine vitiorum carente, quam temporalium superfluitas, cum timore perdendi hoc, et anxia cura, quemadmodum scriptum est : Melius est modicum justo, super divitias peccatorum multas.
paras.en: [[4:5|The fool foldeth his hands together|Stultus complicat manus suas]], that is, folds them together by holding back from labour, [[4:5|and eateth his own flesh|et comedit carnes suas]], that is, wastes himself away with want and leanness, because he shrinks from labouring for what he needs. He also pines away in spiritual poverty, because he refuses to toil at the works of virtue. [[4:5|saying|Dicens]]: [[4:6|Better is a handful|Melior est pugillus]], that is, some little thing, [[4:6|with rest|cum requie]], that is, bodily repose, [[4:6|than both hands full|quam plena utraque manus]], that is, much, or abundance, [[4:6|with labour, and vexation of mind|cum labore et afflictione animi]], that is, with anxious labour and toilsome occupation, and care to obtain in plenty the things needed for food. In this way the sluggard and the negligent man excuses himself, and wrongly applies words that can have a true meaning in themselves to excuse his idleness. For truly [[4:6|better is a handful with rest|melior est pugillus cum requie]], rest of spirit, that is, and tranquillity of mind free from the unrest of vices, than an abundance of temporal things with the fear of losing it and anxious care, as it is written: [[Ps 36:16|Better is a little to the just, than the great riches of the wicked.|Melius est modicum justo, super divitias peccatorum multas]]

paras.t: Considerans, reperi et aliam vanitatem sub sole. Unus est, id est aliquis homo singularis, et secundum non habet, id est cohabitatorem propinquum aut socium, non filium, non fratrem, id est nullum cui de jure competat ei in hereditate succedere; et tamen laborare non cessat pro rebus terrenis augendis, quum habeat satis; nec satiantur oculi ejus divitiis : quia quo plura acquirit, plus appetit. Pecunia enim appetitum non satiat, sed irritat. Nec recogitat, dicens : Cui laboro? id est, cur tam superflue me fatigo, qui heredem non habeo? et fraudo animam meam bonis, id est, me ipsum, seu vitam meam animalem, privo competenti usu opum mearum? In hoc quoque est vanitas, id est stulta cupiditas et avara tenacia, et afflictio pessima : quia res ista continet malum culpæ ac pœnæ. Ideo fertur in Psalmo : Verumtamen in imagine pertransit homo, sed et frustra conturbatur. Thesaurizat, et ignorat cui congregabit ea. Talibus Jacobus loquitur : Divitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, et vestimenta vestra a tineis comesta sunt. Aurum et argentum vestrum æruginavit : et ærugo eorum in testimonium vobis erit, et manducabit carnes vestras sicut ignis.
paras.en: [[4:7|Considering I found also another vanity under the sun|Considerans, reperi et aliam vanitatem sub sole]]. [[4:8|There is but one|Unus est]], that is, some solitary man, [[4:8|and he hath not a second|et secundum non habet]], that is, no near housemate or companion, [[4:8|no child, no brother|non filium, non fratrem]], that is, no one to whom it would by right fall to succeed him in the inheritance; [[4:8|and yet he ceaseth not to labour|et tamen laborare non cessat]] to increase his earthly goods, though he has enough; [[4:8|neither are his eyes satisfied with riches|nec satiantur oculi ejus divitiis]]: for the more he acquires, the more he desires. For money does not satisfy the appetite but provokes it. [[4:8|neither doth he reflect, saying|Nec recogitat, dicens]]: [[4:8|For whom do I labour|Cui laboro]]? that is, why do I weary myself so needlessly, who have no heir? [[4:8|and defraud my soul of good things|et fraudo animam meam bonis]], that is, deprive myself, or my bodily life [*vita animalis*: Denis takes *soul* here for the life of the body], of the fitting use of my wealth? [[4:8|in this also is vanity|In hoc quoque est vanitas]], that is, foolish greed and miserly clinging, [[4:8|and a grievous vexation|et afflictio pessima]]: because this thing holds the evil of guilt and of punishment. Therefore it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 38:7|Surely man passeth as an image: yea, and he is disquieted in vain. He storeth up: and he knoweth not for whom he shall gather these things.|Verumtamen in imagine pertransit homo, sed et frustra conturbatur. Thesaurizat, et ignorat cui congregabit ea]] To such men James says: [[Jas 5:2|Your riches are corrupted: and your garments are motheaten.|Divitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, et vestimenta vestra a tineis comesta sunt]] [[Jas 5:3|Your gold and silver is cankered: and the rust of them shall be for a testimony against you and shall eat your flesh like fire|Aurum et argentum vestrum æruginavit : et ærugo eorum in testimonium vobis erit, et manducabit carnes vestras sicut ignis]].

paras.t: Melius est ergo duos esse simul quam unum, id est utilius et magis humanum, quum, teste Philosopho, homo naturaliter sit animal politicum et sociale ; habent enim emolumentum, id est mutuum lucrum et commodum, societatis suæ. Si unus ceciderit in aliquam adversitatem, tentationem, aut culpam, ab altero fulcietur, id est, sustentabitur, erigetur, custodietur : sicut et in exteriori itinere, si unus in aquam foveamve corruerit, a consorte extrahitur. Væ soli, qui cum alio communionem societatis et amicitiæ prorsus non habet; quia quum ceciderit in mala pœnæ aut culpæ, non habet sublevantem se hominem.
paras.en: [[4:9|It is better therefore that two should be together, than one|Melius est ergo duos esse simul quam unum]], that is, more useful and more human, since, as the Philosopher testifies, man is by nature a political and social animal; [[4:9|for they have the advantage|habent enim emolumentum]], that is, mutual gain and benefit, [[4:9|of their society|societatis suæ]]. [[4:10|If one fall|Si unus ceciderit]] into some adversity, temptation or fault, [[4:10|he shall be supported by the other|ab altero fulcietur]], that is, he shall be held up, raised, guarded: as also on an outward journey, if one falls into water or a pit, he is pulled out by his companion. [[4:10|woe to him that is alone|Væ soli]], who has no fellowship of society and friendship with another at all; [[4:10|for when he falleth|quia quum ceciderit]] into evils of punishment or of guilt, [[4:10|he hath none to lift him up|non habet sublevantem se hominem]].

paras.t: Et si dormierint duo, fovebuntur mutuo : id est, sicut corporaliter pariter dormientes invicem calefaciunt se, sic amicabiliter cohabitantes ac invicem conversantes, mutuo se accendunt per verba et facta caritate Dei et proximi. Unus quomodo calefiet? id est, sicut difficulter calefit tempore frigido, qui solus dormit in lecto; sic qui solus est, difficulter caritate accenditur. Imo faciliter in torporem cadit pigritiæ, et in desideria carnalitatis cujusdam ac consolationis externæ, ut Cassianus testatur. Et si quispiam, scilicet invisibilis aut visibilis inimicus, prævaluerit contra unum, duo resistunt adversario tali, se invicem exhortando; succurritque socius socio superato, pro ipso orando, ipsum monendo, et per opera exemplaria inflammando, suaque merita ei communicando. Hinc Plato loquitur in Phædone : Adversus duos nec Hercules fertur satis potens.
paras.en: [[4:11|And if two lie together, they shall warm one another|Et si dormierint duo, fovebuntur mutuo]]: that is, as those who sleep together bodily warm one another, so those who live together in friendship and converse with one another kindle each other by word and deed with the charity of God and of their neighbour. [[4:11|how shall one alone be warmed|Unus quomodo calefiet]]? That is, as he who sleeps alone in bed in cold weather is hardly warmed, so he who is alone is hardly kindled with charity. Nay, he easily falls into the torpor of sloth, and into desires of a certain carnality and of outward consolation, as Cassian testifies. [[4:12|And if a man|Et si quispiam]], namely an enemy, invisible or visible, [[4:12|prevail against one|prævaluerit contra unum]], [[4:12|two shall withstand|duo resistunt]] such an adversary by exhorting one another; and the companion comes to the help of his companion when he is overcome, by praying for him, admonishing him, and inflaming him by the example of his deeds, and sharing his merits with him. Hence Plato says in the Phaedo: Against two, not even Hercules is said to be strong enough.

paras.t: Ex præinductis vita socialis laudatur. Ad cujus commendationem insinuandam, Dominus et Salvator discipulos suos combinatos misit ad prædicandum. Unde et Psalmista decantat : Ecce quam bonum et quam jucundum, habitare fratres in unum! Hinc sancti et expertissimi Patres, Benedictus, Bernardus, Climacus, Cassianus, vitam cœnobitalem, in qua plures religiosæ personæ sub spirituali patre in sancta obedientia militant Deo, multum commendant, securioremque asserunt; vitam vero solitariam, quamvis sublimem, tamen periculosam esse testantur, nec convenire nisi exercitatis in omni virtute, prout de hoc in regula S. Hieronymus sapienter disseruit. Unde et Aristoteles naturali ratione inductus, testatus est, quod homo solus, est Deus aut bestia, id est divinus aut bestialis. Nihilo minus (prout S. Thomas in secunda secundæ determinat et declarat) absolute loquendo, vita illa omnino solitaria anachoretica, vitæ cœnobitali ac sociali præfertur, tanquam perfectior atque divinior. Nec hoc repugnat præhabitis, quoniam Salomon loquitur hic secundum legem communem, atque de homine secundum congruentiam suæ naturæ, non secundum præeminentiam gratiæ, quæ transcendit naturam, nec lege arctatur communi.
paras.en: By the words just set out, the social life is praised. To commend it, our Lord and Saviour sent his disciples out two by two to preach. Hence the Psalmist too sings: [[Ps 132:1|Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity|Ecce quam bonum et quam jucundum, habitare fratres in unum!]]. Hence the holy and most experienced Fathers, Benedict, Bernard, Climacus, Cassian, greatly commend the cenobitic life, in which many religious persons fight for God under a spiritual father in holy obedience, and declare it the safer; but the solitary life, though sublime, they declare to be dangerous, and fitting only for those trained in every virtue, as St Jerome wisely discussed in his Rule. Hence Aristotle too, led by natural reason, declared that man alone is either a god or a beast, that is, godlike or beastly. Nevertheless (as St Thomas determines and declares in the Secunda Secundæ [the second part of the second part of his Summa, q. 188, a. 8]), speaking absolutely, that wholly solitary life of the anchorites is preferred to the cenobitic and social life, as more perfect and more divine. Nor does this conflict with what was said before, since Solomon speaks here according to the common law, and of man according to what befits his nature, not according to the pre-eminence of grace, which transcends nature and is not bound by the common law.

paras.t: Ex inductis etiam verbis monstratur, quam utile et salubre sit, habere fidelem amicum ac socium probum, qui ad omne bonum honestum integre adstet : cui homini tanquam sibi ipsi possit credere, communicare, confidere. Hinc Seneca dixit : Vita sine amico, visceratio est leonis ac lupi. Errat qui amicum in atrio quærit, in convivio probat. Et rursus : Diu cogita an aliquis recipiendus sit tibi in amicum. Quum placuerit fieri, toto pectore illum admitte; tam audacter cum illo loquere, quam tecum. Si aliquem amicum existimas, cui non tantumdem credis sicut tibi, vehementer erras, nec satis nosti naturam amicitiæ veræ. Omnia cum amico delibera, sed de ipso prius. Post amicitiam vero credendum est ei, sed ante amicitiam deliberandum. Itaque qui pariter conversantur, præsertim religiosi, diligentissime satagant ita cohabitare, ut se invicem adjuvent, ædificent, elevent, et caritate accendant; et nequaquam scandalizent, molestent, perturbent se mutuo. Nisi enim caritate conjuncti sint, et morum conformitate conveniant, cohabitatio eorum maxime est damnosa, amara, ac dura.
paras.en: These words also show how useful and wholesome it is to have a faithful friend and an upright companion, who stands by one wholeheartedly in everything good and honest: a man whom one can trust, share with and confide in as in oneself. Hence Seneca said: A life without a friend is the feeding of a lion or a wolf [*visceratio*, a meal of flesh: to live without a friend is to feed like a beast of prey]. He errs who seeks a friend in the hall and tests him at the banquet. And again: Think long whether someone should be received by you as a friend. When you have decided on it, admit him with your whole heart; speak as boldly with him as with yourself. If you count anyone a friend whom you do not trust as much as yourself, you are badly mistaken, and do not know well enough the nature of true friendship. Deliberate everything with a friend, but first about the friend himself. After friendship you must trust him, but before friendship you must deliberate. Therefore those who live together, religious above all, should take the utmost care so to live together that they help, edify and raise up one another and kindle one another with charity, and in no way scandalize, trouble or disturb one another. For unless they are joined by charity and agree in likeness of manners, their living together is most harmful, bitter and hard.

paras.t: Funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur : id est, sicut corporaliter est de funiculo ex tribus chordis contexto et juncto; sic spiritualiter caritas quæ est vinculum cordis, uniens et colligans amantem dilecto, difficulter violari poterit aut dissolvi, si triplici nutriatur et conservetur fomento, videlicet consideratione bonitatis rei amatæ, potissime summi boni, consideratione quoque beneficiorum dilecti, et intuitione præmii caritatis. Vel per triplicem funiculum, intelliguntur ipse qui diligit, et dilectus ejus, et condilectus utrinque : quemadmodum amor inter conjugatos est fortior, quando eamdem habent prolem ambobus caram. Vel ideo ait, Funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur, quia si tres ad invicem commorentur ac mutuo suffragentur, difficulter poterunt superari, eo quod tot sint coadjutores, quot cohabitatores.
paras.en: [[4:12|a threefold cord is not easily broken|Funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur]]: that is, as it is bodily with a cord woven and joined of three strands, so spiritually charity, which is the bond of the heart, uniting and binding the lover to the beloved, can hardly be violated or dissolved if it is nourished and preserved by a threefold kindling: namely the consideration of the goodness of the thing loved, above all of the highest good; the consideration also of the benefits of the beloved; and the contemplation of the reward of charity. Or by the threefold cord are understood the one who loves, his beloved, and one loved by both together [*condilectus*, a third whom both love]: as love between the married is stronger when they have the same offspring dear to both. Or he says, [[4:12|a threefold cord is not easily broken|Funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur]], because if three dwell together and help one another, they can hardly be overcome, since there are as many helpers as there are housemates.

paras.t: Melior est puer pauper in temporalibus, et sapiens, id est in spiritualibus locuples (quia nec vera prudentia, nec vera sapientia sine aliis habetur virtutibus, quamvis sapientia informis et acquisita queat cum vitiis esse), rege sene et stulto, qui nescit prævidere in posterum, id est, ex præteritis ac præsentibus, nescit conjicere de futuris : quod tamen præcipue spectat ad præsidentes, ut sic de communi utilitate suorum provideant subditorum. Unde, ut Tullius docet, ad prudentem, maxime ad regem, pertinent memoria præteritorum, consideratio præsentium, providentia futurorum. Nescit, inquam, prævidere periculum proprium, utpote quod de carcere catenisque interdum quis egrediatur ad regnum, agnita ejus prudentia, innocentia, idoneitate. Quemadmodum Joseph de carcere fuit promotus super regnum Ægypti, primus post regem, juxta illud in Psalmo : Misit rex, et solvit eum; constituit eum dominum domus suæ. Et in libro Sapientiæ : In vinculis non dereliquit eum, donec afferret illi sceptrum regni. Et alius natus in regno, utpote heres ac filius regis, inopia consumatur : quemadmodum quarto Regum contigisse legitur Sedeciæ. Hinc scriptum est : Deus reges in solio collocat, et illic eriguntur. Et si fuerint in catenis, et vinciantur funibus paupertatis, indicabit eis opera eorum, quia violenti fuerunt, ut revertantur ab iniquitate. Si audierint et observaverint, complebunt dies suos in bono, et annos suos in gloria; si autem non audierint, transibunt per gladium, et consumentur in stultitia.
paras.en: [[4:13|Better is a child that is poor|Melior est puer pauper]] in temporal things, [[4:13|and wise|et sapiens]], that is, rich in spiritual things (for neither true prudence nor true wisdom is had without the other virtues, though wisdom that is unformed and acquired [that is, not quickened by charity, and gained by study rather than given by God] can exist with vices), [[4:13|than a king that is old and foolish|rege sene et stulto]], [[4:13|who knoweth not to foresee for hereafter|qui nescit prævidere in posterum]], that is, does not know how to judge of the future from the past and the present: which yet belongs above all to those who rule, that so they may provide for the common good of their subjects. Hence, as Tully teaches, to the prudent man, and most of all to a king, belong memory of things past, consideration of things present, and foresight of things to come. He knoweth not, I say, to foresee his own danger, namely that [[4:14|out of prison and chains sometimes a man cometh forth to a kingdom|de carcere catenisque interdum quis egrediatur ad regnum]], when his prudence, innocence and fitness are recognized. So Joseph was raised from prison over the kingdom of Egypt, first after the king, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:20|The king sent, and he released him|Misit rex, et solvit eum]]; [[Ps 104:21|He made him master of his house|constituit eum dominum domus suæ]]. And in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 10:14|in bands she left him not, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom|In vinculis non dereliquit eum, donec afferret illi sceptrum regni]]. [[4:14|and another born king|Et alius natus in regno]], that is, the heir and son of the king, [[4:14|is consumed with poverty|inopia consumatur]]: as we read in the fourth book of Kings happened to Sedecias. Hence it is written: God [[Job 36:7|placeth kings on the throne|reges in solio collocat]], [[Job 36:7|and they are exalted|et illic eriguntur]]. [[Job 36:8|And if they shall be in chains, and be bound with the cords of poverty:|Et si fuerint in catenis, et vinciantur funibus paupertatis]] [[Job 36:9|He shall shew them their works|indicabit eis opera eorum]], [[Job 36:9|because they have been violent|quia violenti fuerunt]], [[Job 36:10|that they may return from iniquity|ut revertantur ab iniquitate]]. [[Job 36:11|If they shall hear and observe, they shall accomplish their days in good, and their years in glory.|Si audierint et observaverint, complebunt dies suos in bono, et annos suos in gloria]] [[Job 36:12|But if they hear not, they shall pass by the sword, and shall be consumed in folly.|si autem non audierint, transibunt per gladium, et consumentur in stultitia]] [Job 36:7–12, given in part; the margin gives no reference].

paras.t: Origenes et Victorinus per puerum pauperem et sapientem, intelligunt Christum: de quo loquitur Isaias, Puer natus est nobis. Per regem senem et fatuum, intelligunt diabolum: qui a mundi fuit exordio, et in veritate non stetit; et sapientiam perdidit in decore suo, ut ait Ezechiel; atque inveteratus est in peccato: quem Christus devicit.
paras.en: Origen and Victorinus understand by [[4:13|a child that is poor and wise|puerum pauperem et sapientem]] Christ, of whom Isaias says: [[Is 9:6|a CHILD IS BORN to us|Puer natus est nobis]] [Denis gives the words as the Christmas Introit has them; the Vulgate reads *Parvulus enim natus est nobis*]. By [[4:13|a king that is old|regem senem]] and foolish they understand the devil, who was from the beginning of the world, and [[John 8:44|he stood not in the truth|in veritate non stetit]]; and lost his wisdom in his beauty, as Ezechiel says[[Ezech 28:17||]]; and has grown old in sin: and him Christ overcame.

paras.t: Vidi cunctos, id est multos de omnibus, viventes, qui ambulant sub sole, cum adolescente secundo, id est adhærentes adolescenti filio regis antiqui, qui patri suo secundus est, id est primus post eum, atque interdum ex ambitione usurpat sibi regnum, patre suo adhuc vivente, habetque populum pro majori parte sibi faventem. Hinc subditur : qui consurgit pro eo, id est, pro patre suo incipit regnare. Infinitus, id est nobis innumerabilis et valde magnus, numerus est populi omnium qui fuerunt ante eum, id est, patri suo ante suum principatum obedierunt, et nunc sibi obtemperant; et qui postea futuri sunt, id est posteri obedientium sibi, non lætabuntur in eo, id est, despicient eum senescentem, eo quod patrem suum de regno expulerit, vel ex alia causa, et ita abjicient eum, et filio ejus hærebunt. Sed et hoc vanitas est, sic scilicet regnum invadere, et patre seniore relicto, filium ambitiosum in regem suscipere; et afflictio spiritus, id est valde afflictivum regi antiquo.
paras.en: [[4:15|I saw all men|Vidi cunctos]], that is, many of all, [[4:15|living, that walk under the sun with the second young man|viventes, qui ambulant sub sole, cum adolescente secundo]], that is, cleaving to the young man, the son of the old king, who is second to his father, that is, first after him, and who sometimes out of ambition usurps the kingdom for himself while his father is still living, and has the people for the most part on his side. Hence it is added: [[4:15|who shall rise up in his place|qui consurgit pro eo]], that is, begins to reign in place of his father. [[4:16|The number of the people, of all that were before him|numerus est populi omnium qui fuerunt ante eum]] [[4:16|is infinite|Infinitus]], that is, numberless to us and very great: that is, of those who obeyed his father before his own rule, and now obey him; [[4:16|and they that shall come afterwards|et qui postea futuri sunt]], that is, the descendants of those who obey him, [[4:16|shall not rejoice in him|non lætabuntur in eo]], that is, they will despise him as he grows old, because he drove his father from the kingdom, or for some other cause, and so they will cast him off and cleave to his son. [[4:16|but this also is vanity|Sed et hoc vanitas est]], namely so to seize the kingdom, and, forsaking the older father, to take the ambitious son as king; [[4:16|and vexation of spirit|et afflictio spiritus]], that is, very grievous to the old king.

paras.t: Custodi pedem tuum, ingrediens domum Dei : id est, cum reverentia et humilitate vade et intra in templum sive ecclesiam, et recta intentione vanum refrenando affectum, ne sacra loca inhonores, et Deum in locis suæ honorificentiæ deputatis offendas, sicut multi ingrediuntur indevote, irreverenter, superbe, vana et lasciva affectione cupientes hominibus complacere. Quorum meminit Scriptura dicens : Optimates, capita populorum, ingredientes pompatice domum Israel; et iterum, Visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur super limen. Et appropinqua prædicatoribus, doctoribus, et prælatis, ut audias auribus cordis et corporis verbum Dei et præcepta Ecclesiæ. Multo enim melior est obedientia cordis, qua implentur præcepta, quam stultorum victimæ, id est exteriora sacrificia Deo oblata, quæ non sunt ei accepta : præsertim loquendo de sacrificiis legis, quæ non nisi ex fide, devotione et caritate offerentium, Domino placuerunt.
paras.en: [[4:17|Keep thy foot, when thou goest into the house of God|Custodi pedem tuum, ingrediens domum Dei]]: that is, go and enter the temple or church with reverence and humility, and with a right intention, curbing vain affection, lest you dishonour holy places and offend God in the places appointed for his honour, as many enter undevoutly, irreverently, proudly, longing with vain and wanton affection to please men. Of these Scripture makes mention, saying: [[Amos 6:1|ye great men, heads of the people, that go in with state into the house of Israel|Optimates, capita populorum, ingredientes pompatice domum Israel]]; and again: [[Soph 1:9|I will visit|Visitabo]] [[Soph 1:9|upon every one that entereth arrogantly over the threshold|super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur super limen]]. [[4:17|and draw nigh|Et appropinqua]] to preachers, doctors and prelates, [[4:17|to hear|ut audias]] with the ears of heart and body the word of God and the precepts of the Church. [[4:17|For much better is obedience|Multo enim melior est obedientia]] of the heart, by which the precepts are fulfilled, [[4:17|than the victims of fools|quam stultorum victimæ]], that is, outward sacrifices offered to God which are not acceptable to him: speaking above all of the sacrifices of the law, which pleased the Lord only through the faith, devotion and charity of those who offered them.

paras.t: Qui nesciunt quid faciunt mali : id est, sua vitia non attendunt, sua excæcati elatione aliisque peccatis, in tantum ut mala sua reputent bona. Quibus in Isaia Dominus comminatur : Væ qui dicitis malum, bonum ; et bonum, malum. Istud multum potentibus magis solet competere, qui voluntate utuntur pro lege, juxta illud Sapientiæ : Sit fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ. Unde et quarto Politicorum Aristoteles ait, quod multum potentes, nec sciunt, nec volunt subdi. Postremo, huic quod dictum est, Melior est obedientia, etc., consonat illud primi Regum : Melior est obedientia, quam victimæ. Unde per prophetam Amos Dominus ait iniquis : Non accipiam odorem cœtuum vestrorum. Quod si obtuleritis mihi holocausta, non suscipiam. Qui et in Osee testatur : Misericordiam volui, et non sacrificium.
paras.en: [[4:17|who know not what evil they do|Qui nesciunt quid faciunt mali]]: that is, they do not heed their own vices, blinded by their pride and other sins, so far that they reckon their evils good. To such the Lord threatens in Isaias: [[Is 5:20|Woe to you that call evil good, and good evil|Væ qui dicitis malum, bonum ; et bonum, malum]]. This is wont to fit the very powerful most of all, who use their will as law, according to that saying of Wisdom: [[Wis 2:11|let our strength be the law of justice|Sit fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ]]. Hence too Aristotle says in the fourth book of the Politics that the very powerful neither know how nor wish to be subject. Lastly, with what was said, [[4:17|better is obedience|Melior est obedientia]], etc., agrees that saying of the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 15:22|obedience is better than sacrifices|Melior est obedientia, quam victimæ]]. Hence the Lord says to the wicked through the prophet Amos: [[Amos 5:21|I will not receive the odour of your assemblies|Non accipiam odorem cœtuum vestrorum]]. [[Amos 5:22|And if you offer me holocausts|Quod si obtuleritis mihi holocausta]], [[Amos 5:22|I will not receive them|non suscipiam]]. And in Osee he testifies: [[Osee 6:6|I desired mercy, and not sacrifice|Misericordiam volui, et non sacrificium]].

5.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI QUINTI : NE TEMERE QUID LOQUARIS.
5.title_en: Declaration of the fifth chapter: Speak not any thing rashly.

paras.t: Videtur Salomon in libro isto frequenter in verbis suis derogare providentiæ Dei, et justis judiciis ejus, dicendo: Quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat? et, Nihil habet homo amplius jumento; et consimilia: quæ ex persona carnalium imperitorumque loquitur. Ne ergo putetur talia dixisse ex animo, propriaque persona, et ne quis ejus exemplo ad similia proferenda erumpat; recte nunc ait:
paras.en: Solomon seems in this book often to disparage in his words the providence of God and His just judgments, saying: [[Eccles 3:21|Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend|Quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat]]? and, [[Eccles 3:19|man hath nothing more than beast|Nihil habet homo amplius jumento]]; and the like: which he speaks in the person of carnal and unlearned men. So that he may not be thought to have said such things from his heart and in his own person, and so that no one may break out, by his example, into saying the like, he now rightly says:
