paras.t: Ne temere quid loquaris: id est, nullum verbum proferas veritati Scripturæ aut honestati virtutum contrarium; et præsertim incaute aut præsumptuose nihil loquaris de Deo, et de natura et attributis ipsius: quia, ut ait Apostolus, Corrumpunt mores bonos colloquia mala. Et ad reprimendum nos ab immoderato Deitatis ac judiciorum ejus scrutinio, dictum est in libro Proverbiorum: Qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria.
paras.en: [[5:1|Speak not any thing rashly|Ne temere quid loquaris]]: that is, utter no word contrary to the truth of Scripture or to the uprightness of the virtues; and above all say nothing incautiously or presumptuously of God, and of His nature and attributes: because, as the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 15:33|Evil communications corrupt good manners|Corrumpunt mores bonos colloquia mala]]. And to hold us back from an immoderate searching into the Godhead and His judgments, it is said in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 25:27|he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|Qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria]].

paras.t: Neque cor tuum sit velox ad proferendum sermonem coram Deo: id est, ex consideratione divinæ præsentiæ omnia intuentis ac judicantis retrahi debes, ne præceps sis ad loquendum, potissime de divinis in arduis, et in his ubi non habetur manifesta et certa determinatio ex Scripturis aut doctrinis Ecclesiæ: quia, ut divinus Dionysius et post eum Damascenus testantur, non est audendum aliquid loqui de Deo, præter tradita in sacris eloquiis. Hinc etiam in Proverbiis dictum est: Vidisti hominem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio. Jacobus quoque apostolus: Sit, inquit, omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum. Ideo Seneca loquitur: Sicut sapienti viro incessus modestior convenit, ita oratio (id est locutio) pressa, non audax. Tardiloquum te esse jubeo. Prope est a te Deus: bonus vir sine Deo non est. Et iterum: Sic vive cum hominibus, tanquam Deus videat; sic loquere cum Deo, tanquam homines audiant.
paras.en: [[5:1|and let not thy heart be hasty to utter a word before God|Neque cor tuum sit velox ad proferendum sermonem coram Deo]]: that is, the thought of the divine presence, which beholds and judges all things, ought to hold thee back from being headlong in speaking, above all of divine things in hard matters, and in those where there is no plain and certain determination from the Scriptures or the teachings of the Church: because, as the divine Dionysius and after him Damascene testify, one must not dare to say anything of God beyond what is handed down in the sacred oracles. Hence it is also said in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:20|Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment|Vidisti hominem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio]]. The apostle James also: [[Jas 1:19|let|Sit]], he says, [[Jas 1:19|every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak|omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum]]. Therefore Seneca says: As a more modest gait befits a wise man, so does a restrained, not a bold, speech (that is, way of talking). I bid thee be slow of speech. God is near thee: a good man is not without God. And again: Live so with men as if God saw; speak so with God as if men heard.

paras.t: Deus enim in cœlo, id est, ipse Deus rector, creator, et dominus est cœlorum, et in eis ob suam excellentiam specialiter esse habitareque dicitur. Ideo eum comprehendere nequis, sed temperate ac timorate loqui debes. Et tu super terram, id est, terrenus, mortalis et incola terræ es: ideoque valde inferior Deo. Idcirco non ingeras te divinis inconsiderate. Nam et quamvis ipse in cœlis tanquam omnium summus Judex resideat, nihilo minus inferiora omnia intuetur. Imo ipse in sua natura incircumscriptibilis est omnino, illocalis et intemporalis, ubique præsens, quamvis in cœlo specialiter esse dicatur, eo quod ibi eminentius operetur, ac clarius videatur. Hinc scriptum est: Suspice cœlum et intuere, et contemplare aera, quod altior te sit. Hæc ergo eminentia Creatoris, et incomprehensibilitas judiciorum Altissimi, debet nos refrenare a locutione incauta de ipso ac ejus judiciis, et a periculoso scrutinio, imo ab omni verbo et actu illicito. Propter quod ipse per Isaiam ait: Non enim cogitationes meæ, cogitationes vestræ; neque viæ meæ, viæ vestræ: quia sicut exaltantur cœli a terra, sic exaltatæ sunt viæ meæ a viis vestris, et cogitationes meæ a cogitationibus vestris. Idcirco sint pauci sermones tui, id est moderati, non superflui, potius ad minus, quam ad majus tendentes: et hoc, consideratis circumstantiis rei et causæ atque materiæ: quia secundum audientium dispositionem, capacitatem, indigentiam, et secundum objecti dignitatem, eminentiam, difficultatem, aut incomprehensibilitatem, oportet moderari, extendere, breviare sermonem: ad quod servandum, unctio docet, discretio dirigit, experientia juvat. Denique Glossa fatetur, quod etiam vera de Deo dicere, periculosum sit: quanto magis incerta aut falsa?
paras.en: [[5:1|For God is in heaven|Deus enim in cœlo]], that is, God Himself is the ruler, creator and lord of the heavens, and on account of His excellence He is said to be and to dwell in them in a special way. Therefore thou canst not comprehend Him, but must speak with measure and with fear. [[5:1|and thou upon earth|Et tu super terram]], that is, thou art earthly, mortal and a dweller on the earth: and therefore far beneath God. So do not thrust thyself into divine things without consideration. For although He sits in the heavens as the supreme Judge of all, He nonetheless beholds all things below. Indeed in His nature He is altogether uncircumscribable, not in place and not in time, present everywhere, although He is said to be in heaven in a special way, because there He works more eminently and is seen more clearly. Hence it is written: [[Job 35:5|Look up to heaven and see, and behold the sky, that it is higher than thee|Suspice cœlum et intuere, et contemplare aera, quod altior te sit]]. This eminence of the Creator, then, and the incomprehensibility of the judgments of the Most High, ought to restrain us from incautious speech about Him and His judgments, and from perilous searching, indeed from every unlawful word and deed. For which reason He Himself says through Isaias: [[Is 55:8|For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor your ways my ways|Non enim cogitationes meæ, cogitationes vestræ; neque viæ meæ, viæ vestræ]]: [[Is 55:9|For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts|quia sicut exaltantur cœli a terra, sic exaltatæ sunt viæ meæ a viis vestris, et cogitationes meæ a cogitationibus vestris]]. [[5:1|therefore let thy words be few|Idcirco sint pauci sermones tui]], that is, measured, not superfluous, tending to less rather than to more: and this with due regard to the circumstances of the matter, the case and the subject: because one must moderate, lengthen or shorten one's speech according to the disposition, capacity and need of the hearers, and according to the dignity, eminence, difficulty or incomprehensibility of the object: and for keeping to this, unction teaches, discretion directs, experience helps. Lastly, the Gloss admits that it is perilous to say even true things of God: how much more uncertain or false ones?

paras.t: Multas curas sequuntur somnia, et in multis sermonibus invenitur stultitia: id est, sicut post multas et magnas sollicitudines in vigilia habitas, sequuntur somnia proportionabilia de rebus eisdem in nocte, tempore somni (quæ enim tractantur in vigilia multum intente et anxie, occurrunt in somno per sua phantasmata); sic multos sermones comitatur insipientia, culpa, dispersio cordis, conscientiæ læsio, et audientium scandalum. Unde in Proverbiis dictum est: In multiloquio peccatum non deerit; et, Totum spiritum suum profert stultus.
paras.en: [[5:2|Dreams follow many cares: and in many words shall be found folly.|Multas curas sequuntur somnia, et in multis sermonibus invenitur stultitia]]: that is, as after many and great anxieties had while awake there follow in the night, in the time of sleep, dreams corresponding to them about the same things (for what is handled very intently and anxiously while awake comes up again in sleep through its images); so folly, fault, scattering of heart, hurt to conscience and scandal to the hearers go along with many words. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|In multiloquio peccatum non deerit]]; and, [[Prov 29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus]].

paras.t: Ex præinductis docemur, ex consideratione præsentiæ majestatis divinæ, cuncta cernentis ac audientis, nos in omnibus custodite habere, non solum in verbis oris, sed etiam cordis, hoc est in cogitationibus, atque in affectionibus quæ ex cogitationibus oriuntur. Nam si præsentia viri sapientis ac probi, reprimeret nos a negligentia, inhonestate, excessibusque verborum: quanto magis præsentia Dei, ab omni interiori exteriorique culpa nos debet restringere? Hinc sapientes docuerunt, ut ubique imaginemur quasi præsentialiter adesse, atque inspicere nos virum prudentem et virtuosum, sicque in cunctis agere sapienter, et verecundari de omni indecentia et fœditate, ob viri illius præsentiam: ut vel sic assuescamus ex divinæ consideratu præsentiæ, hoc ipsum implere. Hinc Seneca dixit: Aliquis vir bonus eligendus est nobis, ac semper ante oculos habendus, ut sic semper tanquam illo spectante vivamus, et omnia tanquam illo judice faciamus. Maxima pars vitiorum vitatur et tollitur, si peccatori testis adsistat. Qui sic semper veretur, cito erit verendus. Hanc ipsam practicam docet et S. Bernardus in Epistola ad Fratres de Monte Dei. Præterea etiam sanctorum angelorum præsentia, ad idem incitare nos debet. Et mirum ac deplorandum, quod non attendimus ista, nec divinæ majestatis intuitum perpendimus, veremur ac veneramur. Unde elicitur, quam infinita sit insipientia, miseria, imperfectio, ac perversitas nostra, qui humanum amplius quam divinum honoramus adspectum.
paras.en: From what has gone before we are taught that, from the thought of the presence of the divine majesty, which sees and hears all things, we must keep ourselves guardedly in all things, not only in the words of the mouth but also in those of the heart, that is, in our thoughts and in the affections that arise from our thoughts. For if the presence of a wise and upright man would restrain us from carelessness, unseemliness and excesses of speech, how much more ought the presence of God to hold us back from every fault, inward and outward? Hence the wise have taught that we should everywhere imagine a prudent and virtuous man to be present, as it were in person, and looking at us, and so act wisely in all things, and be ashamed of every unseemliness and foulness because of that man's presence: so that even in this way we may grow used to doing this very thing from the thought of the divine presence. Hence Seneca said: We must choose some good man and always keep him before our eyes, so that we may always live as if he were watching, and do everything as if he were judging. The greatest part of sins is avoided and done away with if a witness stands by the one about to sin. He who always reveres someone in this way will soon himself be worthy of reverence. St. Bernard too teaches this very practice in the Letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu. Moreover the presence of the holy angels also ought to spur us to the same. And it is a wonder and a thing to be lamented that we pay no heed to these things, and do not weigh, fear and revere the gaze of the divine majesty. From which one gathers how boundless are our folly, wretchedness, imperfection and perversity, who honour the gaze of man more than the gaze of God.

paras.t: Si quid vovisti Deo, ne moreris reddere, id est votum implere. Periculum etenim est in mora. Nam si quis ex dilatione non necessaria fiat impotens ad persolvendum votum, incurrit grande periculum. Et quamvis præcepta quæ obligant semper, non obligent ad semper, obligant tamen pro tempore opportuno. Idcirco qui religionem vovit intrare, debet hoc adimplere celerius quo congrue potest. Nec solum reddendum quod Deo vovetur, sed etiam quod hominibus promittitur. Quod si quis promittat aliquid homini, quod ad ipsius hominis pertineat commodum aut honorem, potest homo id relaxare, et promittentem a tali promissione seu obligatione absolvere. Si vero promittat quid alteri, quod Dei honorem, servitutem, aut cultum directe concernat, ut quotidie legere septem psalmos, aut celebrare, non potest homo cui id promittitur, talem relaxare promissionem: quoniam Deo intelligitur principaliter facta, non homini. Hinc ait Psalmista: Vovete, et reddite Domino Deo vestro. In Deuteronomio quoque sic legitur: Quod semel egressum est de labiis tuis, observabis, et facies sicut promisisti Domino Deo tuo.
paras.en: [[5:3|If thou hast vowed any thing to God, defer not to pay it|Si quid vovisti Deo, ne moreris reddere]], that is, to fulfil the vow. For there is danger in delay. For if anyone through needless putting off becomes unable to discharge his vow, he incurs a great danger. And although precepts that bind always do not bind for always [that is, an affirmative precept is always in force but does not oblige one to act at every moment], yet they bind for the fitting time. Therefore he who has vowed to enter religion ought to fulfil it as quickly as he fittingly can. And not only must what is vowed to God be paid, but also what is promised to men. But if someone promises a man something that concerns that man's own advantage or honour, the man can remit it and release the one who promised from such a promise or obligation. If, however, he promises another something that directly concerns the honour, service or worship of God, such as to read the seven [penitential] psalms daily, or to celebrate [Mass], the man to whom it is promised cannot remit such a promise: since it is understood to have been made principally to God, not to man. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 75:12|Vow ye, and pay to the Lord your God|Vovete, et reddite Domino Deo vestro]]. In Deuteronomy too we read thus: [[Deut 23:23|that which is once gone out of thy lips, thou shalt observe, and shalt do as thou hast promised to the Lord thy God|Quod semel egressum est de labiis tuis, observabis, et facies sicut promisisti Domino Deo tuo]].

paras.t: Displicet enim ei infidelis, id est non impleta, et stulta, id est indiscreta, promissio. Quemadmodum enim tres sunt comites juramenti, scilicet discretio, veritas, justitia (ut ait Hieronymus super illud in Jeremia, Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in judicio et veritate et justitia); ita iidem sunt tres comites voti, ita quod quidquid veritati, discretioni, aut justitiæ contrariatur, non est vovendum neque jurandum. Et quamvis promissum sit aut juratum, non est tamen implendum: nec peccat, qui promisit aut juravit, talia non implendo; sed peccavit, tale quid jurando aut promittendo. Hinc ait Isidorus: In malis promissis rescinde fidem; in turpi voto muta decretum. Quod incaute vovisti, non facias: impia est promissio, quæ scelere adimpletur.
paras.en: [[5:3|for an unfaithful|Displicet enim ei infidelis]], that is, unfulfilled, [[5:3|and foolish|et stulta]], that is, indiscreet, [[5:3|promise displeaseth him|promissio]]. For just as there are three companions of an oath, namely discretion, truth and justice (as Jerome says on the passage in Jeremias, [[Jer 4:2|thou shalt swear: As the Lord liveth, in truth, and in judgment, and in justice|Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in judicio et veritate et justitia]] [Denis has the order "in judgment and truth and justice"]), so the same three are the companions of a vow; so that whatever is contrary to truth, discretion or justice is not to be vowed or sworn. And even if it has been promised or sworn, it is still not to be fulfilled: nor does he who promised or swore sin by not fulfilling such things; but he sinned by swearing or promising such a thing. Hence Isidore says: In evil promises break thy word; in a shameful vow change thy resolve. What thou hast vowed incautiously, do not do: that promise is impious which is fulfilled by a crime.

paras.t: Sed quodcumque voveris, redde: præsertim quia votum plus obligat quam juramentum. Violatio etenim voti contrariatur fidelitati quam homo tenetur Deo; violatio autem juramenti repugnat veritati. Et hoc Thomas in secunda secundæ magis declarat. Votum quoque est actus latriæ, quæ inter virtutes morales videtur primatum sortiri, propter propinquitatem ejus ad theologicas virtutes, et quoniam circa Deum versatur, cui cultum cæremoniamque impendit. Ideo, sicut valde laudabile ac meritorium est, vota implere; ita prorsus damnabile vitiosumque censetur, ea non observare. Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Non te vovisse pœniteat; imo gaude jam tibi non licere, quod cum tuæ detrimento salutis licuisset. Felix necessitas, quæ ad meliora compellit. Unde sicut vovere, est spontaneæ voluntatis; sic ea implere, est necessitatis. Multoque melius est non vovere, quam post votum promissa non reddere.
paras.en: [[5:3|but whatsoever thou hast vowed, pay it|Sed quodcumque voveris, redde]]: above all because a vow binds more than an oath. For the breaking of a vow is contrary to the fidelity which man owes to God, while the breaking of an oath is opposed to truth. And Thomas explains this further in the Secunda Secundæ. A vow is also an act of latria [that is, of the worship owed to God alone, here the virtue of religion], which seems to hold the first place among the moral virtues, because of its nearness to the theological virtues, and because it is concerned with God, to whom it pays worship and ceremony. Therefore, as it is very praiseworthy and meritorious to fulfil vows, so it is held utterly damnable and wicked not to keep them. Hence Augustine says: Do not repent of having vowed; rather rejoice that what would have been lawful to thee to the loss of thy salvation is now no longer lawful. Happy necessity, which drives one to better things. So, as to vow is a matter of free will, so to fulfil vows is a matter of necessity. [[5:4|And it is much better not to vow, than after a vow not to perform the things promised.|Multoque melius est non vovere, quam post votum promissa non reddere]].

paras.t: Præterea infidele est votum eorum, qui necessitatis articulo imminente aliquid vovent, et necessitate illa cessante, vovisse se dolent, nec implent. Votum quoque factum de impossibili, stultum est: similiter quod fit Deo de re indifferenti. Constat item ex dictis, multo plus meritorium esse, facere bonum ex voto, quam sine voto. Ponderent hæc religiosi qui nec substantialia suæ religioni observant, quam enormiter atque gravissime peccent.
paras.en: Moreover, the vow of those is unfaithful who vow something when a moment of need is upon them, and, when that need has passed, regret having vowed and do not fulfil it. A vow made about something impossible is also foolish: likewise one made to God about an indifferent thing. It is also plain from what has been said that it is much more meritorious to do good by vow than without a vow. Let religious who do not keep even the substantials of their religion [that is, the essential vows of their rule] weigh how enormously and most gravely they sin.

paras.t: Ne dederis os tuum, ut peccare facias carnem tuam: id est, non dicas ex corde, te non posse præcepta implere, nec concupiscentias carnis frenare, aut in medio hominum caste et sobrie vivere: quod esset iniquitatem in Creatorem, auctorem naturæ, retorquere, juxta illud Psalmistæ, Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala. Unde rursus pro hac iniquitate vitanda, orat Psalmista: Non declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis. Qui autem dicunt se non posse peccata vitare, carni suæ præstant peccandi licentiam. Quocontra ait Hieronymus: Maledictus qui dicit Deum aliquid impossibile præcepisse. Vel sic: Ne dederis os tuum, ut peccare facias carnem tuam: id est, oscula et verba lasciva, ex quibus caro ad peccandum accenditur, fuge; nec etiam aperias os tuum gulæ et ebrietati, ex quibus carnis vitia nutriuntur.
paras.en: [[5:5|Give not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin|Ne dederis os tuum, ut peccare facias carnem tuam]]: that is, do not say from the heart that thou canst not fulfil the commandments, nor rein in the desires of the flesh, nor live chastely and soberly in the midst of men: for that would be to turn the iniquity back upon the Creator, the author of nature, according to that word of the Psalmist, [[Ps 20:12|For they have intended evils against thee|Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala]] [literally "they have turned evils aside upon thee", which is how Denis takes it here]. Hence again, to avoid this iniquity, the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 140:4|Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins|Non declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis]] [the margin gives Ps. cxi, 4; the words are Ps 140:4]. But those who say they cannot avoid sins give their flesh licence to sin. Against which Jerome says: Cursed is he who says that God has commanded anything impossible [the saying comes from the confession of faith of Pelagius once ascribed to Jerome]. Or thus: [[5:5|Give not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin|Ne dederis os tuum, ut peccare facias carnem tuam]]: that is, shun the kisses and wanton words by which the flesh is kindled to sin; and do not open thy mouth to gluttony and drunkenness either, by which the vices of the flesh are fed.

paras.t: Neque dicas coram angelo tibi ad custodiam deputato: Non est providentia: id est, Deus non habet curam et providentiam actuum humanorum. Quo dato, sequitur nec angelos hominibus custodiendis desuper missos. Quocontra ait Apostolus: Nonne omnes sunt administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi propter eos qui hereditatem capiunt salutis? Imo etiam in Evangelio Dominus: Angeli, inquit, eorum in cœlis semper vident faciem Patris mei. Sicque tale verbum, est verbum blasphemiæ atque perfidiæ et ingratitudinis maximæ, non solum in Dei, sed et in angelorum redundans injuriam. Potest tamen per angelum, etiam sacerdos intelligi, juxta illud Malachiæ: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem requirent ex ore ejus, quia angelus Domini est. Ne forte iratus Dominus contra sermones tuos, dissipet cuncta opera manuum tuarum, id est, destruat cuncta quæ habes, sicque ostendat per effectum, providentiam se habere; dissipet quoque opera manuum tuarum, id est, bona tua præterita, propter hanc culpam privet mercede æterna. De taliter enim loquentibus atque dicentibus illud in Isaia, Comedamus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur, Dominus ait: Revelata est iniquitas ista in auribus meis. Si dimittetur (id est non dimittetur) vobis iniquitas hæc donec moriamini. Unde ad Ezechielem Dominus loquitur: Peccatum domus Israel magnum est valde nimis. Dixerunt etenim: Reliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt. Propterea et ego non parcam, nec miserebor, sed arguam in furore.
paras.en: [[5:5|and say not before the angel|Neque dicas coram angelo]] appointed to guard thee: [[5:5|There is no providence|Non est providentia]]: that is, God has no care and providence over human acts. Grant this, and it follows that neither are angels sent from above to guard men. Against which the Apostle says: [[Heb 1:14|Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for them who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?|Nonne omnes sunt administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi propter eos qui hereditatem capiunt salutis?]]? Indeed the Lord too, in the Gospel: [[Matt 18:10|their angels|Angeli]], He says, [[Matt 18:10|in heaven always see the face of my Father|eorum in cœlis semper vident faciem Patris mei]]. And so such a word is a word of blasphemy and faithlessness and the greatest ingratitude, overflowing into an injury not only to God but also to the angels. Yet by the angel a priest can also be understood, according to that word of Malachias: [[Mal 2:7|the lips of the priests shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth: because he is the angel of the Lord|Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem requirent ex ore ejus, quia angelus Domini]]. [[5:5|lest God be angry at thy words, and destroy all the works of thy hands|Ne forte iratus Dominus contra sermones tuos, dissipet cuncta opera manuum tuarum]], that is, destroy all that thou hast, and so show by the effect that He has providence; and may also [[5:5|destroy|dissipet]] [[5:5|the works of thy hands|opera manuum tuarum]], that is, thy past good works: on account of this fault deprive thee of the eternal reward. For of those who speak so and say that word in Isaias, [[Is 22:13|Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die|Comedamus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur]], the Lord says: This iniquity has been revealed in my ears[[Is 22:14||]]. If this iniquity shall be forgiven you (that is, it shall not be forgiven) [[Is 22:14|till you die|donec moriamini]] ["If it shall be forgiven" is a Hebrew form of oath meaning "surely it shall not be forgiven", as the Douay-Rheims renders it]. Hence the Lord says to Ezechiel: The sin of the house of Israel [[Ezech 9:9|is exceeding great|magnum est valde nimis]]. For they have said: [[Ezech 9:9|The Lord hath forsaken the earth, and the Lord seeth not|Reliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt]]. Therefore I too will not spare[[Ezech 9:10||]], nor will I have pity, but I will rebuke them in fury[[Ezech 25:17||]] [Denis joins Ezech 9:9–10 and 25:17 freely].

paras.t: Ubi multa sunt somnia, ibi plurimæ sunt vanitates, et sermones innumeri. Hoc intelligendum est de his qui somniis suis faciliter credunt, et quidquid eis in somno apparet, repræsentatur, occurrit, putant mysticum esse, et aliquid significare, atque a Deo vel angelo revelari. Quibus contingunt multæ deceptiones; et ipsi de suis somniis plurima fabulantur, et tandem fiunt phantastici. Ideo in Ecclesiastico inducitur: Somnia extollunt imprudentes. Quasi qui apprehendit umbram, et persequitur ventum, secundum hoc visio somniorum. Sicut parturientis, cor tuum phantasias patitur, nisi ab Altissimo fuerit visitatio emissa. Multos errare fecerunt somnia. Unde in Jeremia et Ezechiele Dominus loquitur de pseudoprophetis: Errare fecerunt populum meum propter somnia sua, quæ narrat unusquisque proximo suo, dicens: Somniavi, somniavi. Verumtamen ista non sunt intelligenda, quasi somnia sint semper spernenda aut deceptiva. Sunt enim quandoque a Deo per angelos, interdum ex causa pure naturali. Unde in Numeris Dominus ait ad Aaron: Si fuerit inter vos Propheta, in visione apparebo ei, aut per somnium loquar ad eum. In libro Job quoque legitur: Per somnium in visione nocturna, aperit Deus aures virorum. In Evangelio etiam legitur sæpe angelus apparuisse Joseph in somnis. De hac materia super Genesim plenius scripsi, et super præallegatum Ecclesiastici capitulum, suo loco (præstante Domino) scribam. Hæc pro nunc tetigisse sufficiat. Tu vero time Deum filiali timore, non somnia vana, imaginationesque stultas: a quarum deceptione ora liberari a Domino.
paras.en: [[5:6|Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities, and words without number|Ubi multa sunt somnia, ibi plurimæ sunt vanitates, et sermones innumeri]]. This is to be understood of those who readily believe their dreams, and think that whatever appears, is presented or comes up to them in sleep is mystical and signifies something, and is revealed by God or an angel. Many deceptions befall them; and they tell a great many tales about their dreams, and at length become fanciful. Therefore it is brought in in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:1|dreams lift up fools|Somnia extollunt imprudentes]]. [[Ecclus 34:2|is like to him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind|Quasi qui apprehendit umbram, et persequitur ventum]]: so is [[Ecclus 34:3|The vision of dreams|visio somniorum]]. [[Ecclus 34:6|the heart fancieth as that of a woman in travail: except it be a vision sent forth from the most High|Sicut parturientis, cor tuum phantasias patitur, nisi ab Altissimo fuerit visitatio emissa]]. [[Ecclus 34:7|For dreams have deceived many|Multos errare fecerunt somnia]]. Hence in Jeremias and Ezechiel the Lord speaks of the false prophets: [[Ezech 13:10|they have deceived my people|Errare fecerunt populum meum]][[Ezech 13:6||]] [[Jer 23:27|through their dreams, which they tell every man to his neighbour|propter somnia sua, quæ narrat unusquisque proximo suo]], saying: [[Jer 23:25|I have dreamed, I have dreamed|Somniavi, somniavi]]. Yet these things are not to be understood as though dreams were always to be spurned or were deceitful. For they are sometimes from God through angels, sometimes from a purely natural cause. Hence in Numbers the Lord says to Aaron: [[Num 12:6|if there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I will appear to him in a vision, or I will speak to him in a dream|Si fuerit inter vos Propheta, in visione apparebo ei, aut per somnium loquar ad eum]]. In the book of Job too we read: [[Job 33:15|By a dream in a vision by night|Per somnium in visione nocturna]], [[Job 33:16|he openeth the ears of men|aperit Deus aures virorum]]. In the Gospel too we read that an angel often appeared to Joseph in sleep[[Matt 1:20||]][[Matt 2:13||]][[Matt 2:19||]]. I have written more fully on this matter on Genesis, and shall write on the chapter of Ecclesiasticus cited above in its place (the Lord granting). Let it suffice to have touched on these things for now. [[5:6|but do thou fear God|Tu vero time Deum]] with filial fear, not vain dreams and foolish imaginings: and pray to be freed by the Lord from their deception.

paras.t: Si videris calumnias egenorum, quas sustinent a divitibus atque potentibus, et violenta judicia, id est censuras, pœnas, similesve effectus, quos impii judices ac potentes jubent per violentiam infirmioribus inferioribusque inferri, et subverti justitiam in provincia, ita quod innocentes opprimuntur, et justi persecutionibus infestantur; non mireris super hoc negotio, id est, de istis eventibus non mireris admiratione immoderata, turbativa, aut diffidentiali. Solent enim quidam pusilli nondum satis illuminati vel in Scripturis exercitati, vehementer mirari, fluctuare, deficere, dum cernunt quosdam justos, sapientes, innocentes ac sanctos, a pessimis tribulari, spoliari, fugari, occidi, quasi Scriptura non dicat: Multæ tribulationes justorum; et, Quia per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum cœlorum; et rursus, Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam. Siquidem in hac vita electi et justi per impiorum manus purgantur, exercentur, et ad cœleste regnum mittuntur. De hac re Cassianus primo libro Collationum, in collatione abbatis Theodori de Nece Sanctorum, tractat diffuse. Unde in talium pusillorum sic admirantium persona Habacuc loquens: Quare non respicis, inquit, Domine, super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se?
paras.en: [[5:7|If thou shalt see the oppressions of the poor|Si videris calumnias egenorum]] which they suffer from the rich and powerful, [[5:7|and violent judgments|et violenta judicia]], that is, sentences, penalties or like effects, which wicked judges and powerful men command to be inflicted by violence on the weaker and lower, [[5:7|and justice perverted in the province|et subverti justitiam in provincia]], so that the innocent are oppressed and the just are harassed by persecutions; [[5:7|wonder not at this matter|non mireris super hoc negotio]], that is, do not wonder at these events with a wonder that is immoderate, troubling, or distrustful. For some little ones, not yet enlightened enough or practised in the Scriptures, are wont to wonder greatly, to waver and to fail, when they see certain just, wise, innocent and holy men troubled, despoiled, put to flight and slain by the worst of men: as though Scripture did not say: [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|Multæ tribulationes justorum]]; and, that [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom|per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum]] of heaven; and again, [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]]. For in this life the elect and the just are purged, exercised and sent on to the heavenly kingdom through the hands of the wicked. Cassian treats of this at length in the first book of the Conferences, in the conference of Abbot Theodore on the Slaying of the Saints. Hence Habacuc, speaking in the person of such little ones who wonder in this way: [[Hab 1:13|Why lookest thou upon|Quare non respicis]], he says, O Lord, [[Hab 1:13|them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se?]][[Hab 1:3||]]? [Denis reads "Why dost thou not look"; the margin gives "Cf. Habac. i, 13, 3".]

paras.t: Quia excelso excelsior est alius: id est, unus in potestate atque officio constitutus, est alio officiato sublimior, sicque si justus est, potest illius errata corrigere; vel si tyrannus est ille excelsior, potens est inferiorem opprimere. Et super hos quoque eminentiores, id est excelsiores, sunt alii: quemadmodum super barones et comites, sunt duces et reges, seu angeli qui præsunt provinciis, nec sustinerent talia fieri, nisi præstolarentur divini tempus judicii. Et insuper universæ terræ rex, id est monarcha totius regni, imperat servienti, id est suis ministris: ad quem pertinet aliorum emendare injurias et errata. Vel, per Universæ terræ regem, intelligitur Deus omnipotens: de quo ait Psalmista, Quoniam Deus magnus Dominus, et rex magnus super omnem terram. Qui prætacta mala non sineret fieri, nisi suo tempore vellet et posset universa dijudicare, et male judicata rejudicare. Qui ait: Quum accepero tempus, ego justitias judicabo. De quo et in Job scriptum est: Deus inultum abire non patitur; et in Ecclesiastico, Altissimus est patiens redditor.
paras.en: [[5:7|for he that is high hath another higher|Quia excelso excelsior est alius]]: that is, one set in power and office is higher than another officer, and so, if he is just, he can correct the other's errors; or if that higher one is a tyrant, he is able to oppress the lower. [[5:7|and there are others still higher than these|Et super hos quoque eminentiores]], that is, loftier ones: as over barons and counts there are dukes and kings, or the angels who preside over provinces, who would not suffer such things to be done unless they were awaiting the time of the divine judgment. [[5:8|Moreover there is the king that reigneth over all the land|Et insuper universæ terræ rex]], that is, the monarch of the whole kingdom, [[5:8|subject to him|imperat servienti]], that is, he commands his ministers: to whom it belongs to amend the injuries and errors of the others. Or, by the King of all the land, almighty God is understood: of whom the Psalmist says, [[Ps 94:3|For the Lord is a great God|Quoniam Deus magnus Dominus]], and [[Ps 46:3|a great king over all the earth|rex magnus super omnem terram]] [the margin gives Ps. xciv, 3, which ends "above all gods"; "over all the earth" is from Ps 46:3]. He would not let the evils mentioned be done unless He willed and were able in His own time to judge all things and to judge again what was ill judged. He says: [[Ps 74:3|When I shall take a time, I will judge justices|Quum accepero tempus, ego justitias judicabo]]. Of Him too it is written in Job: [[Job 24:12|God doth not suffer it to pass unrevenged|Deus inultum abire non patitur]]; and in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 5:4|the most High is a patient rewarder|Altissimus est patiens redditor]].

paras.t: Avarus non implebitur pecunia, id est, affectus avari non satiatur pecuniis: quoniam quo plures acquirit, plures desiderat, sicut hydropicus, quanto plus bibit, tanto plus sitit. De hoc dicta sunt multa. Et qui amat divitias temporales immoderate, et tanquam finem, seu propter se ipsas, fructum non capiet ex eis, id est usum salubrem: quia non proficiunt ei ad salutem, sed obsunt; et vix audet eis ad sufficientiam uti, ac Deo de eis ingratus est, nec communicat pauperibus. Idcirco in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Nihil iniquius quam amare pecuniam. Et Salvator in Evangelio: Quam difficile, inquit, qui pecunias habent, intrabunt in regnum cœlorum! Facilius est camelum per foramen acus transire, quam divitem intrare in regnum cœlorum. Porro divitiæ in tantum possunt amari, in quantum utiles ac necessariæ sunt ad spiritualia bona, hoc est ad bene vivendum, ad serviendum Altissimo, ad habendum necessaria vitæ, ad cultus virtuosos, ad Dei honorem. Et hoc ergo vanitas.
paras.en: [[5:9|A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money|Avarus non implebitur pecunia]], that is, the covetous man's craving is not sated with money: since the more he gains, the more he desires, like a man with dropsy, who the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. Much has been said of this. [[5:9|and he that loveth riches|Et qui amat divitias]] of this world immoderately, and as an end, or for their own sake, [[5:9|shall reap no fruit from them|fructum non capiet ex eis]], that is, no wholesome use: because they do not profit him for salvation but harm him; and he hardly dares to use them as much as he needs, and is ungrateful to God for them, and does not share them with the poor. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:10|There is not a more wicked thing than to love money|Nihil iniquius quam amare pecuniam]]. And the Saviour in the Gospel: [[Luke 18:24|How hardly|Quam difficile]], He says, [[Luke 18:24|shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom|qui pecunias habent, intrabunt in regnum]] of heaven! [[Luke 18:25|it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom|Facilius est camelum per foramen acus transire, quam divitem intrare in regnum]] of heaven [Denis's "kingdom of heaven" is the wording of Matt 19:23–24; Luke has "kingdom of God"]. But riches may be loved so far as they are useful and necessary for spiritual goods, that is, for living well, for serving the Most High, for having the necessaries of life, for virtuous worship, for the honour of God. [[5:9|so this also is vanity|Et hoc ergo vanitas]].

paras.t: Ubi multæ sunt opes, multi et qui comedunt, id est consumunt, eas. Quod frequenter contingit. Quidam tamen divites tenent secum perpaucos, et opes reponunt. Et quid prodest possessori, nisi quod cernit divitias suas oculis suis? Sicque ex earum apprehensione delectatur inaniter, et est sicut Tantalus in mediis undis.
paras.en: [[5:10|Where there are great riches, there are also many to eat|Ubi multæ sunt opes, multi et qui comedunt]], that is, to consume, [[5:10|them|eas]]. Which often happens. Some rich men, however, keep very few about them, and store up their wealth. [[5:10|And what doth it profit the owner, but that he seeth the riches with his eyes?|Et quid prodest possessori, nisi quod cernit divitias suas oculis suis?]]? And so he takes an empty delight in grasping them, and is like Tantalus in the midst of the waters.

paras.t: Dulcis est somnus operanti, post suum laborem, sive parum sive multum comedat. Nam propter lassitudinem et diuturnum laborem, natura indiget recreatione. Similiter occupato in exercitiis virtuosis, et vitæ activæ operibus, dulce est interdum quieti contemplationis vacare, præsertim si cum Apostolo sciat abundare et penuriam pati, saturari et esuriem sustinere. Saturitas autem divitis non sinit eum dormire diu et quiete: quia ex saturitate dyscrasiam, torsiones, ægritudinesque incurrit; est quoque propter divitias suas sollicitus. Similiter carnalis sua saturitas impedit eum ab obdormitione in Deo per contemplationis soporem; nec dicere potest, In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam. Verum, ut Seneca in Proverbiis suis testatur, bene dormit, qui non sentit quam male dormit.
paras.en: [[5:11|Sleep is sweet to a labouring man|Dulcis est somnus operanti]], after his labour, [[5:11|whether he eat little or much|sive parum sive multum comedat]]. For because of weariness and long labour, nature needs refreshment. Likewise, to one busied in virtuous exercises and the works of the active life it is sweet at times to give himself to the quiet of contemplation, especially if, with the Apostle, he knows how to abound and to suffer need, to be full and to bear hunger[[Phil 4:12||]]. [[5:11|but the fulness of the rich will not suffer him to sleep|Saturitas autem divitis non sinit eum dormire]] long and quietly: because from fulness he incurs dyscrasia [that is, an ill balance of the bodily humours], gripings and illnesses; he is also anxious on account of his riches. Likewise his carnal fulness hinders him from falling asleep in God through the slumber of contemplation; nor can he say, [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam]]. But, as Seneca testifies in his Proverbs, he sleeps well who does not feel how badly he sleeps.

paras.t: Est et alia infirmitas, id est enervatio ac debilitas cordis, robori virtutum contraria, pessima, id est valde mala, quam vidi sub sole: divitiæ conservatæ in malum domini sui, id est, quod ipse dives, præsertim avarus, frequenter congregat et reservat divitias in damnum et periculum sui ipsius, dum fures, raptores, latrones et tyranni, insidiantur ei propter suas divitias, et tollunt eas, aut etiam ipsum occidunt. Ideo Seneca dixit: Maximo periculo custoditur, quod multis placet.
paras.en: [[5:12|There is also another|Est et alia]] [[5:12|evil|infirmitas]] [Latin *infirmitas*, "sickness", "weakness"], that is, a sapping and weakness of heart, contrary to the strength of the virtues, [[5:12|grievous|pessima]], that is, very bad, [[5:12|which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the hurt of the owner|quam vidi sub sole: divitiæ conservatæ in malum domini sui]]: that is, the rich man himself, especially the covetous one, often gathers and stores up riches to his own loss and peril, when thieves, robbers, brigands and tyrants lie in wait for him on account of his riches, and take them away, or even kill him. Therefore Seneca said: That which pleases many is guarded at the greatest peril.

paras.t: Pereunt enim in afflictione pessima, id est, divitiæ auferuntur suo possessori cum amara ejus tristitia et desolatione, quia invitissime eas amittit. Generavit filium, qui in summa egestate erit: quia opes patris direptæ sunt, nec eas potest recuperare.
paras.en: [[5:13|For they are lost with very great affliction|Pereunt enim in afflictione pessima]], that is, the riches are taken from their owner with his bitter sorrow and desolation, because he loses them most unwillingly. [[5:13|he hath begotten a son, who shall be in extremity of want|Generavit filium, qui in summa egestate erit]]: because his father's wealth has been plundered and he cannot recover it.

paras.t: Sicut egressus est nudus ille possessor sic spoliatus, seu filius ejus bonis paternis privatus, de utero matris suæ; sic revertetur pauper et nudus in terram, et nihil auferet secum de labore suo, dum moritur, id est de suis bonis terrenis, laboriose acquisitis. Attamen opera, id est merita ac demerita, singulos eos sequuntur, juxta illud in Apocalypsi: Opera illorum sequuntur illos. Hinc fertur in Psalmo: Dormierunt somnum suum, et nihil invenerunt omnes viri divitiarum in manibus suis. Job quoque: Dives (inquit) quum dormierit, nihil secum auferet; apprehendet eum quasi aqua inopia. Ideo ait Apostolus: Nihil intulimus in hunc mundum; haud dubium quia nec auferre quid possumus. Miserabilis prorsus infirmitas! Quo modo venit, sic revertetur. Quid ergo prodest ei quod laboravit in ventum, id est inaniter et incerte? Cunctis diebus vitæ suæ comedit in tenebris cordis, id est in malis pœnæ et culpæ, et in curis multis, quæ mentem affligunt et pungunt ut spinæ, et in ærumna atque tristitia, id est anxietate et mœrore.
paras.en: [[5:14|As he came forth naked|Sicut egressus est nudus]], that owner thus despoiled, or his son deprived of his father's goods, [[5:14|from his mother's womb|de utero matris suæ]], [[5:14|so shall he return|sic revertetur]], poor and naked, to the earth, [[5:14|and shall take nothing away with him of his labour|et nihil auferet secum de labore suo]] when he dies, that is, of his earthly goods, gained with toil. Yet their works, that is, their merits and demerits, follow each of them, according to that word in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 14:13|their works follow them|Opera illorum sequuntur illos]]. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 75:6|They have slept their sleep; and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands|Dormierunt somnum suum, et nihil invenerunt omnes viri divitiarum in manibus suis]]. Job too: [[Job 27:19|The rich man|Dives]] (he says) [[Job 27:19|when he shall sleep shall take away nothing with him|quum dormierit, nihil secum auferet]]: [[Job 27:20|Poverty like water shall take hold on him|apprehendet eum quasi aqua inopia]]. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 6:7|For we brought nothing into this world: and certainly we can carry nothing out|Nihil intulimus in hunc mundum; haud dubium quia nec auferre quid possumus]]. [[5:15|A most deplorable evil|Miserabilis prorsus infirmitas]]! [[5:15|as he came, so shall he return|Quo modo venit, sic revertetur]]. [[5:15|What then doth it profit him that he hath laboured for the wind?|Quid ergo prodest ei quod laboravit in ventum]], that is, in vain and with no sure gain? [[5:16|All the days of his life he eateth in darkness|Cunctis diebus vitæ suæ comedit in tenebris]] of heart, that is, in the evils of punishment and of guilt, [[5:16|and in many cares|et in curis multis]], which afflict and prick the mind like thorns, [[5:16|and in misery, and sorrow|et in ærumna atque tristitia]], that is, in anxiety and grief.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, divitiæ conservantur in malum domini sui, dum quis ad tempus spiritualiter crescit in scientia atque virtutibus, et non perseverat usque in finem. Imo bona cooperantur ei in malum, et melius ei esset non cognovisse viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem reverti retrorsum. Similiter accidit ei qui de spirituali opulentia meritorum suorum extollitur, nec permanet gratus Deo, humiliterque subjectus. Talis generat filios, id est discipulos ac subditos, pauperes, quia scandalizantur in eo, et recidivationem ejus sequendo, pereunt simul cum ipso: sicut de talibus ait Apostolus, Errantes et in errorem mittentes.
paras.en: Spiritually, [[5:12|riches kept to the hurt of the owner|divitiæ conservantur in malum domini sui]], when someone grows spiritually for a time in knowledge and virtues, and does not persevere to the end. Indeed his good things work together for his harm, and [[2 Pet 2:21|it had been better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after they have known it, to turn back|melius ei esset non cognovisse viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem reverti retrorsum]]. The like happens to one who is puffed up by the spiritual wealth of his merits, and does not remain grateful to God and humbly subject. Such a one begets sons, that is, disciples and subjects, who are poor, because they are scandalized in him, and by following his relapse they perish together with him: as the Apostle says of such, [[2 Tim 3:13|erring, and driving into error|Errantes et in errorem mittentes]].

paras.t: Hoc itaque visum est mihi bonum, ut comedat quis et bibat, et fruatur lætitia ex labore suo, quo laboravit ipse sub sole numero dierum vitæ suæ, quos dedit ei Deus: et hæc est pars illius: id est, melius est temperate et delectabiliter uti terrenis, quam tam anxie propter ea sollicitari, et in tenebris prætactis uti eisdem. Frui autem, frequenter pro Uti accipitur. Nam proprie non est fruendum nisi Deo.
paras.en: [[5:17|This therefore hath seemed good to me, that a man should eat and drink, and enjoy the fruit of his labour, wherewith he hath laboured under the sun, all the days of his life, which God hath given him: and this is his portion.|Hoc itaque visum est mihi bonum, ut comedat quis et bibat, et fruatur lætitia ex labore suo, quo laboravit ipse sub sole numero dierum vitæ suæ, quos dedit ei Deus: et hæc est pars illius]]: that is, it is better to use earthly things temperately and with enjoyment than to be so anxiously troubled about them, and to use them in the darkness spoken of. Now *frui* ["to enjoy"] is often taken for *uti* ["to use"]. For, properly, God alone is to be enjoyed [that is, loved for His own sake as our last end, while all else is used for His sake].

paras.t: Et omni homini, cui Deus dedit divitias atque substantiam, id est mobilia et immobilia bona, potestatemque ei tribuit ut comedat ex eis, et fruatur parte sua, et lætetur de labore suo, id est, delectabiliter sua portione utatur: hoc est donum Dei, id est quoddam beneficium ejus, et melius usu prætacto: et ex gratia id procedit, quod homo temporalibus ordinate utatur. — Spiritualiter, bonum est refici sacramentis Christi, pane lacrimarum, et actibus virtuosis, atque ex eis et gratia Dei, præstolari vitam beatam, ejusque exspectatione gaudere.
paras.en: [[5:18|And every man to whom God hath given riches, and substance|Et omni homini, cui Deus dedit divitias atque substantiam]], that is, movable and immovable goods, [[5:18|and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to enjoy his portion, and to rejoice of his labour|potestatemque ei tribuit ut comedat ex eis, et fruatur parte sua, et lætetur de labore suo]], that is, let him use his portion with enjoyment: [[5:18|this is the gift of God|hoc est donum Dei]], that is, a certain benefit of His, and better than the use spoken of before: and it comes from grace that a man uses temporal things in an ordered way. Spiritually, it is good to be refreshed with the sacraments of Christ, with the bread of tears and with virtuous acts, and from these and the grace of God to await the blessed life, and to rejoice in the expectation of it.

paras.t: Non enim satis recordabitur dierum vitæ suæ, id est, tempus vitæ suæ non videbitur sibi valde longum, nec tædiosum, eo quod Deus occupet deliciis cor ejus, id est, vitam jucundam ei concedat, secundum modum nunc introductum. Iis autem qui in deliciis vivunt, tempus videtur breve, quamvis sit longum: sicut e contrario, iis qui desolatam, tristem, amaram ducunt vitam, tempus, quamvis breve, videtur longum, ut in damnatis maxime patet. Iis quoque qui conantur quotidie multa expedire et agere, dies valde breves apparent, quia non valent satisfacere suo affectui. Conformiter hominibus virtuosis, contemplativis, perfectis, tempus breve videtur, quia in assidua mentis tranquillitate, et bonæ conscientiæ securitate, spiritualique gaudio serviunt Deo; et quoniam quidquid hic agere queunt, quantumcumque diu vixerint, permodicum reputant intuitu et amore retributionis futuræ. Interdum tamen præ desiderio dissolvendi et exsistendi cum Christo, ac perfruendi beatifice Deo, tempus potest eis longum apparere, ita ut dicant: Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est; et, Quando veniam et apparebo ante faciem Dei?
paras.en: [[5:19|For he shall not much remember the days of his life|Non enim satis recordabitur dierum vitæ suæ]], that is, the time of his life will not seem to him very long, nor wearisome, [[5:19|because God entertaineth his heart with delight|eo quod Deus occupet deliciis cor ejus]], that is, grants him a pleasant life, in the way now set out. For to those who live in delights time seems short, although it is long: as on the contrary to those who lead a desolate, sad and bitter life, time, though short, seems long, as is most plain in the damned. To those too who try every day to dispatch and do many things, the days seem very short, because they cannot satisfy their desire. In the same way time seems short to virtuous, contemplative and perfect men, because they serve God in constant tranquillity of mind, in the security of a good conscience and in spiritual joy; and because whatever they can do here, however long they live, they reckon very small in view of, and for love of, the reward to come. Sometimes, however, through desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ[[Phil 1:23||]], and to enjoy God in beatitude, the time may seem long to them, so that they say: [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] and: [[Ps 41:3|when shall I come and appear before the face of God?|Quando veniam et apparebo ante faciem Dei?]]

6.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI SEXTI : EST ET ALIUD MALUM QUOD VIDI SUB SOLE.
6.title_en: Explanation of the sixth chapter: There is also another evil, which I have seen under the sun.

paras.t: Rursus cupidorum et divitum vanitatem, miseriasque describit. Est et aliud malum quod vidi sub sole, et quidem frequens apud homines, id est sæpe contingens hominibus. Deinde exprimit illud. Vir cui dedit Deus divitias et substantiam, id est bona mobilia ac immobilia, bona terrena, opesque naturales ac artificiales, et honorem, id est dignitatem præsidentiæ, famam, et humanæ reverentiæ exhibitionem; et nihil deest animæ suæ, id est personæ ejus, sumendo partem pro toto, seu vitæ animali, ex omnibus quæ desiderat, id est de his quæ ad temporalem spectare videntur prosperitatem. Nec tribuit ei potestatem Deus ut comedat ex eo, id est, tempus vitæ ei non præstat, sed subtrahit eum per mortem; sed homo extraneus vorabit illud, id est, bona ejus consumet. Hoc vanitas, id est instabilitas, et miseria magna est. Non tamen est culpa in se, nec ex parte Dei subtrahentis, nec ex parte subtracti, nisi forsan ob culpam suam tam cito tollatur.
paras.en: Again he describes the vanity and the miseries of the covetous and the rich. [[6:1|There is also another evil, which I have seen under the sun, and that frequent among men|Est et aliud malum quod vidi sub sole, et quidem frequens apud homines]], that is, which often befalls men. Then he states what it is. [[6:2|A man to whom God hath given riches, and substance|Vir cui dedit Deus divitias et substantiam]], that is, goods movable and immovable, earthly goods, and wealth both natural and artificial [that is, natural riches such as food, livestock and land, which serve life directly, and artificial riches such as money], [[6:2|and honour|et honorem]], that is, the dignity of high office, renown, and the showing of men's reverence; [[6:2|and his soul wanteth nothing|et nihil deest animæ suæ]], that is, his person (taking the part for the whole), or his animal life, [[6:2|of all that he desireth|ex omnibus quæ desiderat]], that is, of the things which seem to belong to temporal prosperity. [[6:2|yet God doth not give him power to eat thereof|Nec tribuit ei potestatem Deus ut comedat ex eo]], that is, He does not grant him time of life, but takes him away by death; [[6:2|but a stranger shall eat it up|sed homo extraneus vorabit illud]], that is, shall consume his goods. [[6:2|This is vanity|Hoc vanitas]], that is, instability, [[6:2|and a great misery|et miseria magna est]]. Yet there is no fault in this in itself, neither on the part of God who takes him away nor on the part of the one taken, unless perhaps he is taken away so soon because of his own fault.

paras.t: Si genuerit quispiam centum liberos. In Scripturis autem (ni fallor) non legitur quis genuisse ultra septuaginta filios, nisi forsitan addito uno aut duobus, sicut in libro Judicum recitatur Abimelech filius Gedeonis occidisse septuaginta viros fratres suos filios Gedeonis. Quibus tamen superstes fuit Joatham frater illorum, imo et ipse Abimelech. Similiter quarto Regum narratur Jehu occidisse septuaginta filios Achab: ante quos occiderat filium ejus Joram. Verumtamen aliqui habuerunt plures quam septuaginta duas proles, ut patet de Roboam rege, qui viginti octo genuit filios, sexagintaque filias. Et vixerit multos annos, et plures dies ætatis habuerit, sicque fecunditatem habeat prolis, ac vitæ diuturnitatem, et anima illius, id est ipsemet, non utatur bonis substantiæ suæ, necessaria vitæ sumendo ex ipsis, eo quod sibi subtracta sint, vel ipse in captivitatem traductus, sepulturaque careat: sicut de Joakim rege Jeremias prædixit, Sepultura asini sepelietur. De hoc ego pronuntio, quod melior illo sit abortivus: qui actualiter non peccavit, et ad limbum puerorum deducitur. Hæc autem intelligenda sunt, faciendo comparationem istorum ad invicem, quantum ad mala vitæ præsentis. Potest tamen contingere, quod aliquis dives spolietur et captivetur, atque in tantis adversis sit patiens, ac Deo intentus, sicque melior sit ac felicior abortivo.
paras.en: [[6:3|If a man beget a hundred children|Si genuerit quispiam centum liberos]]. Now in the Scriptures (unless I am mistaken) no one is read to have begotten more than seventy sons, save perhaps with one or two added: as it is related in the book of Judges that Abimelech, the son of Gedeon, slew seventy men, his brothers, the sons of Gedeon[[Judg 9:5||]]. Yet Joatham their brother survived them[[Judg 9:5||]], and indeed so did Abimelech himself. Likewise it is told in the fourth book of Kings that Jehu slew seventy sons of Achab[[4 Kings 10:6||]][[4 Kings 10:7||]], before whom he had slain his son Joram[[4 Kings 9:24||]]. Yet some had more than seventy-two children, as is clear of King Roboam, who begot twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters[[2 Par 11:21||]]. [[6:3|and live many years, and attain to a great age|Et vixerit multos annos, et plures dies ætatis habuerit]], and so have both fruitfulness in offspring and length of life, [[6:3|and his soul|et anima illius]], that is, he himself, [[6:3|make no use of the goods of his substance|non utatur bonis substantiæ suæ]] by taking from them what is needful for life, because they have been taken from him, or he himself has been led away into captivity, [[6:3|and he be without burial|sepulturaque careat]]: as Jeremias foretold of King Joakim, [[Jer 22:19|He shall be buried with the burial of an ass|Sepultura asini sepelietur]]. [[6:3|of this man I pronounce, that the untimely born is better than he|De hoc ego pronuntio, quod melior illo sit abortivus]]: for it has not sinned actually [that is, by any act of its own; it bears only original sin], and is taken down to the limbo of children. These things are to be understood by comparing the two with each other as to the evils of the present life. Yet it can happen that some rich man is despoiled and taken captive, and in such great adversities is patient and intent on God, and so is better and happier than the untimely born.

paras.t: Porro sequentia dupliciter exponuntur: Primo, de abortivo. Frustra enim venit in uterum et ad conceptum, quia non potuit pervenire ad nativitatem ex utero, nec ad vitam beatam; et pergit ad tenebras, id est ad limbum, quem dicunt aliqui tenebrosum, vel quia in eo est pœna damni; vel, Ad tenebras, id est ad sepulcrum; et oblivione delebitur nomen ejus, id est, ipsemet cito erit a memoria hominum omnino deletus, nec habuit nomen sibi impositum. Non vidit solem, id est, quia non prodiit vivus ex ventre ad lucem: neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali, id est, differentiam inter bonum et malum non est expertus in mundo, quia non venit ad usum rationis in vita præsenti.
paras.en: Now what follows is expounded in two ways. First, of the untimely born. [[6:4|For he came in vain|Frustra enim venit]] into the womb and to conception, since he could not come to birth from the womb, nor to the life of bliss; [[6:4|and goeth to darkness|et pergit ad tenebras]], that is, to limbo, which some call dark, or else because in it there is the pain of loss [that is, the loss of the sight of God, as distinct from the pain of sense]; or, [[6:4|to darkness|Ad tenebras]], that is, to the grave; [[6:4|and his name shall be wholly forgotten|et oblivione delebitur nomen ejus]], that is, he himself will soon be wholly blotted out of men's memory, nor had he a name given him. [[6:5|He hath not seen the sun|Non vidit solem]], that is, because he did not come forth alive from the womb into the light; [[6:5|nor known the distance of good and evil|neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali]], that is, he did not experience in the world the difference between good and evil, since he did not come to the use of reason in the present life.

paras.t: Secundo, exponuntur hæc de homine divite, diu vivente, fecundo, nec tamen potente uti divitiis suis: qui frustra venit ad opes, vel in mundum, in quo non est consecutus felicitatem, et pergit ad tenebras, id est ad tormenta ac desolationes; et oblivione delebitur nomen ejus: eo modo quo in Proverbiis dictum est: Nomen impiorum putrescet; et in Psalmo, Nomen eorum delesti in æternum, et in sæculum sæculi. Non vidit solem, id est, prosperitatem atque lætitiam non est expertus, nec Solem justitiæ consideravit; neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali: id est, sola adversa expertus est, non prospera, et ita non novit utrumque perfecte: quia (ut fertur communiter) qui non est paupertatem aut infirmitatem expertus, nescit quid sit opulentia aut sanitas. Vel, Non cognovit distantiam boni et mali, id est, non discrevit inter virtutes et vitia. Imo quæ illicita sunt, licita reputavit.
paras.en: Secondly, these words are expounded of a rich man who lives long and is fruitful, yet cannot use his riches. He [[6:4|came in vain|frustra venit]] to wealth, or into the world, in which he has not attained happiness, [[6:4|and goeth to darkness|et pergit ad tenebras]], that is, to torments and desolations; [[6:4|and his name shall be wholly forgotten|et oblivione delebitur nomen ejus]], in the way in which it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 10:7|the name of the wicked shall rot|Nomen impiorum putrescet]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 9:6|thou hast blotted out their name for ever and ever|Nomen eorum delesti in æternum, et in sæculum sæculi]]. [[6:5|He hath not seen the sun|Non vidit solem]], that is, he has not experienced prosperity and gladness, nor has he contemplated the Sun of justice; [[6:5|nor known the distance of good and evil|neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali]]: that is, he has experienced only adversity, not prosperity, and so does not know both perfectly; for (as is commonly said) he who has not experienced poverty or sickness does not know what wealth or health is. Or, [[6:5|nor known the distance of good and evil|Non cognovit distantiam boni et mali]], that is, he did not discern between virtues and vices; nay rather, what is unlawful he reckoned lawful.

paras.t: Etiam si duobus millibus annis vixerit homo: quum tamen nemo in Scripturis legatur mille annis vixisse; sed Mathusalem qui ceteris diutius invenitur vixisse, annis nongentis sexaginta novem vixisse narratur in Genesi; et non fuerit perfruitus bonis, sed jugiter malis, adhuc tamen abortivo miserior est, præsertim si non fuerit perfruitus bonis gratiæ ac virtutum. Nonne ad unum locum properant omnia?
paras.en: [[6:6|Although he lived two thousand years|Etiam si duobus millibus annis vixerit]] (though no one is read in the Scriptures to have lived a thousand years; but Mathusala, who is found to have lived longer than the rest, is related in Genesis to have lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years[[Gen 5:27||]]), [[6:6|and hath not enjoyed good things|et non fuerit perfruitus bonis]], but continually evil ones, he is still more wretched than the untimely born, above all if he has not enjoyed the goods of grace and of the virtues. [[6:6|do not all make haste to one place?|Nonne ad unum locum properant omnia?]]

paras.t: Omnis labor hominis in ore ejus: id est, quidquid laborando acquirit de rebus terrenis, ore seu comestione consumit; sed anima ejus non implebitur: id est, cor ejus plura desiderabit, nec sufficientia erit contentum (potissime loquendo de cupido), ac postea iterum cupiet manducare. — Spiritualiter, omnis labor hominis est in ore ejus, quando jugiter laborat addiscere aliquid, ut instruat alios, vel ut ornate loquatur, et sapienter eloqui videatur.
paras.en: [[6:7|All the labour of man is for his mouth|Omnis labor hominis in ore ejus]]: that is, whatever he gains of earthly things by labouring, he consumes with his mouth, that is, by eating; [[6:7|but his soul shall not be filled|sed anima ejus non implebitur]]: that is, his heart will desire more, and will not be content with sufficiency (speaking chiefly of the covetous man), and afterwards he will want to eat again. Spiritually, [[6:7|All the labour of man is for his mouth|omnis labor hominis est in ore ejus]] when he labours continually to learn something in order to teach others, or to speak elegantly and seem to speak wisely.

paras.t: Quid habet amplius sapiens a stulto? et quid pauper, supple, a divite? id est, in quo excedit sapiens decoratus sapientia (quæ est donum seu notitia Scripturarum cum impletione earum) stultum, id est iniquum in quo puerilitatis vitium viget? Unde in Proverbiis dictum est: Usquequo stulti ea quæ sibi nociva sunt, cupient? Propter quod admonet Paulus: Nolite pueri effici sensibus. Et in quo pauper spiritu, id est humilis, seu propter Deum libenter egenus, excedit divitem cupidum? Nisi ut pergat, tam sapiens talis, quam pauper, illuc ubi est vita gloriæ, id est beatitudo æterna, cui nihil de mortalitate et calamitate miscetur. Unde scriptum est: Neminem diligit Deus, nisi qui cum sapientia inhabitat. Et in Isaia: Non est populus sapiens, ideo non miserebitur ejus, qui fecit illum. Et in Matthæo loquitur Veritas: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum: atque in Psalmo, Parcet pauperi et inopi, et animas pauperum salvas faciet. Sed, heu! multi sunt, in quibus detestanda puerilitas regnat. Propter quod Seneca protestatur: Multa bona nostra nobis nocent. Adhuc enim in nobis non pueritia, sed quod est gravius, puerilitas remanet. Et hoc quidem pejor est, quod auctoritatem senum habemus, et vitia puerorum.
paras.en: [[6:8|What hath the wise man more than the fool?|Quid habet amplius sapiens a stulto?]] [[6:8|and what the poor man|et quid pauper]], supply: more than the rich man? That is, in what does the wise man adorned with wisdom (which is the gift, or knowledge, of the Scriptures together with the fulfilling of them) surpass the fool, that is, the wicked man in whom the vice of childishness flourishes? Hence it is said in Proverbs: How long shall [[Prov 1:22|fools covet those things which are hurtful to themselves|stulti ea quæ sibi nociva sunt, cupient]]? For this reason Paul warns: [[1 Cor 14:20|do not become children in sense|Nolite pueri effici sensibus]]. And in what does the poor in spirit, that is, the humble man, or the man gladly needy for God's sake, surpass the covetous rich man? [[6:8|but to go|Nisi ut pergat]], the wise man so described as well as the poor man, [[6:8|thither, where there is life|illuc ubi est vita]] of glory, that is, eternal beatitude, with which nothing of mortality and calamity is mingled. Hence it is written: [[Wis 7:28|God loveth none but him that dwelleth with wisdom|Neminem diligit Deus, nisi qui cum sapientia inhabitat]]. And in Isaias: [[Is 27:11|it is not a wise people, therefore he that made it, shall not have mercy on it|Non est populus sapiens, ideo non miserebitur ejus, qui fecit illum]] [the margin gives Is. xxxiii, 11; the words are from Is 27:11]. And in Matthew the Truth says: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:13|He shall spare the poor and needy: and he shall save the souls of the poor|Parcet pauperi et inopi, et animas pauperum salvas faciet]]. But alas, there are many in whom a detestable childishness reigns. For this reason Seneca declares: “Many of our goods do us harm. For there still remains in us, not childhood, but, what is graver, childishness. And this indeed is worse, that we have the authority of old men and the vices of children.”

paras.t: Melius est videre, id est cognoscere, quod cupias, id est, quod merito et salubriter appetere debes, videlicet ultimum finem, et omnia necessaria seu utilia ad eum adipiscendum, quam desiderare quod nescias, id est, quod tibi expedit ignorare magis quam scire, ut sunt superstitiosa, magica, frivola. Falsum quoque non scitur, quamvis sciri putetur, ut ait Philosophus. Sed et hoc vanitas est, et præsumptio spiritus, scilicet desiderare quod nescias: juxta expositionem nunc tactam.
paras.en: [[6:9|Better it is to see|Melius est videre]], that is, to know, [[6:9|what thou mayst desire|quod cupias]], that is, what thou oughtest rightly and wholesomely to seek, namely the last end, and all things necessary or useful for attaining it, [[6:9|than to desire that which thou canst not know|quam desiderare quod nescias]], that is, what it is better for thee to be ignorant of than to know, such as superstitious, magical and frivolous things. Also, what is false is not known, though it be thought to be known, as the Philosopher says. [[6:9|But this also is vanity, and presumption of spirit|Sed et hoc vanitas est, et præsumptio spiritus]], namely, to desire what thou canst not know, according to the exposition just touched on.

paras.t: Qui futurus est, jam vocatum est nomen ejus: id est, omnium qui nascentur nomina Deo præcognita sunt; vel, alii qui præcesserunt, similes illis in specie, similia nomina habuerunt. Et scitur quod homo sit, id est, de omnibus illis scitur, quod mortales et fragiles creaturæ sunt, fuerunt, aut erunt. Idcirco non debent se ultra mensuram sui gradus et status seu conditionis extendere ad vana, præsumptuosa et curiosa. Et non possit contra fortiorem se in judicio contendere: id est, Creatori suo non poterit respondere, vanitatem et culpam propriam defendendo, aut aliquid contra Dei providentiam efficaciter allegando. Unde ait Apostolus: O homo, tu quis es, qui respondeas Deo? Numquid dicit figmentum ei qui se finxit, Quid me fecisti sic? Hinc fertur in Job: Sapiens corde est, et fortis robore. Quis restitit ei, et habuit pacem? Si voluerit homo cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille. Hoc est quod in Isaia scriptum est: Væ qui contradicit factori suo. Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?
paras.en: [[6:10|He that shall be, his name is already called|Qui futurus est, jam vocatum est nomen ejus]]: that is, the names of all who shall be born are foreknown to God; or, others who went before, like them in kind, had like names. [[6:10|and it is known, that he is a man|Et scitur quod homo sit]], that is, of all of them it is known that they are, were, or will be mortal and frail creatures. Therefore they ought not to stretch themselves beyond the measure of their degree and state or condition to vain, presumptuous and curious things. [[6:10|and cannot contend in judgment with him that is stronger than himself|Et non possit contra fortiorem se in judicio contendere]]: that is, he will not be able to answer his Creator by defending his own vanity and fault, or by alleging anything with effect against God's providence. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 9:20|O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it: Why hast thou made me thus?|O homo, tu quis es, qui respondeas Deo? Numquid dicit figmentum ei qui se finxit, Quid me fecisti sic?]] Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 9:4|He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength: who hath resisted him, and hath had peace?|Sapiens corde est, et fortis robore. Quis restitit ei, et habuit pacem?]] [[Job 9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand|Si voluerit homo cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille]]. This is what is written in Isaias: [[Is 45:9|Woe to him that gainsayeth his maker|Væ qui contradicit factori suo]]. [[Is 45:9|shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it: What art thou making|Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?]]

paras.t: Verba sunt plurima, eorum qui secreta et incomprehensibilia, seu curiosa et superstitiosa scire cupiunt et scrutantur: qui frequenter verbis utuntur superfluis. De qualibus ait Apostolus: Semper discentes, et nunquam ad veritatis notitiam pervenientes; et Isaias, Ubi sunt augures tui, qui contemplabantur sidera, ut ex his annuntiarent tibi quæ ventura sunt? Multamque in disputando habentia vanitatem: quia errant in multis, et argumentis topicis ac frivolis, tanquam demonstrativis ac solidis, innituntur et occupantur. Hoc clarissime patet in multis philosophis atque astronomis, qui contra fidei christianæ veritatem plurima conscripserunt ac disputaverunt: qui enormiter sunt mentiti, et in rudissimos ac nefandissimos corruerunt errores, sicut Averroes peripateticus, qui tandem in disputationibus suis contra Catholicos, negavit providentiam Dei, et animam humanam dixit esse mortalem, ac unum numero intellectum in cunctis hominibus. Similiter Porphyrius Platonicus, qui licet concesserit legem Moysi datam a Deo, nihilo minus idololatriam approbavit, quæ tamen in lege Moysis apertissime reprobatur. Albumasar quoque astrologus in Introductorio majori, et Alkindus in sua Theorica, et libro de Radiis stellicis, mirabiliter ac miserabiliter erraverunt. De talibus ad Timotheum scribens Apostolus, ait: Quemadmodum Jannes et Mambres restiterunt Moysi, ita et hi resistunt veritati, homines mente corrupti, reprobi circa fidem; sed ultra non proficient: insipientia enim eorum manifesta erit omnibus, sicut et illorum fuit.
paras.en: [[6:11|There are many words|Verba sunt plurima]], of those who desire to know and search out things secret and incomprehensible, or curious and superstitious, and who often use superfluous words. Of such the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 3:7|Ever learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth|Semper discentes, et nunquam ad veritatis notitiam pervenientes]]; and Isaias: Where are thy augurs, [[Is 47:13|they that gazed at the stars|qui contemplabantur sidera]], [[Is 47:13|that from them they might tell the things that shall come to thee|ut ex his annuntiarent tibi quæ ventura sunt?]] [Denis quotes Isaias freely.] [[6:11|that have much vanity in disputing|Multamque in disputando habentia vanitatem]]: for they err in many things, and rely on and busy themselves with topical and frivolous arguments [that is, arguments that are merely probable, drawn from commonplaces, as against demonstrative arguments, which prove with certainty] as though they were demonstrative and solid. This is most clearly seen in many philosophers and astronomers who have written and disputed a great deal against the truth of the Christian faith: who have lied outrageously and fallen into the crudest and most abominable errors, like Averroes the Peripatetic, who at last, in his disputations against the Catholics, denied the providence of God, and said that the human soul is mortal, and that there is one intellect, numerically one, in all men. Likewise Porphyry the Platonist, who, though he granted that the law of Moses was given by God, nevertheless approved idolatry, which is yet most plainly condemned in the law of Moses[[Ex 20:3||]][[Ex 20:4||]][[Ex 20:5||]]. Albumasar the astrologer too, in his Greater Introduction, and Alkindus in his Theorica and in the book On the Rays of the Stars, erred wondrously and woefully. Of such the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: [[2 Tim 3:8|Now as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith|Quemadmodum Jannes et Mambres restiterunt Moysi, ita et hi resistunt veritati, homines mente corrupti, reprobi circa fidem]]; [[2 Tim 3:9|But they shall proceed no farther: for their folly shall be manifest to all men, as theirs also was|sed ultra non proficient: insipientia enim eorum manifesta erit omnibus, sicut et illorum fuit]].

7.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI SEPTIMI : QUID NECESSE EST HOMINI MAJORA SE QUÆRERE ?
7.title_en: Elucidation of the seventh chapter: What needeth a man to seek things that are above him?

paras.t: Capitulum istud sententiis atque moralibus documentis est plenum, in quibus non vanitas, sed via ac meritum ad veram consistit salutem.
paras.en: This chapter is full of maxims and moral teachings, in which consists not vanity but the way to true salvation and the merit of it.

paras.t: Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere, id est, ea scrutari et comprehendere velle, quæ intellectus sui capacitatem transcendunt? Unde in sequentibus dicitur : Non plus sapias quam necesse est, ne obstupescas. Et in Ecclesiastico legitur : Altiora te ne quæsieris; non enim tibi necesse est ea quæ abscondita sunt, videre oculis tuis. Quum ignoret quid conducat sibi in vita sua, id est, quid sibi conveniat seu utile necessariumve exsistat in isto exsilio ad beatitudinem impetrandam. Nam et Apostolus ait : Quid oremus sicut oportet, nescimus. Quocirca sciendum, quod quædam ex suo genere bona sunt et necessaria ad salutem, ut præcepta Dei atque Ecclesiæ; vel ad salutem utilia, ut evangelica Christi consilia. Et de talibus scimus quid nobis conducat in vita nostra. Quædam vero sunt indifferentia in se, quibus possumus bene et male uti; nec cunctis expediunt, sed nec semper : ut infirmitas, sanitas, opulentia, paupertas externa. De quibus nescimus quid, sicut oportet, oremus, et quid nobis magis conveniat. Unde Dominum exorare debemus, ut de talibus provideat nobis quod amplius nobis expediens est, et ipse inspirare dignetur quid appetamus. A cognitione autem et consideratione necessariorum et utilium salubriumve saluti, frequenter nos impedit curiosa, subtilis, seu præsumptuosa investigatio altiorum talium. Idcirco vitanda est, et nociva. Et illud Ecclesiastici est servandum : Quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper. Hinc ait et Seneca : Cito a corpore ad animum redi. Illum excole et exorna. Modico labore colitur ille. Bonum illud apprehendere cura, quod vetustate fit melius. Non te jubeo libro et pugillaribus jugiter imminere : dandum est animo aliquod intervallum. Hinc Plato loquitur in Timæo : Hoc meis sit precibus comprehensum, ut potissimum ea dicantur, quæ Deitati sunt placita.
paras.en: [[7:1|What needeth a man to seek things that are above him|Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere]], that is, to wish to search out and comprehend things that go beyond the capacity of his understanding? Hence it is said further on: [[7:17|be not more wise than is necessary, lest thou become stupid|Non plus sapias quam necesse est, ne obstupescas]]. And we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:22|Seek not the things that are too high for thee|Altiora te ne quæsieris]]; [[Ecclus 3:23|For it is not necessary for thee to see with thy eyes those things that are hid|non enim tibi necesse est ea quæ abscondita sunt, videre oculis tuis]] [the margin gives Eccli. xi, 22, 23; the words are Ecclus 3:22–23]. [[7:1|whereas he knoweth not what is profitable for him in his life|Quum ignoret quid conducat sibi in vita sua]], that is, what befits him, or what is useful or necessary in this exile for obtaining beatitude. For the Apostle too says: [[Rom 8:26|we know not what we should pray for as we ought|Quid oremus sicut oportet, nescimus]]. Therefore we must know that some things are good of their kind and necessary for salvation, as the commandments of God and of the Church; or useful for salvation, as the evangelical counsels of Christ. And of such things we know what is profitable for us in our life.
