But some things are indifferent in themselves, things we can use well or ill; they are not expedient for all, nor always: such as sickness, health, wealth, outward poverty. Of these we know not what we should pray for as we ought, nor what better befits us. Hence we ought to beseech the Lord to provide us, in such matters, with what is more expedient for us, and to deign himself to inspire what we should desire. But from the knowledge and consideration of the things necessary and useful or wholesome for salvation, a curious, subtle or presumptuous inquiry into higher things of this sort often hinders us. Therefore it is to be avoided, and it is harmful. And that saying of Ecclesiasticus is to be kept: [[Ecclus 3:22|the things that God hath commanded thee, think on them always|Quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper]]. Hence Seneca too says: Return quickly from the body to the mind. Cultivate it and adorn it. It is cultivated with little labour. Take care to lay hold of that good which grows better with age. I do not bid you to be ever bent over book and writing-tablets: some respite must be given to the mind. Hence Plato says in the Timaeus: Let this be included in my prayers, that those things above all be said which are pleasing to the Deity.

paras.t: Itaque nescit homo quid conducat ei in vita sua numero dierum peregrinationis suæ, id est conversationis præsentis, qua tendit ad patriam Beatorum, sicut ait Apostolus : Dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino. Unde et Jacob patriarcha in Genesi : Dies, inquit, peregrinationis meæ super terram, centum triginta annorum sunt. Et tempore quod velut umbra præterit. Quemadmodum quodam loco David loquitur Deo : Peregrini sumus coram te et advenæ, sicut omnes patres nostri; dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora. Sanctus quoque Job ait : Homo quasi flos egreditur et conteritur, et fugit velut umbra, et nunquam in eodem statu permanet.
paras.en: So man knows not what is profitable for him in his life [[7:1|in all the days of his pilgrimage|numero dierum peregrinationis suæ]], that is, of his present way of life, by which he is making for the fatherland of the Blessed, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:6|while we are in the body we are absent from the Lord|Dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino]]. Hence the patriarch Jacob too, in Genesis: [[Gen 47:9|The days|Dies]], he says, [[Gen 47:9|of my pilgrimage are a hundred and thirty years|peregrinationis meæ super terram, centum triginta annorum sunt]] [Denis adds *super terram*, upon earth]. [[7:1|and the time that passeth like a shadow?|Et tempore quod velut umbra præterit]] As David in a certain place says to God: [[1 Par 29:15|we are sojourners before thee, and strangers, as were all our fathers. I Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Peregrini sumus coram te et advenæ, sicut omnes patres nostri; dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]. Holy Job too says: Man [[Job 14:2|cometh forth like a flower, and is destroyed, and fleeth as a shadow, and never continueth in the same state|quasi flos egreditur et conteritur, et fugit velut umbra, et nunquam in eodem statu permanet]].

paras.t: Aut quis ei poterit indicare quid post eum futurum sub sole sit? id est, quis hominum poterit alteri prædicere quid certive post ejus mortem continget (loquendo de futuris pure contingentibus)? Scimus tamen ex Scripturis multa quæ fient post nos; sed præfata contingentia certe præscire ac prænuntiare, Deo appropriatur. Propter quod in Isaia inducitur : Quæ futura sunt, annuntiate, et sciemus quia dii estis. Hinc in Scripturis quidam vocantur divini, qui de talibus prænuntiandis et revelandis secretis se intromittunt.
paras.en: [[7:1|Or who can tell him what shall be after him under the sun?|Aut quis ei poterit indicare quid post eum futurum sub sole sit?]] that is, which man can foretell to another what will with any certainty happen after his death (speaking of things to come that are purely contingent [that is, things that may or may not come about, depending on free choice or chance, not fixed by necessity])? Yet we know from the Scriptures many things that will happen after us; but to know beforehand and foretell such contingent things with certainty belongs to God. For this reason it is put thus in Isaias: [[Is 41:23|Shew the things that are to come hereafter, and we shall know that ye are gods|Quæ futura sunt, annuntiate, et sciemus quia dii estis]]. Hence in the Scriptures some are called diviners, who meddle with foretelling such things and revealing secrets.

paras.t: Melius est nomen bonum, id est fama ædificatoria et honesta, quam unguenta pretiosa. Nam bonum nomen est ad gloriam Dei, ædificationemque proximi, et ei qui bonæ famæ est, ad multa accommodum. Idcirco, secundum Augustinum, qui negligit famam, crudelis est, quoniam quantum in se est, interimit proximos qui audiunt malum de eo. Deo itaque debemus conscientiam puram, proximo bonam famam. Hinc ait Apostolus : Christi bonus odor sumus in omni loco. Et Seneca contestatur : Honestus rumor, alterum est patrimonium. Verumtamen multi devoti doctores affirmant pertinere ad humilem, ut velit ab omnibus vituperari, contemni, et conculcari. Quomodo igitur appetit nomen bonum? Et respondendum, quod quantum in se est, ex consideratione suorum peccaminum, ac desiderio conformandi se aliqualiter Christo propter se passo, appetit talia; sed ne alii scandalizentur in ipso, atque ex hoc Deus inhonoretur, bonam desiderat famam.
paras.en: [[7:2|A good name|Melius est nomen bonum]], that is, an upright reputation that edifies, [[7:2|is better than precious ointments|quam unguenta pretiosa]]. For a good name serves the glory of God and the edification of one's neighbour, and is of use in many things to him who has a good reputation. Therefore, according to Augustine, he who neglects his reputation is cruel, since as far as in him lies he kills the neighbours who hear evil of him. So we owe God a pure conscience, and our neighbour a good reputation. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 2:15|we are the good odour of Christ|Christi bonus odor sumus]] [[2 Cor 2:14|in every place|in omni loco]] [the margin gives II Cor. ii without a verse; Denis joins v. 15 with the last words of v. 14]. And Seneca bears witness: An honourable report is a second patrimony. Yet many devout doctors affirm that it belongs to the humble man to wish to be blamed, despised and trampled on by all. How then does he desire a good name? And the answer must be that, as far as concerns himself, from the consideration of his sins and from the desire to conform himself in some way to Christ who suffered for him, he desires such things; but lest others be scandalized in him, and God be dishonoured by it, he desires a good reputation.

paras.t: Et dies mortis, die nativitatis. Dies nativitatis est, qua generamur in culpa, et natura filii iræ, atque ad multa pericula et tormenta ac vitia. Unde Sancti quidam, tali diei maledixisse legantur, præsertim Job et Jeremias, dicentes : Maledicta dies in qua natus sum. Hinc Jeremiæ quintodecimo dicitur : Væ mihi, mater mea; quare me genuisti, virum rixæ, virum discordiæ? Porro in die mortis evadimus mala ista : ideo melior nuncupatur. Verumtamen, quoniam esse et vivere, sunt naturaliter appetibilia valde, et mala pœnæ possunt ad salutem proficere, atque in vita hac possumus virtutes sortiri, beatitudinemque mereri, et filii adoptivi fieri Creatoris : ideo secundum istum respectum, non est dies mortis melior die nativitatis, sicut nec mors melior vita : nisi intelligatur de electis et Sanctis, quorum dies mortis, vocatur dies natalitius eorum, quia tunc incipiunt feliciter vivere, et confirmati esse in bono. Mors autem peccatorum, pessima. Dies quoque mortis eorum, qui egressi de corpore, purgatorio deputantur, quantum ad hoc, melior est die nativitatis : quia ex tunc assecurantur de æterna felicitate, et immobilitantur in gratia, evadentes multa ac magna pericula. Sed in quantum pœnæ purgatorii valde acriores sunt pœnis vitæ præsentis, nec in purgatorio quis potest mereri, videtur dies mortis illorum non esse melior die nativitatis eorum qui regenerantur in Domino. Reprobis vero expediret magis non nasci, quam ad tot peccata et ad æterna supplicia gigni. Cur ergo Dominus creat eos? Respondet Damascenus : Quoniam Deus facit quod ad suam pertinet bonitatem, nec decet eum omittere hoc ob abusionem et ingratitudinem nostram. Multa quoque bona ex eis et ex eorum elicit damnatione.
paras.en: [[7:2|and the day of death than the day of one's birth|Et dies mortis, die nativitatis]]. The day of birth is that on which we are begotten in guilt, and [[Eph 2:3|by nature children of wrath|natura filii iræ]], and for many dangers and torments and vices. Hence certain Saints are read to have cursed such a day, especially Job[[Job 3:3||]] and Jeremias, saying: [[Jer 20:14|Cursed be the day wherein I was born|Maledicta dies in qua natus sum]]. Hence it is said in the fifteenth of Jeremias: [[Jer 15:10|Woe is me, my mother: why hast thou borne me a man of strife, a man of contention|Væ mihi, mater mea; quare me genuisti, virum rixæ, virum discordiæ?]]? But on the day of death we escape these evils: that is why it is called better. Yet because being and living are by nature greatly to be desired, and the evils of punishment [that is, sufferings, as distinct from the evil of guilt, which is sin] can profit for salvation, and in this life we can acquire virtues, merit beatitude, and become adopted sons of the Creator: in this respect the day of death is not better than the day of birth, just as death is not better than life; unless it be understood of the elect and the Saints, whose day of death is called their birthday, because then they begin to live happily and to be confirmed in good. [[Ps 33:22|The death of the wicked is very evil|Mors autem peccatorum, pessima]]. The day of death, too, of those who on leaving the body are assigned to purgatory is, in this regard, better than the day of birth: for from then on they are made secure of eternal happiness and fixed immovably in grace, escaping many great dangers. But inasmuch as the pains of purgatory are much sharper than the pains of the present life, and no one can merit in purgatory, the day of their death does not seem to be better than the day of birth of those who are reborn in the Lord. For the reprobate, indeed, it would be more expedient not to be born than to be begotten for so many sins and for eternal torments. Why then does the Lord create them? Damascene answers: Because God does what belongs to his goodness, and it is not fitting that he should leave it undone because of our abuse and ingratitude. He also draws many goods out of them and out of their damnation.

paras.t: Melius est ire ad domum luctus, ubi deploratur defunctus, vel ad pœnitentium et sua peccata lugentium congregationem, vel ad locum seu templum ubi fit sermo de novissimis hominum, de stultitiis quoque peccantium, de enormitatibus et turpitudinibus vitiorum, ex quorum prædicatione, audientes inducuntur ad luctum salubrem; quam ad domum convivii : quia in convivio resolvitur cordis compunctio, fitque frequenter excessus in cibo et potu, in verbis, jocis ac risibus, ex quibus oriuntur incitamenta lasciviæ. Unde Judas apostolus in sua fatur Canonica : Hi sunt in epulis suis convivantes sine timore, semetipsos pascentes, nubes sine aqua, despumantes suas confusiones : quibus procella tenebrarum conservata est in æternum. In Exodo quoque asseritur : Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexerunt ludere. Propterea dicit Gregorius : Sicut impossibile est ignem in aqua ardere, sic impossibile est in convivantibus compunctionem vigere. Cur autem sit melius ire ad domum luctus, subjungitur :
paras.en: [[7:3|It is better to go to the house of mourning|Melius est ire ad domum luctus]], where the dead is wept for; or to the gathering of penitents mourning their sins; or to a place or church where there is preaching on the last things of men, on the follies of sinners too, on the enormity and foulness of vices, by the preaching of which the hearers are led to a wholesome mourning; [[7:3|than to the house of feasting|quam ad domum convivii]]: for at a feast the heart's compunction is dissolved, and there is often excess in food and drink, in words, jests and laughter, from which arise the incitements of lust. Hence the apostle Jude says in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jude 1:12|These are|Hi sunt]] [[Jude 1:12|in their banquets, feasting together without fear, feeding themselves: clouds without water|in epulis suis convivantes sine timore, semetipsos pascentes, nubes sine aqua]], [[Jude 1:13|foaming out their own confusion|despumantes suas confusiones]]: [[Jude 1:13|to whom the storm of darkness is reserved for ever|quibus procella tenebrarum conservata est in æternum]]. In Exodus too it is said: [[Ex 32:6|the people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play|Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexerunt ludere]]. Therefore Gregory says: As it is impossible for fire to burn in water, so it is impossible for compunction to flourish among those who feast. And why it is better to go to the house of mourning is added:

paras.t: In illa enim, puta in domo luctus, finis cunctorum admonetur hominum : id est, ex defuncti præsentia inducuntur qui adsunt, ad meditandum de sua morte, quæ finis est vitæ mortalium. Quod etiam ex verbis atque sermonibus fit in congregationibus pœnitentium, et in locis sermocinantium. Et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit sibi, scilicet qualiter morietur et judicabitur a Deo, ac punietur acerrime nisi in præsenti expurgatus fuerit plene. Hæc autem consideratio mortis et concomitantium eam, efficacissima est ad vitandum omne peccatum, ut Climacus scribit. Hinc Plato in Phædone disseruit : Meditatio philosophorum est separatio et dissolutio animæ a corpore. Et rursus : Revera philosophantes, morti se præparant. Si quem videris graviter ferre quum debeat mori, nullo modo erat philosophus. Mors aliud non est quam animæ corporisque divisio. Hæc Plato. Seneca quoque in suis testatur Proverbiis : Omnes vitam differentes, id est diu vivere se putantes, incerta mors prævenit : ideo omnis dies tanquam ultimus ordinandus est. Hoc est quod sanctus pater Macarius docuit, ut semper tam discrete et timorate ac pure vivamus, quasi die quolibet morituri, et quasi centum annis victuri.
paras.en: [[7:3|for in that|In illa enim]], namely in the house of mourning, [[7:3|we are put in mind of the end of all|finis cunctorum admonetur hominum]]: that is, by the presence of the dead those who are there are led to meditate on their own death, which is the end of the life of mortals. This also comes about through the words and sermons in the gatherings of penitents and in the places where preaching is held. [[7:3|and the living thinketh what is to come|Et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit sibi]] for himself, namely how he will die and be judged by God, and be punished most sharply unless he has been fully cleansed in the present. Now this consideration of death and of what goes with it is most effective for avoiding all sin, as Climacus writes. Hence Plato discoursed in the Phaedo: The meditation of philosophers is the separation and loosing of the soul from the body. And again: Those who truly philosophize prepare themselves for death. If you see anyone take it hard when he must die, he was in no way a philosopher. Death is nothing else than the division of soul and body. So far Plato. Seneca too bears witness in his Proverbs: All who put off living, that is, who think they will live long, are forestalled by uncertain death: therefore every day is to be ordered as though it were the last. This is what the holy father Macarius taught: that we should always live as discreetly, fearfully and purely as if we were to die any day, and as if we were to live a hundred years.

paras.t: Melior est ira risu. Hoc intelligendum est de ira per zelum, qua contra propria ac proximorum peccata movemur, ac ea punimus. Sicque (ut Tullius loquitur) vindicativa est pars quædam justitiæ. De hac ira laudabili fatur Chrysostomus : Si ira non fuerit, nec doctrina proficit, nec judicia stant, nec crimina compescuntur. Itaque qui, dum causa est, non irascitur, peccat. Patientia enim irrationabilis vitia seminat, nec solum malos, sed et bonos ad malum invitat. Verumtamen grandi moderatione uti oportet circa hanc iram, ne immoderantius exardescat. Propter quod affirmat Gregorius, quod non debet quasi domina rationem præcedere, sed tanquam ancilla post tergum sequi. Ira quippe per zelum vocatur, quam ratio per imperium sibi assumit, quatenus actum virtutis efficacius exsequatur. Melior ergo est ira hæc risu : quoniam magis caritativum, pium, et justum est peccanti irasci, quam arridere : quemadmodum pater filio suo dilecto ac delinquenti irascitur; qui autem non diligit ipsum, de ejus culpa et insipientia ridet. Hinc subditur : quia per tristitiam vultus, quam ira per zelum causat in facie, corrigitur animus delinquentis : dum pensat alium ob suum contristari excessum, præsertim quando advertit illum sic contristari ex caritate illius ad se, aut ex zelo justitiæ. Unde ait Bernardus, quod animus probus, videns alium pro se ita sollicitum, erubescit illo præsente reprehensibiliter se habere. Hinc etiam in Proverbiis dictum est : Ventus Aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem. Dum ergo quis non audet corripere delinquentem, ad minus ostendat ei faciem tristem, ut sic perpendat quantum culpa sua sibimet noceat, quæ alium sic contristat.
paras.en: [[7:4|Anger is better than laughter|Melior est ira risu]]. This is to be understood of anger through zeal [that is, anger stirred up and governed by reason for the sake of justice, as opposed to anger as a vice], by which we are moved against our own sins and our neighbours', and punish them. And so (as Tully says) the vindictive part [that is, the part concerned with just punishment] is a certain part of justice. Of this praiseworthy anger Chrysostom says: If there is no anger, teaching does not profit, judgements do not stand, crimes are not checked. So he who is not angry when there is cause, sins. For unreasonable patience sows vices, and invites not only the wicked but the good also to evil. Yet great moderation must be used with this anger, lest it blaze up too immoderately. For this reason Gregory affirms that it ought not to go before reason like a mistress, but to follow behind like a handmaid. For that is called anger through zeal which reason takes up by its command, so as to carry out the act of virtue more effectively. This anger then is better than laughter: since it is more charitable, more loving and more just to be angry with one who sins than to smile on him: as a father is angry with his beloved son when he does wrong; but one who does not love him laughs at his fault and folly. Hence it is added: [[7:4|because by the sadness of the countenance|quia per tristitiam vultus]], which anger through zeal causes in the face, [[7:4|the mind of the offender is corrected|corrigitur animus delinquentis]]: when he considers that another is saddened by his excess, especially when he notices that the other is so saddened out of charity towards him, or out of zeal for justice. Hence Bernard says that an upright mind, seeing another so anxious for him, is ashamed to behave blameworthily in his presence. Hence too it is said in the Proverbs: [[Prov 25:23|The north wind driveth away rain, as doth a sad countenance a backbiting tongue|Ventus Aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem]]. So when someone does not dare to rebuke an offender, let him at least show him a sad face, so that he may thus weigh how much his fault harms himself, since it so saddens another.

paras.t: Cor sapientium, ubi tristitia : id est, sapientium est de malo culpæ tristari, peccantibus condolere, mundi hujus miserias deplorare, præsens deflere exsilium, præsertim quod Deus omnipotens indesinenter tam graviter ac multipliciter inhonoratur, offenditur, atque tot animæ pereunt ac damnantur. Hac ex causa (secundum Basilium in regula sua) non licet modo ridere. Hæc est bona et ordinata tristitia : de qua fatetur Apostolus, Quæ secundum Deum est tristitia, pœnitentiam in salutem stabilem operatur. Tristitia vero sæcularis inordinata, quæ est de propria injuria, infirmitate, temporalive damno, est vitiosa. De qua idem dixit Apostolus : Sæculi tristitia mortem operatur. De qua in Proverbiis dictum est : Sicut tinea vestimento, sic tristitia nocet cordi. Denique sapiens contristatur de propria imperfectione, et pronitate in malum, et quod tam longe distat a perfectione optata cœlestique gloria.
paras.en: [[7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning|Cor sapientium, ubi tristitia]]: that is, it belongs to the wise to be sad over the evil of guilt, to grieve with sinners, to lament the miseries of this world, to weep over the present exile, especially because almighty God is so gravely and in so many ways dishonoured and offended without ceasing, and so many souls perish and are damned. For this reason (according to Basil in his Rule) it is not lawful to laugh now. This is the good and ordered sorrow of which the Apostle declares: [[2 Cor 7:10|the sorrow that is according to God worketh penance, steadfast unto salvation|Quæ secundum Deum est tristitia, pœnitentiam in salutem stabilem operatur]]. But disordered worldly sorrow, which is over one's own injury, sickness or temporal loss, is vicious. Of it the same Apostle said: [[2 Cor 7:10|the sorrow of the world worketh death|Sæculi tristitia mortem operatur]]. Of it it is said in the Proverbs: [[Prov 25:20|As a moth doth by a garment|Sicut tinea vestimento]], [[Prov 25:20|so the sadness of a man consumeth the heart|sic tristitia nocet cordi]]. Lastly, the wise man is saddened by his own imperfection, by his proneness to evil, and that he is so far from the perfection he longs for and from the glory of heaven.

paras.t: Et cor stultorum, ubi lætitia : id est, stultorum est inaniter gloriari, sibi ipsi placere, de aliorum ruina ridere. Unde dictum est supra : Risum reputavi errorem, et gaudio dixi : Quid frustra deciperis? Stultissimorum autem est gaudere quum male fecerint, et in rebus pessimis exsultare, seque de iniquitate jactare. Similiter oblivisci periculorum quibus expositi sumus, et risibus, jocis, choreis, lusibusque vacare, insaniæ est. Idcirco de talibus in Job scriptum est : Tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi; ducunt in bonis dies suos, et in puncto ad infernum descendunt. (Verum est alia bona lætitia, in contemplatione, dilectione cultuque Dei, et actione virtutum consistens. De qua ait Scriptura : Gaudete in Domino semper; et iterum, Servite Domino in lætitia.) Hinc etiam docuit Christus : Beati qui lugent; et, Væ vobis qui ridetis.
paras.en: [[7:5|and the heart of fools where there is mirth|Et cor stultorum, ubi lætitia]]: that is, it belongs to fools to glory vainly, to be pleased with themselves, to laugh at the ruin of others. Hence it was said above: [[Eccles 2:2|Laughter I counted error: and to mirth I said: Why art thou vainly deceived?|Risum reputavi errorem, et gaudio dixi : Quid frustra deciperis?]] But it is the mark of the most foolish of all that they [[Prov 2:14|are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in the most wicked things|gaudere quum male fecerint, et in rebus pessimis exsultare]], and boast of their iniquity. Likewise, to forget the dangers to which we are exposed and give oneself to laughter, jests, dances and games is madness. Therefore it is written of such men in Job: [[Job 21:12|They take the timbrel, and the harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ|Tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi]]; [[Job 21:13|They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell|ducunt in bonis dies suos, et in puncto ad infernum descendunt]]. (There is, indeed, another, good mirth, which consists in the contemplation, love and worship of God and in the practice of the virtues. Of it Scripture says: [[Phil 4:4|Rejoice in the Lord always|Gaudete in Domino semper]]; and again, [[Ps 99:2|serve ye the Lord with gladness|Servite Domino in lætitia]].) Hence Christ too taught: [[Matt 5:5|Blessed are they that mourn|Beati qui lugent]]; and, [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that now laugh|Væ vobis qui ridetis]].

paras.t: Melius est a sapiente corrigi, id est verbis ac disciplinis castigari, quam stultorum, id est iniquorum et callidorum, adulatione decipi : qui laudant peccatorem in desideriis animæ suæ, et blandiendo quærunt placere, ac propria commoda consequi, non autem peccantem curare. Hinc Seneca dixit : Admoneris libenter, reprehensionem sume gratanter ac patienter. Si merito objurgarit te aliquis, scito quod prodesse voluit. Non dura, sed adulatoria verba verearis. Esto vitiorum fugax, aliorum vero neque curiosus scrutator, nec reprehensor acerbus, sed sine exprobratione corrector, ita ut admonitionem hilaritate prævenias. Quocirca inquiri potest, qualiter dicat admonitionem hilaritate præveniendam, nec reprehensionem debere acerbam esse, quum jam dictum sit, per tristitiam vultus corrigi animum delinquentis, et quædam vitia acriori indigeant increpatu. Et respondendum, quod admonitionem dicit hilaritate præveniendam, non increpationem. Vel si nomine admonitionis increpationem includit, dicendum quod superiores, et benevoli cito flexibiles, et ex infirmitate peccantes, prævia hilaritate sunt arguendi seu admonendi. Quod si tali non acquieverint reprehensioni et informationi, durius sunt tractandi, præsertim si subditi sint. Idcirco dicit Isidorus : Qui blando verbo castigatus non emendatur, necesse est ut acrius arguatur. Et cum dolore sunt abscindenda, quæ non possunt levi castigatione arceri.
paras.en: [[7:6|It is better to be rebuked by a wise man|Melius est a sapiente corrigi]], that is, to be chastised with words and discipline, [[7:6|than to be deceived by the flattery of fools|quam stultorum adulatione decipi]] (fools, that is, the wicked and the crafty), who praise the sinner in the desires of his soul[[Ps 9:24||]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 3 according to the Hebrew numbering, which is Ps 9:24 in the Vulgate], and by flattering seek to please and to gain their own advantage, but not to cure the sinner. Hence Seneca said: Be glad to be admonished; take reproof gratefully and patiently. If someone rightly rebukes you, know that he wished to do you good. Fear not harsh words but flattering ones. Be a fugitive from vices, but of other men's vices be neither a curious searcher nor a bitter reprover, but a corrector without reproach, so that you go before your admonition with cheerfulness. Here it may be asked how he can say that admonition is to be preceded by cheerfulness, and that reproof ought not to be bitter, when it has already been said that by the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected, and when certain vices need a sharper rebuke. And the answer must be that he says admonition is to be preceded by cheerfulness, not rebuke. Or, if under the name of admonition he includes rebuke, it must be said that superiors, and well-disposed people who are quickly bent, and those who sin out of weakness, are to be reproved or admonished with cheerfulness going before. But if they do not yield to such reproof and instruction, they are to be dealt with more harshly, especially if they are subjects. Therefore Isidore says: He who, chastised with a gentle word, does not amend, must needs be reproved more sharply. And what cannot be kept off by light chastisement must be cut away with pain.

paras.t: Quia sicut sonitus spinarum ardentium sub olla est vehemens atque confusus, sic risus stulti est inconditus et dissolutus, ac cachinnativus, etiam in peccato et ruina alterius. Unde communiter dicitur : Per risum multum, poteris cognoscere stultum. De hoc Seneca scripsit : Reprehensibilis risus est, si immodicus, si pueriliter effusus, si muliebriter fractus. Odibilem quoque hominem facit risus, aut superbus et clarus, aut malignus et furtivus, aut alienis malis evocatus. Non sit tibi scurrilis, sed grata urbanitas; risus sine cachinno, vox sine clamore, incessus sine tumultu, quies sine desidia; et quum ab aliis luditur, sancti et honesti aliquid tracta. Sed et hoc vanitas.
paras.en: [[7:7|For as the crackling of thorns burning under a pot|Quia sicut sonitus spinarum ardentium sub olla]] is loud and confused, [[7:7|so is the laughter of a fool|sic risus stulti]]: unruly, dissolute and cackling, even at the sin and ruin of another. Hence the common saying: By much laughter you may know a fool. Of this Seneca wrote: Laughter is blameworthy if it is immoderate, if it pours out like a child's, if it is broken like a woman's. Laughter also makes a man hateful, whether it is proud and loud, or malicious and stealthy, or called forth by other men's misfortunes. Let your wit be not scurrilous but pleasing; your laughter without cackling, your voice without shouting, your gait without bustle, your rest without sloth; and when others are at play, be about something holy and honourable. [[7:7|now this also is vanity|Sed et hoc vanitas]].

paras.t: Calumnia, id est illatio magnæ injuriæ, conturbat sapientem, et perdet robur cordis ejus, id est, patientiam et constantiam ejus dejiciet. Quomodo verum est hoc, quum scriptum sit alibi, Non contristabit justum, quidquid ei accidet; et sapientis sit, in adversis gaudere, ac passionibus dominari? Gregorius quoque, Justorum (inquit) sapientia est, mala libentius tolerare quam facere, nullam injuriæ ultionem quærere, contumeliam propter veritatem illatam, lucrum putare. Seneca etiam loquitur : Non ex vocibus spectandi sunt sapientes, sed ex perpetuitate virtutis atque constantiæ. Verum ad istud patet responsio, ex verbis Albini et Glossæ, dicentium : Sapiens perfectus nulla arguitione indiget, nulla turbatur calumnia : ideo de sapiente adhuc in profectu constituto, istud est accipiendum, qui aliquando turbatur de iniquitate humani judicii, quando Deus statim non punit. Et de taliter bono seu virtuoso disseruit Seneca : Mutat se bonitas, quum irritatur injuria; et rursus, Bonus animus læsus, gravius multo irascitur. De virtuoso autem et sapiente perfecto, fatetur : Contumeliam pati nec fortis nec ingenuus potest; et denuo, Ingenuitas non recipit contumeliam.
paras.en: [[7:8|Oppression|Calumnia]] [*calumnia*: false accusation or wrongful oppression], that is, the infliction of a great injury, [[7:8|troubleth the wise, and shall destroy the strength of his heart|conturbat sapientem, et perdet robur cordis ejus]], that is, will cast down his patience and constancy. How is this true, since it is written elsewhere: [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum, quidquid ei accidet]]; and since it belongs to the wise man to rejoice in adversity and to master the passions? Gregory too says: It is the wisdom of the just to bear evils more willingly than to do them, to seek no revenge for injury, to count as gain an insult offered for the truth's sake. Seneca also says: The wise are to be judged not by their words but by the lastingness of their virtue and constancy. But the answer to this is plain from the words of Albinus [that is, Alcuin] and the Gloss, who say: The perfect wise man needs no reproof and is troubled by no oppression; so this is to be taken of the wise man still making progress, who is sometimes troubled at the iniquity of human judgement, when God does not punish at once. And of one good or virtuous in this way Seneca discoursed: Goodness changes when it is provoked by injury; and again: A good mind, when wounded, is far more gravely angered. But of the virtuous and perfect wise man he declares: Neither the brave man nor the noble-minded can suffer insult; and again: Noble-mindedness does not admit insult.

paras.t: Melior est finis orationis, quam principium. Finis enim est consummatio rei, et a fine res præcipue sumit denominationem atque virtutem. Unde dicitur : Dum finis bonus est, totum bonum est. Nempe si oratio a devotione incipiat, et in distractione terminetur, invalida esse, aut parum valere censetur. Si autem a distractione inchoetur, et in recollectione, devotione, et fervida unione finiatur, idonea judicatur. Et quamvis principia dicantur maxima esse virtute, et plus quam media totorum, finis tamen primatum sortitur. Propter quod adstruit Veritas : Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit. Hinc Dominus in Levitico jussit sibi caudam in sacrificium immolari.
paras.en: [[7:9|Better is the end of a speech than the beginning|Melior est finis orationis, quam principium]] [*oratio* means both speech and prayer; Denis takes it of prayer]. For the end is the completion of a thing, and it is chiefly from its end that a thing takes its name and its worth. Hence it is said: When the end is good, all is good. Indeed, if a prayer begins in devotion and ends in distraction, it is reckoned to be of no force, or of little worth. But if it begins in distraction and ends in recollection, devotion and fervent union, it is judged fit. And although beginnings are said to be greatest in power, and more than the half of the whole [a proverb: well begun is half done], yet the end holds the first place. For this reason the Truth affirms: [[Matt 24:13|he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved|Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit]]. Hence the Lord in Leviticus bade the tail be offered to him in sacrifice[[Lev 3:9||]][[Lev 7:3||]].

paras.t: Melior est patiens arrogante. In patientia enim anima possidetur, in superbia perditur. Atque per arrogantiam maxime fit homo servus, membrum filiusque diaboli, qui est rex super omnes filios superbiæ.
paras.en: [[7:9|Better is the patient man than the presumptuous|Melior est patiens arrogante]]. For in patience the soul is possessed[[Luke 21:19||]], in pride it is lost. And it is above all through arrogance that a man becomes the slave, member and son of the devil, who [[Job 41:25|is king over all the children of pride|est rex super omnes filios superbiæ]].

paras.t: Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quia ira in sinu, id est, corde, stulti requiescit. Siquidem eo ipso, quo quis iram per vitium, de qua intelligitur istud, non solum admittit, sed etiam intra se retinet ita quod quiescit in eo, stulto assimilatur et luce sapientiæ caret : ac stultus est, non solum eo modo, quo omnis qui in mortali est culpa, stultus asseritur; sed et tanto specialius, quo ira mentem intus magis excæcat, et hominem in apparatu vultus, exteriorique gestu, stulto, imo et furioso facit similiorem. Hinc fertur in Job : Virum stultum interficit iracundia. Et congrue ait, Interficit : quoniam ex suo genere peccatum est mortale, tam ratione immoderatæ suæ impetuositatis, qua ratione penitus dominatur, quam propter excessum ultionis, quam expetit seu infligit : quæ dum offensæ injuriam vehementer transcendit, directe contrariatur justitiæ æqualitati. Ideo ait Hieronymus : Quid iracundo furor suus confert, quem sævissimis exagitat stimulis passionis, et ita ab omni consilio ac mente deturpat, ut dum irascitur, insanire credatur? Amplius, quam nociva, turbativa, et intolerabilis ira exsistat, pandit Gregorius, dicens : Per iram justitia relinquitur, gratia vitæ socialis amittitur, mititas superatur. De hoc dictum est plenius super illud Proverbiorum, Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere? Et sicut Seneca Tulliusque testantur, menti furore ebriæ rectum videtur, quidquid judicat et operatur; perversumque arbitratur, quidquid judicio suæ commotionis contrarium ei denuntiatur. Ista ira omnino vitanda est. Et si primi motus non præveniantur, ne oriantur, reprimantur tamen, ne augeantur aut immorentur. Nam (ut Seneca fassus est) in bono viro cito moritur iracundia. Qui iterum ait : Esto tardus ad iram, promptus ad misericordiam. Nempe quum ira ex suo genere sit mortalis, consuetudo irascendi periculosissima est, quum et irrefrenata venialium consuetudo, mortalis perhibeatur.
paras.en: [[7:10|Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom|Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quia ira in sinu]], that is, in the heart, [[7:10|of a fool|stulti requiescit]]. For by the very fact that someone not only admits anger as a vice (of which this is understood) but also keeps it within him, so that it rests in him, he becomes like a fool and lacks the light of wisdom: and he is a fool not only in the way in which everyone in mortal sin is called a fool, but the more especially in that anger blinds the mind within the more, and makes a man, in the bearing of his face and his outward gestures, more like a fool, nay, like a madman. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 5:2|Anger indeed killeth the foolish|Virum stultum interficit iracundia]]. And it says fittingly [[Job 5:2|killeth|Interficit]]: for of its kind it is a mortal sin [that is, anger as a vice is grave matter in itself, though it may be venial through lack of full consent or slight matter], both by reason of its immoderate violence, by which it utterly overmasters reason, and because of the excess of vengeance which it seeks or inflicts: for when this far exceeds the injury of the offence, it is directly contrary to the equality of justice. Therefore Jerome says: What does his fury profit the angry man, whom it drives with the fiercest goads of passion, and so disfigures, robbing him of all counsel and mind, that while he is angry he is thought to be mad? Further, how harmful, disturbing and intolerable anger is, Gregory shows, saying: Through anger justice is abandoned, the grace of social life is lost, gentleness is overcome. Of this more has been said on that saying of the Proverbs: [[Prov 18:14|a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere?]] And as Seneca and Tully bear witness, to a mind drunk with fury whatever it judges and does seems right; and whatever is pointed out to it as contrary to the judgement of its own agitation it thinks perverse. This anger is to be avoided altogether. And if the first movements are not forestalled so that they do not arise, let them at least be repressed, so that they do not grow or linger. For (as Seneca has said) in a good man anger dies quickly. He says again: Be slow to anger, quick to mercy. Indeed, since anger is of its kind mortal, the habit of growing angry is most dangerous, since even an unbridled habit of venial sins is said to be mortal.

paras.t: Ne dicas : Quid putas causæ est, quod priora tempora meliora fuere quam nunc sunt? Stulta est enim hujusmodi interrogatio. Dies namque in se ipsis vel ex sua natura, nec boni nec mali sunt; sed quo homines sub tempore aliquo existentes, sunt meliores aut deteriores, eo dies meliores aut pejores sunt. Hinc in Michææ habetur : Non ambulabitis superbi, quoniam tempus pessimum est. Ista autem eminentia bonitatis, et excessus malitiæ, ex libero dependent arbitrio. Ideo Salomon istud inducit contra illorum amentiam, qui impietates suas volunt excusare, retorquendo eas in malitiam temporis.
paras.en: [[7:11|Say not: What thinkest thou is the cause that former times were better than they are now? for this manner of question is foolish|Ne dicas : Quid putas causæ est, quod priora tempora meliora fuere quam nunc sunt? Stulta est enim hujusmodi interrogatio]]. For days in themselves, or by their own nature, are neither good nor evil; but as the men living at any time are better or worse, so the days are better or worse. Hence we have in Michæas: [[Mich 2:3|you shall not walk haughtily, for this is a very evil time|Non ambulabitis superbi, quoniam tempus pessimum est]]. Now this pre-eminence of goodness and excess of malice depend on free will. That is why Solomon brings this in against the folly of those who would excuse their impieties by turning them back upon the wickedness of the times.

paras.t: Propterea dicit Hieronymus : Ne dicas : Priora tempora meliora fuerunt quam nunc sunt. Virtutes faciunt dies bonos, vitia malos. Hinc hortatur Apostolus ut dies malos faciamus bonos, dicendo : Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt. Glossa quoque : Sic (inquit) vivere debes, ut dies præsentes semper sint tibi meliores quam præteriti. Nempe ex consideratione malorum præcedentis diei, cautiores merito efficeremur. Propter quod Seneca loquitur : Discipulus est prioris diei dies posterior.
paras.en: Therefore Jerome says: [[7:11|Say not|Ne dicas]]: [[7:11|former times were better than they are now?|Priora tempora meliora fuerunt quam nunc sunt]] Virtues make the days good, vices make them evil. Hence the Apostle exhorts us to make the evil days good, saying: [[Eph 5:16|redeeming the time, because the days are evil|Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt]]. The Gloss too: So ought you to live (it says) that the present days may always be better for you than the past. Indeed, from considering the evils of the day before we should rightly be made more cautious. For this reason Seneca says: The later day is the pupil of the earlier.

paras.t: Denique, loquendo in generali, triplex ponitur tempus, scilicet : tempus legis naturalis, ab Adam usque ad Moysen; exinde, tempus legis scriptæ, usque ad dationem evangelicæ legis a Christo : sub quo est tempus evangelicæ legis, usque ad finem mundi. In quolibet etiam horum trium temporum, potest distingui prius et posterius. Dicunt igitur aliqui, quod tempus evangelicæ legis fuit melius præcedentibus duobus temporibus : quia in eo est data lex perfectissima, et abundantia gratiarum præcipua (propter quod, tempus gratiæ nuncupatur), et plures quam ante crediderunt in Deum. Similiter tempus legis scriptæ, dicunt melius fuisse tempore legis naturæ : quia in tempore legis scriptæ, multa et magna gratiarum charismata hominibus sunt collata, magis quam ante. Sicque affirmant posteriora tempora fuisse prioribus meliora. — Alii dicunt, quod prima pars temporis legis naturæ, fuit melior quam pars ejus posterior : quoniam tempore Adæ, et diu postea, ipse et posteritas ejus, pro magna parte coluerunt unum verum Deum; postea vero, circa tempora Noe, cœperunt communiter ad carnis vitia declinare, prout in Genesi narratur quod omnis caro corrupit viam suam; et post diluvium ad idololatriam corruerunt. Idem dicunt de tempore legis scriptæ, quod scilicet tempora meliora fuerunt sub Moyse et Aaron ac senioribus, sub quibus facta sunt mirabilia multa et magna; et sub Josue, diuque postea, filii Israel Domino servierunt. Similiter in exordio primitivæ Ecclesiæ, maxima data est copia gratiarum, et innumerabilia tunc fiebant miracula : ideo tempus illud dicunt posteriori tempore melius exstitisse. Sicque affirmant tempora priora fuisse meliora, comparando partem unius temporis, ad aliam ejusdem temporis partem. Verumtamen Boetius videtur sensisse, tempora priora absolute fuisse meliora, dicendo : Felix nimium prior ætas, Contenta fidelibus arvis. Unde et Seneca : Quotidie, inquit, deterior est dies posterior.
paras.en: Lastly, speaking in general, a threefold time is laid down, namely: the time of the natural law, from Adam to Moses; then the time of the written law, up to the giving of the law of the Gospel by Christ; under whom is the time of the law of the Gospel, up to the end of the world. And in each of these three times an earlier and a later can be distinguished. Some therefore say that the time of the law of the Gospel was better than the two preceding times: because in it the most perfect law was given, and a special abundance of graces (for which reason it is called the time of grace), and more believed in God than before. Likewise they say that the time of the written law was better than the time of the law of nature: because in the time of the written law many great gifts of grace were bestowed on men, more than before. And so they affirm that the later times were better than the earlier. Others say that the first part of the time of the law of nature was better than its later part: since in the time of Adam, and long after, he and his posterity for the most part worshipped the one true God; but afterwards, about the times of Noe, they began commonly to turn aside to the vices of the flesh, as it is told in Genesis that [[Gen 6:12|all flesh had corrupted its way|omnis caro corrupit viam suam]]; and after the flood they fell into idolatry. They say the same of the time of the written law: namely that the times were better under Moses and Aaron and the elders, under whom many great wonders were done; and under Josue, and long after, the children of Israel served the Lord. Likewise at the beginning of the primitive Church the greatest abundance of graces was given, and countless miracles were then done: so they say that that time was better than the later. And so they affirm that the earlier times were better, comparing a part of one time with another part of the same time. Yet Boethius seems to have held that the earlier times were better absolutely, saying: Too happy was the former age, content with its faithful fields. Hence Seneca too: Every day, he says, the later day is worse.

paras.t: Hinc videtur dicendum ac respondendum, sub triplici distinctione. Prima est, quod dies dicuntur deteriores seu meliores, non solum propter mala culpæ, sed et propter mala pœnæ. Secunda est, quod dies dicuntur meliores seu pejores dupliciter, utpote intensive et extensive : intensive, propter gratiarum seu prosperitatum exuberantiam; extensive, propter multitudinem suppositorum servientium Deo. Tertia, quod uno et eodem tempore dies apud quosdam sunt meliores, et apud alios deteriores. Ex qua distinctione multæ sumi possunt considerationes ad dissolvendum propositam quæstionem. Siquidem tempore Apostolorum intensive erant tempora meliora, Evangelio nondum undique divulgato : quo sic divulgato, meliora erant extensive. Rursus, tempore primitivæ Ecclesiæ, durante persecutorum tyrannide, tempora erant pejora, loquendo de malo pœnæ. Sed instante Antichristi adventu, erunt pejora, tam malitia culpæ, quam pœnæ. Postremo, tempore evangelicæ legis, Christus in Ecclesia sua magnam frequenter fecit reformationem, nunc in una parte Christianitatis, jam in alia. Sicque quibusdam, tempora posteriora facta sunt aurea et prioribus meliora.
paras.en: Hence it seems that we must speak and answer with a threefold distinction. The first is that days are called worse or better not only because of the evils of guilt but also because of the evils of punishment. The second is that days are called better or worse in two ways, namely intensively and extensively: intensively, because of the overflowing of graces or of prosperity; extensively, because of the number of those subject to God and serving him. The third is that at one and the same time the days are better with some and worse with others. From this distinction many considerations can be drawn for resolving the question put forward. For in the time of the Apostles the times were better intensively, while the Gospel was not yet spread abroad everywhere; once it was so spread, they were better extensively. Again, in the time of the primitive Church, while the tyranny of the persecutors lasted, the times were worse, speaking of the evil of punishment. But when the coming of Antichrist is at hand, they will be worse both in the malice of guilt and in punishment. Lastly, in the time of the law of the Gospel, Christ has often made a great reformation in his Church, now in one part of Christendom, now in another. And so for some the later times have become golden and better than the earlier.

paras.t: Utilior est sapientia cum divitiis, quam sine eis. Nam bonum creatum additum bono creato, efficit ipsum majus. Sapiens autem divitiis bene scit uti, et per eas succurrit egenis. Verumtamen istud dictum videtur secundum cursum et tenorem legis Mosaicæ, in qua indigentia seu paupertas valde fuit horrori, juxta illud Deuteronomii: Omnino indigens et mendicus non erit inter vos. Unde et alibi legitur: Melius est mori, quam egere. Christus autem legem perfecit, et paupertatem exemplo ac verbo edocuit; illamque prædicavit esse altissimam, in qua nec in generali, neque in speciali proprium quid habetur. Universa quoque terrena docuit atque consuluit esse derelinquenda, viam perfectionis ingredi cupienti. Quamvis enim divitiæ non sint malæ in se, multas tamen et magnas habent occupationes et curas annexas: sed et valde difficile est, eis uti sine excessu. Hi quoque qui eas propter Deum omnino relinquunt, nec propria retinent, aliunde multo majora virtuosarum actionum subsidia consequuntur, videlicet gratiarum charismata, quam sint ipsæ corporales divitiæ. Itaque melior est sapientia cum evangelica, spontanea religiosaque paupertate, quam cum divitiis. Hinc gloriosissimus et sapientissimus princeps Apostolorum locutus est claudo ex utero: Argentum et aurum non est mihi; quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do. In nomine Jesu Christi surge et ambula. Vas quoque electionis: Altissima, inquit, paupertas eorum, abundavit in divitias simplicitatis eorum.
paras.en: [[7:12|Wisdom with riches is more profitable|Utilior est sapientia cum divitiis]] than without them. For a created good added to a created good makes it greater. And the wise man knows well how to use riches, and through them he succours the needy. This saying, however, seems to follow the course and tenor of the law of Moses, under which want or poverty was held in great horror, according to that word of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 15:4|there shall be no poor nor beggar among you|Omnino indigens et mendicus non erit inter vos]]. Hence it is read elsewhere too: [[Ecclus 40:29|it is better to die than to want|Melius est mori, quam egere]]. But Christ perfected the law, and taught poverty by example and by word[[Matt 8:20||]]; and He preached that to be the highest poverty in which nothing is held as one's own, neither in common nor in particular[[Matt 5:3||]]. He also taught and counselled that all earthly things are to be left behind by one who desires to enter on the way of perfection[[Matt 19:21||]]. For although riches are not evil in themselves, yet they have many and great occupations and cares bound up with them; and it is also very hard to use them without excess. Those, too, who leave them altogether for God's sake and keep nothing of their own, obtain from elsewhere far greater helps to virtuous actions than bodily riches themselves are, namely the charisms of graces. And so wisdom is better with evangelical, voluntary and religious poverty than with riches. Hence the most glorious and most wise prince of the Apostles said to the man lame from his mother's womb: [[Acts 3:6|Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, I give thee. In the name of Jesus Christ|Argentum et aurum non est mihi; quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do. In nomine Jesu Christi]] [[Acts 3:6|arise and walk|surge et ambula]]. The Vessel of election too: [[2 Cor 8:2|their very deep|Altissima]], he says, [[2 Cor 8:2|poverty hath abounded unto the riches of their simplicity|paupertas eorum, abundavit in divitias simplicitatis eorum]].

paras.t: Præterea quæritur, quomodo Salomon dicat hic, Utilior est sapientia cum divitiis, quum in Proverbiis dixerit, Mendicitatem et divitias ne dederis mihi. Et respondendum, quod per divitias potest hic sufficientia terrenorum intelligi, ibi vero, superfluitas. Regibus quoque et in magnis officiis constitutis, necessariæ sunt divitiæ. Illud vero Proverbiorum, in persona eorum qui de communi sunt statu, potest accipi dictum.
paras.en: It is further asked how Solomon can say here, [[7:12|Wisdom with riches is more profitable|Utilior est sapientia cum divitiis]], when in Proverbs he said, [[Prov 30:8|Give me neither beggary, nor riches|Mendicitatem et divitias ne dederis mihi]]. And the answer is that by riches here can be understood a sufficiency of earthly things, but there, superfluity. Riches are also necessary to kings and to those set in great offices. That saying of Proverbs, on the other hand, can be taken as spoken in the person of those who are of the common state.

paras.t: Et magis prodest videntibus solem. Sicut enim protegit sapientia sapientem, contra insidias visibilium ac invisibilium adversariorum. Propter quod in Proverbiis dictum est: Sapientia protegit gradientes simpliciter. Sapientia etenim facit hominem oculatum, custoditum, Deoque inhærentem: et ita meretur divinum subsidium. Sic protegit et pecunia, id est bonus ac prudens usus pecuniæ, utpote misericordiæ opera; et per eam acquiruntur ac nutriuntur auxiliarii contra hostes. Unde in Evangelio loquitur Dominus: Facite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut quum defeceritis, recipiant vos in æterna tabernacula. Hoc autem plus habet eruditio, quæ est actus sapientiæ, et sapientia, quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti, quod vitam tribuunt possessori suo, id est, causa meritoria sunt vitæ gratiæ, ejusque incrementi, et vitæ gloriæ. Quod quamvis usus præfatus pecuniæ etiam faciat, non tamen ita principaliter et directe. Pecunia enim non est virtus. Sapientia vero uno modo est virtus intellectualis, et alio modo dicitur donum.
paras.en: [[7:12|and bringeth more advantage to them that see the sun|Et magis prodest videntibus solem]]. [[7:13|For as wisdom is a defence|Sicut enim protegit sapientia]] to the wise man, against the snares of visible and invisible adversaries. For which reason it is said in Proverbs that wisdom doth [[Prov 2:7|protect them that walk in simplicity|protegit gradientes simpliciter]] [in the verse it is the Lord who protects; Denis makes wisdom the subject]. For wisdom makes a man watchful, guarded and cleaving to God, and so he merits the help of God. [[7:13|so money is a defence|Sic protegit et pecunia]], that is, the good and prudent use of money, such as the works of mercy; and through it helpers against our enemies are gained and kept. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: [[Luke 16:9|Make unto you friends of the mammon of iniquity: that when you shall fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings|Facite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis, ut quum defeceritis, recipiant vos in æterna tabernacula]]. [[7:13|but learning|Hoc autem plus habet eruditio]], which is the act of wisdom, [[7:13|and wisdom excel in this|et sapientia]], which is a gift of the Holy Ghost, [[7:13|that they give life to him that possesseth them|quod vitam tribuunt possessori suo]]: that is, they are the meritorious cause of the life of grace and of its increase, and of the life of glory. And although the use of money just spoken of does this too, yet not so principally and directly. For money is not a virtue; but wisdom is in one sense an intellectual virtue, and in another it is called a gift.

paras.t: Considera opera Dei, id est secreta et incomprehensibilia ejus judicia, et effectus circa homines, qualiter unum misericorditer vocet intusque trahat (sicut in Evangelio Joannis asserit Christus: Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum; omnis qui audivit a Patre et didicit, venit ad me); alium vero juste relinquat. Unde ait Apostolus: Cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat. Hinc rursum Dominus in Exodo aperte ac terribiliter protestatur: Miserebor cui voluero, et clemens ero in quem mihi placuerit. Hæc autem consideranda sunt reverenter ac timorate et sobrie, in quodam generali, absque scrutinio rationum earumdem in speciali. In communi etenim potest ratio assignari, quia vult Creator omnipotens in quibusdam declarare suam misericordiam et suæ pietatis perfectionem, in aliis suam justitiam, prout ad Romanos plenius docet Apostolus. Tamen in speciali, cur scilicet istum magis quam illum elegerit seu prædestinaverit, ratio a nobis assignari non valet, si totus prædestinationis effectus simul sumatur, prout Richardus de Mediavilla super primum Sententiarum declarat. Certum est tamen, quod Deus altissimus essentialiter bonus, sapiens, justus, nil irrationabiliter injusteve agat, sed rationem dignissimam sui operis intra se intuetur.
paras.en: [[7:14|Consider the works of God|Considera opera Dei]], that is, His secret and incomprehensible judgments, and His workings upon men: how He mercifully calls one and draws him inwardly (as Christ declares in the Gospel of John: [[John 6:44|No man can come to me, except the Father|Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater]] [Denis: "my Father"] [[John 6:44|draw him|traxerit eum]]; [[John 6:45|Every one that hath heard of the Father and hath learned cometh forth me|Omnis qui audivit a Patre et didicit, venit ad me]]), but justly leaves another. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 9:18|he hath mercy on whom he will. And whom he will, he hardeneth|Cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat]]. Hence again the Lord openly and terribly protests in Exodus: [[Ex 33:19|I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be merciful to whom it shall please me|Miserebor cui voluero, et clemens ero in quem mihi placuerit]]. These things, however, are to be considered reverently, fearfully and soberly, in a certain general way, without searching into their reasons in particular. For in general a reason can be assigned: that the almighty Creator wills to show forth His mercy and the perfection of His goodness in some, and His justice in others, as the Apostle teaches more fully in Romans[[Rom 9:23||]][[Rom 9:22||]]. But in particular, that is, why He has chosen or predestined this man rather than that, no reason can be assigned by us, if the whole effect of predestination is taken together, as Richard of Middleton explains on the first book of the Sentences. Yet it is certain that the most high God, being essentially good, wise and just, does nothing without reason or unjustly, but beholds within Himself a most worthy reason for His work.

paras.t: Itaque, Considera opera Dei, et scito quod nemo possit corrigere, id est per verba aut disciplinas seu alio modo convertere, ita ut finaliter perseveret in bonis, quem ille, utpote Deus, despexerit. Porro dupliciter despicit peccatorem. Primo, secundum præsentem justitiam. Sicque despicit omnes qui in mortali sunt culpa, juxta illud Psalmi: Sprevisti omnes discedentes a justitiis tuis. Secundo, per præscientiam æternalem et reprobationem finalem: de qua aspernatione jam sermo. Et quem sic spernit, nullus finaliter corrigere potest, quamvis ad tempus ad pœnitentiam emolliatur. Cujus reprobationis et aspernationis probabile signum, est obduratio hominis in peccato. Quem dum quis talem experitur, debet ab ejus correptione cessare, saltem ad tempus, et orare pro ipso: si tamen sit subditus suus, debet ei opportuno tempore, quod ex officio obligatur, impendere, et propter conservationem boni communis, peccantem arguere seu punire.
paras.en: So then, [[7:14|Consider the works of God|Considera opera Dei]], and know [[7:14|that no man can correct|quod nemo possit corrigere]], that is, convert by words or by discipline or in any other way, so that he perseveres finally in good, [[7:14|whom he|quem ille]], that is, God, [[7:14|hath despised|despexerit]]. Now He despises the sinner in two ways. First, according to present justice; and so He despises all who are in mortal sin, according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 118:118|Thou hast despised all them that fall off from thy judgments|Sprevisti omnes discedentes a justitiis tuis]] [Denis reads *justitiis*, "justices", where the Vulgate has *judiciis*, "judgments"]. Secondly, by eternal foreknowledge and final reprobation [that is, God's eternal decision to leave a man to the consequences of his own final impenitence]; and it is of this despising that we are now speaking. Whom He despises in this way, no one can correct finally, even though for a time he may be softened to penance. A probable sign of this reprobation and despising is a man's hardening in sin. When anyone finds a man to be such, he ought to cease from correcting him, at least for a time, and pray for him; but if he is his subject, he ought at a fitting time to give him what he is bound to by his office, and for the preservation of the common good, rebuke or punish the sinner.

paras.t: In die bona frui bonis, id est, tempore prosperitatis et gratiæ, utere donis Dei jucunde et moderate; et malam diem præcave, id est, diem ultionis, tentationis seu adversitatis stude effugere, ita ut non condemneris, nec tentationibus obruaris, nec adversis frangaris in ea. Unde in Oratione dominica dicimus: Et ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos a malo; atque in Psalmo: Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus.
paras.en: [[7:15|In the good day enjoy good things|In die bona frui bonis]], that is, in the time of prosperity and grace use the gifts of God joyfully and moderately; [[7:15|and beware beforehand of the evil day|et malam diem præcave]], that is, strive to escape the day of vengeance, temptation or adversity, so that in it thou be not condemned, nor overwhelmed by temptations, nor broken by adversities. Hence we say in the Lord's Prayer: [[Matt 6:13|And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil|Et ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos a malo]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 40:2|Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor: the Lord will deliver him in the evil day|Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus]].

paras.t: Quidam exponunt sic: In die bona, id est in diebus solennibus, fruere bonis, id est cibis et potibus lautioribus. Quod tunc licet, juxta illud Nehemiæ: Ite, comedite pinguia, et bibite mulsum, et mittite partes his qui non præparaverunt sibi, quia dies sanctus Domini est. Unde et in Tobia legitur: Quum esset dies festus Domini, et factum esset prandium bonum in domo Tobiæ, dixit filio suo: Vade, et voca aliquos de tribu nostra timentes Deum, ut epulentur nobiscum. Et malam diem præcave, id est, a talibus deliciis cave diebus deputatis afflictioni atque jejuniis: quemadmodum in Levitico fertur de die expiationis, Omnis anima quæ afflicta non fuerit die hoc, peribit de populis suis. Sed non apparet quod dies festi, virtutum actibus deputati et sacri, vocentur in Scripturis mali.
paras.en: Some expound it thus: [[7:15|In the good day|In die bona]], that is, on feast days, [[7:15|enjoy good things|fruere bonis]], that is, richer food and drink. This is lawful then, according to that word of Nehemias: [[2 Esd 8:10|Go, eat fat meats, and drink sweet wine, and send portions to them that have not prepared for themselves: because it is the holy day of the Lord|Ite, comedite pinguia, et bibite mulsum, et mittite partes his qui non præparaverunt sibi, quia dies sanctus Domini est]]. Hence it is read in Tobias too: [[Tob 2:1|when there was a festival of the Lord, and a good dinner was prepared in Tobias's house|Quum esset dies festus Domini, et factum esset prandium bonum in domo Tobiæ]], [[Tob 2:2|He said to his son: Go, and bring some of our tribe that fear God, to feast with us|dixit filio suo: Vade, et voca aliquos de tribu nostra timentes Deum, ut epulentur nobiscum]]. [[7:15|And beware beforehand of the evil day|Et malam diem præcave]], that is, beware of such delights on the days appointed for affliction and fasting, as is said in Leviticus of the day of expiation: [[Lev 23:29|Every soul that is not afflicted on this day, shall perish from among his people.|Omnis anima, quæ afflicta non fuerit die hac, peribit de populis suis:]] But it does not appear that feast days, which are holy and appointed for acts of virtue, are called evil in the Scriptures.

paras.t: Sicut enim hanc, sic et illam fecit Deus. Utramque enim diem instituit Deus ad actus congruos illis. Et sicut dies prosperitatis ac meritorum, est effectus pietatis divinæ; sic dies judicii et ultionis seu adversitatis, opus est divinæ justitiæ. Ut non inveniat homo contra eum justas querimonias, id est, ne rationabiliter conqueri possit, quod Deus injuste quemquam condemnet, aut inconvenienter disponat. Omnia enim in sapientia fecit, et tempus pœnitendi ac promerendi largitur, nec alicui injuriatur. Certamen quoque requirit a suis ministris, ut in tentationibus et adversitatibus viriliter prælientur contra hostes suæ salutis: quoniam non meretur coronari, nisi qui certat legitime. Hinc in Evangelio, murmuranti legitur respondisse: Amice, non facio tibi injuriam. Et sanctus Job dixit: Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini, mala quare non sustineamus? Angelus quoque Tobiæ loquutus est: Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse erat ut tentatio probaret te. Consequenter probat præcavendum malum diem, juxta sensum inductum, et quod sit factus a Domino.
paras.en: [[7:15|for God hath made both the one and the other|Sicut enim hanc, sic et illam fecit Deus]]. For God established each day for the acts that befit it. And as the day of prosperity and merits is the effect of God's goodness, so the day of judgment and vengeance or adversity is the work of God's justice. [[7:15|that man may not find against him any just complaint|Ut non inveniat homo contra eum justas querimonias]]: that is, so that he cannot reasonably complain that God condemns anyone unjustly or orders things unfittingly. For He made all things in wisdom[[Ps 103:24||]] [the margin gives Ps. cvii, 24; the words are Ps 103:24], and grants a time for repenting and meriting, and does wrong to no one. He also requires a contest of His servants, that they should fight manfully in temptations and adversities against the enemies of their salvation, since none deserves to be crowned unless he strives lawfully[[2 Tim 2:5||]]. Hence in the Gospel He is read to have answered the one who murmured: [[Matt 20:13|friend, I do thee no wrong|Amice, non facio tibi injuriam]]. And holy Job said: [[Job 2:10|If we have received good things at the hand of God, why should we not receive evil?|Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini, mala quare non sustineamus?]] The angel too said to Tobias: [[Tob 12:13|because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee|Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse erat ut tentatio probaret te]]. Next he proves that the evil day is to be guarded against, in the sense given, and that it is made by the Lord.

paras.t: Hæc quoque vidi in diebus vanitatis meæ, id est transitoriæ ac miseræ vitæ meæ. Justus perit in justitia sua: id est, juste vivendo, et propter suam justitiam persecutiones mortemque patitur; et impius multo vivit tempore in malitia sua: ita quod vitiose vivendo, prosperatur in mundo. Unde Isaias testatur: Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet. Et tamen istud videtur divinæ derogare justitiæ ac providentiæ provisoris æterni. Et utique derogaret, si non esset vita alia post præsentem, nec futurum Dei judicium, qui juste ac sapienter ista permittit seu agit, quatenus electi et justi taliter patiendo a suis culpis in hac vita purgentur, majoremque gloriam consequantur, ac aliis in exemplum ponantur; impii autem ac reprobi, majora suæ perversitatis sortiantur tormenta. Tamen quia de isto multi solent mirari, in eorum persona loquitur Jeremias: Justus quidem tu es, Domine, si disputem tecum; verumtamen justa loquar ad te. Quare via impiorum prosperatur? Talibus quoque per Malachiam loquitur Deus: Invaluerunt super me verba vestra, et dixistis: Vanus est qui servit Deo; et quod emolumentum, quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et quia ambulavimus tristes coram Domino? Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt facientes impietatem.
paras.en: [[7:16|These things also I saw in the days of my vanity|Hæc quoque vidi in diebus vanitatis meæ]], that is, of my passing and wretched life. [[7:16|A just man perisheth in his justice|Justus perit in justitia sua]]: that is, by living justly, and because of his justice, he suffers persecutions and death; [[7:16|and a wicked man liveth a long time in his wickedness|et impius multo vivit tempore in malitia sua]], so that by living viciously he prospers in the world. Hence Isaias testifies: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet]]. And yet this seems to take away from the justice of God and the providence of the eternal Provider. And it would indeed take away from it, if there were no other life after the present one, and no future judgment of God, who justly and wisely permits or does these things, so that the elect and the just, by suffering in this way, may be purged of their faults in this life, gain greater glory, and be set as an example to others; while the wicked and the reprobate may receive the greater torments of their perversity. Yet because many are wont to wonder at this, Jeremias speaks in their person: [[Jer 12:1|Thou indeed, O Lord, art just, if I plead with thee, but yet I will speak what is just to thee: Why doth the way of the wicked prosper|Justus quidem tu es, Domine, si disputem tecum; verumtamen justa loquar ad te. Quare via impiorum prosperatur?]]? To such, too, God speaks through Malachias: [[Mal 3:13|Your words have been unsufferable to me|Invaluerunt super me verba vestra]], [[Mal 3:14|And you have said|et dixistis]]: [[Mal 3:14|He laboureth in vain that serveth God, and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances, and that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord|Vanus est qui servit Deo; et quod emolumentum, quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et quia ambulavimus tristes coram Domino?]]? [[Mal 3:15|Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up|Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes, siquidem ædificati sunt facientes impietatem]].

paras.t: Noli esse justus multum. Justitia virtus est: quæ tanto fuerit major, tanto et melior. Quomodo ergo ait, Noli esse justus multum? Et respondendum, quod quamvis justitia sit virtus in se, in qua directe non est excessus, quia augmentatio ejus est sua completio; tamen in exercitiis et actibus, quibus ad justitiam seu ejus profectum pertingitur, et quæ ad eam pertinere putantur, potest excessus superfluitasque accidere, sicut et circa caritatem et abstinentiam. Itaque homo non debet se immoderatis, indiscretis, et sibi importabilibus vigiliis, jejuniis, disciplinis, et consimilibus fatigare amore justitiæ obtinendæ aut perficiendæ, vel desiderio proficiendi in caritate aut devotione. Nec debet circa justitiam, per nimium rigorem seu austeritatem excedere, sed medium observare, faciliter indulgere, ac circa proximos potius declinare ad minus, quam ad majus: virtus namque moralis, est quædam medietas inter duo vitiosa extrema; estque clementia justitiæ contemperanda. Juxta hunc modum in Proverbiis dictum est: Prudentiæ tuæ pone modum; et in Jeremia, Quia plus fecit quam potuit, idcirco periit. Hinc ait Chrysostomus: Circa vitam tuam esto austerus; circa aliorum vitam, benignus. Audiant te homines parva præcipientem, et grandia operantem.
paras.en: [[7:17|Be not over just|Noli esse justus multum]]. Justice is a virtue, and the greater it is, the better it is. How then does he say, [[7:17|Be not over just|Noli esse justus multum]]? The answer is that although justice in itself is a virtue in which there is no excess directly, since its increase is its completion, yet in the exercises and acts by which one attains to justice or progress in it, and which are thought to belong to it, excess and superfluity can occur, as also in regard to charity and abstinence. And so a man ought not to wear himself out with immoderate, indiscreet and, for him, unbearable vigils, fasts, disciplines [that is, scourgings undertaken as penance] and the like, for love of obtaining or perfecting justice, or from a desire of advancing in charity or devotion. Nor ought he to go to excess in justice by too great rigour or austerity, but keep the mean, pardon readily, and towards his neighbours lean rather to the less than to the more: for moral virtue is a kind of mean between two vicious extremes, and justice is to be tempered with clemency. In this sense it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 23:4|set bounds to thy prudence|Prudentiæ tuæ pone modum]] [the margin gives Prov. xxii, 4; the words are Prov 23:4]; and in Jeremias: [[Jer 48:36|because he hath done more than he could, therefore they have perished|Quia plus fecit quam potuit, idcirco periit]] [Denis has *periit*, "he perished"]. Hence Chrysostom says: Be austere towards thy own life, kind towards the life of others. Let men hear thee commanding small things and doing great ones.

paras.t: Severitas autem (ut Cicero loquitur) est, per quam judiciaria potestas aut ultio in aliquem districtius exercetur. Qualis vero debeat esse intentio judicis justique correctoris, idem Cicero pandit, dicendo: In corrigendo seu vindicando hæc tria lex secuta est, quæ princeps quoque sequi debet: ut eum quem punit seu reprehendit, emendet; aut pœna ejus ceteros meliores reddat; aut ut iniquis sublatis, ceteri vivant securius. Quantum vero severitas sit vitanda, patet ex verbis Senecæ, qui fatetur: Severitas assiduitate auctoritatem amittit; et rursus: Vide si adhuc malus es, et similibus parce: verum si esse desisti, quare aliis locum emendationis abscindas?
paras.en: Now severity (as Cicero says) is that by which judicial power or punishment is exercised more strictly against someone. What the intention of a judge and of a just corrector ought to be, the same Cicero makes plain, saying: In correcting or punishing, the law has followed these three aims, which the prince also ought to follow: that it may amend him whom it punishes or reproves; or that his punishment may make the rest better; or that, the wicked being removed, the rest may live more securely. How far severity is to be avoided is plain from the words of Seneca, who declares: Severity loses its authority by constant use; and again: See whether thou art still wicked, and then spare those like thee; but if thou hast ceased to be so, why wouldst thou cut off from others the room for amendment?

paras.t: Circa hunc locum ait Albinus: Qui nunquam fraternis ignoscere vult peccatis, sed omnia vindicare secundum impetum animi sui, plus et aliter justus est quam deceat. Quum enim dicat Salvator, Nolite judicare, ut non judicemini; et, Si dimiseritis hominibus, dimittet vobis Pater cœlestis delicta vestra: nec nimis rigidus, nec nimis solutus debet esse prælatus, sed via regia ingredi, et considerare diligenter quid cui conveniat ad salutem animæ suæ.
paras.en: On this place Albinus [that is, Alcuin] says: He who will never pardon his brothers' sins, but would punish everything according to the impulse of his own mind, is just more than is fitting, and otherwise than is fitting. For since the Saviour says, [[Matt 7:1|Judge not, that you may not be judged|Nolite judicare, ut non judicemini]]; and, [[Matt 6:14|if you will forgive men|Si dimiseritis hominibus]], [[Matt 6:14|your heavenly Father will forgive you also your offences|dimittet vobis Pater cœlestis delicta vestra]], a prelate ought to be neither too rigid nor too lax, but walk the royal road, and consider carefully what befits each one for the salvation of his soul.

paras.t: Neque plus sapias quam necesse est: id est, non coneris de secretis et incomprehensibilibus plus intelligere quam convenit tibi: sicut in exordio hujus capituli dictum est, Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere? Neque de tua sapientia aut justitia immoderate præsumas; sed potius te ipsum humilia, propriæ fragilitatis mensuram considera, et Deum formidare non cesses: sicut hortatur Apostolus, Noli altum sapere, sed time. Ne obstupescas, id est, ne mentis stuporem hebetudinemque incurras ex tali scrutinio, aut reputatione tui ipsius.
paras.en: [[7:17|and be not more wise than is necessary|Neque plus sapias quam necesse est]]: that is, do not try to understand more of secret and incomprehensible things than befits thee, as was said at the beginning of this chapter: [[7:1|What needeth a man to seek things that are above him|Quid necesse est homini majora se quærere]]? Nor presume immoderately on thy own wisdom or justice; but rather humble thyself, consider the measure of thy own frailty, and cease not to fear God, as the Apostle exhorts: [[Rom 11:20|Be not highminded, but fear|Noli altum sapere, sed time]]. [[7:17|lest thou become stupid|Ne obstupescas]], that is, lest thou fall into stupor and dullness of mind from such searching, or from thinking much of thyself.

paras.t: Ne impie agas multum. Hoc dicit, non licentiando ut impie agamus, dummodo non multum hoc faciamus, sed ut studeamus omnino vitare mortalia, si venialia in toto vitare non possumus. Omnia equidem, sed non singula, vitare valemus. Sequitur: et noli esse stultus, id est divini transgressor præcepti, et temporalia ac terrena Creatori tuo præponens, quod prorsus stultissimum est; ne moriaris in tempore non tuo, id est præfixo tuæ periodo, si sapiens esses: hoc est, ne peccando merearis per leges humanas cito occidi, et ne Deus propter facinora tua tuam acceleret mortem. Quemadmodum in Job de quibusdam dicitur: Semitam sæculorum calcaverunt viri iniqui, qui ante tempus suum sublati sunt; et in Psalmo, Viri sanguinum et dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos. Sic mortui sunt tempore non suo Dathan et Abiron, Core et Hon. Nempe (ut Augustinus in libro de Doctrina christiana declarat) Deus a quocunque homine vel populo æquanimiter sustinet certum aliquod pondus culparum: quo impleto, ultra non tolerat. Hinc (ut in Genesi habetur) dixit Deus ad Abraham: Nondum completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum. Jeremias quoque asserit: Non poterat vos Dominus ultra portare propter malitiam studiorum vestrorum.
paras.en: [[7:18|Be not overmuch wicked|Ne impie agas multum]]. He says this not to give leave for us to act wickedly so long as we do not do it much, but so that we may strive to avoid mortal sins altogether, if we cannot avoid venial sins entirely. For we can avoid each one of them, but not all of them [Denis's Latin, literally "all, but not each", seems to have the two words reversed; the common teaching is that each venial sin can be avoided, but not all of them together]. There follows: [[7:18|and be not foolish|et noli esse stultus]], that is, a transgressor of God's commandment, setting temporal and earthly things before thy Creator, which is utterly most foolish; [[7:18|lest thou die before thy time|ne moriaris in tempore non tuo]], that is, the time that would be fixed for thy span if thou wert wise: that is, lest by sinning thou deserve to be quickly put to death by human laws, and lest God hasten thy death on account of thy crimes. As it is said of some in Job: [[Job 22:15|the path of ages, which wicked men have spurned|Semitam sæculorum calcaverunt viri iniqui]], [[Job 22:16|Who were taken away before their time|qui ante tempus suum sublati sunt]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 54:24|Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days|Viri sanguinum et dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos]]. So Dathan and Abiron, Core and Hon died before their time[[Num 16:1||]][[Num 16:32||]]. For indeed (as Augustine explains in the book On Christian Doctrine) God patiently bears from any man or people a certain fixed weight of sins: when it is filled up, He bears no further. Hence (as we have it in Genesis) God said to Abraham: [[Gen 15:16|as yet the iniquities of the Amorrhites are not at the full|Nondum completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum]]. Jeremias too declares: [[Jer 44:22|the Lord could no longer bear, because of the evil of your doings|Non poterat vos Dominus ultra portare propter malitiam studiorum vestrorum]].

paras.t: Bonum est te sustentare justum, id est, laudabile est, ut virtuosos pie refoveas, et in temporalibus ac spiritualibus misericordiæ actibus pro posse eis subvenias: quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico scriptum est, Benefac justo, et invenies retributionem magnam.
