Ad Galatas quoque Apostolus: Dum tempus (inquit) habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes, maxime ad domesticos fidei. Sed et ab illo ne subtrahas manum tuam, id est, consilium et subsidium ne deneges justo, ne Deum inhabitatorem illius, qui istud præcepit, offendas; quia qui timet Deum, nihil negligit. Qui enim filiali, aut saltem initiali timore Deum veretur, nullum omittit præceptum, secundum quod talis; tamen, in quantum liberi exstat arbitrii, potest peccare. Itaque timor Dei retrahit a negligentiis et peccatis. Estque timor iste, diligentiæ sollicitator atque custodiæ pater, ita quod quanto plus in timore isto [quis] excreverit, tanto vigilantior ac sollicitior est ad vitandum omnem negligentiam et offensam. Ideo nihil deest ita timenti Deum.
paras.en: [[7:19|It is good that thou shouldst hold up the just|Bonum est te sustentare justum]], that is, it is praiseworthy that thou cherish the virtuous with kindness and help them as far as thou canst by the works of mercy, temporal and spiritual, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 12:2|Do good to the just, and thou shalt find great recompense|Benefac justo, et invenies retributionem magnam]]. The Apostle too, to the Galatians: [[Gal 6:10|whilst we have time|Dum tempus]], he says, [[Gal 6:10|let us work good to all men, but especially to those who are of the household of the faith|operemur bonum ad omnes, maxime ad domesticos fidei]]. [[7:19|yea and from him withdraw not thy hand|Sed et ab illo ne subtrahas manum tuam]], that is, do not deny counsel and help to the just man, lest thou offend God who dwells in him and who commanded this; [[7:19|for he that feareth God, neglecteth nothing|quia qui timet Deum, nihil negligit]]. For he who reveres God with filial, or at least initial, fear [that is, the fear of a son who dreads offending his father, or the fear of a beginner, still mixed with dread of punishment] omits no commandment, in so far as he is such; yet, in so far as he has free will, he can sin. And so the fear of God draws a man back from negligences and sins. This fear is the rouser of diligence and the father of watchfulness, so that the more [anyone] grows in this fear, the more watchful and careful he is to avoid all negligence and offence. Therefore nothing is wanting to one who so fears God[[Ps 33:10||]].

paras.t: Sapientia, quæ est donum, et præsertim increata Sapientia, quæ est Deus, confortavit sapientem super decem principes civitatis, id est, fecit eum spiritualiter fortiorem quibuscumque civitatum rectoribus, sapientiam non habentibus: quoniam tales a vitiis protinus superantur. Vel, Super decem principes, id est, plus roboravit sapientem, quam a quibuscumque principibus possit confortari: quia, ut scriptum est, Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus. Ideo ait Psalmista: Bonum est sperare in Domino, quam sperare in principibus. Hinc ait Scriptura: Melior est sapientia, quam vires; et item, Sapientia vincit malitiam.
paras.en: [[7:20|Wisdom|Sapientia]], which is a gift, and above all the uncreated Wisdom, which is God, [[7:20|hath strengthened the wise more than ten princes of the city|confortavit sapientem super decem principes civitatis]], that is, has made him spiritually stronger than any rulers of cities who have not wisdom, since such men are straightway overcome by vices. Or, [[7:20|more than ten princes|Super decem principes]], that is, it has strengthened the wise man more than he could be strengthened by any princes whatever: for, as it is written, [[Jer 17:5|Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord|Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus]]. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 117:9|It is good to trust in the Lord, rather than to trust in princes.|Bonum est sperare in Domino, quam sperare in principibus.]] Hence Scripture says: [[Wis 6:1|Wisdom is better than strength|Melior est sapientia, quam vires]]; and again, [[Wis 7:30|no evil can overcome wisdom|Sapientia vincit malitiam]] [Denis's wording, *Sapientia vincit malitiam*, "wisdom overcometh malice", gives the sense of the verse in other words].

paras.t: Non est enim homo justus super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet: id est, nemo in hac vita (secundum legem communem) tam virtuosus est, aut tam intentus diligenter actibus bonis, quin aliquando peccet, saltem venialiter. Nam et multæ distractiones, imperfectiones, ac negligentiæ admiscentur actibus nostris bonis. Propter quod loquitur Isaias: Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ. Hinc quoque fertur in Job: Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere? Quod quum ita sit, omnes indigemus sapientia confortante.
paras.en: [[7:21|For there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|Non est enim homo justus super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet]]: that is, no one in this life (by the common law) is so virtuous, or so diligently intent on good acts, that he does not sometimes sin, at least venially. For many distractions, imperfections and negligences are mingled with our good acts too. For which reason Isaias says: [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ]]. Hence it is said in Job as well: [[Job 15:14|What is man that he should be without spot, and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just?|Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere]] This being so, we all need the strengthening of wisdom.

paras.t: Sed et cunctis sermonibus qui dicuntur, ne accommodes cor tuum: id est, mentem auremque cordis non adhibeas per consensum aut credulitatem universis verbis quæ audis, videlicet verbis detractoriis, accusatoriis, mendosis, dolosis, et apparentiam non habentibus, aut discordiæ seminativis, nec verbis malis quæ percipis esse dicta de te, inquirendo an sint dicta adversus te, sicut narratur tibi: quia ex his oriuntur in te inquietudo, indignatio, ira, impatientia, rancor, contra male loquentes de te. Et præsertim non est credendum de facili narrantibus crimina magna de aliis.
paras.en: [[7:22|But do not apply thy heart to all words that are spoken|Sed et cunctis sermonibus qui dicuntur, ne accommodes cor tuum]]: that is, do not give thy mind and the ear of thy heart, by consent or belief, to all the words thou hearest, namely words of detraction, of accusation, lying, deceitful words and words without likelihood, or words that sow discord; nor to evil words which thou learnest were said about thee, inquiring whether they were said against thee as it is told thee: for from these arise in thee disquiet, indignation, anger, impatience and rancour against those who speak ill of thee. And above all, those who tell of great crimes of others are not to be believed easily.

paras.t: Hinc enim ait Joannes apostolus: Carissimi, nolite omni spiritui credere; sed probate spiritus si ex Deo sint. Seneca quoque: Rumoribus, inquit, criminationibus, suspicionibus minime sis credulus, sed potius oppositissimus malignis qui per speciem simplicitatis ad nocendum subrepserint. Iterum protestatur: Difficilem oportet habere aurem ad crimina. Unde Dominus, quasi vix credens tanta esse in Sodomitis facinora, ait in Genesi: Descendam, et videbo, utrum clamorem qui venit ad me, opere compleverint, an non est ita, ut sciam. Itaque magna mala parit credendi facilitas. Tamen in hac re uti oportet discretione. Nam et Godolias fuit occisus ab Ismaele, quia non credidit verbis Johanan sibi insinuanti insidias Ismaelis. In talibus equidem abundans cautela non nocet, ut quasi non credendo credatur, et qualis sit ipse qui loquitur, consideretur.
paras.en: For hence the apostle John says: [[1 John 4:1|Dearly beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God|Carissimi, nolite omni spiritui credere; sed probate spiritus si ex Deo sint]]. Seneca too: Be by no means credulous, he says, of rumours, accusations and suspicions, but rather most opposed to the malicious who have crept in under a show of simplicity to do harm. Again he declares: One ought to have an ear hard of hearing towards accusations. Hence the Lord, as though scarcely believing that the crimes of the Sodomites were so great, says in Genesis: [[Gen 18:21|I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry that is come to me; or whether it be not so, that I may know.|Descendam, et videbo utrum clamorem qui venit ad me, opere compleverint; an non est ita, ut sciam.]] And so easiness of belief brings forth great evils. Yet in this matter discretion must be used. For Godolias was slain by Ismael[[4 Kings 25:25||]][[Jer 41:2||]] because he did not believe the words of Johanan warning him of Ismael's plot[[Jer 40:13||]][[Jer 40:14||]]. In such things abundant caution does no harm, so that one believes as though not believing, and considers what sort of man the speaker is.

paras.t: Ne forte audias servum tuum maledicentem tibi, eo quod cunctis verbis adhibeas aurem; vel, ne percipias servum tuum tibi maledixisse, id est, mala tibi imprecatum fuisse, sicque habeas contra eum grandem commotionem. Etenim qui adhuc faciliter passionantur, sibimetipsis magnam procurant turbationem atque tentationem, de omnibus verbis, præsertim de ipsis (ut eis narratur) dictis, quærendo, et an dicta sint, inquirendo.
paras.en: [[7:22|lest perhaps thou hear thy servant reviling thee|Ne forte audias servum tuum maledicentem tibi]], because thou givest ear to all words; or, lest thou learn that thy servant has reviled thee, that is, called down evils upon thee, and so thou have a great commotion against him. For those who are still easily moved by passion bring great disturbance and temptation on themselves, by inquiring about all words, especially those said (as it is told them) about themselves, and asking whether they were said.

paras.t: Scit enim conscientia tua, quia et tu crebro maledixisti aliis: ideo patienter ferre debes, si et alii maledixerint tibi, juxta illud: Sicut fecisti, fiet tibi. Porro, conscientia teste ac judice, nemo nocens absolvitur. Ideo Seneca dixit: Neminem magis verearis, quam conscientiam tuam. Nam aliorum notitiam potes effugere, sed non tuam.
paras.en: [[7:23|For thy conscience knoweth that thou also hast often spoken evil of others|Scit enim conscientia tua, quia et tu crebro maledixisti aliis]]: therefore thou oughtest to bear it patiently if others too revile thee, according to that word: [[Abd 1:15|as thou hast done, so shall it be done to thee|Sicut fecisti, fiet tibi]]. Moreover, with conscience as witness and judge, no guilty man is acquitted. Therefore Seneca said: Fear no one more than thy own conscience; for thou canst escape the knowledge of others, but not thy own.

paras.t: Cuncta tentavi in sapientia: id est, sapienter, et per sapientiam universa probavi et investigavi ut potui, quatenus de omnibus certam obtinerem notitiam. Unde Apostolus: Omnia (inquit) probate; quod bonum est, tenete. Experientia namque exigit multa. Dixi: Sapiens efficiar: id est, fiduciam habui pertingendi ad sapientiam magnam ex inquisitione et studio. Et ipsa longius recessit a me: id est, quanto plus profeci in ea, tanto limpidius cognovi eminentiam ejus, et vidi quantum ab ejus plenitudine distem. Sapientia etenim proprie est, cognitio divinorum: et quanto in hac vita Deum sublimius contemplamur, tanto perspicacius intuemur quam infinite ab ejus comprehensione deficimus; et tandem per mysticam theologiam conjungimur ei tanquam prorsus ignoto, quantum ad quid est. Propter quod divinus et magnus Dionysius libro de Mystica theologia disseruit: Hoc est Deum vere cognoscere, supersubstantialem supersubstantialiter per omnium ablationem laudare.
paras.en: [[7:24|I have tried all things in wisdom|Cuncta tentavi in sapientia]]: that is, wisely, and through wisdom, I proved and searched out all things as well as I could, so as to obtain certain knowledge of them all. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:21|prove all things|Omnia (inquit) probate]]; [[1 Thess 5:21|hold fast that which is good|quod bonum est, tenete]]. For experience requires many things. [[7:24|I have said: I will be wise|Dixi: Sapiens efficiar]]: that is, I was confident of reaching great wisdom by inquiry and study. [[7:24|and it departed farther from me|Et ipsa longius recessit a me]]: that is, the more I advanced in it, the more clearly I knew its eminence, and saw how far I am from its fullness. For wisdom, properly speaking, is the knowledge of divine things; and the more loftily we contemplate God in this life, the more clearly we see how infinitely we fall short of comprehending Him; and at last, through mystical theology, we are joined to Him as to one wholly unknown as regards what He is. For which reason the divine and great Dionysius taught in the book On Mystical Theology: This is truly to know God: to praise Him who is above all being, in a manner above all being, by the taking away of all things.

paras.t: Multo magis quam erat: id est, transcendit meam capacitatem multo plus quam ante mihi innotuit.
paras.en: [[7:25|Much more than it was|Multo magis quam erat]]: that is, it surpasses my capacity much more than it was known to me before.

paras.t: Et alta profunditas, id est, imperscrutabilis altitudo in Deo est, præsertim quantum ad superbeatissimæ Trinitatis mysterium; quis investigabit eam? id est, nullus poterit eam plene scrutari aut scire. Unde ad Moysen Dominus dixit: Faciem meam videre non poteris; non enim videbit me homo, et vivet. Et Christus in Evangelio: Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius. Ideo dixit Psalmista: Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me; confortata est, et non potero ad eam. Quum enim scire, sit rem per causam cognoscere, ejus illud æternum, independens ac infinitum, infinite excedit omnem mentis creatæ capacitatem. Quapropter ait Apostolus: Videmus per speculum in ænigmate. Denique (juxta Philosophum) unumquodque tantum habet de cognoscibilitate, quantum habet de actualitate. Ideo, sicut Deus incomparabilis et immensus, est infinitæ actualitatis, ita et infinitæ cognoscibilitatis. Propter quod plene comprehendi ac sciri non potest, nisi ab intellectu perspicacitatis et virtutis penitus infinitæ, utpote a se ipso.
paras.en: [[7:25|it is a great depth|Et alta profunditas]], that is, there is an unsearchable height in God, above all as regards the mystery of the most supremely blessed Trinity; [[7:25|who shall find it out|quis investigabit eam]]? that is, no one will be able to search it out or know it fully. Hence the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 33:20|Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me, and live|Faciem meam videre non poteris; non enim videbit me homo, et vivet]]. And Christ in the Gospel: [[Matt 11:27|neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son|Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius]]. Therefore the Psalmist said: [[Ps 138:6|Thy knowledge is become wonderful to me: it is high, and I cannot reach to it.|Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me; confortata est, et non potero ad eam.]] [the margin gives Ps. cxxviii, 6; the verse is Ps 138:6] For since to know [*scire*, to know scientifically] is to know a thing through its cause, His cause, which is eternal, independent and infinite, infinitely exceeds all the capacity of a created mind [the Latin, *ejus illud æternum*, is compressed; the sense seems to be that God has no cause beyond Himself, and His being infinitely exceeds any created mind]. For which reason the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner|Videmus per speculum in ænigmate]]. Lastly (according to the Philosopher), each thing has as much knowability as it has actuality [that is, a thing can be known in so far as it is in act, that is, actually real and complete]. Therefore, as God, being incomparable and immense, is of infinite actuality, so He is also of infinite knowability. For which reason He cannot be fully comprehended and known except by an intellect of utterly infinite insight and power, that is, by Himself.

paras.t: Lustravi, id est, considerando circuivi, universa animo meo, ut scirem, et considerarem, et quærerem sapientiam et rationem de singulis rebus atque eventibus; et ut cognoscerem impietatem stulti, ad evitandum et reprobandum eamdem, et errorem imprudentium, quatenus et mihi ac aliis inde caverem.
paras.en: [[7:26|I have surveyed|Lustravi]], that is, I went round in consideration, [[7:26|all things with my mind, to know, and consider, and seek out wisdom and reason|universa animo meo, ut scirem, et considerarem, et quærerem sapientiam et rationem]] about each thing and event; [[7:26|and to know the wickedness of the fool|et ut cognoscerem impietatem stulti]], so as to avoid and reject it, [[7:26|and the error of the imprudent|et errorem imprudentium]], so that I might guard myself and others against it.

paras.t: Et inveni amariorem morte mulierem: id est, hoc reperi, quod mulier amarissimam faciat separationem mentis a Deo: quæ separatio morte corporali amarior est, quia incomparabiliter pejor, et damnationis perpetuæ inductiva, juxta illud Jeremiæ: Scito et vide, quia malum et amarum est te reliquisse Dominum Deum tuum. Quæ laqueus venatorum est: quia per mulierem dæmones, qui animas venantur ad mortem, fallunt et capiunt adolescentes et juvenes atque viros. Unde in Psalmo: Ipse liberabit me de laqueo venantium. Et sagena cor ejus. Est equidem rete diaboli: et sicut sagena capit quoslibet pisces, sic cor mulieris lasciviæ appetit omnes sibi allicere. Vincula sunt manus illius: quia per manuum contactum et amplexus, vinculo concupiscentiæ ligat virum. Quemadmodum enim asserit Augustinus, Nihil virilem sic dejicit animum, sicut feminea blandimenta, corporumque contactus. Libido quoque ferreas domat mentes. Qui placet Deo, effugiet illam, id est vir timoratus et castus. Interdum tamen et talis dejicitur, quemadmodum David per Bethsabee. Unde Augustinus fatetur: Vidi cedros Libani cecidisse, de quorum ruina non magis suspicabar, quam de casu Hieronymi et Ambrosii. Qui autem peccator est, capietur ab illa. Peccator enim adjiciet ad peccandum, et unum peccatum pondere suo trahit ad aliud; nec talis meretur retrahi per gratiam Dei.
paras.en: [[7:27|And I have found a woman more bitter than death|Et inveni amariorem morte mulierem]]: that is, I found this, that woman brings about a most bitter separation of the mind from God; and this separation is more bitter than bodily death, because it is incomparably worse and leads to everlasting damnation, according to that word of Jeremias: [[Jer 2:19|Know thou, and see that it is an evil and a bitter thing for thee, to have left the Lord thy God|Scito et vide, quia malum et amarum est te reliquisse Dominum Deum tuum]]. [[7:27|who is the hunter's snare|Quæ laqueus venatorum est]]: for through woman the demons, who hunt souls to death, deceive and catch boys and youths and men. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 90:3|he hath delivered me from the snare of the hunters|Ipse liberabit me de laqueo venantium]] [Denis has the future, *liberabit*, "he will deliver"]. [[7:27|and her heart is a net|Et sagena cor ejus]]. It is indeed the devil's net: and as a drag-net [*sagena*] catches fish of every kind, so the heart of a wanton woman seeks to draw all men to herself. [[7:27|her hands are bands|Vincula sunt manus illius]]: for by the touch of her hands and her embraces she binds a man with the bond of concupiscence. For as Augustine declares, Nothing so casts down a man's mind as a woman's caresses and the touching of bodies. Lust also tames minds of iron. [[7:27|He that pleaseth God shall escape from her|Qui placet Deo, effugiet illam]], that is, a God-fearing and chaste man. Yet sometimes even such a one is cast down, as David was through Bethsabee[[2 Kings 11:2||]][[2 Kings 11:4||]]. Hence Augustine confesses: I have seen cedars of Lebanon fall, of whose ruin I had no more suspicion than of the fall of Jerome and Ambrose. [[7:27|but he that is a sinner, shall be caught by her|Qui autem peccator est, capietur ab illa]]. For [[Ecclus 3:29|the sinner will add sin to sin|Peccator enim adjiciet ad peccandum]], and one sin by its own weight drags him to another; nor does such a man deserve to be drawn back by the grace of God.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per mulierem istam, hæretica pravitas designatur, quæ amarissime vulnerat corda, et per quam hæresiarchæ maledicti ac dæmones, plurimos deceperunt.
paras.en: Spiritually, by this woman is signified heretical depravity, which most bitterly wounds hearts, and through which accursed heresiarchs and the demons have deceived very many.

paras.t: Ecce hoc, quod jam dictum est, inveni, id est, considerando et inquirendo cognovi, dixit Ecclesiastes, unum et alterum, id est, ista et illa discutiendo, ut invenirem rationem de singulis, sicut jam tactum est:
paras.en: [[7:28|Lo this|Ecce hoc]], which has just been said, [[7:28|have I found|inveni]], that is, I have come to know by considering and inquiring, [[7:28|said Ecclesiastes, weighing one thing after another|dixit Ecclesiastes, unum et alterum]], that is, by examining these things and those, [[7:28|that I might find out the account|ut invenirem rationem]] of each, as has just been touched on:

paras.t: quam adhuc quærit anima mea. Nam, sicut homo videns a longe rem pulchram, appetit eam clarius cernere, et desiderio quodam accenditur; ita qui studet pro veritate intelligenda, dum incipit eam cognoscere, inflammatur ad pleniorem ejus notitiam obtinendam. Et non inveni eam perfecte. Vix enim possumus de aliqua creatura universas ejus causas assignare aut scire, omnesque ejus proprietates et vires dignoscere, quemadmodum expositum est super illud, Cunctæ res difficiles.
paras.en: [[7:29|Which yet my soul seeketh|quam adhuc quærit anima mea]]. For as a man who sees a beautiful thing from afar longs to see it more clearly and is fired with a certain desire, so one who studies to understand the truth, when he begins to know it, is inflamed to obtain a fuller knowledge of it. [[7:29|and I have not found it|Et non inveni eam]] perfectly. For we can scarcely assign or know all the causes of any creature, or discern all its properties and powers, as was explained on the words, [[Eccles 1:8|All things are hard|Cunctæ res difficiles]].

paras.t: Virum de mille unum reperi: id est, tantam inveni in hominibus defectuositatem, quod de mille viris vix reperi unum nomine viri dignum, utpote virtuosum, perfectum, feminea blandimenta spernentem. In quibus verbis ponitur numerus determinatus pro indeterminato, ad innuendum paucitatem bonorum respectu malorum, quemadmodum ait Salvator: Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi. Et Apostolus ait: Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt. Atque in Psalmo: Omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt. Mulierem ex omnibus non inveni: id est, in feminis tantam inveni fragilitatem, ut nulla in eis virtuosa appareat. Non quod penitus nulla sit virtuosa, sed respective et per hyperbolen dictum est hoc: quia quod modicum est, pro nihilo reputatur, et quia in naturalibus mulieres imperfectiores sunt viris communiter, quamvis non sit ita de singulis. Sicque per verba hæc videtur insinuari, quod plures sint virtuosi viri quam feminæ. Et credibile satis apparet, quod plures sint viri perfecti, quam feminæ, sicut et in naturalibus viri præfulgent. Unde in regula sua beatus ait Hieronymus, quod quantumcumque virtuosa sit mulier, si virtus in viro deficiat, tandem deficit et in muliere.
paras.en: [[7:29|One man among a thousand I have found|Virum de mille unum reperi]]: that is, I found such defectiveness in men that out of a thousand men I scarcely found one worthy of the name of man [*vir*], that is, virtuous, perfect, and scorning a woman's caresses. In these words a definite number is put for an indefinite one, to suggest how few the good are in comparison with the wicked, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 20:16|many are called but few chosen|Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi]][[Matt 22:14||]]. And the Apostle says: [[Phil 2:21|all seek the things that are their own|Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 52:4|All have gone aside, they are become unprofitable together|Omnes declinaverunt, simul inutiles facti sunt]]. [[7:29|a woman among them all I have not found|Mulierem ex omnibus non inveni]]: that is, I found such frailty in women that none among them appears virtuous. Not that there is no virtuous woman at all; but this is said comparatively and by hyperbole: because what is little is reckoned as nothing, and because in natural gifts women are commonly less perfect than men, though it is not so in every single case. And so these words seem to suggest that there are more virtuous men than women. And it seems credible enough that there are more perfect men than women, as men also excel in natural gifts. Hence blessed Jerome says in his rule that however virtuous a woman may be, if virtue fails in the man, it fails at last in the woman too.

paras.t: Solummodo, id est præcipue, hoc inveni, quod fecerit Deus hominem rectum: id est, protoplastum parentem in originali justitia condidit, scientiis virtutibusque perfectum; vel, quemlibet hominem Deus efficit rectum, id est in naturalibus bonum, ad virtutes dispositum, habentem in se quamdam inchoationem scientiarum atque virtutum concreatam. De primo tamen homine magis potest intelligi, ut ex Genesis primo ac secundo capitulis elucescit. Nam et alibi asseritur: Deus creavit hominem inexterminabilem. In Ecclesiastico quoque de primis parentibus legitur: Creavit illis scientiam spiritus, sensu implevit corda illorum. Et ipse se infinitis miscuerit quæstionibus, id est innumerabilibus, non solum quæstionibus utilibus, fructuosis et licitis, sed insuper curiosis, superstitiosis, illicitis: per quarum occupationem negligit quæ sunt salutis, et tempus infructuose consumit.
paras.en: [[7:30|Only|Solummodo]], that is, chiefly, [[7:30|this I have found, that God made man right|hoc inveni, quod fecerit Deus hominem rectum]]: that is, He created our first-formed parent in original justice [that is, the state of grace and integrity in which Adam was created], perfect in knowledge and virtues; or, God makes every man right, that is, good in his natural endowments, disposed to the virtues, having within him a certain beginning of knowledge and virtues created together with him. Yet it can rather be understood of the first man, as is clear from the first and second chapters of Genesis. For it is said elsewhere too: [[Wis 2:23|God created man incorruptible|Deus creavit hominem inexterminabilem]]. And in Ecclesiasticus it is read of our first parents: [[Ecclus 17:6|He created in them the science of the spirit, he fired their heart with wisdom|Creavit illis scientiam spiritus, sensu implevit corda illorum]]. [[7:30|and he hath entangled himself with an infinity of questions|Et ipse se infinitis miscuerit quæstionibus]], that is, innumerable ones; not only useful, fruitful and lawful questions, but also curious, superstitious and unlawful ones, by being taken up with which he neglects the things of salvation and spends his time without fruit.

paras.t: Quis talis ut sapiens est? Secundum Glossam videtur hoc Salomon implicite et oblique dicere de se ipso, ut sit sensus: Quis talis ut sapiens est? id est, quis tantæ scientiæ, ut ego Salomon, qui antonomastice Sapiens vocor? et tamen in rerum plenaria perscrutatione in tantum deficio. Ideo alii debent de immoderato et curioso scrutinio supersedere. Et quis cognovit solutionem verbi, id est difficilium quæstionum per verba propositarum? Vel, Solutionem verbi, id est rei significatæ per verba. Sic enim verbum pro re frequenter accipitur, ut ibi: Quod est verbum quod factum est? Quasi dicat: Talem solutionem ego præ aliis scio, nec tamen respondere ad omnia valeo: quanto magis alii debent manum superponere ori? Vel sic: Quis talis ut sapiens? id est, quum tam arduum sit et rarum, ad sapientiam pervenire, quis talis, id est, quis in sæculo isto tam appretiandus et commendandus, sicut vir qui ad sapientiam veram pertingit? Et quis novit solutionem verbi, nisi hujusmodi sapiens?
paras.en: [[7:30|Who is as the wise man|Quis talis ut sapiens est]]? According to the Gloss, Solomon seems to say this implicitly and obliquely of himself, so that the sense is: [[7:30|Who is as the wise man|Quis talis ut sapiens est]]? that is, who is of such knowledge as I, Solomon, who am called by antonomasia [that is, by way of eminence, the title standing for the name] the Wise? And yet I fall so far short in a full searching out of things. Therefore others ought to refrain from immoderate and curious searching. [[7:30|and who hath known the resolution of the word|Et quis cognovit solutionem verbi]], that is, of difficult questions put forward in words? Or, [[7:30|the resolution of the word|Solutionem verbi]], that is, of the thing signified by the words. For in this way *word* is often taken for the thing, as here: [[2 Kings 1:4|What is the matter that is come to pass|Quod est verbum quod factum est]]? [the Vulgate has *verbum*, "word", where the Douay-Rheims has "matter"] As if he said: I know such resolution beyond others, and yet I cannot answer everything; how much more ought others to lay their hand upon their mouth? Or thus: [[7:30|Who is as the wise man|Quis talis ut sapiens]]? that is, since it is so hard and so rare to come to wisdom, who is such, that is, who in this world is so much to be prized and commended, as a man who attains to true wisdom? [[7:30|and who hath known the resolution of the word|Et quis novit solutionem verbi]], except a wise man of this kind?

8.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI SEPTIMI : QUID NECESSE EST HOMINI MAJORA SE QUÆRERE ?
8.title_en: Elucidation of the seventh chapter: What needeth a man to seek things that are above him?
8.note: This article treats chapter 7 and the first verse of chapter 8; its commentary on chapter 7 is shown under that chapter.

paras.t: Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus, id est in apparatu atque modestia faciei. Interiora namque per exteriora noscuntur, et dispositio ac qualitas mentis, in vultu et oculis præcipue repræsentantur, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus. De hoc dictum est super illud Proverbiorum: Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium, sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus. Insuper, Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus, id est, per oris responsionem innotescit sapientia intellectus: similiter per gestus ipsius vultus, sicut per risus refrenationem, dum vana et frivola videntur et audiuntur; per bonam mœstitiam, dum verba detractoria aut lasciva seu consimilia proferuntur; per diligentem auscultationem verborum ad rem spectantium.
paras.en: [[8:1|The wisdom of a man shineth in his countenance|Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus]], that is, in the bearing and modesty of the face. For inward things are known by outward ones, and the disposition and quality of the mind are shown above all in the face and the eyes, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:26|A man is known by his look, and a wise man, when thou meetest him, is known by his countenance.|Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus.]] Of this we spoke on that word of Proverbs: [[Prov 27:19|As the faces of them that look therein, shine in the water, so the hearts of men are laid open to the wise.|Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium, sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus.]] Further, [[8:1|The wisdom of a man shineth in his countenance|Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus]], that is, the wisdom of the understanding becomes known by the answer of the mouth; and likewise by the bearing of the face itself, as by restraining laughter when vain and frivolous things are seen and heard; by a good sadness when words of detraction, wantonness or the like are uttered; by attentive listening to words that bear on the matter.

paras.t: Et Potentissimus faciem illius commutabit: id est, Deus omnipotens faciem sapientis interiorem et exteriorem ad placitum suum diversimode alterabit, afficiet et movebit, nunc jucunditatem, nunc tristitiam, nunc spei fiduciam, nunc timoris vehementiam infundendo. Unde in Proverbiis scriptum est: Cor regis in manu Dei est; quocumque voluerit, vertet illud; atque in Job, Qui immutat cor principum terræ. Hinc loquitur Isaias: Qui sperant in Domino, mutabunt fortitudinem.
paras.en: [[8:1|and the most mighty will change his face|Et Potentissimus faciem illius commutabit]]: that is, almighty God will alter, affect and move the inner and outer face of the wise man in various ways at His pleasure, pouring in now gladness, now sadness, now the confidence of hope, now the vehemence of fear. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 21:1|the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord: whithersoever he will, he shall turn it|Cor regis in manu Dei est; quocumque voluerit, vertet illud]]; and in Job: [[Job 12:24|He changeth the heart of the princes|Qui immutat cor principum terræ]]. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 40:31|they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength|Qui sperant in Domino, mutabunt fortitudinem]].

8.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI OCTAVI : EGO OS REGIS OBSERVO, ET PRÆCEPTA JURAMENTI DEI.
8.title_en: Exposition of the eighth chapter: I observe the mouth of the king, and the commandments of the oath of God.

paras.t: Dixit Salomon in fine præcedentis capituli : Potentissimus faciem illius, scilicet hominis, commutabit. Ideo docet hic, quid ipse ad hoc egit, et quid nobis agendum sit, ut facies nostra commutetur in melius, atque in resurrectione communi faciem gloriosam recipiamus a Domino. Nam (ut ait Apostolus) omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur.
paras.en: Solomon said at the end of the preceding chapter: [[8:1|the most mighty will change his face|Potentissimus faciem illius, scilicet hominis, commutabit]], that is, the face of man. Therefore he teaches here what he himself did to this end, and what we must do, so that our face may be changed for the better, and that in the common resurrection we may receive a glorious face from the Lord. For (as the Apostle says) [[1 Cor 15:51|We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed|omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur]].

paras.t: Ego os regis observo, id est, verba a Deo omnipotente procedentia, diligenter adverto, et mandata Decalogi ore ejus prolata custodio : et præcepta juramenti Dei, id est etiam præcepta cærimonialia ac judicialia : quæ contulit Deus cum juramento seu firma assertione, quod obedientibus sibi conferret præmia copiosa. Quæ etiam præcepta populus Israel accepit cum grandi affirmatione, quod obediret, juxta illud in Exodo : Omnia quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus, et erimus obedientes. Porro cærimonialia legis præcepta, Evangelio divulgato, jam cessaverunt, quoniam erant figurativa rerum nunc impletarum. Præcepta quoque judicialia, populum Israel specialiter concernebant.
paras.en: [[8:2|I observe the mouth of the king|Ego os regis observo]], that is, I carefully attend to the words that proceed from almighty God, and I keep the commandments of the Decalogue uttered by his mouth: [[8:2|and the commandments of the oath of God|et præcepta juramenti Dei]], that is, also the ceremonial and judicial precepts, which God gave with an oath or firm assurance that he would bestow abundant rewards on those who obey him. These precepts the people of Israel also received with a great affirmation that they would obey, according to that in Exodus: [[Ex 24:7|All things that the Lord hath spoken, we will do, we will be obedient|Omnia quæ locutus est Dominus, faciemus, et erimus obedientes]]. But the ceremonial precepts of the law have now ceased, since the Gospel has been spread abroad, because they were figures of things now fulfilled. The judicial precepts, too, concerned the people of Israel in particular.

paras.t: Ne festines recedere a facie ejus, id est ab ipso Deo omnia intuente, seu ab ejus sapientia, per inobedientiam atque stultitiam, seu per aversionem mentis tuæ a consideratione et honorificentia gratiosæ ac summæ præsentiæ ejus : sicut Cain, qui egressus a facie Domini, habitavit profugus in terra, ut dicitur in Genesi. Jonas quoque peccavit surgendo ut fugeret a facie Domini. Denique quidam peccant ex infirmitate, id est passionis vehementia et fragilitate humana : qui ad horam resistunt, sed superari se sinunt. Isti non festinant a facie Dei recedere, sed recedunt. Alii vero peccant ex consuetudine prava, ex deliberatione, ex proposito et certa scientia. Isti festinant a Deo recedere, et currunt ad vitia ac infernum. De quibus apud Jeremiam legitur : Induraverunt facies suas supra petram, et noluerunt reverti. De quibus Deus, quasi de eorum perversitate admirans, rursus per Jeremiam locutus est : Quare aversus est populus iste aversione contentiosa? Unde et Zacharias de talibus ait : Noluerunt attendere, et averterunt scapulam recedentes ; et cor suum posuerunt ut adamantem, ne audirent legem. Neque permaneas in opere malo, vel in omissione operis boni. Quamvis humanum sit peccare, diabolicum tamen est in vitio permanere. Qui autem ex infirmitate aut ignorantia peccant, facta informatione et passione cessante, faciliter pœnitent ; qui autem ex habitu pravo, difficulter et raro.
paras.en: [[8:3|Be not hasty to depart from his face|Ne festines recedere a facie ejus]], that is, from God himself, who beholds all things, or from his wisdom, by disobedience and folly, or by turning your mind away from considering and honouring his gracious and supreme presence: like Cain, who [[Gen 4:16|went out from the face of the Lord, and dwelt as a fugitive on the earth|egressus a facie Domini, habitavit profugus in terra]], as is said in Genesis. Jonas too sinned when he [[Jon 1:3|rose up to flee|surgendo ut fugeret]] from the face of the Lord. Now some sin from infirmity, that is, from the violence of passion and human frailty: they resist for a while, but let themselves be overcome. These do not hasten to depart from the face of God, but they do depart. Others sin from wicked habit, from deliberation, of set purpose and with sure knowledge. These hasten to depart from God, and run to vices and to hell. Of them we read in Jeremias: [[Jer 5:3|they have made their faces harder than the rock, and they have refused to return|Induraverunt facies suas supra petram, et noluerunt reverti]]. Of them God, as though marvelling at their perversity, spoke again by Jeremias: [[Jer 8:5|Why then is this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn revolting?|Quare aversus est populus iste aversione contentiosa?]] Hence Zacharias too says of such men: [[Zach 7:11|they would not hearken, and they turned away the shoulder to depart|Noluerunt attendere, et averterunt scapulam recedentes]]; [[Zach 7:12|they made their heart as the adamant stone, lest they should hear the law|et cor suum posuerunt ut adamantem, ne audirent legem]]. [[8:3|and do not continue in an evil work|Neque permaneas in opere malo]], or in the omission of a good work. Though to sin is human, yet to remain in vice is devilish. Those who sin from infirmity or ignorance repent easily once they are instructed and the passion ceases; but those who sin from wicked habit repent with difficulty and seldom.

paras.t: Quia omne quod voluerit Dominus, faciet. Est enim omnipotens et infinite beatus, ideo voluntati ejus nil deest. Qui per Isaiam testatur : Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus fecit, in cœlo et in terra, in mari et in omnibus abyssis.
paras.en: [[8:3|for he will do all that pleaseth him|Quia omne quod voluerit Dominus, faciet]]: for he is almighty and infinitely blessed, and so nothing is wanting to his will. He testifies by Isaias: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]]. Wherefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 134:6|Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done, in heaven, in earth, in the sea, and in all the deeps|Omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus fecit, in cœlo et in terra, in mari et in omnibus abyssis]].

paras.t: Et sermo illius potestate plenus est, id est efficax ad agendum, præsertim sermo ejus in ipso manens. Unde sæpe in Genesi dicitur : Dixit Deus, Fiat hoc aut illud; et factum est ita. Proprie autem sermo Dei loquentis, est unigenitus Filius ejus, sermo ac Verbum æterni Patris. De quo ad Hebræos ait Apostolus : Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti. Hic sermo omnipotens est sicut et Pater ; et utriusque, imo totius superessentialis, incomprehensibilis et supergloriosissimæ Trinitatis, est una et indivisa potestas. De hoc sermone alibi sic habetur : Omnipotens sermo tuus, Domine, a regalibus sedibus venit. Hinc dixisse Dei, fecisse est : cui, quum voluerit, subest posse.
paras.en: [[8:4|And his word is full of power|Et sermo illius potestate plenus est]], that is, effective in acting, above all his word abiding in himself. Hence it is often said in Genesis: God said, Let this or that be made; and it was so done[[Gen 1:3||]] [the margin gives Gen. i, 3, 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 15, 24]. But properly the word of God speaking is his only-begotten Son, the Word and Utterance of the eternal Father [*sermo* and *Verbum*, both "word"]. Of him the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword|Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax, et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti]]. This Word is almighty as the Father also is; and there is one undivided power of both, nay, of the whole superessential, incomprehensible and most supremely glorious Trinity. Of this Word it is said elsewhere: [[Wis 18:15|Thy Almighty word|Omnipotens sermo tuus]], O Lord, came [[Wis 18:15|from thy royal throne|a regalibus sedibus]]. Hence for God, to have said is to have done: [[Wis 12:18|thy power is at hand when thou wilt|cui, quum voluerit, subest posse]].

paras.t: Nec dicere ei quisquam potest : Quare ita facis? Hoc, de jure et licite seu per resistentiam efficacem, nullus potest dicere Deo, qui est causa, mensura et regula prima omnis juris et virtutis ac totius ordinis rerum, juxta illud Isaiæ : Cum quo iniit consilium, et instruxit eum, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi? Unde ait Apostolus : Ex ipso, et per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia. Cui alio loco dicitur : Virtus tua, justitiæ initium est. Quum ergo nequeamus Omnipotenti resistere, nec ejus sapientiam aut judicia increpare, nec manum ejus effugere, nec appellare ab ipso; hoc solum restat et consulendum ac necessarium nobis est, ut confugiamus ad ipsum, obediendo eidem humiliter, sine discussione temeraria præceptorum, consiliorum et judiciorum ipsius. Ideo dixit Propheta : Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam? Sed et sanctus Job istud perpendens, ait : Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest; et anima ejus quodcumque voluit, hoc fecit. Idcirco a facie ejus turbatus sum, et considerans eum, timore sollicitor. Hinc saluberrime ait, et sapientissime consulit Scriptura, dicendo : Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem, et per hoc habebis fructus optimos.
paras.en: [[8:4|neither can any man say to him: Why dost thou so?|Nec dicere ei quisquam potest : Quare ita facis?]] No one can say this to God by right and lawfully, or with effective resistance, for he is the first cause, measure and rule of all right and virtue and of the whole order of things, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 40:14|With whom hath he consulted, and who hath instructed him|Cum quo iniit consilium, et instruxit eum]], [[Is 40:14|and shewed him the way of understanding|et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi]]? Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 11:36|of him, and by him, and in him, are all things|Ex ipso, et per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia]]. To him it is said in another place: [[Wis 12:16|thy power is the beginning of justice|Virtus tua, justitiæ initium est]] [*virtus*, "power", is also "virtue"]. Since, then, we can neither resist the Almighty, nor find fault with his wisdom or his judgments, nor escape his hand, nor appeal from him, this alone remains for us, and is to be counselled and is necessary: that we take refuge in him, obeying him humbly, without rash debate over his precepts, counsels and judgments. Therefore the Prophet said: [[Ps 138:7|Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face?|Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? et quo a facie tua fugiam?]] And holy Job too, weighing this, says: [[Job 23:13|he is alone, and no man can turn away his thought: and whatsoever his soul hath desired, that hath he done|Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest; et anima ejus quodcumque voluit, hoc fecit]]. [[Job 23:15|therefore I am troubled at his presence, and when I consider him, I am made pensive with fear|Idcirco a facie ejus turbatus sum, et considerans eum, timore sollicitor]]. Hence Scripture says most wholesomely and counsels most wisely: [[Job 22:21|Submit thyself then to him, and be at peace: and thereby thou shalt have the best fruits|Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem, et per hoc habebis fructus optimos]].

paras.t: Qui custodit præceptum, id est universa præcepta Dei, et vicariorum ipsius. De quibus denuntiat : Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit. Qui autem offendit in uno, fit omnium reus. Non experietur quidquam mali, id est, nihil sustinebit supplicii in futuro, dummodo perseveraverit usque in finem, et tam perfecte ea impleverit, ut nihil purgandum deferat secum. Quod si lignum, fœnum, stipulam portaverit secum, purgatorium sustinebit; ac (juxta Apostolum) salvus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem. Et non solum nil mali experietur, sed et plenam beatitudinem consequetur.
paras.en: [[8:5|He that keepeth the commandment|Qui custodit præceptum]], that is, all the commandments of God and of his vicars, of whom he declares: [[Luke 10:16|He that heareth you heareth me: and he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. And whosoever shall [[Jas 2:10|offend in one point, is become guilty of all|offendit in uno, fit omnium reus]]. [[8:5|shall find no evil|Non experietur quidquam mali]], that is, he will suffer no punishment in the life to come, provided he perseveres to the end and fulfils them so perfectly that he carries nothing with him to be purged. But if he carries with him [[1 Cor 3:12|wood, hay, stubble|lignum, fœnum, stipulam]], he will suffer purgatory[[1 Cor 3:13||]]; and (according to the Apostle) [[1 Cor 3:15|he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire|salvus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem]]. And not only will he find no evil, but he will also obtain full beatitude.

paras.t: Tempus et responsionem cor sapientis intelligit, id est, considerat quid cui tempori congruat, et quod ipsum tempus incessabiliter currat ac defluat. Tempus quoque judicii pensat, et qualiter debeat respondere, advertit. Attendit quoque aliorum responsa, ut proficiat ex eisdem, vel erronea reprobet. Hinc princeps Apostolorum hortatur : Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem de ea, quæ in vobis est, fide et spe. Mansuete ergo, opportune ac sapienter est respondendum. Propter quod in Job scriptum est : Numquid sapiens respondebit quasi in ventum loquens, et implebit ardore stomachum suum?
paras.en: [[8:5|The heart of a wiser man understandeth time and answer|Tempus et responsionem cor sapientis intelligit]], that is, it considers what befits each time, and that time itself runs on and flows away without ceasing. It weighs also the time of judgment, and takes heed how it ought to answer. It attends also to the answers of others, so as to profit by them, or to reject those that are mistaken. Hence the prince of the Apostles exhorts: [[1 Pet 3:15|being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you|Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem de ea, quæ in vobis est, fide et spe]] [Denis reads "of that faith and hope which is in you"]. One must answer, then, gently, at the right time and wisely. Wherefore it is written in Job: [[Job 15:2|Will a wise man answer as if he were speaking in the wind, and fill his stomach with burning heat?|Numquid sapiens respondebit quasi in ventum loquens, et implebit ardore stomachum suum?]]

paras.t: Omni negotio tempus est et opportunitas : id est, unumquodque opus fieri debet suo loco et tempore opportuno. Locus quippe et tempus, sunt circumstantiæ generales in omni actu virtutis humanæ. Propter quod dictum est supra : Omnia tempus habent. Hinc legi naturæ et sacramentis ac sacrificiis ejus, successit lex Moysis cum sacramentis et sacrificiis suis : quibus evangelica lex cum sacrificiis et sacramentis suis successit. Unde et in Esther scriptum est : Nec æstimare debetis, si pro temporum varietate diversa jubeamus, ex animi nostri levitate venire, sed pro qualitate et necessitate temporum, ut rei publicæ poscit utilitas, ferre sententiam.
paras.en: [[8:6|There is a time and opportunity for every business|Omni negotio tempus est et opportunitas]], that is, each work ought to be done in its own place and at the fitting time. For place and time are general circumstances in every act of human virtue. Wherefore it was said above: [[Eccles 3:1|All things have their season|Omnia tempus habent]]. Hence the law of nature with its sacraments and sacrifices was succeeded by the law of Moses with its sacraments and sacrifices, and these were succeeded by the law of the Gospel with its sacrifices and sacraments. Hence it is written also in Esther: [[Esth 16:9|Neither must you think|Nec æstimare debetis]], if according to the variety of times [[Esth 16:9|we command different things|diversa jubeamus]], [[Esth 16:9|that it cometh of the levity of our mind|ex animi nostri levitate venire]], [[Esth 16:9|but that we give sentence according to the quality and necessity of times, as the profit of the commonwealth requireth|sed pro qualitate et necessitate temporum, ut rei publicæ poscit utilitas, ferre sententiam]].

paras.t: Et multa hominis afflictio, quia ignorat præterita, et futura nullo potest scire nuntio. Circa hoc quidam scribit : Futura præmia non potest homo scire per se, vel per alium humana investigatione : et hoc causat afflictionem aliquam in adimpletione præceptorum. Si enim sciret futura præmia, non esset aliqua afflictio in impletione præceptorum, sed magis consolatio. Istud inidonee dictum videtur. Primo, quoniam quamvis futura præmia demonstrative non scimus, tamen indubitanter hæc credimus. Et quamvis major dicatur certitudo scientiæ, quam fidei, loquendo de certitudine evidentiæ : loquendo tamen de certitudine adhærentiæ, fides certior exstat scientia. Secundo, quoniam afflictio in actibus bonis fidelium, non consurgit ex defectu nescientiæ seu incertitudinis præmiorum, de quibus nil ambigunt; sed ex rebellione sensualitatis ac fomite, et vitiorum reliquiis, et gravitate ac lassitudine corporis, quod aggravat animam, ex dæmonum etiam tentamentis. Tertio, quia et Paulus præmia illa clare intuitus et expertus, reversus ad se, interdum sensit afflictiones in actibus bonis : quia et stimulum carnis sustinuit, et diversa pœnalia, quæ ad Corinthios narrat.
paras.en: [[8:6|and great affliction for man|Et multa hominis afflictio]], [[8:7|Because he is ignorant of things past, and things to come he cannot know by any messenger|quia ignorat præterita, et futura nullo potest scire nuntio]]. On this a certain writer says: Man cannot know the rewards to come by himself, or through another, by human inquiry; and this causes some affliction in fulfilling the commandments. For if he knew the rewards to come, there would be no affliction in fulfilling the commandments, but rather consolation. This seems to be ill said. First, because, although we do not know the rewards to come by demonstration, yet we believe them without doubting. And although the certitude of knowledge is said to be greater than that of faith, speaking of the certitude of evidence, yet, speaking of the certitude of adherence, faith is more certain than knowledge [that is, knowledge is more certain in that its object is seen, faith in the firmness with which the mind holds to its object]. Secondly, because affliction in the good acts of the faithful does not arise from want of knowledge or from uncertainty about the rewards, of which they have no doubt, but from the rebellion of sensuality and the fomes [that is, the tinder of sin, the inclination to evil left by original sin], and the remnants of vices, and the weight and weariness of the body, which [[Wis 9:15|is a load upon the soul|aggravat animam]], and also from the temptations of the demons. Thirdly, because Paul too, after clearly beholding and experiencing those rewards[[2 Cor 12:4||]], when he came back to himself, at times felt afflictions in good acts: for he both bore the sting of the flesh[[2 Cor 12:7||]] and the various sufferings that he tells to the Corinthians[[2 Cor 12:10||]].

paras.t: Est itaque exponendum : Et multa hominis afflictio, quia ignorat præterita. Si enim sciret præterita, qualiter ab initio mundi, electi et sancti Dei passi sunt multa et magna adversa, et qualiter Deus sæpe ac dire etiam in sæculo isto punivit iniquos, et consolatus est coronavitque justos ; posset se consolari in multis, et bonis actibus alacriter immorari, vitiisque indefesse reniti. Et futura nullo scire potest nuntio : id est, nullus hominum, nisi super hoc informatus, potest ei prænunciare pro certo futura pure contingentia, sibi aliisque ventura. Ideo sæpe sibi occurrunt tristia et adversa, dum speravit læta et prospera. Sicque dupliciter affligitur : quoniam improvise talia ei occurrunt (jacula enim prævisa minus affligunt), et quia spei suæ inveniuntur contraria. Unde et Jeremias locutus est : Sustinuimus pacem, et non venit : et tempus curationis, et ecce turbatio. Et Poeta : Nescia mens hominum fati sortisque futuræ. Semper igitur simus ad quæcumque adversa parati, ac clypeo patientiæ præmuniti.
paras.en: It is therefore to be explained thus: [[8:6|and great affliction for man|Et multa hominis afflictio]], [[8:7|Because he is ignorant of things past|quia ignorat præterita]]. For if he knew things past, how from the beginning of the world the elect and saints of God suffered many and great adversities, and how God has often and severely punished the wicked even in this world, and has consoled and crowned the just, he could console himself in many things, and dwell eagerly on good acts, and resist vices untiringly. [[8:7|and things to come he cannot know by any messenger|Et futura nullo scire potest nuntio]], that is, no man, unless he has been informed of it, can foretell to him with certainty things to come that are purely contingent [that is, that depend on free choice or chance, and so are not determined in their causes], which will befall him and others. Therefore sad and adverse things often befall him while he hoped for joyful and prosperous ones. And so he is afflicted in two ways: because such things come upon him unforeseen (for darts foreseen wound less), and because they are found contrary to his hope. Hence Jeremias too spoke: We waited for peace, and it came not[[Jer 8:15||]]: and [[Jer 14:19|for the time of healing, and behold trouble|tempus curationis, et ecce turbatio]] [the margin gives Jer. viii, 15; xiv, 19; Denis's words are closest to xiv, 19]. And the Poet: The mind of men knows not fate and the lot to come [Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 501]. Let us therefore be always ready for any adversities whatever, and armed beforehand with the shield of patience.

paras.t: Non est in hominis ditione, prohibere spiritum : id est, in potestate ac dominio hominis non est, aliorum corda seu spiritum ad suum libitum immutare, ac prohibere a conceptu et opere eis placentibus ; nec potentiorum animos valet reprimere a persecutione et oppressione infirmiorum, nec propriam mentem a fluctuatione cogitationum et varietate affectionum. Propter quod ait Bernardus : Non puto quod animum clausit a cogitationibus, qui cœlum clausit orationibus, puta Elias. Nec his obstat quod ait Apostolus : Spiritus Prophetarum, Prophetis subjecti sunt. Hoc enim dixit contra quosdam hæreticos, asserentes Prophetas esse locutos tanquam arreptitios et insanos. Contra quod docet Apostolus, quod per liberum usum rationis dominabantur sibimetipsis, quemadmodum et nos possumus cogitationibus affectibusque perversis resistere, quamvis eorum ortum non valeamus jugiter prævenire ac prohibere.
paras.en: [[8:8|It is not in man's power to stop the spirit|Non est in hominis ditione, prohibere spiritum]] [Denis reads *ditione*, "dominion"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *potestate*, "power"], that is, it is not in man's power and dominion to change the hearts or spirit of others at his pleasure, and to stop them from what they please to conceive and do; nor can he restrain the minds of the more powerful from persecuting and oppressing the weaker, nor his own mind from the wavering of thoughts and the changing of affections. Wherefore Bernard says: I do not think that he shut his mind against thoughts, who shut heaven by his prayers, that is, Elias[[3 Kings 17:1||]][[3 Kings 17:7||]]. Nor does what the Apostle says stand against this: [[1 Cor 14:32|the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets|Spiritus Prophetarum, Prophetis subjecti sunt]]. For he said this against certain heretics who asserted that the Prophets spoke as men possessed and out of their minds. Against this the Apostle teaches that by the free use of reason they were masters of themselves, just as we too can resist perverse thoughts and affections, though we cannot always forestall and stop their rising.

paras.t: Insuper non est in hominis ditione, prohibere spiritum suum quum suo tempore recedat a corpore. Ideo subditur : nec habet potestatem in die mortis retinere animam suam in corpore. Horum quoque qui persequuntur nunc et opprimunt alios, tunc cessat potestas. Nec sinitur quiescere ingruente bello : quia dum homo impugnatur a dæmonibus, mundo, aut acie vitiorum, non potest quiescere, sed oportet eum resistere aut succumbere. Quod bellum tempore mortis a dæmonibus fortissime ac periculosissime excitatur in homine. Neque salvabit impietas impium : imo gravabit atque damnabit eum. Quidam autem in suis simulationibus, fraudibus, malitiisque confidunt, quasi per talia queant salvari. Qui dicunt in Isaia : Posuimus mendacium spem nostram, et mendacio protecti sumus. De quibus et apud alium Prophetam legitur : Væ qui lætamini in nihilo, et dicitis : Numquid non in fortitudine nostra assumpsimus nobis cornua?
paras.en: Moreover, it is not in man's power to stop his own spirit when in its time it departs from the body. Therefore he adds: [[8:8|neither hath he power in the day of death|nec habet potestatem in die mortis]] to keep his soul in the body. The power, too, of those who now persecute and oppress others ceases then. [[8:8|neither is he suffered to rest when war is at hand|Nec sinitur quiescere ingruente bello]]: for while a man is assailed by the demons, the world, or the battle line of vices, he cannot rest, but must resist or give way. And this war is stirred up in man by the demons most fiercely and most dangerously at the time of death. [[8:8|neither shall wickedness save the wicked|Neque salvabit impietas impium]]: nay, it will weigh him down and damn him. Some trust in their pretences, frauds and malice, as though they could be saved by such things. They say in Isaias: [[Is 28:15|we have placed our hope in lies, and by falsehood we are protected|Posuimus mendacium spem nostram, et mendacio protecti sumus]]. Of them we read also in another Prophet: Woe to you [[Amos 6:14|that rejoice in a thing of nought: you that say: Have we not taken unto us horns by our own strength?|qui lætamini in nihilo, et dicitis : Numquid non in fortitudine nostra assumpsimus nobis cornua?]]

paras.t: Omnia hæc præinducta ac subsequentia consideravi, et dedi cor meum, id est, applicui illud ad considerandum, in cunctis operibus, id est in quibusdam de cunctis generibus operum, quæ fiunt sub sole : præsertim inter homines. Interdum dominatur homo homini in malum suum, id est ad majorem suam damnationem, quando videlicet negligenter, carnaliter, scandalose, aut superbe se habet in officio præsidentiæ suæ : quia tunc Dominus requirit de manu ipsius animas pereuntium subditorum sub ipso. Et quo ejus gradus est altior, et quo pluribus præest, eo ruina ipsius est gravior. Et unusquisque prælatus ac præsidens tot mortibus, tot damnationibus dignus est, quot subditi scandalizantur sub eo, et ex ejus vitiis periclitantur, ut ait Gregorius. Nempe qui coram aliis male agit, quantum in ipso est, eos a quibus videtur, occidit, ut asserit Augustinus. Denique taliter præsidens, dominatur subditis etiam in magnum malum ipsorum : quia sub ejus regimine pereunt, prout in Jeremia fertur : Quia stulte egerunt pastores, omnis grex eorum dissipatus est.
paras.en: [[8:9|All these things|Omnia hæc]], those set down before and those that follow, [[8:9|I have considered, and applied my heart|consideravi, et dedi cor meum]], that is, I applied it to consider, [[8:9|to all the works|in cunctis operibus]], that is, to some of all the kinds of works [[8:9|that are done under the sun|quæ fiunt sub sole]], above all among men. [[8:9|Sometimes one man ruleth over another to his own hurt|Interdum dominatur homo homini in malum suum]], that is, to his own greater damnation: namely when he behaves negligently, carnally, scandalously or proudly in his office of authority; for then the Lord requires at his hand the souls of the subjects under him who perish[[Ezech 3:18||]][[Ezech 3:20||]][[Ezech 33:6||]][[Ezech 33:8||]]. And the higher his rank, and the more men he is set over, the heavier is his fall. And every prelate and ruler deserves as many deaths, as many damnations, as there are subjects scandalized under him and endangered by his vices, as Gregory says. Indeed, he who does evil before others kills, as far as in him lies, those by whom he is seen, as Augustine asserts. Again, one who rules in such a way rules his subjects also to their great hurt, for they perish under his government, as is said in Jeremias: [[Jer 10:21|Because the pastors have done foolishly|Quia stulte egerunt pastores]], [[Jer 10:21|all their flock is scattered|omnis grex eorum dissipatus est]].

paras.t: Vidi impios sepultos, id est sepultos quosdam, qui ante et usque ad mortem iniqui fuerunt, nec pœnituerunt; qui etiam quum adhuc viverent, in loco sancto erant, id est in sacris officiis constituti, ita quod erant Dei vicarii ac ministri, et laudabantur in civitate quasi justorum operum, id est, a subditis suis commendabantur ut justi, vel ex adulatione, vel ex timore, vel proprii commodi cupiditate, vel ex ficta justitia. Ex his namque et consimilibus causis, multi subditorum suos laudant superiores, quamvis iniquos. Sed et hoc vanitas est : quia (ut ait Gregorius) culpa vehementer diffunditur, dum is qui peccat, propter sui dignitatem officii honoratur.
paras.en: [[8:10|I saw the wicked buried|Vidi impios sepultos]], that is, certain men buried who had been wicked before and up to their death, and did not repent; [[8:10|who also when they were yet living were in the holy place|qui etiam quum adhuc viverent, in loco sancto erant]], that is, set in sacred offices, so that they were God's vicars and ministers, [[8:10|and were praised in the city as men of just works|et laudabantur in civitate quasi justorum operum]], that is, they were commended as just by their subjects, whether from flattery, or from fear, or from desire of their own advantage, or because of a feigned justice. For from these and like causes many subjects praise their superiors, though they are wicked. [[8:10|but this also is vanity|Sed et hoc vanitas est]]: for (as Gregory says) the fault spreads widely when he who sins is honoured for the dignity of his office.

paras.t: Etenim, quia non cito profertur contra malos sententia divini judicii : Deus enim pluribus diu parcit, ut convertantur, juxta illud Sapientiæ, Dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam ; absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala. Hoc de intimoratis et excæcatis hominibus est intelligendum : qui ex dilatione vindictæ, fiunt ad peccandum audaciores, non considerantes rigorem divini judicii, vel persuadentes sibi vanissime quod postea pœnitebunt, vel quod sufficiat pœnitere in fine vitæ, quemadmodum per Ezechielem Dominus loquitur : Quacumque hora peccator ingemuerit, omnium peccatorum suorum non recordabor. Et quoniam vident alios diu impune peccasse, putant sibi quoque periculum non instare. Isti ingrati ac obdurati, non pensantes occulta ac metuenda Dei judicia, abutuntur patientia Dei. Quibus ad Romanos loquitur Paulus : Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit ? Secundum duritiam autem tuam, et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die justi judicii Dei. O quam paucissimi eorum, qui tempore sanitatis ac juventutis Deum tam intimorate et irrefrenate offendunt, in fine aut senio veraciter pœnitent ! Verumtamen ex tanta dilatione punitionis pravorum, non debet quis pronior esse ad culpam. Propterea subditur :
paras.en: [[8:11|For because sentence is not speedily pronounced against the evil|Etenim, quia non cito profertur contra malos sententia]], the sentence of the divine judgment (for God spares many for a long time, that they may be converted, according to that of Wisdom: [[Wis 11:24|overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|Dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]]), [[8:11|the children of men commit evils without any fear|absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala]]. This is to be understood of fearless and blinded men, who become bolder in sinning because punishment is delayed, not considering the rigour of the divine judgment, or persuading themselves most vainly that they will repent later, or that it is enough to repent at the end of life, according as the Lord speaks by Ezechiel: In what hour soever the sinner shall groan, I will remember no more all his sins[[Ezech 18:21||]][[Ezech 18:22||]] [this saying is a common paraphrase of Ezechiel rather than his words; the margin gives Ezech. xviii, 21, 22]. And because they see that others have long sinned unpunished, they think that no danger threatens them either. These ungrateful and hardened men, not weighing the hidden and fearful judgments of God, abuse the patience of God. To them Paul speaks in Romans: [[Rom 2:4|Knowest thou not that the benignity of God leadeth thee to penance?|Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit]] [[Rom 2:5|But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath|Secundum duritiam autem tuam, et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram]] in the day of [[Rom 2:5|the just judgment of God|justi judicii Dei]]. O how very few of those who in the time of health and youth offend God so fearlessly and so unrestrainedly truly repent at the end or in old age! Yet no one ought to be more prone to sin because the punishment of the wicked is so long delayed. Therefore he adds:

paras.t: Attamen peccator ex eo quod centies, id est diu ac sæpissime, facit malum, id est peccata mortalia, etiam bona debita omittendo. Itaque numerus determinatus pro indeterminato hic ponitur, quum dicitur, Centies : sicut in Evangelio : Non dico tibi, Usque septies; sed, Usque septuagesies septies. Et per patientiam sustentatur, id est, misericorditer sustinetur, conservatur, et nutritur a Deo in vita naturæ, non obstantibus tot et tantis ejus sceleribus. Ego cognovi quod erit bonum timentibus Deum filiali timore, qui verentur faciem ejus omnia intuentis, ita quod dicere queunt : Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo. Si enim Deus iniquis ac reprobis, ingratis et pessimis largitur et diu conservat dona naturæ, bona fortunæ, et beneficia multa in præsenti hac vita, non dubium quin gratis, justis, ac timoratis dabit bona incomparabiliter meliora, videlicet charismata gratiæ in præsenti, et dona gloriæ in futuro, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt. Hinc per Malachiam ait Altissimus : Convertimini, et videbitis quid sit inter justum et impium ; et inter servientem Deo, et non servientem ei. Ecce enim dies veniet succensa quasi ignis, et erunt omnes superbi et omnes facientes impietatem, stipula, et inflammabit eos ; et orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ, et sanitas in pennis vestris.
paras.en: [[8:12|But though a sinner do evil a hundred times|Attamen peccator ex eo quod centies]]: *a hundred times*, that is, for a long time and very often; [[8:12|do evil|facit malum]], that is, mortal sins, also by omitting the good he owes. So a definite number is put here for an indefinite one when it says *a hundred times*: as in the Gospel: [[Matt 18:22|I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times|Non dico tibi, Usque septies; sed, Usque septuagesies septies]]. [[8:12|and by patience be borne withal|Et per patientiam sustentatur]], that is, he is mercifully borne with, preserved and nourished by God in the life of nature, in spite of so many and so great crimes of his. [[8:12|I know from thence that it shall be well with them that fear God|Ego cognovi quod erit bonum timentibus Deum]] with filial fear, [[8:12|who dread his face|qui verentur faciem ejus]], who beholds all things, so that they can say: [[Ps 118:168|I have kept thy commandments and thy testimonies: because all my ways are in thy sight|Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo]]. For if God lavishes on the wicked and reprobate, the ungrateful and the very worst, and long preserves to them, the gifts of nature, the goods of fortune and many benefits in this present life, no doubt he will give to the grateful, the just and the God-fearing goods incomparably better: the charisms of grace in the present, and in the future the gifts of glory, which [[1 Cor 2:9|eye hath not seen, nor ear heard: neither hath it entered into the heart of man|nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt]]. Hence the Most High says by Malachias: Be converted, and you [[Mal 3:18|shall see the difference between the just and the wicked: and between him that serveth God, and him that serveth him not|videbitis quid sit inter justum et impium ; et inter servientem Deo, et non servientem ei]]. [[Mal 4:1|For behold the day shall come kindled as a furnace: and all the proud, and all that do wickedly shall be stubble|Ecce enim dies veniet succensa quasi ignis, et erunt omnes superbi et omnes facientes impietatem, stipula]] [Denis reads *quasi ignis*, "as a fire", for *quasi caminus*, "as a furnace"], and [[Mal 4:1|shall set them on fire|inflammabit eos]]; and [[Mal 4:2|unto you that fear my name, the Sun of justice shall arise|orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ]], and health in your wings [Denis reads *vestris*, "your", for *ejus*, "his"].

paras.t: Præterea, quia iniqui et reprobi, indigni et ingrati sunt prætactis beneficiis Dei, Salomon zelo justitiæ subdit : Non sit bonum, id est temporalis prosperitas, impio : quia abutitur ea; nec prolongentur dies ejus, id est, non diu vivat : quia quo vivit diutius, peccat enormius, et graviorem sibi damnationem mereatur. Sed quasi umbra transeant, qui non timent faciem Domini, quem tam graviter inhonorant, et alios scandalizant. Itaque transeant quasi umbra, non diu tendendo ad mortem, sed cito corruendo in eam. Istud itaque dicitur non zelo invidiæ aut vindictæ, sed potius ex amore et zelo justitiæ. Ideo non repugnat verbo Psalmistæ, dicentis : Noli æmulari in malignantibus.
paras.en: Further, because the wicked and reprobate are unworthy of the benefits of God just mentioned, and ungrateful for them, Solomon adds out of zeal for justice: [[8:13|But let it not be well|Non sit bonum]] (*well*, that is, temporal prosperity) [[8:13|with the wicked|impio]], because he abuses it; [[8:13|neither let his days be prolonged|nec prolongentur dies ejus]], that is, let him not live long: for the longer he lives, the more grievously he sins, and the heavier the damnation he earns. [[8:13|but as a shadow let them pass away that fear not the face of the Lord|Sed quasi umbra transeant, qui non timent faciem Domini]], whom they so grievously dishonour, and they scandalize others. Let them pass away, then, as a shadow, not drawing slowly towards death, but quickly falling into it. This, then, is said not out of the zeal of envy or revenge, but rather out of love and zeal for justice. Therefore it does not conflict with the word of the Psalmist, who says: [[Ps 36:1|Be not emulous of evildoers|Noli æmulari in malignantibus]].

paras.t: Est et alia vanitas, quæ fit super terram : quia in casu qui sequitur, quamvis sit justa ac sapientialis dispositio Dei, tamen in eodem est etiam inordinatio culpæ, sicut patebit. Sunt justi quibus mala pœnæ proveniunt : multæ enim tribulationes justorum; quasi opera egerint impiorum, id est, ac si peccando meruerint illa pati, et omnino injusti sint. Unde amici Job, videntes eum tam dire percussum, putaverunt eum fuisse hypocritam et iniquum, ac pro suis percussum sceleribus : quemadmodum et amici ac uxor Tobiæ, visa excæcatione ejus tam inopinata. Quum enim pœna debeatur culpæ, dum justi sic affliguntur, putantur suis id meruisse peccatis : sed Deus infligit pœnas suis electis non solum propter eorum demerita, sed etiam ut exercitentur, aliisque in exemplum ponantur, et incrementa gratiæ in præsenti, ac gloriæ in futuro obtineant : vel, ut in curatione seu liberatione eorum, potestas Dei monstretur, sicut de cæco nato ait Salvator : Neque hic peccavit, neque parentes ejus, ut scilicet cæcus nasceretur : sed ut manifestentur opera Dei in illo. De Lazaro quoque ait : Infirmitas hæc non est ad mortem, sed ad gloriam Dei. Et sunt impii qui ita securi sunt, id est tam immunes ac liberi ab adversis, et tam parum aut nihil formidantes de inferni suppliciis, quasi justorum facta habeant, id est, tanquam suis meritis istam securitatem sortiti sint. Nam et perfecta caritas justorum, excludit timorem suppliciorum. Sed et hoc vanissimum judico, quod scilicet impii tam periculosa securitate fruantur.
paras.en: [[8:14|There is also another vanity, which is done upon the earth|Est et alia vanitas, quæ fit super terram]]: for in the case that follows, although God's disposition is just and wise, yet there is in it also the disorder of fault, as will appear. [[8:14|There are just men to whom evils|Sunt justi quibus mala]] of punishment [[8:14|happen|proveniunt]] (for [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|multæ enim tribulationes justorum]]) [[8:14|as though they had done the works of the wicked|quasi opera egerint impiorum]], that is, as if by sinning they had deserved to suffer them, and were altogether unjust. Hence the friends of Job, seeing him so terribly stricken, thought that he had been a hypocrite and wicked, and stricken for his own crimes[[Job 4:7||]][[Job 8:11||]][[Job 11:14||]][[Job 20:4||]][[Job 22:5||]][[Job 34:7||]][[Job 34:36||]][[Job 36:17||]] [the margin gives Job iv, 7–11; viii, 11–19; xi, 14; xx, 4, 5; xxii, 5–10; xxiv, 7, 8, 36, 37; xxxvi, 17; "xxiv" is evidently xxxiv, where Eliu speaks against Job]; as did also the friends and the wife of Tobias, when they saw his blindness come upon him so unexpectedly[[Tob 2:15||]][[Tob 2:16||]][[Tob 2:22||]][[Tob 2:23||]]. For since punishment is due to fault, when the just are so afflicted they are thought to have deserved it by their own sins. But God inflicts punishments on his elect not only for their demerits, but also that they may be exercised, and set as an example to others, and obtain increase of grace in the present and of glory in the future; or that in their healing or deliverance the power of God may be shown, as the Saviour says of the man born blind: [[John 9:3|Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents|Neque hic peccavit, neque parentes ejus]], namely [[John 9:2|that he should be born blind|cæcus nasceretur]]; [[John 9:3|but that the works of God should be made manifest in him|sed ut manifestentur opera Dei in illo]]. Of Lazarus too he says: [[John 11:4|This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God|Infirmitas hæc non est ad mortem, sed ad gloriam Dei]]. [[8:14|and there are wicked men, who are as secure|Et sunt impii qui ita securi sunt]], that is, so free and exempt from adversities, and fearing the torments of hell so little or not at all, [[8:14|as though they had the deeds of the just|quasi justorum facta habeant]], that is, as though they had obtained this security by their own merits. For it is the [[1 John 4:18|perfect charity|perfecta caritas]] of the just that [[1 John 4:18|casteth out fear|excludit timorem]] of punishments. [[8:14|but this also I judge most vain|Sed et hoc vanissimum judico]]: namely, that the wicked enjoy so perilous a security.

paras.t: Verumtamen, quod justi præfata sustinent mala, ex providentia venit divina. Nec malum est, nisi ex parte affligentium justos, qui eos persequendo, enormiter peccant. Verumtamen iste eventus sæpe perturbat et in admirationem convertit pusillos, qui ad præsentia oculos habent, nec pensant quam multipliciter atque ineffabiliter prosit electis et justis, tribulationibus exerceri in vita præsenti. Idcirco in pusillorum persona loquitur Habacuc Deo : Mundi sunt oculi tui, ne videas malum ; et respicere ad iniquitatem non potes. Quare non respicis contemptores, et taces conculcante impio justiorem se ? Sed Gregorius in persona viri perfecti fatetur : Quamvis mira sint judicia Dei, dum justis adversa, et impiis prospera in mundo isto eveniunt; mirabiliora tamen sunt, dum hic justis prospera, et reprobis adversa contingunt.
paras.en: Yet that the just suffer the evils spoken of comes from divine providence. Nor is it evil, except on the part of those who afflict the just, who sin grievously in persecuting them. Yet this happening often troubles the little ones and turns them to wonder, who have their eyes on present things and do not weigh in how many ways and how unspeakably it profits the elect and the just to be exercised by tribulations in the present life. Therefore Habacuc speaks to God in the person of the little ones: [[Hab 1:13|Thy eyes are too pure to behold evil, and thou canst not look on iniquity|Mundi sunt oculi tui, ne videas malum ; et respicere ad iniquitatem non potes]]. Why dost thou not look upon the despisers[[Hab 1:3||]], [[Hab 1:13|and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|et taces conculcante impio justiorem se]] [the margin gives "Cf. Habac. i, 13, 3"; Denis's "Why dost thou not look upon the despisers" differs from the Vulgate's "Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things"] But Gregory, in the person of the perfect man, confesses: Though the judgments of God are wonderful when adversity befalls the just in this world and prosperity the wicked, yet they are more wonderful when here prosperity befalls the just and adversity the reprobate.

paras.t: Laudavi igitur lætitiam, quod non esset homini bonum sub sole, nisi quod comederet et biberet, atque gauderet; et hoc solum secum auferret, id est, consequeretur, nec aliud desuper præmium præstolaretur, de labore suo omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, quos dedit ei Deus sub sole.
