Si istud, ut textus videtur prætendere, intelligatur de carnali lætitia, et corporali manducatione atque potatione; tunc Salomon loquitur ista in carnalis viri persona, ut dictum est sæpe. Si vero hæc spiritualiter exponantur, possunt pertinere ad sapientem : ad quem spectant conscientiæ bonæ lætitia, esus et potus sacramentalis, panisque vitæ et intellectus, et aqua sapientiæ salutaris.
paras.en: [[8:15|Therefore I commended mirth, because there was no good for a man under the sun, but to eat, and drink, and be merry|Laudavi igitur lætitiam, quod non esset homini bonum sub sole, nisi quod comederet et biberet, atque gauderet]]; [[8:15|and that he should take nothing else with him|et hoc solum secum auferret]] [literally "and should take this alone with him"], that is, obtain, and look for no other reward from above, [[8:15|of his labour in the days of his life, which God hath given him under the sun|de labore suo omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, quos dedit ei Deus sub sole]]. If this, as the text seems to put forward, is understood of carnal mirth and of bodily eating and drinking, then Solomon says these things in the person of a carnal man, as has often been said. But if they are explained spiritually, they can belong to the wise man, to whom belong the joy of a good conscience, sacramental eating and drinking, [[Ecclus 15:3|the bread of life and understanding|panisque vitæ et intellectus]], and [[Ecclus 15:3|the water of wholesome wisdom|aqua sapientiæ salutaris]].

paras.t: Et apposui cor meum ut scirem sapientiam, et intelligerem distinctionem, id est discretionem variumque eventum, qui contingit hominibus : ita quod unus prosperatur, alter adversis affligitur; unus prævenitur a Domino, et gratiis adimpletur ab eo, iste indesinenter peccare, ac obdurari permittitur; unus cæcus, alter surdus, aut claudus generatur sive efficitur : quæ versatur in terra. Est homo qui diebus et noctibus somnum sufficientem modicum, non capit oculis suis. Quod autem modicum est, reputatur pro nihilo. Talis igitur vigilat, ut studendo, considerando, sciscitando, valeat horum invenire rationem et causam in speciali : quod curiosum superfluumque consistit. Quamvis enim monstruosorum effectuum quasdam rationes assignent philosophi, talia tamen principaliter referenda sunt ad providentiam Dei. Nec potest quis tradere rationem distinctam, cur anima ista infundatur corpori monstruoso, alia corpori integro, sed ignobili, alia corpori nobili et illustri. Hinc subditur :
paras.en: [[8:16|And I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to understand the distraction|Et apposui cor meum ut scirem sapientiam, et intelligerem distinctionem]] [Denis reads *distinctionem*, "distinction", for the Vulgate's *distentionem*, "distraction"], that is, the difference and varied fortune that befalls men: so that one prospers, another is afflicted with adversities; one is forestalled by the Lord and filled by him with graces, another is permitted to sin without ceasing and to be hardened; one is born or made blind, another deaf or lame: [[8:16|that is upon earth|quæ versatur in terra]]. [[8:16|for there are some that day and night take no sleep|Est homo qui diebus et noctibus somnum]] (that is, no sufficient sleep, but a little) [[8:16|with their eyes|non capit oculis suis]]. For what is little is reckoned as nothing. Such a man, then, keeps watch so that, by studying, considering and inquiring, he may find the reason and cause of these things in particular: which is curious and superfluous. For though the philosophers assign certain reasons for monstrous effects, yet such things are to be referred chiefly to the providence of God. Nor can anyone give a distinct reason why this soul is infused into a monstrous body, another into a sound but ignoble body, another into a noble and illustrious one. Hence he adds:

paras.t: Et intellexi quod omnium operum Dei, videlicet talium abditorum, nullam possit homo invenire rationem eorum quæ fiunt sub sole. Et quanto plus laboraverit ad quærendum talium rationem in particulari, tanto minus invenient : quia justo judicio Deus permittet eum errare, et falsa pro veris inducere : sicut Origeni accidisse timetur. Qui, quum post Apostolos esset præcipuus doctor Ecclesiæ, voluit considerationem suam circa talia nimium profundare; atque ex hoc videtur magnos incidisse errores, sicut in libris Periarchon et Stromatum, et super Threnos, ac Danielem, locisque aliis invenitur. Etiamsi dixerit sapiens, id est in Scripturis eruditus, et qui inter homines sapiens reputatur, aut esse se credit, se nosse talium rationem, non poterit invenire rationem illorum.
paras.en: [[8:17|And I understood that man can find no reason of all those works of God|Et intellexi quod omnium operum Dei]], namely of such hidden things, [[8:17|that are done under the sun|nullam possit homo invenire rationem eorum quæ fiunt sub sole]]. [[8:17|and the more he shall labour to seek|Et quanto plus laboraverit ad quærendum]] the reason of such things in particular, [[8:17|so much the less shall he find|tanto minus invenient]]: for by a just judgment God will permit him to go astray and to bring in false things for true, as it is feared happened to Origen. He, though after the Apostles he was a foremost doctor of the Church, wished to sink his consideration too deep into such things, and from this he seems to have fallen into great errors, as is found in the books *Periarchon* [that is, *Peri Archon*, "On First Principles"] and the *Stromata*, and on Lamentations and Daniel, and in other places. [[8:17|yea, though the wise man shall say|Etiamsi dixerit sapiens]], that is, one learned in the Scriptures, who is reputed wise among men or believes himself so, [[8:17|that he knoweth it|se nosse]], the reason of such things, [[8:17|he shall not be able to find it|non poterit invenire]], the reason of them.

9.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI OCTAVI : EGO OS REGIS OBSERVO, ET PRÆCEPTA JURAMENTI DEI.
9.title_en: Exposition of the eighth chapter: I observe the mouth of the king, and the commandments of the oath of God.
9.note: This article treats chapter 8 and the first verse of chapter 9; its commentary on chapter 8 is shown under that chapter.

paras.t: Omnia hæc tractavi in corde meo per diligentem considerationem, ut curiose intelligerem talium rationem. Quod tamen vitandum est, dicente Apostolo : Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus! Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini? In Jeremia quoque scriptum est : Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit, et audivit sermonem ejus?
paras.en: [[9:1|All these things have I considered in my heart|Omnia hæc tractavi in corde meo]] by diligent consideration, [[9:1|that I might carefully understand|ut curiose intelligerem]] the reason of such things [*curiose*, "carefully" in the Douay-Rheims, also means "with curiosity", the sense Denis takes here]. Yet this is to be avoided, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 11:33|How incomprehensible are his judgments|Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus]]! [[Rom 11:34|For who hath known the mind of the Lord|Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini]]? It is written also in Jeremias: [[Jer 23:18|who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath seen and heard his word?|Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit, et audivit sermonem ejus?]]

paras.t: HIC reprimit hominem ab omni vana securitate, elatione et præsumptione, eo quod nesciat an placeat Deo, an habeat caritatem infusam, an finaliter sit salvandus.
paras.en: Here he restrains man from all vain security, elation and presumption, because he does not know whether he pleases God, whether he has infused charity, or whether he is finally to be saved.

paras.t: Sunt justi atque sapientes habentes sapientiam quæ est donum; et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt, id est, actus eorum interiores et exteriores, ab ipsis oblati, exhibiti, et commissi sunt Deo, tanquam creatori ac judici. Sunt quoque opera eorum in manu Dei, quia conservantur a Deo, et ipse potest judicare de eis ut vult. Et tamen nescit homo, id est, certitudinalem notitiam de isto non habet, videlicet utrum amore an odio dignus sit. Hoc, inquam, nescit homo, quamvis virtuosus ac sapiens sit; quoniam nescit an sit in caritate et statu salutis, an in peccato mortali; sicque ignorat an mereatur et dignus sit amari a Deo, an odio haberi ab eo. Et quamvis experiatur se Deum diligere, ignorat tamen an diligat Deum caritate infusa, an solum naturali et acquisito amore: eo quod tanta sit similitudo et convenientia actuum harum duarum dilectionum, quod homo non valet inter eos certo discernere, ut communiter dicunt doctores. Verumtamen multi pro certo sciunt, aut scire possunt, se esse in peccatis mortalibus, atque ob hoc Deo esse odibiles secundum præsentem justitiam; quid autem finaliter fiet de eis, ignorant.
paras.en: [[9:1|there are just men and wise men|Sunt justi atque sapientes]], having the wisdom which is a gift; [[9:1|and their works are in the hand of God|et opera eorum in manu Dei]]: that is, their acts, interior and exterior, are offered, shown forth and committed by them to God, as to their Creator and Judge. Their works are also in the hand of God because they are preserved by God, and He can judge of them as He wills. [[9:1|and yet man knoweth not|Et tamen nescit homo]], that is, he has no certain knowledge of this, namely [[9:1|whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|utrum amore an odio dignus sit]]. This, I say, man does not know, however virtuous and wise he may be; for he does not know whether he is in charity and in the state of salvation, or in mortal sin; and so he does not know whether he deserves and is worthy to be loved by God, or to be hated by Him. And though he experiences that he loves God, he still does not know whether he loves God with infused charity, or only with a natural and acquired love: because the acts of these two loves are so alike and so much in agreement that man cannot discern between them with certainty, as the doctors commonly say. Yet many know for certain, or can know, that they are in mortal sins, and are therefore hateful to God according to present justice [that is, as they now stand, whatever God foresees of their end]; but what will finally become of them they do not know.

paras.t: Sed omnia in futurum reservantur incerta: id est, Deus interim ista occultat hominibus, sed in futuro generali judicio omnibus innotescet quis a Deo electus sit et dilectus, et quis præscitus; eo quod universa, scilicet prospera et adversa, vita longa et brevis, vitia et virtutes, atque, id est indifferenter, quantum ad apparentiam exteriorem, quamvis coram Deo diversa sit ratio, eveniant justo et impio, quantum ad virtutes infusas, et vitia eis contraria, bono et malo, id est habenti virtutes morales, et eis carenti, mundo, per fidem et sapientiam, et immundo per hæresim, perfidiam et errores, immolanti victimas, et sacrificia contemnenti. Sicut bonus, sic et peccator habet jam dicta. Nam et quidam electi quandoque vitiis sunt subjecti. Similiter virtuosi et electi interdum prosperantur in sæculo, et divitiis ac honore abundant, et reprobi quidam premuntur adversis. Ut perjurus, ita et ille qui verum dejerat, id est, valde affirmat, et multum assertive jurat, prout primo Regum habetur: Addidit Jonathas dejerare David.
paras.en: [[9:2|But all things are kept uncertain for the time to come|Sed omnia in futurum reservantur incerta]]: that is, God meanwhile hides these things from men, but in the future general judgment it will be made known to all who has been chosen and loved by God, and who foreknown [that is, foreseen by God as one who will be lost]; [[9:2|because all things|eo quod universa]], namely prosperity and adversity, long life and short, vices and virtues, [[9:2|equally|atque]] [Denis's text has *atque*, "and", where the Vulgate reads *æque*, "equally"; his gloss gives the sense of *æque*], that is, indifferently as to outward appearance, though before God the account is different, [[9:2|happen to the just and to the wicked|eveniant justo et impio]], as regards the infused virtues and the vices contrary to them, [[9:2|to the good and to the evil|bono et malo]], that is, to him who has the moral virtues and to him who lacks them, [[9:2|to the clean|mundo]] through faith and wisdom, [[9:2|and to the unclean|et immundo]] through heresy, faithlessness and errors, [[9:2|to him that offereth victims, and to him that despiseth sacrifices|immolanti victimas, et sacrificia contemnenti]]. [[9:2|As the good is, so also is the sinner|Sicut bonus, sic et peccator]]: that is, the sinner has the things just named as the good man has them. For even some of the elect are at times subject to vices. Likewise the virtuous and the elect sometimes prosper in the world and abound in riches and honour, and some of the reprobate are pressed by adversities. [[9:2|as the perjured, so he also that sweareth truth|Ut perjurus, ita et ille qui verum dejerat]], that is, who affirms strongly and swears with great assertion, as is found in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 20:17|And Jonathan swore again to David|Addidit Jonathas dejerare David]] [*dejerare*, "to swear solemnly": the same word as in *verum dejerat*, "sweareth truth"].

paras.t: Hoc est pessimum inter omnia quæ fiunt sub sole, quia eadem cunctis eveniunt, id est, similia contingunt quibusdam de omni genere hominum. Sed quum istud ex divina providentia, non sine rationabili causa procedat, quomodo pessimum est? Et respondendum, quod pessimum est, id est valde periculosum quampluribus, atque occasio vitiorum multorum. Propter quod subditur:
paras.en: [[9:3|This is a very great evil among all things that are done under the sun, that the same things happen to all men|Hoc est pessimum inter omnia quæ fiunt sub sole, quia eadem cunctis eveniunt]], that is, like things befall some men of every kind. But since this proceeds from divine providence, and not without a reasonable cause, how is it a very great evil [*pessimum*, literally "the worst"]? The answer is that it is a very great evil, that is, very dangerous to a great many, and an occasion of many vices. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Unde et corda filiorum hominum implentur malitia, id est, in vitiis perseverant ac habituantur, sine timore peccando, ut dictum est, quum videant omnia quasi indifferenter bonis et malis hominibus evenire. Verumtamen talia, quæ in se non sunt bona aut mala moraliter, quæ scilicet justis et injustis communia sunt, philosophi vocant bona media seu indifferentia; sed vulgo sæpe pessima, aut etiam optima esse videntur. Siquidem dona gratiæ gratis datæ, ut potestas faciendi miracula, donum prophetiæ, genera linguarum, maxime reputantur a plebe communi. Sapientes autem dona gratiæ gratum facientis, incomparabiliter amplius magni pendunt et appetunt. Implentur etiam et contemptu in vita sua, ita quod ex superbia se invicem aspernantur, vel superiores suos et eorum jussiones despiciunt, et circa præcepta Dei tam parvam aut nullam habent curam et diligentiam, quod ipso facto ostendunt se præcepta Dei, imo et Deum præcipientem, contemnere. Talibus Dominus per Jeremiam ait : A sæculo confregisti jugum, rupisti vincula, et dixisti, Non serviam; et rursus per Osee, Sicut vacca lasciviens declinavit Israel.
paras.en: [[9:3|whereby also the hearts of the children of men are filled with evil|Unde et corda filiorum hominum implentur malitia]], that is, they persevere in vices and become hardened in the habit of them, sinning without fear, as has been said, since they see all things befall good and bad men as if indifferently. Yet such things as are not in themselves morally good or evil, namely those common to the just and the unjust, the philosophers call middle or indifferent goods; but to the crowd they often seem the worst, or even the best, of things. For the gifts of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: gifts such as miracles and prophecy, given for the good of others, which do not of themselves make the receiver holy], such as the power of working miracles, the gift of prophecy, kinds of tongues, are esteemed most highly by the common people. But the wise value and desire the gifts of sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*: the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God] incomparably more. They are filled also [[9:3|and with contempt while they live|et contemptu in vita sua]], so that out of pride they despise one another, or scorn their superiors and their commands, and have so little care and diligence about the commandments of God, or none, that by that very fact they show that they despise the commandments of God, and indeed God who commands them. To such the Lord says by Jeremias: [[Jer 2:20|Of old time thou hast broken my yoke, thou hast burst my bands, and thou saidst: I will not serve|A sæculo confregisti jugum, rupisti vincula, et dixisti, Non serviam]]; and again by Osee: [[Osee 4:16|Israel hath gone astray like a wanton heifer|Sicut vacca lasciviens declinavit Israel]].

paras.t: Et post hæc ad inferos deducentur. Quibus dicturus est Judex : Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum. Interim vero, quantum ad animas, in infernum dejiciuntur, quemadmodum in Ezechiele habetur : Omnes hi descenderunt ad terram ultimam; et portaverunt ignominiam suam cum his qui descendunt in lacum; et descenderunt ad infernum.
paras.en: [[9:3|and afterwards they shall be brought down to hell|Et post hæc ad inferos deducentur]]. To them the Judge will say: [[Matt 25:41|Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire|Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum]]. Meanwhile, as to their souls, they are cast down into hell, as is found in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 32:24|all of them|Omnes hi]] [[Ezech 32:24|went down uncircumcised to the lowest parts of the earth|descenderunt ad terram ultimam]]; [[Ezech 32:24|and they have borne their shame with them that go down into the pit|et portaverunt ignominiam suam cum his qui descendunt in lacum]]; and they [[Ezech 32:27|went down to hell|descenderunt ad infernum]] [the margin gives Ezech. xxxii, 24, 27: Denis joins words from both verses].

paras.t: Nemo est qui semper vivat vita naturæ in sæculo isto : quia oportet omnem hominem solvere debitum mortis, quum constet ex contrariis elementis, et propter reatum originalis peccati. Unde et quotidie famem, sitim, et consimilia naturæ incommoda, tanquam quotidianas sustinemus infirmitates : contra quas cibo, potu, somno, tanquam medicinalibus remediis utimur. Hinc ait Psalmista : Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem? Et impii dum moriuntur, in infernum labuntur. Et qui hujus rei habeat fiduciam.
paras.en: [[9:4|There is no man that liveth always|Nemo est qui semper vivat]] by the life of nature in this world: for every man must pay the debt of death, since he is made of contrary elements, and because of the guilt of original sin. Hence also we daily bear hunger, thirst and like discomforts of nature as daily infirmities, against which we use food, drink and sleep as medicinal remedies. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 88:49|Who is the man that shall live, and not see death|Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem]]? And the wicked, when they die, slip down into hell. [[9:4|or that hopeth for this|Et qui hujus rei habeat fiduciam]] [literally "and who has confidence in this thing", that is, in living always].

paras.t: Melior est canis vivus leone mortuo. Hoc juxta superficiem litteræ constat, quod res viva, quamvis ratione carens, melior sit, non moraliter, sed bonitate rei, ente non vivo atque cadavere. Iste tamen non est sensus litteralis; sed Salomon metaphorice loquens, per canem vivum, intelligit hominem in carne viventem, utpote peccatorem, qui propter iracundiæ impetum, aut animi sui irrationabilitatem, canis vocatur. Unde de quibusdam in Isaia dicitur : Speculatores ejus cæci omnes; canes muti, non valentes latrare. Per leonem vero mortuum, intelligit hominem iniquum, superbum, jam mortuum corpore : quo melior dicitur peccator adhuc vivens, quoniam potest se emendare, ac vitam promereri beatam; nec est obstinatus in malo totaliter, sicut qui in mortali decesserunt peccato. Hinc subditur :
paras.en: [[9:4|a living dog is better than a dead lion|Melior est canis vivus leone mortuo]]. On the surface of the letter it is plain that a living thing, though it lacks reason, is better (not morally, but in the goodness of the thing) than a thing not living, a carcass. Yet this is not the literal sense; but Solomon, speaking metaphorically, means by the living dog a man living in the flesh, that is, a sinner, who is called a dog because of the violence of his anger or the unreasonableness of his mind. Hence it is said of some in Isaias: [[Is 56:10|His watchmen are all blind|Speculatores ejus cæci omnes]]; [[Is 56:10|dumb dogs not able to bark|canes muti, non valentes latrare]]. By the dead lion he means a wicked and proud man now dead in body: than whom the sinner still living is said to be better, since he can amend himself and merit the blessed life, and is not wholly obstinate in evil, as are those who have died in mortal sin. Hence it is added:

paras.t: Viventes enim sciunt se esse morituros: ideo ex consideratione suæ mortalitatis, possunt per pœnitentiam corrigere vitam, seque parare ad mortem; mortui vero, nihil noverunt amplius. De injustis mortuis loquitur Salomon : quos affirmat nil amplius scire, videlicet in inferno, eo sensu quo infra ait in isto capitulo, quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos : quod paulo post exponetur. Nil quippe salubriter sciunt, quo ad consolationem, relevamen aut pœnitentiam possint juvari. Nec habent ultra mercedem : quia damnati sunt, nec sunt in statu merendi ac demerendi. In hac autem vita, etiam vitiose vivendo, habuerunt quamdam mercedem : quoniam pro quibusdam bonis ex genere, quæ interdum egerunt, contulit eis pius et justus Deus aliquid temporalis prosperitatis, vitæve longioris. Unde diviti condemnato Abraham dixit : Recepisti bona in vita tua. Verum post vitam hanc, cessat hujusmodi merces. Quia oblivioni tradita est memoria eorum : id est, Deus oblitus est eorum, ita quod misericordiam suam aufert ab eis in sempiternum, juxta illud Job : Obliviscatur ejus misericordia; dulcedo illius, vermes. Unde in Osee Dominus loquitur : Quia oblitus es mei, obliviscar et ego tui. Hanc oblivionem misericordiæ Dei merentur iniqui, non Deo, sed vanitatibus inhærendo, quemadmodum scriptum est : Qui custodiunt vanitates, frustra misericordiam suam derelinquunt. Quocontra dicitur de electo : In memoria æterna erit justus. Verumtamen puniuntur citra condignum, idcirco non penitus privantur misericordia.
paras.en: [[9:5|For the living know that they shall die|Viventes enim sciunt se esse morituros]]: therefore, from considering their mortality, they can correct their life through penance and prepare themselves for death; [[9:5|but the dead know nothing more|mortui vero, nihil noverunt amplius]]. Solomon is speaking of the unjust dead, who he declares know nothing more, namely in hell, in the sense in which he says below in this chapter that [[9:10|neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell|nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos]]: which will be explained a little later. For they know nothing to their salvation, nothing by which they could be helped to consolation, relief or penance. [[9:5|neither have they a reward any more|Nec habent ultra mercedem]]: for they are damned, and are not in the state of meriting and demeriting. But in this life, even while living viciously, they had a certain reward: for in return for certain things good in their kind [that is, good in the kind of act, though not meritorious] which they sometimes did, the kind and just God gave them some temporal prosperity, or a longer life. Hence Abraham said to the condemned rich man: [[Luke 16:25|thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime|Recepisti bona in vita tua]]. But after this life such reward ceases. [[9:5|for the memory of them is forgotten|Quia oblivioni tradita est memoria eorum]]: that is, God has forgotten them, so that He takes His mercy away from them for ever, according to that of Job: [[Job 24:20|Let mercy forget him: may worms be his sweetness|Obliviscatur ejus misericordia; dulcedo illius, vermes]]. Hence the Lord says in Osee: Because thou hast forgotten me, I also will forget thee[[Osee 4:6||]] [no margin reference; Denis's words are nearest to Osee 4:6, "thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I also will forget thy children"]. The wicked deserve this forgetting by the mercy of God by cleaving not to God but to vanities, as it is written: [[Jon 2:9|They that in vain observe vanities, forsake their own mercy|Qui custodiunt vanitates, frustra misericordiam suam derelinquunt]]. On the contrary it is said of the elect: [[Ps 111:7|The just shall be in everlasting remembrance|In memoria æterna erit justus]]. Yet since the damned are punished less than they deserve [*citra condignum*, short of what their sins strictly merit], they are not wholly deprived of mercy.

paras.t: Amor quoque, et odium, et invidiæ simul perierunt : id est, inordinatæ et vitiosæ eorum affectiones, quibus quosdam carnaliter amarunt, et Deum aut justos odio habuerunt, jam cum ipsis damnatæ sunt, nec possunt eos juvare. Nec habent partem in hoc sæculo : id est, a corpore Ecclesiæ sunt omnino abscisi, nec caritatis communionem aut participationem cum viventibus habent, nec possidere possunt aliquid hujus mundi; et in opere quod sub sole geritur, id est, in operibus pietatis, quæ pro mortuis fiunt, non habent partem, quia per suffragia talia non juvantur.
paras.en: [[9:6|Their love also, and their hatred, and their envy are all perished|Amor quoque, et odium, et invidiæ simul perierunt]]: that is, their disordered and vicious affections, with which they loved some carnally and held God or the just in hatred, are now damned with them and cannot help them. [[9:6|neither have they any part in this world|Nec habent partem in hoc sæculo]]: that is, they are wholly cut off from the body of the Church, and have no communion or sharing of charity with the living, nor can they possess anything of this world; [[9:6|and in the work that is done under the sun|et in opere quod sub sole geritur]], that is, in the works of piety which are done for the dead, they have no part, for they are not helped by such suffrages.

paras.t: Præterea, per canem vivum, quidam intelligunt pauperem justum, vilem reputatum, tamen instar canis Domino suo fidelem, et pro Deo contra peccata latrantem : qui melior est leone mortuo, id est potente sæculi hujus defuncto.
paras.en: Moreover, by the living dog some understand the just poor man, held to be vile, yet faithful like a dog to his Lord, and barking against sins for God: who is [[9:4|better than a dead lion|melior est leone mortuo]], that is, than a mighty man of this world who has died.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per canem vivum, designatur populus gentilis, in fide et gratia Christi vivens. Unde ad Chananeam dixit Salvator : Non est bonum sumere panem filiorum, et mittere canibus. Canis iste melior est leone mortuo, id est populo Judæorum sua incredulitate perempto, et jam corporaliter pro maxima parte destructo : qui de veritatibus fidei catholicæ nil aut parum agnoscit, atque a Deo relictus est. Quorum amor inordinatus ad legem, et odium ac invidia contra Christum et ejus Apostolos, perierunt.
paras.en: Spiritually, the living dog signifies the Gentile people, living in the faith and grace of Christ. Hence the Saviour said to the woman of Chanaan: [[Matt 15:26|It is not good to take the bread of the children, and to cast it to the dogs|Non est bonum sumere panem filiorum, et mittere canibus]]. This dog is [[9:4|better than a dead lion|melior est leone mortuo]], that is, than the Jewish people, slain by its unbelief and now for the most part destroyed in body: which knows nothing or little of the truths of the Catholic faith, and has been forsaken by God. Their disordered love for the Law, and their hatred and envy against Christ and His Apostles, [[9:6|are all perished|perierunt]].

paras.t: Vade ergo, et comede in lætitia panem tuum, et bibe cum gaudio vinum tuum : id est, corporalem ac spiritualem refectionem sume cum hilaritate in Deo : sicut istud jam sæpe præhabitum est; quia Deo placent opera tua, si feceris ita, et quia hoc ipsum potes sperare, et vivere cum jucunditate in spe.
paras.en: [[9:7|Go then, and eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with gladness|Vade ergo, et comede in lætitia panem tuum, et bibe cum gaudio vinum tuum]]: that is, take bodily and spiritual refreshment with cheerfulness in God, as has often been said already; [[9:7|because thy works please God|quia Deo placent opera tua]], if thou dost so, and because thou canst hope for this very thing, and live with gladness in hope.

paras.t: Omni tempore sint vestimenta tua candida, id est, opera tua, quibus anima vestitur, decoratur, protegitur, sint pura et casta. Unde in Apocalypsi legitur : Qui vicerit, vestietur vestimentis albis. Ubi et Dominus protestatur : Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis. De hujusmodi vestimentis sanctus Job loquitur Deo : Si fulserint velut mundissimæ manus meæ, tamen sordibus intinges me, et abominabuntur me vestimenta mea. Atque in Ezechiele Dominus loquitur Synagogæ : Indui te discoloribus, et posui amictum meum super te. Et oleum de capite tuo non deficiat, id est, pietas nunquam a tua mente recedat, nec unctio gratiæ mentem illustrans, tibi desit. Potest quoque per oleum spiritualis lætitia, sed et claritas bonæ famæ intelligi, quum de Christo legatur : Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis: et in Isaia, Oleum gaudii pro luctu; atque in Canticis, Oleum effusum nomen tuum.
paras.en: [[9:8|At all times let thy garments be white|Omni tempore sint vestimenta tua candida]], that is, let thy works, with which the soul is clothed, adorned and protected, be pure and chaste. Hence we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:5|He that shall overcome shall thus be clothed in white garments|Qui vicerit, vestietur vestimentis albis]]. Where the Lord also declares: Those [[Apoc 3:4|which have not defiled their garments: and they shall walk with me in white|Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis]]. Of such garments holy Job speaks to God: If [[Job 9:30|my hands shall shine ever so clean|fulserint velut mundissimæ manus meæ]], [[Job 9:31|Yet thou shalt plunge me in filth, and my garments shall abhor me|tamen sordibus intinges me, et abominabuntur me vestimenta mea]]. And in Ezechiel the Lord says to the Synagogue: [[Ezech 16:10|I clothed thee with embroidery|Indui te discoloribus]], [[Ezech 16:8|and I spread my garment over thee|et posui amictum meum super te]] [the margin gives Ezech. xvi, 10, 8; Denis has *indui*, "I clothed", for the Vulgate's *vestivi*, and *posui*, "I put", for *expandi*]. [[9:8|and let not oil depart from thy head|Et oleum de capite tuo non deficiat]], that is, let piety never depart from thy mind, nor the anointing of grace that enlightens the mind be lacking to thee. By oil may also be understood spiritual joy, and also the brightness of a good name, since we read of Christ: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis]]; and in Isaias: [[Is 61:3|the oil of joy for mourning|Oleum gaudii pro luctu]]; and in the Canticles: [[Cant 1:2|Thy name is as oil poured out|Oleum effusum nomen tuum]].

paras.t: Perfruere vita cum uxore, quam diligis, cunctis diebus vitæ instabilitatis tuæ, qui dati sunt tibi sub sole, omni tempore vanitatis tuæ. Hæc est enim pars tua in vita, et in labore tuo. Quidam dicunt istud ad litteram spiritualiter et metaphorice esse intelligendum, ita ut per uxorem, intelligatur mentis sponsa, videlicet Sapientia increata, aut sapientia salutaris infusa, quæ est donum, per quam contemplamur cum gustu interno divina. Unde de sapientia illud dicitur : Quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere, et amator factus sum formæ illius. Cum hac perfruendum est vita, id est, occupandum est cor in amplexu, contemplatu, amore et quiete Sapientiæ æternalis, sicut ibidem additur : Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa.
paras.en: [[9:9|Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest, all the days of thy unsteady life|Perfruere vita cum uxore, quam diligis, cunctis diebus vitæ instabilitatis tuæ]], [[9:9|which are given to thee under the sun, all the time of thy vanity|qui dati sunt tibi sub sole, omni tempore vanitatis tuæ]]: [[9:9|for this is thy portion in life, and in thy labour|Hæc est enim pars tua in vita, et in labore tuo]]. Some say that this is to be understood, according to the letter, spiritually and metaphorically [that is, the metaphor is itself the literal sense intended], so that by the wife is understood the spouse of the mind, namely uncreated Wisdom, or the saving infused wisdom which is a gift, by which we contemplate divine things with an inward taste. Hence it is said of wisdom: I [[Wis 8:2|have desired to take for my spouse, and I became a lover of her beauty|Quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere, et amator factus sum formæ illius]]. With her we must live joyfully, that is, the heart must be occupied in the embrace, contemplation, love and rest of eternal Wisdom, as is added in the same place: [[Wis 8:16|When I go into my house, I shall repose myself with her|Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa]].

paras.t: Alii exponunt hæc de uxore legitima : cum qua, qui omnino continere non potest, aut non vult, debet delectabiliter vivere cum honestate et castimonia conjugali, ut omnem fornicationem devitet. Sicque conversari cum conjugali, est pars sua, id est præcipuum quid ad suam spectans vocationem.
paras.en: Others explain these words of a lawful wife: with her, he who cannot, or will not, keep wholly continent ought to live with delight, in the honesty and chastity of marriage, so as to avoid all fornication. And so to live with his wife is his portion, that is, something principal belonging to his calling.

paras.t: Quodcumque potest facere manus tua, id est, quidquid boni agere valet tua potestas seu virtus operativa, instanter operare, id est, sine dilatione et cessatione prosequ[…]re et adimple : quia, ut in Evangelio ait Christus, Venit nox, quando nemo potest operari. Unde et ipse idem : Vigilate, inquit (nescitis enim quando Dominus veniat : sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu), ne, quum venerit repente, inveniat vos dormientes. Ideo subjungitur :
paras.en: [[9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do|Quodcumque potest facere manus tua]], that is, whatever good thy power or working strength is able to do, [[9:10|do it earnestly|instanter operare]], that is, without delay or ceasing pursue[…] and fulfil it: for, as Christ says in the Gospel, [[John 9:4|the night cometh, when no man can work|Venit nox, quando nemo potest operari]]. Hence He likewise says: [[Mark 13:35|Watch ye|Vigilate]], He says (for [[Mark 13:35|you know not when the lord of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cock crowing|nescitis enim quando Dominus veniat : sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu]]), [[Mark 13:36|Lest coming on a sudden, he find you sleeping|ne, quum venerit repente, inveniat vos dormientes]]. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia, erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas. Albinus et alii quidam, per inferos intelligunt mortem, in qua ista non sunt, sed suspenduntur præ nimia mortis angustia, juxta illud : Quoniam non est in morte qui memor sit tui. — Alii, per inferos intelligunt limbum patrum : quia Salomon loquebatur Judæis pro tempore illo, quo justi omnino purgati, descenderunt in limbum illum seu Abrahæ sinum : in quo limbo non erant opus, ratio, sapientia, aut scientia ad promerendum, sed bene ad alia. Et pro tempore isto, per inferos intelligunt purgatorium, in quo etiam nullum istorum ad promerendum consistit. Nam Salomon loquitur justo, qui non properat ad infernum damnatorum. Hæc autem duo loca creduntur esse in superiori parte inferni, et quandoque inferni nomine designantur, sicut et limbus puerorum.
paras.en: [[9:10|for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening|Quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia, erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas]]. Albinus [that is, Alcuin] and certain others understand by hell death, in which these things are not, but are suspended through the excessive anguish of death, according to that: [[Ps 6:6|For there is no one in death, that is mindful of thee|Quoniam non est in morte qui memor sit tui]]. Others understand by hell the limbo of the fathers: because Solomon was speaking to the Jews for that time, in which the just, wholly purged, went down into that limbo, or Abraham's bosom; in which limbo there was no work, reason, wisdom or knowledge for meriting, though there was for other things. And for this present time [that is, since Christ opened heaven] they understand by hell purgatory, in which also none of these things avails for meriting. For Solomon is speaking to a just man, who is not hastening to the hell of the damned. These two places are believed to be in the upper part of hell, and are sometimes called by the name of hell, as is the limbo of children also.

paras.t: Porro doctores super quartum Sententiarum communiter auctoritatem istam allegant de inferiori reproborum inferno : in quo non est opus, id est aliqua meritoria actio, nec ratio, id est usus rationis ad discernendum salubriter, nec sapientia ad contemplandum divina, nec scientia ad considerandum pœnitentialiter propriam conditionem. Sapientia quoque et scientia, ut sunt dona, nequaquam sunt in damnatis, sicut nec caritas. Atque, ut aliqui opinantur, ratio ex vehementia suppliciorum totaliter absorbetur in illis, præsertim post diem judicii. Sed obviare videtur, quod dives epulo positus in inferno, deprecatus est Abraham, ut mitteret Lazarum in domum patris sui. Dæmones quoque, quamvis damnati, valde vigent acumine intellectus. Thomas autem super quartum testatur, quod ea quæ augent dolorem, et infernalium miseriarum sunt augmentativa, damnati possunt considerare, imo considerant ; non autem ea quæ alleviativa sunt tormentorum. Unde super Apocalypsim scribit Albertus, quod damnati acrius affliguntur in mente, dum attendunt miseriam suam æternaliter duraturam, quam ab igne tartareo.
paras.en: Further, the doctors on the fourth book of the Sentences commonly cite this text of the lower hell of the reprobate: in which there is no work, that is, no meritorious action; nor reason, that is, the use of reason to discern to salvation; nor wisdom to contemplate divine things; nor knowledge to consider one's own condition with penitence. Wisdom and knowledge, too, as they are gifts [that is, gifts of the Holy Ghost], are in no way in the damned, as neither is charity. And, as some hold, reason is wholly swallowed up in them by the violence of their torments, especially after the day of judgment. But against this seems to be the fact that the rich feaster, placed in hell, begged Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house[[Luke 16:27||]]. The demons too, though damned, are very strong in sharpness of intellect. But Thomas, on the fourth book, testifies that the damned can consider, and indeed do consider, the things that increase their pain and add to their hellish miseries, but not the things that would lighten their torments. Hence Albert writes on the Apocalypse that the damned are more sharply afflicted in mind, when they attend to their misery that will last for ever, than by the fire of hell.

paras.t: Porro Salomon intendebat instruere in his libris, non solum Judæos, sed et universos fideles. Idcirco, quod ait, Quo tu properas, dixit comminando, vel advisando, vel asserendo. Nam et verbum istud potuit dirigere ad iniquum, imo ad quemlibet hominem, quia et venialiter peccando, properat homo ad infernum dispositive. Vel, quod ait, Quo tu properas, intelligendum est sub conditione implicita, utpote, nisi emendes te, seu obedieris Deo.
paras.en: Further, Solomon meant in these books to instruct not only the Jews but all the faithful. Therefore when he said, [[9:10|whither thou art hastening|Quo tu properas]], he said it by way of threat, or of warning, or of assertion. For he could also direct this word to the wicked man, indeed to any man, since even by sinning venially a man hastens to hell dispositively [that is, venial sin disposes a man towards mortal sin, and so towards hell]. Or else, when he says, [[9:10|whither thou art hastening|Quo tu properas]], it is to be understood under an implied condition, namely: unless thou amend thyself, or obey God.

paras.t: Verti me ad aliud considerandum, videlicet, an homines viribus suis possint implere quod monui, dicens, Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare. Et vidi sub sole, id est, Deo illustrante cognovi, nec velocium esse cursum, id est, veloces et fervidos in actibus bonis, suis viribus non posse bona meritoria agere, ita quod cursus, id est expedita actio virtuosa, et conversatio fervida, qua non solum eunt, sed etiam currunt ad beatificum finem, non est eorum, id est, ipsis adscribenda non est principaliter, sed Deo et ejus gratioso auxilio, sicut ait Apostolus : Gratia Dei sum id quod sum. Rursus quoque quum dixisset, Plus omnibus laboravi ; mox addidit : Non autem ego, sed gratia Dei mecum. Unde Salvator : Sine me, inquit, nihil potestis facere. Et in Osee : Perditio tua ex te; in me tantummodo auxilium tuum. Et juxta hunc sensum subjungitur :
paras.en: [[9:11|I turned me to another thing|Verti me ad aliud]] to consider, namely, whether men can by their own strength fulfil what I counselled when I said: [[9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly|Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare]]. [[9:11|and I saw that under the sun|Et vidi sub sole]], that is, I came to know by God's enlightening, [[9:11|the race is not to the swift|nec velocium esse cursum]]: that is, that the swift and fervent in good acts cannot do meritorious good works by their own strength; so that the race, that is, ready virtuous action and fervent conduct, by which they not only go but even run to the blessed end, is not theirs: that is, it is not to be ascribed chiefly to them, but to God and his gracious help, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:10|by the grace of God, I am what I am|Gratia Dei sum id quod sum]]. And again, when he had said, [[1 Cor 15:10|I have laboured more abundantly than all they|Plus omnibus laboravi]], he at once added: [[1 Cor 15:10|Yet not I, but the grace of God with me|Non autem ego, sed gratia Dei mecum]]. Hence the Saviour: [[John 15:5|without me|Sine me]], he says, [[John 15:5|you can do nothing|nihil potestis facere]]. And in Osee: [[Osee 13:9|Destruction is thy own|Perditio tua ex te]]; [[Osee 13:9|thy help is only in me|in me tantummodo auxilium tuum]]. And in keeping with this sense there follows:

paras.t: Nec fortium bellum : id est, resistentia ac triumphus servorum et militum Dei, contra invisibiles hostes vitiorumque aciem præliantium, non ipsis, sed Deo et ejus pio subsidio, sunt adscribendi. Cui ait Propheta : In te eripiar a tentatione, et in Deo meo transgrediar murum. Imo et in corporali bello ab ipso datur victoria, sicut ait Scriptura : De cœlo victoria est. Nec sapientium panem : id est, panem vitæ et intellectus, et omnem salubrem refectionem, qua sapientes prælati prædicatores reficiunt audientes ac subditos seu se ipsos, a Deo habent, non a se. Imo in vanum laborat lingua prædicatoris, si desit inspiratio Creatoris. Ideo loquitur Isaias : Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum, qui lassus est, verbo. Propter quod etiam orat Apostolus : Ut detur mihi sermo in apertione oris mei. Nec doctorum divitias, id est, spirituales opes doctorum, esse Domino attribuendas. De quibus in Proverbiis dictum est : Redemptio animæ viri, divitiæ ejus; atque in Psalmo, Gloria et divitiæ in domo ejus. Nec artificum gratiam, id est, acceptabilitatem prudentiamque artificum, qui industriose fabricant in se et in aliis structuram virtutum, perfectionisque turrim, non esse eorum, sed donum Dei.
paras.en: [[9:11|nor the battle to the strong|Nec fortium bellum]]: that is, the resistance and triumph of the servants and soldiers of God against the invisible foes and the battle-line of the vices that fight against them are to be ascribed not to them, but to God and his loving aid. To him the Prophet says: [[Ps 17:30|by thee I shall be delivered from temptation; and through my God I shall go over a wall|In te eripiar a tentatione, et in Deo meo transgrediar murum]]. Indeed, even in bodily war the victory is given by him, as Scripture says: From heaven is the victory[[1 Mach 3:19||]] [the margin gives Mach. iii, 19, where the verse reads: strength cometh from heaven]. [[9:11|nor bread to the wise|Nec sapientium panem]]: that is, the bread of life and of understanding, and all the wholesome refreshment with which wise prelates and preachers refresh their hearers and subjects, or themselves, they have from God, not from themselves. Indeed the preacher's tongue labours in vain if the inspiration of the Creator is wanting. Therefore Isaias says: [[Is 50:4|The Lord hath given me a learned tongue, that I should know how to uphold by word him that is weary|Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum, qui lassus est, verbo]]. For this reason too the Apostle prays: [[Eph 6:19|that speech may be given me, that I may open my mouth|Ut detur mihi sermo in apertione oris mei]]. [[9:11|nor riches to the learned|Nec doctorum divitias]]: that is, the spiritual wealth of the learned is to be attributed to the Lord. Of these it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 13:8|The ransom of a man's life are his riches|Redemptio animæ viri, divitiæ ejus]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 111:3|Glory and wealth shall be in his house|Gloria et divitiæ in domo ejus]]. [[9:11|nor favour to the skilful|Nec artificum gratiam]] [gratia means both "favour" and "grace"]: that is, the acceptableness and prudence of the craftsmen who industriously build, in themselves and in others, the structure of the virtues and the tower of perfection, is not theirs but the gift of God.

paras.t: Sed tempus casumque in omnibus : id est, in universis prædictis inveni variam mutationem, per temporum intervalla : quoniam unus a celsitudine gratiæ labitur ad bassitudinem culpæ. Et qui hodie vincit, cras vincitur; et qui nunc docet et corripit alium, paulo post indiget increpari. Ideo nullus debet præsumere, neque inaniter gloriari : tum quia quidquid gratiæ et virtutis seu meriti habet, a Deo accepit; tum quia ignorat quam diu perseverabit in eis, et quia indesinenter eget conservatione ac protectione divina. Propter quod Paulus hortatur : Qui stat, videat ne cadat. Denique huic Salomonis sententiæ consonat illud quod Jeremias ait : Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus; nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos. Similiter illud ad Romanos : Igitur non volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei.
paras.en: [[9:11|but time and chance in all|Sed tempus casumque in omnibus]]: that is, in all the things aforesaid I found varied change through the intervals of time: for one man falls from the height of grace to the lowness of guilt; and he who conquers today is conquered tomorrow; and he who now teaches and rebukes another, a little later needs to be rebuked himself. Therefore no one ought to presume, nor to glory vainly: both because whatever grace and virtue or merit he has, he has received from God; and because he does not know how long he will persevere in them, and because he needs God's preserving and protection unceasingly. For this reason Paul exhorts: [[1 Cor 10:12|he that thinketh himself to stand, let him take heed lest he fall|Qui stat, videat ne cadat]] [Denis reads simply "he that standeth"]. Lastly, with this saying of Solomon agrees what Jeremias says: [[Jer 10:23|I know, O Lord, that the way of a man is not his: neither is it in a man to walk, and to direct his steps|Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus; nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos]]. Likewise that to the Romans: [[Rom 9:16|So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy|Igitur non volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei]].

paras.t: Quidam exponunt hunc passum superficialiter valde, dicendo : Vidi nec velocium esse cursum : quia quandoque contingit, quod velocior cursor non venit prior ad terminum; nec fortium bellum : quia quandoque fortior a minus forti superatur; etc. Verum de tali cursu non loquitur hic Scriptura, sed magis de eo de quo ait Apostolus : Cursum consummavi; et item, Sic currite, ut comprehendatis; et Psalmista, Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri.
paras.en: Some expound this passage very superficially, saying: [[9:11|I saw|Vidi]] [[9:11|the race is not to the swift|nec velocium esse cursum]], because it sometimes happens that the swifter runner does not reach the goal first; [[9:11|nor the battle to the strong|nec fortium bellum]], because sometimes the stronger is overcome by one less strong; etc. But Scripture is not speaking here of such a race, but rather of the one of which the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 4:7|I have finished my course|Cursum consummavi]]; and again: [[1 Cor 9:24|So run that you may obtain|Sic currite, ut comprehendatis]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 118:32|I have run the way of thy commandments|Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri]].

paras.t: Nescit homo finem suum, id est terminum vitæ præsentis, seu diem et horam mortis, nisi reveletur a judice Deo, vel jure humano aut per violentiam tradatur ad mortem, ita quod prænuntietur ei quando sit moriturus. Hinc orat Psalmista : Notum fac mihi, Domine, finem meum, et numerum dierum meorum, quis est. Nescit etiam homo finem suum supernaturalem : quoniam Deus qui est objectum beatitudinis nostræ, seu finis objectalis, incomprehensibilis est. Similiter beatifica visio Dei, quæ est finis et salus nostra formalis, tanta res est, quod ejus dignitatem ac eminentiam in hac vita plene agnoscere non valemus, juxta quod scriptum est : Oculus non vidit, Deus, absque te, quæ præparasti exspectantibus te. Sed sicut pisces capiuntur hamo improvise, et sicut aves laqueo comprehenduntur deceptorie; sic capiuntur homines, id est, de vita hac subtrahuntur, tempore malo, id est hora diræ mortis ac particularis sui judicii, quum eis extemplo, id est repente, supervenerit. Ideo Dominus admonet : Vigilate, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit; itemque, Estote parati, quia qua hora non putatis, Filius hominis veniet.
paras.en: [[9:12|Man knoweth not his own end|Nescit homo finem suum]], that is, the term of the present life, or the day and hour of death, unless it is revealed by God the judge, or he is handed over to death by human law or by violence, so that it is told him beforehand when he is to die. Hence the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 38:5|O Lord, make me know my end. And what is the number of my days|Notum fac mihi, Domine, finem meum, et numerum dierum meorum, quis est]]. Again, [[9:12|man knoweth not his own end|Nescit etiam homo finem suum]], his supernatural end: for God, who is the object of our beatitude, or our objective end, is incomprehensible. Likewise the beatific vision of God, which is our formal end and salvation [the objective end is God himself, the thing possessed; the formal end is the act of seeing him, by which he is possessed], is so great a thing that we cannot fully recognise its dignity and eminence in this life, according to what is written: [[Is 64:4|the eye hath not seen, O God, besides thee, what things thou hast prepared for them that wait for thee|Oculus non vidit, Deus, absque te, quæ præparasti exspectantibus te]]. [[9:12|but as fishes are taken with the hook|Sed sicut pisces capiuntur hamo]] unawares, [[9:12|and as birds are caught with the snare|et sicut aves laqueo comprehenduntur]] by deceit, [[9:12|so men are taken|sic capiuntur homines]], that is, are taken away from this life, [[9:12|in the evil time|tempore malo]], that is, in the hour of dire death and of their particular judgment, [[9:12|when it shall suddenly|quum eis extemplo]], that is, all at once, [[9:12|come upon them|supervenerit]]. Therefore the Lord warns: [[Matt 24:42|Watch ye therefore, because you know not what hour your Lord will come|Vigilate, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit]]; and again: [[Luke 12:40|Be you then also ready: for at what hour you think not the Son of man will come|Estote parati, quia qua hora non putatis, Filius hominis veniet]][[Matt 24:44||]] [the margin gives Matt. xxiv, 42, 44 and Luke xii, 40; Denis's words here are those of Luke].

paras.t: Hanc quoque sub sole vidi sapientiam, id est sapientialem seu prudentem effectum : quia quod sequitur, potuit esse res gesta, vel ponitur pro exemplo : quamvis et aliter exponatur, sicut tangetur : et probavi magnam, id est valde magnam. Civitas parva, et pauci in ea viri. Venit contra eam rex magnus, et vallavit eam, exstruxitque munitiones per gyrum, et perfecta est obsidio. Inventusque est in ea vir pauper et sapiens, et liberavit urbem per sapientiam suam, dando consilium, qualiter hostibus multis pauci cives prævalerent, vel adjutorium implorarent a Deo, vel adversariis persuaderent recedere. Tale quid accidit sæpe. Et nullus deinceps civium urbis illius, recordatus est hominis illius pauperis. In quo patent eorum insipientia, ingratitudo, improbitas.
paras.en: [[9:13|This wisdom also I have seen under the sun|Hanc quoque sub sole vidi sapientiam]], that is, a wise or prudent deed: for what follows may have been a thing that really happened, or it is put as an example; though it is also expounded otherwise, as will be touched on: [[9:13|and it seemed to me to be very great|et probavi magnam]] [Denis reads magnam, "great", where the Vulgate has maximam], that is, exceedingly great. [[9:14|A little city, and few men in it: there came against it a great king, and invested it, and built bulwarks round about it, and the siege was perfect.|Civitas parva, et pauci in ea viri. Venit contra eam rex magnus, et vallavit eam, exstruxitque munitiones per gyrum, et perfecta est obsidio]] [[9:15|Now there was found in it a man poor and wise, and he delivered the city by his wisdom|Inventusque est in ea vir pauper et sapiens, et liberavit urbem per sapientiam suam]], by giving counsel how the few citizens might prevail against many enemies, or might implore help from God, or might persuade the adversaries to withdraw. Such a thing often happens. [[9:15|and no man afterward remembered that poor man|Et nullus deinceps civium urbis illius, recordatus est hominis illius pauperis]] of the citizens of that city. In this their folly, ingratitude and wickedness are plain.

paras.t: Et dicebam ego, meliorem esse sapientiam fortitudine corporali. Sapientia quoque quæ donum est, est dignior fortitudine quæ est donum. Similiter sapientia quæ est virtus intellectualis, dicitur dignior fortitudine quæ est virtus cardinalis. Quomodo ergo sapientia pauperis contempta est ab illis ingratis, et verba ejus non sunt audita ab ipsis, cessante necessitatis articulo? Nam durante obsidione, fuerunt audita. Verba sapientium audiuntur in silentio, id est a quietis prudentibusque hominibus, in quibus est tranquillitas mentis, non passionum et vitiorum inquietudo : ideo stulti non audiunt ea; magis, id est attentius, quam clamor principis inter stultos, id est passionatos et imprudentes, qui non advertunt nisi sibi placentia.
paras.en: [[9:16|And I said that wisdom is better than strength|Et dicebam ego, meliorem esse sapientiam fortitudine]] of body. Wisdom too that is a gift [that is, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost] is worthier than fortitude that is a gift. Likewise wisdom that is an intellectual virtue is said to be worthier than fortitude that is a cardinal virtue. [[9:16|how then is the wisdom of the poor man slighted|Quomodo ergo sapientia pauperis contempta est]] by those ungrateful men, [[9:16|and his words not heard|et verba ejus non sunt audita]] by them, once the moment of need had passed? For while the siege lasted, they were heard. [[9:17|The words of the wise are heard in silence|Verba sapientium audiuntur in silentio]], that is, by quiet and prudent men, in whom there is tranquillity of mind, not the restlessness of passions and vices: therefore fools do not hear them; [[9:17|more|magis]], that is, more attentively, [[9:17|than the cry of a prince among fools|quam clamor principis inter stultos]], that is, among the passionate and imprudent, who heed nothing but what pleases them.

paras.t: Præterea, per civitatem hanc parvam, multi intelligunt Ecclesiam humilem, propria reputatione parvam, et quæ in exordio suo fuit parva, sicut in Evangelio ait Salvator : Nolite timere, pusillus grex. Contra quam venit rex magnus, id est diabolus : cui in Zacharia dicitur : Quis tu, mons magne, contra Zorobabel in planum? Quem Christus principem mundi hujus appellat : qui est rex super omnes filios superbiæ. Hic per se et angelos suos, ac per tyrannos, per hæresiarchas atque philosophos, multipliciter oppugnavit Ecclesiam. Christus autem propter nos pauper factus, per evangelicæ legis sapientiam, liberavit Ecclesiam : Ego, inquiens, dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri. In Ecclesia autem sunt pauci viri virtutum, et pauci electi; sed paucissimi deinceps sunt memores Salvatoris : quoniam omnes, quæ sua sunt, quærunt, non quæ Christi. — Insuper potest per urbem istam, intelligi quilibet homo : in quo sunt pauci viri, id est boni cogitatus atque affectus viriles ; in quo rex est ratio ; quem circumdat diabolus : et fomes tanquam tyrannus impugnat eumdem. Sed vir pauper, id est intellectus aut synderesis, liberat eum, remurmurando iniquitati, et erudiendo qualiter sit resistendum. Habita autem victoria, interiores exterioresque sensus, et appetitus irascibilis ac concupiscibilis, tanquam fatui cives, censuram intellectus atque synderesis respuentes, cito ac faciliter recidivant.
paras.en: Moreover, by this [[9:14|little city|civitatem hanc parvam]] many understand the humble Church, little in its own esteem, and which at its beginning was little, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:32|Fear not, little flock|Nolite timere, pusillus grex]]. Against it there came [[9:14|a great king|rex magnus]], that is, the devil, to whom it is said in Zacharias: [[Zach 4:7|Who art thou, O great mountain, before Zorobabel?|Quis tu, mons magne, contra Zorobabel]] [[Zach 4:7|thou shalt become a plain|in planum]]. Christ calls him [[John 12:31|the prince of this world|principem mundi hujus]]; he is [[Job 41:25|king over all the children of pride|rex super omnes filios superbiæ]]. He, by himself and his angels, and through tyrants, heresiarchs and philosophers, has assailed the Church in many ways. But Christ, made poor for our sakes[[2 Cor 8:9||]], delivered the Church by the wisdom of the gospel law, saying: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]]. Now in the Church there are few men of virtue, and few elect; but very few are mindful of the Saviour afterward: for [[Phil 2:21|all seek the things that are their own not the things that are Jesus Christ's|omnes, quæ sua sunt, quærunt, non quæ Christi]]. — Further, by this city any man can be understood: in whom are [[9:14|few men|pauci viri]], that is, good thoughts and manly affections; in whom the king is reason; whom the devil surrounds; and the fomes [that is, the tinder of sin, the inclination to evil left by original sin] assails him like a tyrant. But [[9:15|a man poor|vir pauper]], that is, the intellect or synderesis [the natural habit of the mind that holds the first principles of conduct and murmurs against evil], delivers him, by murmuring against iniquity, and by teaching him how to resist. But once the victory is won, the interior and exterior senses, and the irascible and concupiscible appetites, like foolish citizens rejecting the judgment of the intellect and of synderesis, quickly and easily fall back.

paras.t: Melior est sapientia, quam arma bellica corporalia, aut etiam, quam arma bellica quædam spiritualia (de quibus ait Apostolus : Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo), id est, quam morales et inferiores virtutes intellectuales. Siquidem ex sua specie, et ratione sui objecti, est illis præstantior. Plus etiam valet ad obtinendum victoriam tam in spirituali quam corporali pugna, quam bellica arma.
paras.en: [[9:18|Better is wisdom, than weapons of war|Melior est sapientia, quam arma bellica]] of the body, or even than certain spiritual weapons of war (of which the Apostle says: [[Eph 6:13|take unto you the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day|Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo]]), that is, than the moral virtues and the lower intellectual virtues. For by its species, and by reason of its object, it is more excellent than they. It also avails more than weapons of war for winning the victory, in spiritual as well as in bodily combat.

paras.t: Et qui in uno peccaverit, id est, quodcumque mortale peccatum inciderit, multa bona perdet : quia peccando amittit caritatem, ceterasque virtutes infusas formatas, ad minus quantum ad esse earum formatum : quoniam formantur et decorantur, atque ad operandum meritorie redduntur idoneæ a caritate, quæ est forma, vita, decor et vertex virtutum, motrix et imperatrix earum. Amittit etiam omnia merita sua præhabita, communionemque mystici corporis Christi; et desinit esse membrum, minister ac miles Dei, fitque servus et membrum diaboli. Sed et summum et incommutabile bonum, Deum creatorem ac salvatorem suum amittit, et pretiosissima bona gloriæ æternalis. Ideo Jacobus dixit apostolus : Quicumque totam legem impleverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Ecce quanta est peccantis stultitia, qui pro modica voluptate incurrit et infligit sibi ipsi tot damna, et sapientiam aspernatur. Videat sibi unusquisque, ne sapientem despiciat, aut sapientiam parvi pendat : quoniam hoc est unum de maximis malis, quæ geruntur sub sole; et plane tam malum, ut in Ecclesiastico dicatur : In duobus contristatum est cor meum : vir bellator deficiens per inopiam, et vir sensatus contemptus.
paras.en: [[9:18|and he that shall offend in one|Et qui in uno peccaverit]], that is, falls into any mortal sin whatever, [[9:18|shall lose many good things|multa bona perdet]]: for by sinning he loses charity, and the other infused virtues that were formed [that is, given life by charity; without it they are "unformed" and cannot merit], at least as to their formed being: for they are formed and adorned, and made fit to work meritoriously, by charity, which is the form, life, beauty and summit of the virtues, their mover and their empress. He loses also all the merits he had before, and the communion of the mystical body of Christ; and he ceases to be a member, minister and soldier of God, and becomes a slave and member of the devil. And he loses too the highest and unchangeable good, God his creator and saviour, and the most precious goods of eternal glory. Therefore James the apostle said: [[Jas 2:10|whosoever shall keep the whole law, but offend in one point, is become guilty of all|Quicumque totam legem impleverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus]]. See how great is the folly of the sinner, who for a little pleasure incurs and inflicts on himself so many losses, and spurns wisdom. Let each man look to himself, that he despise not the wise man, nor hold wisdom cheap: for this is one of the greatest evils that are done under the sun; and plainly so evil that it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 26:25|At two things my heart is grieved|In duobus contristatum est cor meum]]: [[Ecclus 26:26|A man of war fainting through poverty, and a man of sense despised:|vir bellator deficiens per inopiam, et vir sensatus contemptus]]

paras.t: Circa præhabita quæritur, an homo posset certo scire se esse in caritate, et per consequens quod dignus sit amore, id est amari a Deo. Ad hanc quæstionem pro utraque parte multæ possent auctoritates adduci. Quod enim posset hoc scire, etiam sine revelatione, apparet ex eo quod princeps Apostolorum in sua ait Canonica : Per bona opera certam faciatis vocationem vestram. Joannes quoque in sua prima affirmat epistola : In hoc scimus quia in Deo manemus, et Deus in nobis, quoniam de Spiritu suo dedit nobis; et rursus, Scimus quia ex Deo sumus. Paulus etiam fatetur : Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. In oppositum est auctoritas hujus capituli ; et quod alibi Salomon loquitur : Quis gloriabitur mundum se habere cor? Et demum, quod beatus Job protestatur : Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum : et si abierit, non intelligam.
paras.en: Concerning what has gone before, it is asked whether a man could know for certain that he is in charity, and so that he [[9:1|be worthy of love|dignus sit amore]], that is, of being loved by God. On this question many authorities could be brought for either side. For that he could know this, even without revelation, appears from what the prince of the Apostles says in his Canonical Epistle: [[2 Pet 1:10|by good works you may make sure your calling|Per bona opera certam faciatis vocationem vestram]]. John too affirms in his first epistle: [[1 John 4:13|In this we know that we abide in him, and he in us: because he hath given us of his spirit|In hoc scimus quia in Deo manemus, et Deus in nobis, quoniam de Spiritu suo dedit nobis]] [the margin gives 1 John iii, 24; Denis's wording is that of 1 John 4:13]; and again: [[1 John 5:19|We know that we are of God|Scimus quia ex Deo sumus]] [the margin gives Ibid. iv, 6, that is, 1 John 4:6, "We are of God"; Denis's wording is that of 1 John 5:19]. Paul also declares: [[1 Cor 2:12|we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]. On the other side is the authority of this chapter[[9:1||]]; and what Solomon says elsewhere: Who shall glory that he hath a clean heart?[[Prov 20:9||]] [Denis quotes an older Latin form of the verse; the Douay-Rheims reads: Who can say: My heart is clean]; and lastly, what blessed Job protests: [[Job 9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him: if he depart, I shall not understand.|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum : et si abierit, non intelligam]]

paras.t: Ad hanc quæstionem Antisiodorensis in secunda parte Summæ suæ respondet : Aliqui dicunt, quod quidam sciunt se non habere caritatem : ut qui sunt in proposito vel actu peccandi. Aliqui dubitant se caritatem habere, quoniam habent rationes æque fortes pro parte utraque : ut qui incipiunt facere quod in ipsis est, et proponunt non peccare de cetero. Alii putant se habere caritatem : ut qui jam fecerunt multa bona opera, et diu est quod non fuerunt in proposito vel actu peccandi. Tamen adhuc sustinent primos motus, et turpia imaginantur, patiunturque inquietudinem muscarum morientium, quæ perdunt suavitatem unguenti (id est cogitationum distractiones, quæ orationis dulcedinem tollunt). Alii sciunt se caritatem habere : qui scilicet gustant dulcedinem Dei, et in quibus fomes fere exstinctus est, ut in Maria Magdalene et Maria Ægyptiaca, post plurimos fletus. Denique duplex est scientia, scilicet experimenti, quæ est per signa; et scientia proprie dicta, videlicet cognitio alicujus per se noti, ut in primis principiis, vel alicujus ex illis deducti. Primo modo potest quis scire se caritatem habere, puta per signa ; quæ sunt tria, videlicet jucunditas spiritualis, desideria bona, et opera bona. Secundo modo nullus potest scire se caritatem habere, nisi ex revelatione. Sciendum est etiam, quod duplex est dilectio Dei, videlicet naturalis, et gratuita : quæ tantam habent affinitatem et conjunctionem ad invicem, quod non potest aliquis discernere utrum suum diligere sit motus dilectionis naturalis, an gratuitæ. Nam et naturalis dilectio habet delicias suas. Itaque voluit Deus nos aliquo modo scire, quod simus in caritate, tribus de causis : prima, ut aliquam consolationem habeamus in miseriis sæculi hujus; secunda, ut Deo gratias referamus; tertia, ut provocemur ad meliora. Voluit quoque nos istud aliquo modo nescire, ut cautiores simus, et magis solliciti de nostra salute. Auctoritatem autem Salomonis, dicentis, Nescit homo an amore sit dignus, quidam exponunt de amore prædestinationis. Hæc Antisiodorensis.
paras.en: To this question William of Auxerre [Denis calls him Antisiodorensis, "the man of Auxerre"], in the second part of his Summa, replies: Some say that certain men know that they do not have charity: such as those who are in the purpose or in the act of sinning. Some are in doubt whether they have charity, since they have equally strong reasons on either side: such as those who are beginning to do what is in them, and purpose not to sin from now on. Others think that they have charity: such as those who have already done many good works, and it is long since they were in the purpose or act of sinning. Yet they still suffer the first motions [that is, the first stirrings of desire before the will consents], and imagine foul things, and suffer the disquiet of the dying flies, which [[Eccles 10:1|spoil the sweetness of the ointment|perdunt suavitatem unguenti]] (that is, distractions of thought, which take away the sweetness of prayer). Others know that they have charity: those, namely, who taste the sweetness of God, and in whom the fomes is almost extinguished, as in Mary Magdalene and Mary of Egypt, after very many tears. Further, knowledge is twofold: namely, the knowledge of experience, which is by signs; and knowledge properly so called, that is, the knowing of something known through itself, as in first principles, or of something deduced from them. In the first way a man can know that he has charity, namely by signs; which are three: spiritual joy, good desires and good works. In the second way no one can know that he has charity, except by revelation. It must also be known that the love of God is twofold, natural and gratuitous [that is, given by grace]: and these have such affinity and connexion with each other that no one can discern whether his loving is a motion of natural or of gratuitous love. For natural love too has its delights. So God willed that we should in some way know that we are in charity, for three reasons: first, that we may have some consolation in the miseries of this world; second, that we may give thanks to God; third, that we may be spurred on to better things. He willed also that we should in some way not know it, that we may be more cautious, and more solicitous for our salvation. But the authority of Solomon, who says, [[9:1|man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love|Nescit homo an amore sit dignus]], some expound of the love of predestination. Thus far William of Auxerre.

paras.t: Præterea, super primum Sententiarum, distinctione 17, S. Thomas respondet : Potentias et habitus non possumus cognoscere, nisi per actus et conatus qui proportionantur eorum naturæ, et actus per objecta. In actu autem animæ, est plura considerare, scilicet speciem actus, quæ sumitur ab objecto, et modum, ac effectum. Si ergo accipiamus actum caritatis, qui est diligere Deum et proximum, ex specie actus, non discernitur an sit a caritate gratuita, vel naturali, quia utraque versatur circa idem objectum. Modus vero, quem ponit habitus in opere, est facilitas et delectatio. Per hunc autem modum non discernitur an sit a caritate infusa, vel naturali seu acquisita. Proprius vero effectus caritatis seu actus caritatis, est in virtute merendi : quod nullo modo cadit in nostram cognitionem. Ideo nemo certitudinaliter scire potest se esse in caritate. Hæc Thomas. Cui Richardus de Mediavilla satis concordat.
paras.en: Further, on the first book of the Sentences, distinction 17, St. Thomas replies: We cannot know powers and habits except through the acts and efforts that are proportioned to their nature, and acts through their objects. Now in an act of the soul there are several things to consider: namely the species of the act, which is taken from the object, and its mode, and its effect. If, then, we take the act of charity, which is to love God and neighbour, by the species of the act it is not discerned whether it comes from gratuitous charity or from natural, since both are concerned with the same object. The mode, again, that a habit puts into the work is ease and delight; and by this mode it is not discerned whether it comes from infused charity, or from natural or acquired. But the proper effect of charity, or of the act of charity, lies in the power of meriting: which in no way falls within our knowledge. Therefore no one can know with certainty that he is in charity. Thus far Thomas. With him Richard of Middleton fairly well agrees.

paras.t: Porro Petrus de Tarentasia, præallegata ait distinctione : Illos habitus, qui habent actus omnino diversos, et dissimiles ab aliis, ut fides et spes, possumus cognoscere sub propria ratione. Illos vero, qui habent actus similes actibus aliorum habituum, vel innatorum, vel acquisitorum, ut caritas, non possumus cognoscere cognitione perfecta in propria ratione, sed solum in universali. Unde scire possumus habere nos dilectionem, sed non caritatem. Et hoc, quadruplici ratione : primo, quia caritas importat Dei acceptationem, quæ nos latet; secundo, quia intellectus noster obumbratus ex carne, hebes est ad supernaturalia; tertio, quoniam actus caritatis similis est actui dilectionis acquisitæ et naturalis; quarto, propter judicium Dei, qui ad humiliandum nos, vult nos bona nostra latere. Proprium quoque effectum caritatis, quem addit supra naturalem dilectionem, scire non possumus, quia hic effectus, est quædam ineffabilis unio ad Deum : de qua Salvator loquitur ad Patrem, Ut sint unum sicut et nos. Hæc Petrus.
paras.en: Peter of Tarentaise, again, on the distinction already cited, says: Those habits whose acts are wholly different from and unlike those of others, such as faith and hope, we can know under their proper character. But those whose acts are like the acts of other habits, whether innate or acquired, such as charity, we cannot know with perfect knowledge in their proper character, but only in general. Hence we can know that we have love, but not that we have charity. And this for four reasons: first, because charity implies God's acceptance, which is hidden from us; second, because our intellect, darkened by the flesh, is dull toward supernatural things; third, because the act of charity is like the act of acquired and natural love; fourth, because of the judgment of God, who to humble us wills that our good things be hidden from us. Nor can we know the proper effect of charity, which it adds over natural love, because this effect is a certain ineffable union with God, of which the Saviour speaks to the Father: [[John 17:11|that they may be one, as we also are|Ut sint unum sicut et nos]][[John 17:22||]]. Thus far Peter.

paras.t: Postremo ad idem probandum, Alexander de Hales et Dominus Antisiodorensis adducunt hoc argumentum : Spiritum Sanctum esse in te, et caritatem esse in te, sunt duo convertibilia. Primum nescis, quoniam Spiritum Sanctum esse in te, non est scibile, sed credibile : ergo nec secundum scis.
paras.en: Lastly, to prove the same, Alexander of Hales and the lord of Auxerre bring this argument: That the Holy Ghost is in thee, and that charity is in thee, are two convertible things [that is, each follows from the other]. The first thou knowest not, since that the Holy Ghost is in thee is not a thing that can be known, but believed: therefore neither dost thou know the second.

paras.t: De hac materia, et de signis per quæ probabiliter scitur, quod caritas habeatur, multum consolatorie loquitur S. Bernardus; et multa de his dici possent. Sed prolixitas est vitanda : ideo pro præsenti sufficiant ista.
paras.en: On this matter, and on the signs by which it is known with probability that charity is possessed, St. Bernard speaks very consolingly; and much could be said about these things. But prolixity is to be avoided: so for the present let this suffice.

10.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI DECIMI : MUSCÆ MORIENTES PERDUNT SUAVITATEM UNGUENTI.
10.title_en: Explanation of the tenth chapter: Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment.

paras.t: Multa moralia documenta in isto continentur capitulo. Nec est hic continuatio ejusdem materiæ, sicut nec in Proverbiis.
paras.en: Many moral lessons are contained in this chapter. Nor is there here a continuation of one and the same subject, just as there is none in Proverbs.

paras.t: Muscæ morientes perdunt suavitatem unguenti. Ad litteram, dum musca infirma cadit in unguentum suave, manendo et moriendo in illo, destruit ejus valorem atque odorem. Sic, qui in uno reus est, plurima perdit bona; et tota meritorum congeries, uno mortali peccato destruitur. Unus quoque perversus et scandalosus ac pestilens, totam perturbat ac inficit communitatem. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Modicum fermentum totam massam corrumpit.
paras.en: [[10:1|Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment|Muscæ morientes perdunt suavitatem unguenti]]. Literally: when a sickly fly falls into sweet ointment, by staying and dying in it, it destroys its worth and its fragrance. So he who is guilty in one thing loses a great many good things, and the whole heap of merits is destroyed by one mortal sin. Likewise one perverse, scandalous and pestilent man troubles and infects a whole community. For which reason the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 5:6|a little leaven corrupteth the whole lump?|Modicum fermentum totam massam corrumpit]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, muscæ morientes, sunt cogitationes vanæ, inutiles, affectiones illicitæ, distractiones morosæ, præsertim in divino Officio: quæ perdunt suavitatem unguenti, id est experimentalem dulcedinem spiritualium exercitiorum, quæ sentiri solet in orationibus, meditationibus, contemplationibus, psalmodiis, recollecta ac stabili mente Deo oblatis. Imo in cunctis actibus virtuosis hanc utique tollit et impedit muscarum istarum admixtio, hoc est misera et detestanda illa distractio, ita quod homo sine sapore et gustu, vaga et vana mente orat, psallit et meditatur, ac cetera bona exercet. Hinc in Summa sua Antisiodorensis disseruit: Psalmista ait: In custodiendis illis, scilicet Dei mandatis, retributio multa. Non enim tantum pro custodiendis, sed etiam in custodiendis mandatis Dei, retributio multa. Et hoc, propter jucunditatem mentis, et prægustationem dulcedinis Dei, quæ habetur in divinorum custodia mandatorum.
paras.en: Spiritually, [[10:1|dying flies|muscæ morientes]] are vain and useless thoughts, unlawful affections, lingering distractions [*morosæ*: dwelt on and lingered over, as in the moralists' morose delectation, not merely passing], above all in the divine Office; which [[10:1|spoil the sweetness of the ointment|perdunt suavitatem unguenti]], that is, the felt sweetness of spiritual exercises, which is wont to be tasted in prayers, meditations, contemplations and psalmody offered to God with a recollected and steady mind.
