Indeed in all virtuous acts the mingling of these flies, that is, that wretched and detestable distraction, takes this sweetness away and hinders it, so that a man prays, sings the psalms and meditates, and does his other good works, without savour or relish, with a wandering and empty mind. Hence the doctor of Auxerre [William of Auxerre, in his *Summa aurea*] argued in his Summa: The Psalmist says: [[Ps 18:12|in keeping them|In custodiendis illis]], that is, God's commandments, [[Ps 18:12|there is a great reward|retributio multa]]. For not only for keeping God's commandments, but also in keeping them, there is a great reward. And this because of the gladness of mind and the foretaste of God's sweetness which is had in keeping the divine commandments.

paras.t: Pretiosior est sapientia, parvaque gloria, id est cum gloria modica, seu cum parvo honore, ad tempus stultitia, id est temporali insipientia: quamvis ei adjuncta sit honorificentia magna, quemadmodum dictum est supra: Melior est puer pauper et sapiens, rege sene et stulto.
paras.en: [[10:1|Wisdom and glory is more precious|Pretiosior est sapientia, parvaque gloria]] [Denis reads *parvaque gloria*, and a little glory, joining *parva*, small, to glory], that is, wisdom with a modest glory or with small honour, than [[10:1|shortlived folly|ad tempus stultitia]], that is, than temporal foolishness, even though great honour be joined to it; as was said above: [[Eccles 4:13|Better is a child that is poor and wise, than a king that is old and foolish|Melior est puer pauper et sapiens, rege sene et stulto]].

paras.t: Vel: Pretiosior est sapientia, quæ simplicitate et innocentia decoratur, parvaque gloria, id est humilis gloriatio de Deo in ipso, vel de se in Deo, juxta illud, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur; ad tempus stultitia, id est superba sui ipsius exaltatione atque jactantia.
paras.en: Or: [[10:1|Wisdom|Pretiosior est sapientia]] is more precious, wisdom adorned with simplicity and innocence, [[10:1|and glory|parvaque gloria]], a little glory, that is, a humble glorying in God himself, or in oneself in God, according to that saying: [[1 Cor 1:31|He that glorieth may glory in the Lord|Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur]][[2 Cor 10:17||]]; than [[10:1|shortlived folly|ad tempus stultitia]], that is, than the folly of proud self-exaltation and boasting.

paras.t: Cor sapientis, in dextera ejus: id est, ratio et intentio sapientis, dirigitur et versatur circa spiritualia et cœlestia bona, ut bene conversando, obtineat ea; et cor stulti, id est iniqui, est in sinistra illius, id est, circa carnalia et terrena, animæ suæ nociva, intentum est. Per dexteram enim, bona et prospera; per sinistram vero, designantur adversa et noxia. Hoc (ni fallor) est, quod in Matthæo ait Salvator: Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex, id est recta intentio, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit, id est, operum tuorum congeries erit virtuosa et clara, et nomine sapientis ac condignus, atque ad dexteram Judicis stabis; si autem oculus tuus nequam fuerit, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit.
paras.en: [[10:2|The heart of a wise man is in his right hand|Cor sapientis, in dextera ejus]]: that is, the reason and intention of the wise man is directed to and busied about spiritual and heavenly goods, so that by living well he may obtain them; [[10:2|and the heart of a fool|et cor stulti]], that is, of the wicked man, is [[10:2|in his left hand|in sinistra illius]], that is, it is bent on carnal and earthly things, harmful to his soul. For by the right hand are signified good and prosperous things, by the left adverse and harmful ones. This (unless I am mistaken) is what the Saviour says in Matthew: [[Matt 6:22|If thy eye be single|Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex]], that is, a right intention, [[Matt 6:22|thy whole body shall be lightsome|totum corpus tuum lucidum erit]], that is, the whole sum of thy works will be virtuous and bright, and fully worthy of the name of wise, and thou shalt stand at the right hand of the Judge; [[Matt 6:23|But if thy eye be evil thy whole body shall be darksome|si autem oculus tuus nequam fuerit, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit]].

paras.t: Sed et in via stultus ambulans, id est peccator in sæculo degens et conversans, quum ipse insipiens sit, constituendo sibi finem in rebus carnalibus et caducis, omnes stultos æstimat, id est, omnes reputat similes sibi, seu omnes putat peccare, et alicui vitio deservire, sicut et ipse: sicque ex qualitate sui ipsius, accipit formam judicandi de aliis. Hinc sæculares, communiter reputant religiosos aut avaros, aut invidos, aut alicui vitio simili obnoxios.
paras.en: [[10:3|Yea, and the fool when he walketh in the way|Sed et in via stultus ambulans]], that is, the sinner living and going about in the world, [[10:3|whereas he himself is a fool|quum ipse insipiens sit]], by setting his end in carnal and perishable things, [[10:3|esteemeth all men fools|omnes stultos æstimat]], that is, he reckons all men like himself, or thinks that all men sin and are slaves to some vice, as he is: and so he takes his rule for judging others from his own condition. Hence worldly people commonly reckon religious [that is, monks, friars and nuns, those bound by vows in a religious order] to be either covetous, or envious, or subject to some like vice.

paras.t: Vel, Omnes æstimat stultos, qui aliter sentiunt quam ipse, et terrena ista despiciunt, quæ ipse maxime appretiatur. Unde, ut legitur quarto Regum, quum unus ex filiis prophetarum unxisset ipsum Jehu in regem, principes dixerunt: Quid venit insanus iste ad te? Ideo et in Job dicitur: Deridetur justi simplicitas; lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum, parata ad tempus statutum. Et Apostolus: Nos, inquit, stulti propter Christum. Unde, ut in Evangelio legitur, Christo contra avaritiam et ambitionem prædicante, Scribæ et Pharisæi qui erant ambitiosi ac cupidi, audientes, deriserunt eum, dicentes: Insanit; quid eum auditis? Hinc reprobi tandem dicturi sunt illud Sapientiæ: Ii sunt, quos aliquando habuimus in derisum, et in similitudinem improperii. Nos insensati, vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam. Non igitur contristetur vir bonus, nec doleat sapiens, quando ab imprudentibus et carnalibus, a negligentibus et intimoratis contemnitur, deridetur, vituperatur. Hinc in Proverbiis suis Seneca protestatur: Malis displicere, laudari est; et rursus, Nondum felix es, si nondum te turba deridet. Causam quoque hujus tam erronei judicii impiorum, tangit Seneca, dicens: Omnis affectus habet, ut in quo ipse insanit, ceteros furere putet. Hinc sancti patres Cassianus et Climacus dicunt, quod qui alicui passioni aut vitio subjacet, pronus est alium de eadem passione aut vitio judicare.
paras.en: Or: he [[10:3|esteemeth all men fools|Omnes æstimat stultos]] who think otherwise than he does and despise these earthly things which he prizes most highly. Hence, as we read in the fourth book of Kings, when one of the sons of the prophets had anointed Jehu king, the princes said: [[4 Kings 9:11|why came this madman to thee?|Quid venit insanus iste ad te?]] And so it is said in Job too: [[Job 12:4|the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn|Deridetur justi simplicitas]]; [[Job 12:5|The lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, is ready for the time appointed.|lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum, parata ad tempus statutum]]. And the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:10|We are fools for Christs sake|Nos, inquit, stulti propter Christum]]. Hence, as we read in the Gospel, when Christ preached against avarice and ambition[[Luke 16:13||]], the Scribes and Pharisees, who were ambitious and covetous, hearing it, [[Luke 16:14|derided him|deriserunt eum]], saying: He [[John 10:20|is mad. Why hear you him?|Insanit; quid eum auditis?]] Hence at last the reprobate will say those words of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:3|These are they, whom we had sometime in derision, and for a parable of reproach|Ii sunt, quos aliquando habuimus in derisum, et in similitudinem improperii]]. [[Wis 5:4|We fools esteemed their life madness|Nos insensati, vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam]]. Let not the good man be saddened, then, nor the wise man grieve, when he is despised, derided and reviled by the imprudent and carnal, by the negligent and those without the fear of God. Hence Seneca declares in his Proverbs: To displease the wicked is to be praised; and again: Thou art not yet happy, if the crowd does not yet laugh at thee. Seneca also touches on the cause of this so erroneous judgment of the wicked, saying: Every passion has this about it, that it thinks others mad in the very thing in which it is itself mad. Hence the holy fathers Cassian and Climacus say that whoever is subject to some passion or vice is prone to judge another guilty of that same passion or vice.

paras.t: Si spiritus potestatem habentis ascenderit super te: id est, si impulsus diaboli tentaverit et impugnaverit te, ut ex mystico corpore Christi trajiciat te in corpus suum, hoc est in ecclesiam malignantium, ut te faciat membrum et servum suum; vel, Si spiritus potestatem habentis, id est exagitatio fomitis, quæ pluribus dominatur, impugnaverit te: vel, Spiritus, id est indignatio, habentis potestatem, id est alicujus te fortioris, ascenderit super te, ut te persequatur et opprimat; locum tuum ne dimiseris: id est, a mystico corpore Christi, a congregatione devota, a statu gratiæ ac stabilitate virtutum, a patientia sancta, nequaquam recedas, nec acquiescas iniquis; sed invoca Deum, et per virtutes resiste, ac tanto instantius occupa te in bonis, quanto acrius impugnaris. Hinc Jacobus exhortatur: Resistite diabolo, et fugiet a vobis. Et Paulus: Deus, inquit, pacis conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris velociter. Porro diabolus potens est valde. De quo Christus, victor ipsius, fatetur, Dum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum; et de quo in Job asseritur, Non est potestas super terram quæ comparetur ei. Denique, si hæreticus potens in philosophia aut in Scripturis, aut tyrannus insurgat adversum nos, locum et doctrinam Ecclesiæ nullatenus dimittamus.
paras.en: [[10:4|If the spirit of him that hath power, ascend upon thee|Si spiritus potestatem habentis ascenderit super te]]: that is, if the onset of the devil tempt and assail thee, to carry thee over from the mystical body of Christ into his own body, that is, into the church of the malignant, so as to make thee his member and his slave; or: [[10:4|If the spirit of him that hath power|Si spiritus potestatem habentis]], that is, the stirring of the fomes [that is, the tinder of sin, the inclination to evil left in man after original sin], which lords it over many, assail thee; or: [[10:4|the spirit|Spiritus]], that is, the indignation, [[10:4|of him that hath power|habentis potestatem]], that is, of someone stronger than thou, [[10:4|ascend upon thee|ascenderit super te]], to persecute and oppress thee; [[10:4|leave not thy place|locum tuum ne dimiseris]]: that is, by no means withdraw from the mystical body of Christ, from the devout congregation, from the state of grace and steadfastness in the virtues, from holy patience, nor give in to the wicked; but call upon God, and resist by the virtues, and busy thyself in good works the more earnestly, the more fiercely thou art assailed. Hence James exhorts: [[Jas 4:7|resist the devil: and he will fly from you|Resistite diabolo, et fugiet a vobis]]. And Paul says: [[Rom 16:20|the God of peace crush Satan under your feet speedily|Deus, inquit, pacis conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris velociter]]. Now the devil is very mighty. Of him Christ, his conqueror, declares: [[Luke 11:21|When a strong man armed keepeth his court|Dum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum]]; and of him it is asserted in Job: [[Job 41:24|There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him|Non est potestas super terram quæ comparetur ei]]. Lastly, if a heretic mighty in philosophy or in the Scriptures, or a tyrant, rise up against us, let us by no means leave the place and the teaching of the Church.

paras.t: Quia curatio, id est resistentia talis contra peccata, qua anima a læsione præservatur, et sanitatem recuperat; vel, Curatio, id est fomitis sanatio, seu mitigatio per resistentiam contra concupiscentiam; Curatio quoque, id est contritio seu pœnitentia de peccatis, et superatio interioris tentationis; cessare faciet peccata maxima, id est vitia multa atque enormia, quæ ex fomite et interiori tentatione nascuntur, nisi idonee resistatur. Nempe, ut Jacobus ait, Unusquisque tentatur a concupiscentia sua abstractus et illectus: deinde concupiscentia, quum conceperit, parit peccatum; peccatum vero, quum consummatum fuerit, generat mortem. Unde Hieronymus ait: Primum peccatum est, cogitasse quæ mala sunt, cum mora superflua, aut complacentia aliqua; secundum est, cogitationibus acquievisse; tertium, quod deterius est, opere complevisse; quartum, post peccatum non pœnitere, et in suo sibi complacere delicto. Merito igitur dixit Propheta: Si mei non fuerint dominati, tunc immaculatus ero, et emundabor a delicto maximo.
paras.en: [[10:4|because care|Quia curatio]] [*curatio*: care, but also cure or healing, which Denis's readings draw on], that is, such resistance against sins, by which the soul is preserved from hurt and recovers its health; or: [[10:4|care|Curatio]], that is, the healing of the fomes, or its easing by resisting concupiscence; and also [[10:4|care|Curatio]], that is, contrition or penance for sins, and the overcoming of inward temptation, [[10:4|will make the greatest sins to cease|cessare faciet peccata maxima]], that is, the many and enormous vices which arise from the fomes and from inward temptation, unless it is fitly resisted. For, as James says, [[Jas 1:14|every man is tempted by his own concupiscence, being drawn away and allured|Unusquisque tentatur a concupiscentia sua abstractus et illectus]]: [[Jas 1:15|Then, when concupiscence hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin. But sin, when it is completed, begetteth death.|deinde concupiscentia, quum conceperit, parit peccatum; peccatum vero, quum consummatum fuerit, generat mortem]]. Hence Jerome says: The first sin is to have thought of evil things with needless lingering or some complacency; the second, to have consented to the thoughts; the third, which is worse, to have fulfilled them in deed; the fourth, not to repent after the sin, and to take pleasure in one's own wrongdoing. Rightly, then, did the Prophet say: [[Ps 18:14|If they shall have no dominion over me, then shall I be without spot: and I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin|Si mei non fuerint dominati, tunc immaculatus ero, et emundabor a delicto maximo]].

paras.t: Est et aliud malum quod vidi sub sole, quasi per errorem egrediens a facie principis. Si per principem intelligatur Deus omnipotens, tunc malum istud quod sequitur mox in textu, non egreditur ab eo veraciter per errorem, sed quasi per errorem: quia insipientibus videtur erroneum et injustum, quum tamen juste permittatur a Deo. Si vero per principem intelligatur quicumque princeps terrenus, sic malum quod subditur, vere ex errore pravitateque accidit sæpe: videlicet, positum stultum in dignitate sublimi. Vitiosi enim, ambitiosi, imperiti, frequenter ad officia promoventur, melioribus derelictis. De quibus subjungitur: et divites sedere deorsum, id est, spiritualibus gratiis locupletes et virtuosos, subesse. Vidi servos in equis, id est, ignobiles et vitiis subditos, per violentiam ad præsidentiam ascendisse; et principes ambulantes super terram quasi servos, id est, eos quibus ex jure competebat præesse, oppressos et pulsos ab impiis illis. Istud Deus fieri sinit propter subditorum flagitia: quia frequenter dantur hominibus principes ac prælati secundum ipsorum demerita hominum. Ideo per Osee Dominus loquitur: Dabo tibi regem in furore meo, et principes in indignatione mea. De quo etiam in Job inducitur: Qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi. Verumtamen, quod talia non sint directe et effective a Deo, constat ex hoc, quod ipse rursus in Osee testatur: Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me; principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi. Aliqui tamen sua promotione fuerunt digni, et directe a Deo promoti; sed tempore procedente, potestate abusi sunt, et tyranni effecti, sicut et Saul.
paras.en: [[10:5|There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were by an error proceeding from the face of the prince|Est et aliud malum quod vidi sub sole, quasi per errorem egrediens a facie principis]] [Denis's text reads: There is also another evil]. If by the prince is understood almighty God, then the evil that follows next in the text does not truly proceed from him by error, but *as it were* by error: for to the foolish it seems erroneous and unjust, though in fact it is justly permitted by God. But if by the prince is understood any earthly prince, then the evil next named does often truly come about through error and wickedness: namely, [[10:6|A fool set in high dignity|positum stultum in dignitate sublimi]]. For the vicious, the ambitious and the unskilled are often promoted to offices, and better men passed over. Of these it is added: [[10:6|and the rich sitting beneath|et divites sedere deorsum]], that is, that those rich in spiritual graces, and the virtuous, are made subject. [[10:7|I have seen servants upon horses|Vidi servos in equis]], that is, the base-born and those enslaved to vice have climbed to authority by violence; [[10:7|and princes walking on the ground as servants|et principes ambulantes super terram quasi servos]], that is, those to whom it belonged by right to rule, oppressed and driven out by those wicked men. God allows this to happen because of the crimes of subjects: for princes and prelates are often given to men according to the demerits of those very men. Therefore the Lord speaks through Osee: [[Osee 13:11|I will give thee a king in my wrath|Dabo tibi regem in furore meo]], and princes in my indignation [the Vulgate goes on: and will take him away in my indignation]. Of which also it is brought in in Job: [[Job 34:30|Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people.|Qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi]]. Yet that such things are not directly and effectively from God is clear from this, that he testifies again in Osee: [[Osee 8:4|They have reigned, but not by me: they have been princes, and I knew not|Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me; principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi]]. Some, however, were worthy of their promotion and were promoted directly by God; but as time went on they abused their power and became tyrants, as Saul did.

paras.t: Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam: id est, qui alteri quærit nocere, et deceptionis laqueum præparare atque extendere, lædit se ipsum in anima, et debitas luet pœnas, ac similia patietur. Hinc in Proverbiis scriptum est: In insidiis suis capientur iniqui. Et iterum ait Scriptura: Qui expandit laqueum, capietur in illo. Etenim uniuscujusque malum redundat in suum auctorem; et propriam linguam detractor coinquinat; propriam mentem invidiosus exulcerat, se ipsum iracundus conturbat. Ideo ait Psalmista de impio: Lacum aperuit, et effodit eum; et incidit in foveam quam fecit. Denique qui vitiorum occasiones non vitant, sed sponte assumunt, sibi ipsis foveam parant, et in eam labuntur, dum ex occasionibus talibus corruunt in peccata: sicut qui pergunt ad loca suspecta, et prava admittunt consortia.
paras.en: [[10:8|He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it|Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam]]: that is, he who seeks to harm another, and to prepare and spread the snare of deceit, hurts himself in his soul, and will pay the penalty due, and will suffer the like. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 11:6|the unjust shall be caught in their own snares|In insidiis suis capientur iniqui]]. And again Scripture says: [[Ecclus 27:29|he that layeth a snare for another, shall perish in it|Qui expandit laqueum, capietur in illo]] [Denis's wording, he that spreadeth a snare shall be caught in it, is not quite that of the Vulgate]. For each man's evil recoils upon its author: the detractor defiles his own tongue, the envious man ulcerates his own mind, the angry man troubles himself. Therefore the Psalmist says of the wicked man: [[Ps 7:16|He hath opened a pit and dug it: and he is fallen into the hole he made.|Lacum aperuit, et effodit eum; et incidit in foveam quam fecit]]. Lastly, those who do not avoid the occasions of vice but take them up of their own accord prepare a pit for themselves and slip into it, when through such occasions they fall headlong into sins: like those who go to suspect places and admit evil company.

paras.t: Et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber. Hoc corporaliter quandoque sic accidit. Sed sensus est, quod qui canonicas Patrum sanctiones et ecclesiasticam disciplinam, quibus muniuntur fideles, transgreditur, a dæmone punietur: qui in Genesi serpens vocatur. Unde et alibi scriptum est: Mordeat eum coluber.
paras.en: [[10:8|and he that breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him|Et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber]]. This sometimes happens so in the body. But the sense is that he who transgresses the canonical decrees of the Fathers and the discipline of the Church, by which the faithful are fenced about, will be punished by the demon, who in Genesis is called the serpent[[Gen 3:1||]][[Gen 3:4||]][[Gen 3:13||]][[Gen 3:14||]]. Hence it is written elsewhere too: [[Amos 5:19|a serpent should bite him|Mordeat eum coluber]].

paras.t: Qui transfert lapides de loco suo ad locum indebitum, affligetur in eis: id est, qui fideles (qui sunt lapides vivi, ex quibus ædificatur Ecclesia) fallit, et de Ecclesia ad hæreticorum, aut schismaticorum, aut perversorum consortia trahit, enormiter peccat et tormenta sustinebit perpetua, ecclesiasticis quoque percutietur censuris. De talibus lapidibus loquitur beatissimus Petrus in prima sua epistola, dicens: Et vos tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini, domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, offerre hostias spirituales, acceptabiles Deo per Jesum Christum. Unde per Isaiam Dominus promisit Ecclesiæ: Fundabo te in sapphiris.
paras.en: [[10:9|He that removeth stones|Qui transfert lapides]] from their own place to a place where they do not belong, [[10:9|shall be hurt by them|affligetur in eis]]: that is, he who deceives the faithful (who are the living stones of which the Church is built), and draws them out of the Church into the company of heretics, schismatics or perverse men, sins enormously and will suffer everlasting torments, and will also be struck with the censures of the Church. Of such stones the most blessed Peter speaks in his first epistle, saying: [[1 Pet 2:5|Be you also as living stones built up, a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.|Et vos tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini, domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, offerre hostias spirituales, acceptabiles Deo per Jesum Christum]]. Hence the Lord promised the Church through Isaias: I [[Is 54:11|will lay thy foundations with sapphires|Fundabo te in sapphiris]].

paras.t: Et qui scindit ligna, vulnerabitur ab eis. Per ligna quoque et arbores, passim signantur credentes. Unde ait Salvator: Aut facite arborem bonam, aut facite arborem malam. Qui itaque ligna scindit, id est, credentes scandalizat, et pusillos a bono incepto avertit, atque a Christo præscindit; nunc vulnera incidit vitiorum, passurus deinceps vulnera infelicium supplicium. Nempe, Væ homini per quem scandalum venit. Et in Proverbiis dictum est: Mallei percutientes præparati corporibus stultorum.
paras.en: [[10:9|and he that cutteth trees, shall be wounded by them|Et qui scindit ligna, vulnerabitur ab eis]]. By wood and trees, too, believers are signified throughout Scripture. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 12:33|Either make the tree good|Aut facite arborem bonam]], [[Matt 12:33|or make the tree evil|aut facite arborem malam]]. He, then, who [[10:9|cutteth trees|ligna scindit]], that is, who scandalizes believers, and turns the little ones from a good beginning and cuts them off from Christ, falls now into the wounds of vices, and will afterwards suffer the wounds of the punishments of the wretched. For: [[Matt 18:7|woe to that man by whom the scandal cometh|Væ homini per quem scandalum venit]]. And it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 19:29|striking hammers for the bodies of fools|Mallei percutientes præparati corporibus stultorum]].

paras.t: Si retusum fuerit ferrum, id est, si acumen suum amiserit securis aut clavus ex percussione super saxum, et hoc non ut prius, id est, non parum ita acciderit, sed hebetatum fuerit, id est omnino obtusum, multo labore exacuetur. Quod autem istud non dicatur ad litteram de ferro, sed metaphorice de homine negligente ac duro, constat ex eo quod subditur: et post industriam sequetur sapientia. Tanquam dicat: Si homo acuti ingenii, et in Scripturis competenter instructus, postposito eo quod novit, in superbiam aut luxuriam corruat, et mente obtenebrata, hebes ac deses fiat ad ea quæ Dei sunt ac suæ salutis; non faciliter ad veram pertinget contritionem, nec recuperabitur levi labore, sed ex intimo corde oportet ingemiscere eum, et omnem carnalitatem hebetantem abjicere, atque ad spiritualem consurgere intellectum, considerando Dei justitiam, et sua novissima: sicque post talem industriam et laborem sequetur sapientia, et ipse sapientiam assequetur. Ideo monet Apostolus: Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis. Unde per Ezechielem Dominus contestatur: Multo labore sudatum est, ut auferretur ab ea nimia rubigo ejus; et iterum, Non mundaberis priusquam requiescere in te faciam indignationem meam.
paras.en: [[10:10|If the iron be blunt|Si retusum fuerit ferrum]], that is, if an axe or a nail has lost its edge from striking on a rock, [[10:10|and be not as before|et hoc non ut prius]], that is, if this has happened in no small measure, [[10:10|but be made blunt|sed hebetatum fuerit]], that is, wholly dulled, [[10:10|with much labour it shall be sharpened|multo labore exacuetur]]. That this is not said literally of iron, but metaphorically of a negligent and hardened man, is clear from what is added: [[10:10|and after industry shall follow wisdom|et post industriam sequetur sapientia]]. As if he said: If a man of sharp wit, and competently instructed in the Scriptures, sets aside what he knows and falls into pride or lust, and with darkened mind becomes dull and sluggish toward the things of God and of his own salvation, he will not easily come to true contrition, nor be recovered with light labour; but he must groan from his inmost heart, cast off all the carnality that dulls him, and rise up to spiritual understanding, considering the justice of God and his own last things: and so after such industry and labour wisdom will follow, and he will attain to wisdom. Therefore the Apostle warns: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]. Hence the Lord protests through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 24:12|Great pains have been taken|Multo labore sudatum est]], that its great rust might be taken from it [Denis's reading; the Vulgate has: and its great rust is not gone out of it]; and again: [[Ezech 24:13|neither shalt thou be cleansed, before I cause my indignation to rest in thee|Non mundaberis priusquam requiescere in te faciam indignationem meam]].

paras.t: Periculosum est ergo peccare; periculosius, in peccatis manere; periculosissimum, usque ad mortem, aut infirmitatem vel senium, pœnitentiam ipsam differre: quia tunc vix aliquis veraciter pœnitet, inveterata consuetudine pressus et victus, de qua ex fundo cordis resipiscere, difficulter nimis contingit, nisi quod per omnipotentis Dei gratiam prævenientem faciliter fieri potest, quod per naturam vix effici valet. Et tamen ipse Omnipotens, apud quem non est impossibile, imo nec difficile, omne verbum, in hoc ipso difficultatem quamdam ostendit, asserens per Prophetam: Abominabilis facta es, quia mundare te volui, et non es mundata; et per Isaiam iterum, Præbuisti mihi laborem in iniquitatibus tuis. Et in Malachia habetur: Laborare fecistis Dominum in sermonibus vestris.
paras.en: It is dangerous, then, to sin; more dangerous to remain in sins; most dangerous to put off penance itself until death, or sickness, or old age: for then scarcely anyone repents truly, weighed down and overcome by long-standing habit, from which it is exceedingly hard to come to one's senses from the bottom of the heart; save that by the prevenient grace [that is, the grace that goes before and moves the will] of almighty God that can easily be done which by nature can scarcely be brought about. And yet the Almighty himself, with whom no word is impossible[[Luke 1:37||]], nay, nor hard[[Jer 32:17||]][[Jer 32:27||]], shows a certain difficulty in this very thing, declaring through the Prophet: Thou art become abominable [Denis's wording; the Vulgate has: Thy uncleanness is execrable], [[Ezech 24:13|because I desired to cleanse thee, and thou art not cleansed|quia mundare te volui, et non es mundata]]; and again through Isaias: [[Is 43:24|thou hast wearied me with thy iniquities|Præbuisti mihi laborem in iniquitatibus tuis]] [literally, thou hast given me labour: the same *labor* as in the much labour of v. 10]. And in Malachias we have: [[Mal 2:17|You have wearied the Lord with your words|Laborare fecistis Dominum in sermonibus vestris]].

paras.t: Si mordeat mordens serpens in silentio, nihil eo minus habet qui occulte detrahit fratri suo: id est, sicut letaliter nocet corpori serpens qui morsu occulto ei infundit venenum, ita detractor propriam animam detrahendo occidit. Similiter animam audientis, quantum in ipso est, et eum cui obloquitur, occidit, quantum ad esse bonæ reputationis ac famæ, quod in cordibus habuit proximorum. Unde, ut S. Clemens refert, sacratissimus Petrus asseruit, tria esse homicidii genera: unum corporale, aliud odium, tertium detractionem. Merito igitur detractores sunt Deo odibiles; et, Jacobo protestante apostolo, Qui detrahit fratri suo, detrahit legi. Præterea, per serpentem silenter mordentem, intelligi potest diabolus, pestifera suggestione mentem inficiens: quam necat silentio, dum eam sic detinet in peccato, quod vitia sua excusat, nec confitetur. Audi hoc, o detractor malevole et infelix; vide cui assimileris. Certe non solum terreno, sed infernali colubro comparat te Scriptura. Resipisce ergo, insipiens; et quod tibi fieri indignaris, non facias proximis.
paras.en: [[10:11|If a serpent bite in silence|Si mordeat mordens serpens in silentio]], [[10:11|he is nothing better that backbiteth secretly|nihil eo minus habet qui occulte detrahit]] his brother [Denis's text adds *fratri suo*, his brother, and reads *mordeat mordens*, bite with a bite]: that is, as a serpent that pours its venom into the body by a hidden bite harms it mortally, so the detractor kills his own soul by detracting. Likewise he kills the soul of the hearer, as far as in him lies, and him against whom he speaks, as regards the being of good repute and fame which he had in the hearts of his neighbours. Hence, as St Clement relates, the most holy Peter declared that there are three kinds of homicide: one bodily, another hatred, the third detraction. Rightly, then, are detractors [[Rom 1:30|hateful to God|Deo odibiles]]; and, as the apostle James protests, [[Jas 4:11|He that detracteth his brother|Qui detrahit fratri suo]], [[Jas 4:11|detracteth the law|detrahit legi]]. Moreover, by the serpent biting silently can be understood the devil, infecting the mind with pestilent suggestion: he kills it in silence, while he so holds it fast in sin that it excuses its vices and does not confess them. Hear this, O malevolent and unhappy detractor; see whom thou art likened to. Surely Scripture compares thee not only to an earthly serpent but to the serpent of hell. Come to thy senses, then, thou fool; and what thou wouldst be indignant to have done to thee, do not to thy neighbours.

paras.t: Verba oris sapientis, gratia, id est gratiosa et accepta, facientia eum Deo hominibusque benevolis amabilem et placentem, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Sapiens se ipsum in verbis amabilem facit. Unde de Christo refert Evangelista: Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus. De quo Psalmista prædixit: Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis. Et labia insipientis præcipitabunt eum in foveam vitiorum, deinde in voraginem tormentorum. In multa quoque damna, pericula, afflictionesque cordis et corporis incidit homo ex verbis suis insipientibus, pungitivis, mordacibus. Unde in Proverbiis dictum est: Labia insipientis supplantabunt eum; itemque, Qui inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala.
paras.en: [[10:12|The words of the mouth of a wise man are grace|Verba oris sapientis, gratia]], that is, gracious and acceptable, making him lovable and pleasing to God and to well-disposed men, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:13|A man wise in words shall make himself beloved|Sapiens se ipsum in verbis amabilem facit]]. Hence the Evangelist relates of Christ: All [[Luke 4:22|wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth|Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus]]. Of whom the Psalmist foretold: [[Ps 44:3|grace is poured abroad in thy lips|Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis]]. [[10:12|but the lips of a fool shall throw him down headlong|Et labia insipientis præcipitabunt eum]] into the pit of vices, and then into the abyss of torments. Into many losses, too, and dangers and afflictions of heart and body a man falls through his foolish, stinging and biting words. Hence it is said in Proverbs: The lips of the fool shall trip him up[[Prov 22:12||]] [the margin gives Cf. Prov. xxii, 12, where the words of the unjust are overthrown; Denis's words are not found as such in Proverbs]; and again: [[Prov 13:3|he that hath no guard on his speech shall meet with evils|Qui inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala]].

paras.t: Initium verborum ejus, stultitia, id est, stulte incipit loqui, et sine deliberatione ac consideratione matura, sicut alibi dictum est: Os fatuorum ebullit stultitiam. Et novissimum oris illius, error pessimus: quia quanto plus ac diutius loquitur, tanto gravius peccat loquendo; et tandem ad detractiones, mendacia, perjuria, contentiones, contumeliosaque verba prorumpit. Multi quoque per suam facundiam vel potius loquacitatem, inciderunt hæreticam pravitatem. Ideo, qui imponit stulto silentium, mitigat iras, et præcidit varias culpas.
paras.en: [[10:13|The beginning of his words is folly|Initium verborum ejus, stultitia]], that is, he begins to speak foolishly, without deliberation and ripe consideration, as is said elsewhere: [[Prov 15:2|the mouth of fools bubbleth out folly|Os fatuorum ebullit stultitiam]]. [[10:13|and the end of his talk is a mischievous error|Et novissimum oris illius, error pessimus]]: for the more and the longer he talks, the more gravely he sins in talking; and at last he breaks out into detractions, lies, perjuries, quarrels and insulting words. Many, too, through their eloquence, or rather their talkativeness, have fallen into heretical depravity. Therefore [[Prov 26:10|he that putteth a fool to silence, appeaseth anger|qui imponit stulto silentium, mitigat iras]], and cuts off many kinds of fault.

paras.t: Stultus verba multiplicat. Non enim habet in loquendo discretionem; et sæpe per verba superflua nititur et intendit suam jactare scientiam, quum potius suam pandat stultitiam. Ideo in Proverbiis conscriptum est: Totum spiritum suum profert stultus. Compendiose ergo loquendum est, nec sine necessitate, fructu, seu rationabili causa protrahendus est sermo. In multiloquio enim non deest peccatum.
paras.en: [[10:14|A fool multiplieth words|Stultus verba multiplicat]]. For he has no discretion in speaking; and often by needless words he strives and aims to show off his knowledge, when rather he lays bare his folly. Therefore it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus]]. We must speak briefly, then, and not draw out our speech without necessity, fruit or reasonable cause. For [[Prov 10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|In multiloquio enim non deest peccatum]].

paras.t: Ignorat homo quid ante se fuerit. De multis enim præteritis ignorantiam habemus; et quæ ex relatione, scripturis, aut chronicis agnoscimus de præteritis, pauca et modicissima sunt respectu horum quæ nescimus de talibus. Et præsertim stultus non studiosus, de talibus est ignarus. Et quod post se futurum est, quis ei poterit indicare? quasi dicat, Hominum nullus: loquendo de futuris omnino contingentibus, nec a Deo in sacro eloquio, aut alias revelatis. Ideo stultus, horum tam nescius, non debet verba multiplicare, nec apud imperitos per loquacitatem velle doctus videri. Qui enim moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est; vir autem linguosus non dirigetur in terra.
paras.en: [[10:14|A man cannot tell what hath been before him|Ignorat homo quid ante se fuerit]]. For of many past things we are ignorant; and what we know of the past from report, writings or chronicles is little and very slight compared with what we do not know of such things. And above all the fool who does not study is ignorant of them. [[10:14|and what shall be after him, who can tell him?|Et quod post se futurum est, quis ei poterit indicare?]] as if to say: No man can; speaking of future things that are wholly contingent [that is, that may or may not come to pass], and not revealed by God in holy writ or otherwise. Therefore the fool, so ignorant of these things, ought not to multiply words, nor wish to seem learned among the unskilled by his talkativeness. For [[Prov 10:19|he that refraineth his lips, is most wise|Qui enim moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est]]; but [[Ps 139:12|A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth|vir autem linguosus non dirigetur in terra]].

paras.t: Labor stultorum affliget eos: id est, inane et immoderatum studium iniquorum, quod habent in curiosa inquisitione, ornata locutione, illicita actione, ingeret eis pœnam, tam in sæculo isto, quam in futuro. Multam enim in talibus inquietudinem, molestiam, sollicitudinem, patiuntur. Ideo dicunt illud Sapientiæ: Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles. De qualibus ait Psalmista: Labor labiorum ipsorum operiet eos.
paras.en: [[10:15|The labour of fools shall afflict them|Labor stultorum affliget eos]]: that is, the empty and immoderate striving of the wicked, which they spend on curious inquiry, ornate speech and unlawful action, will bring punishment upon them, both in this world and in the next. For they suffer much restlessness, trouble and anxiety in such things. Therefore they say those words of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways|Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles]]. Of such the Psalmist says: [[Ps 139:10|the labour of their lips shall overwhelm them|Labor labiorum ipsorum operiet eos]].

paras.t: Qui nesciunt in urbem pergere, id est ad patriam tendere Beatorum, et incorporari Ecclesiæ militanti per fidem et caritatem. De qua urbe fertur in Psalmo: Gloriosa dicta sunt de te, civitas Dei. Sicut lætantium omnium habitatio est in te. Et in Apocalypsi: Civitas non eget sole neque luna. Et in Ezechiele: Nomen civitatis, Dominus ibidem. Interdum autem civitas in malo accipitur, ut quum Dominus ait per Osee prophetam: Non ingrediar civitatem. Denique labor hæreticorum, paganorum et philosophorum, præsertim eorum qui contra Religionem christianam verbis et scriptis plurimis acriter disputaverunt, ut Porphyrius atque Averroes, æternaliter eos affliget. Qui sapientes fuerunt ut facerent mala, bene facere autem, id est civitatem Domini virtutum ingredi, nescierunt.
paras.en: [[10:15|that know not how to go to the city|Qui nesciunt in urbem pergere]], that is, to make for the fatherland of the Blessed, and to be incorporated into the Church militant by faith and charity. Of which city it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 86:3|Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God.|Gloriosa dicta sunt de te, civitas Dei]] [[Ps 86:7|The dwelling in thee is as it were of all rejoicing.|Sicut lætantium omnium habitatio est in te]] And in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:23|the city hath no need of the sun, nor of the moon|Civitas non eget sole neque luna]]. And in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 48:35|the name of the city|Nomen civitatis]], [[Ezech 48:35|The Lord is there|Dominus ibidem]]. But sometimes *city* is taken in a bad sense, as when the Lord says through the prophet Osee: [[Osee 11:9|I will not enter into the city|Non ingrediar civitatem]]. Lastly, the labour of heretics, pagans and philosophers, above all of those who have argued sharply against the Christian Religion in words and in very many writings, like Porphyry and Averroes, will afflict them eternally. They [[Jer 4:22|are wise to do evil|sapientes fuerunt ut facerent mala]], [[Jer 4:22|but to do good|bene facere autem]], that is, to enter the city of the Lord of hosts, [[Jer 4:22|they have no knowledge|nescierunt]].

paras.t: Væ tibi, terra, id est politia seu regnum, cujus rex, id est princeps, dux, comes, aut prælatus, seu præsul, puer est, non solum ætate, sed et moribus et inexperientia ac imperitia. Dum enim supremus in populo, talis est, multa pericula, damna, turbationes imminent subditis. Nam, ut ait Philosophus, in omni genere oportet primum esse potissimum et perfectum. Et quo pluribus aliquis præsidet, eo ampliori prudentia virtuositateque eget. Pueri autem sunt inexperti, et per consequens imprudentes: quia, ut Aristoteles docet, ad prudentiam experientia requiritur. Hinc rursus in Politicis scribit, quod nemo eligit pueros in principes. Et cujus principes mane comedunt, id est, gulæ ac luxui vacant, nec sobrietati student atque prudentiæ, abstinentes quousque causas ac judicia expedierint subditorum: ad quod ante comestionem aptiores essent, quam postea. Hanc eamdem sententiam allegat Tullius a Platone dictam et scriptam, sicut et eam quæ subditur.
paras.en: [[10:16|Woe to thee, O land|Væ tibi, terra]], that is, commonwealth or kingdom, [[10:16|when thy king|cujus rex]], that is, prince, duke, count, or prelate or bishop, [[10:16|is a child|puer est]], not only in age, but also in character, inexperience and unskilfulness. For when he who is highest among the people is such, many dangers, losses and disturbances threaten his subjects. For, as the Philosopher says, in every kind the first must be the most excellent and perfect. And the more men one rules over, the greater the prudence and virtue he needs. But children are inexperienced, and consequently imprudent: for, as Aristotle teaches, experience is required for prudence. Hence again he writes in the Politics that no one chooses children for princes. [[10:16|and when the princes eat in the morning|Et cujus principes mane comedunt]], that is, give themselves to gluttony and luxury, and do not study sobriety and prudence by abstaining until they have dispatched the causes and judgments of their subjects: for which they would be fitter before eating than after. Tully cites this same saying as spoken and written by Plato, and the one that follows also.

paras.t: Beata terra, cujus rex nobilis est, non solum carnis propagine, quæ nobilitas (secundum Aristotelem in libro Politicorum) non est nisi antiquata opulentia, sed et sapientiæ ac virtutum præclaritate. De qua in Actibus Apostolorum sic dicitur: Nobiliores ex eis susceperunt verbum Dei cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas. Dum hæ duæ nobilitates in eodem concurrunt, se invicem ornant, dicente Gregorio: Dum una alteri sociatur, quasi gemma carbunculi in ornamento auri locatur. Et cujus principes, scilicet judices et ceteri officiati, vescuntur in tempore suo, expeditis pro posse causis reipublicæ et litibus subditorum, ad reficiendum corpora sua moderate, post laborem et fatigationem pro bono communi, et non ad luxuriam: per quam ratio maxime obscuratur: ideo summe principibus et prælatis cavenda. De talibus præsidentibus in Isaia inducitur: Princeps ea quæ digna sunt principe, cogitabit; et ipse super duces stabit. Hinc Antigonus dixisse legitur Alexandro: Indignus es imperare, propter incontinentiam tuam et juventutem.
paras.en: [[10:17|Blessed is the land, whose king is noble|Beata terra, cujus rex nobilis est]], not only by descent of the flesh (a nobility which, according to Aristotle in the book of the Politics, is nothing but long-established wealth), but also by the brightness of wisdom and virtue. Of this nobility it is said thus in the Acts of the Apostles: The [[Acts 17:11|more noble|Nobiliores]] of them [[Acts 17:11|received the word with all eagerness, daily searching the scriptures|susceperunt verbum Dei cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas]]. When these two nobilities meet in the same man, they adorn each other, as Gregory says: When the one is joined to the other, it is as if a carbuncle gem were set in an ornament of gold. [[10:17|and whose princes|Et cujus principes]], namely the judges and other officers, [[10:17|eat in due season|vescuntur in tempore suo]], having dispatched as best they can the causes of the commonwealth and the lawsuits of their subjects, [[10:17|for refreshment|ad reficiendum]] of their bodies in moderation, after labour and fatigue for the common good, [[10:17|and not for riotousness|et non ad luxuriam]], by which reason is darkened most of all: and so princes and prelates must beware of it above all. Of such rulers it is said in Isaias: [[Is 32:8|the prince will devise such things as are worthy of a prince, and he shall stand above the rulers|Princeps ea quæ digna sunt principe, cogitabit; et ipse super duces stabit]]. Hence Antigonus is read to have said to Alexander: Thou art unworthy to rule, because of thy incontinence and thy youth.

paras.t: Allegorice, Beata terra, id est militans Ecclesia: cujus rex nobilis est, scilicet Christus Filius Dei Patris ac reginæ Virginis Matris: cujus principes, id est Apostoli, sobriissimi exstiterunt, primum quærentes regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, incessabiliterque intenti ad procurandam hominum universorum salutem.
paras.en: Allegorically, [[10:17|Blessed is the land|Beata terra]], that is, the Church militant, [[10:17|whose king is noble|cujus rex nobilis est]], namely Christ, Son of God the Father and of the Virgin Mother, the queen; [[10:17|and whose princes|cujus principes]], that is, the Apostles, were most sober, seeking [[Matt 6:33|first the kingdom of God, and his justice|primum quærentes regnum Dei et justitiam ejus]], and unceasingly intent on procuring the salvation of all men.

paras.t: In pigritiis humiliatur contignatio. Contignatio vocatur conjunctio seu coaptatio lignorum et lignorum in ædificio domus. Quemadmodum ergo contignatio talis humiliatur, id est, dissolvitur et cadit, ex pigritia rectorum ac civium urbis, qui ex sua ignavia permittunt turres et domos civitatis perire; sic ex acedia uniuscujusque hominis, perit in eo virtutum constructio, et caritatis prosternitur altitudo. Ex negligentia quoque prælatorum sic deformatur Ecclesia, et munimenta ipsius labuntur. De quibus ait Bernardus: Arcem Sion obtinuerunt, et potestative deinceps totam tradunt incendio civitatem. Misera eorum conversatio, plebis tuæ, o Domine Jesu, subversio est. Non jam ornant Ecclesiam, sed spoliant, scandalizant, evertunt. Hinc est quod Ecclesia hispida est, exsanguis, deformis, et facie miseranda.
paras.en: [[10:18|By slothfulness a building shall be brought down|In pigritiis humiliatur contignatio]] [*contignatio*, which the Douay-Rheims renders building, is properly a framing of beams]. *Contignatio* is the name for the joining or fitting together of timbers with timbers in the building of a house. As, then, such a framing is brought down, that is, comes apart and falls, through the sloth of the rulers and citizens of a town, who through their idleness let the towers and houses of the city go to ruin, so through the acedia [that is, spiritual sloth, a sorrowful weariness of the things of God] of each man the structure of the virtues perishes in him, and the height of charity is laid low. Through the negligence of prelates, too, the Church is thus disfigured, and her defences give way. Of them Bernard says: They have taken the citadel of Sion, and thenceforth by their power hand over the whole city to the fire. Their wretched way of life is the overthrow of thy people, O Lord Jesus. They no longer adorn the Church, but strip, scandalize and overturn her. Hence it is that the Church is rough, bloodless, disfigured, and pitiable to look upon.

paras.t: Et in infirmitate manuum, perstillabit domus: id est, ex remissione et debilitate manuum ad operandum, et reparandum confracta in tecto, contingit quod guttæ cadunt per tectum. Sic ex caritatis defectu et tepefactione virtutum anima ictibus passionum colliditur, imbribus adversitatum et ventis tentationum dejicitur, quemadmodum in Matthæo ait Salvator: Omnis qui audit verba mea, et non facit ea, similis erit viro stulto, qui ædificavit domum suam super arenam: et descendit pluvia, et venerunt flumina, et flaverunt venti, et irruerunt in domum illam; et cecidit, et fuit ruina ejus magna. Hinc tepido in Apocalypsi dicitur: Utinam calidus esses aut frigidus; nunc autem quia tepidus es, incipiam te evomere ex ore meo. Atque in Isaia Dominus loquitur: Confortamini, manus fatigatæ, et, genua debilia, roboramini. Paulus quoque: Manus, inquit, remissas erigite, et rectos facite gressus pedibus vestris.
paras.en: [[10:18|and through the weakness of hands, the house shall drop through|Et in infirmitate manuum, perstillabit domus]]: that is, through slackness and feebleness of the hands in working and in repairing what is broken in the roof, it comes about that drops fall through the roof. So through want of charity and the cooling of the virtues the soul is battered by the blows of the passions, and thrown down by the rains of adversity and the winds of temptation, as the Saviour says in Matthew: [[Matt 7:26|every one that heareth these my words and doth them not, shall be like a foolish man that built his house upon the sand|Omnis qui audit verba mea, et non facit ea, similis erit viro stulto, qui ædificavit domum suam super arenam]]: [[Matt 7:27|And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and they beat upon that house, and it fell, and great was the fall thereof|et descendit pluvia, et venerunt flumina, et flaverunt venti, et irruerunt in domum illam; et cecidit, et fuit ruina ejus magna]]. Hence it is said to the lukewarm in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:15|I would thou wert cold or hot|Utinam calidus esses aut frigidus]]; but now [[Apoc 3:16|because thou art lukewarm|quia tepidus es]], [[Apoc 3:16|I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth|incipiam te evomere ex ore meo]]. And in Isaias the Lord says: [[Is 35:3|Strengthen ye the feeble hands, and confirm the weak knees.|Confortamini, manus fatigatæ, et, genua debilia, roboramini]] [Denis's reading turns the verse into an address: Be strengthened, ye weary hands, and ye feeble knees, be made strong]. Paul too says: [[Heb 12:12|lift up the hands which hang down|Manus, inquit, remissas erigite]], [[Heb 12:13|And make straight steps with your feet|et rectos facite gressus pedibus vestris]].

paras.t: Conformiter ex carnalitate, perversitate et negligentia prælatorum et prædicatorum, contingunt hæc mala in singulis quibusque Ecclesiis: quoniam deformata, lapsa, infirma, confracta non reformant, erigunt, roborant, neque consolidant.
paras.en: In like manner, through the carnality, perversity and negligence of prelates and preachers, these evils come about in each and every Church: for they do not reform, raise up, strengthen or make firm what is disfigured, fallen, weak and broken.

paras.t: Sed, sicut subjungitur, In risu faciunt panem et vinum: id est, cum jucunditate carnali procurant et præparant sibi victualia delicata, et populo blandiuntur, atque placentia potius quam salubria sermocinantur, ut propria commoda consequantur. De quibus in Osee conqueritur Dominus: Peccata populi mei comedunt, et ad iniquitatem sublevant animas eorum. Vix aliquem pro suis peccatis caritative et juste corripiunt, ne temporalium detrimentum incurrant. Propter quod subditur, ut epulentur bibentes. De quibus per Isaiam loquitur Deus: Ipsi pastores ignoraverunt intelligentiam, videntes vana, et dormientes, canes impudentissimi, nescientes saturitatem; et iterum per Ezechielem: Nonne oves pascuntur a pastoribus? Lac comedebatis, et lana operiebamini; gregem autem meum non pascebatis.
paras.en: But, as is added, [[10:19|For laughter they make bread, and wine|In risu faciunt panem et vinum]]: that is, with carnal merriment they procure and prepare dainty fare for themselves, and flatter the people, and preach what pleases rather than what heals, so as to obtain their own advantage. Of them the Lord complains in Osee: [[Osee 4:8|They shall eat the sins of my people, and shall lift up their souls to their iniquity.|Peccata populi mei comedunt, et ad iniquitatem sublevant animas eorum]]. They scarcely ever rebuke anyone for his sins with charity and justice, lest they incur temporal loss. For which reason it is added: [[10:19|that the living may feast|ut epulentur bibentes]] [Denis reads *bibentes*, drinking, for the Vulgate's *viventes*, the living]. Of them God speaks through Isaias: [[Is 56:11|the shepherds themselves knew no understanding|Ipsi pastores ignoraverunt intelligentiam]], [[Is 56:10|seeing vain things, sleeping|videntes vana, et dormientes]], [[Is 56:11|most impudent dogs, they never had enough|canes impudentissimi, nescientes saturitatem]]; and again through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 34:2|should not the flocks be fed by the shepherds?|Nonne oves pascuntur a pastoribus?]] [[Ezech 34:3|You ate the milk, and you clothed yourselves with the wool|Lac comedebatis, et lana operiebamini]]; [[Ezech 34:3|but my flock you did not feed|gregem autem meum non pascebatis]].

paras.t: Et pecuniæ obediunt omnia: id est, quia per pecuniam omnia ista delectabilia, utilia et honesta hujus sæculi procurantur; ideo omnes avaritiæ student, et amore pecuniæ relinquunt justitiam. Nec hi qui præsunt, subditis debitam adhibent disciplinam, ne illis offensis, aut certe correctis et juste agentibus, cessent adipisci ab eis pecuniam. Sunt equidem quidam tam obtenebrati et sceleratissimi, ut malint subditos peccare atque in vitiis perseverare, quam pecuniarum (quas loco emendationis accipiunt) emolumenta amittere. Quocontra Seneca ait: Pecuniæ imperare oportet, non obedire. Et sanctus pater Bernardus: Filii Adam, genus avarum et ambitiosum, audite: Quid vobis cum terrenis divitiis, quæ nec veræ nec vestræ sunt? Aurum et argentum quid sunt, nisi terra alba et rubea, quæ hominum error pretiosiora facit, quam sunt? Verumtamen veri et perfecti discipuli Christi, aurum arbitrantur ut lutum, et pecuniam aspernantur ut stercora, in tantum ut nec tangere eam dignentur, et videre vix acquiescant.
paras.en: [[10:19|and all things obey money|Et pecuniæ obediunt omnia]]: that is, because all the pleasant, useful and honourable things of this world are procured by money, all men therefore give themselves to avarice, and abandon justice for love of money. Nor do those who are set over others apply due discipline to their subjects, lest, if these are offended, or indeed corrected and living justly, they should cease to get money from them. There are indeed some so darkened and so very wicked that they would rather have their subjects sin and persevere in vice than lose the profit of the money which they take in place of amendment [that is, fines and payments accepted instead of correcting the sinner]. Against this Seneca says: Money should be commanded, not obeyed. And the holy father Bernard: Sons of Adam, covetous and ambitious race, hear: What have you to do with earthly riches, which are neither true nor yours? What are gold and silver but white and red earth, which the error of men makes more precious than they are? But the true and perfect disciples of Christ count gold as mud, and spurn money as dung[[Phil 3:8||]], so much so that they do not deign to touch it, and scarcely consent to look at it.

paras.t: In cogitatione tua regi ne detrahas, et in secreto cubiculi tui ne maledixeris diviti: id est, tam diligenter præcave obloqui superioribus tuis, principibus ac prælatis, et potentioribus, ut nec in corde tuo murmures contra eos, aut obtrectare proponas, nec in secretissimo loco id facias, quamvis iniqui sint; sed committe eos divino judicio, et superioribus suis quos habent in terra, aut summo Pontifici, seu synodo generali, ubi ordinate poterunt accusari. Dic ergo cogitatui tuo: Ecce ipsi sunt judices mei, non ego eorum. Non est meum judicare meos superiores, quibus (quamvis dyscolis) oportet me obedire, et cum reverentia subdi, intuitu et amore illius a quo omnis potestas, cujus vicarii sunt. Quia et aves cœli portabunt vocem tuam, et qui habet pennas annuntiabit sententiam: id est, quocumque modo ipsi superiores tui percipient tuam detractionem et maledictionem: quia quod sæpe cogitaveris, tandem effundes, quoniam ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Et quoniam multi quærunt placere majoribus suis, aliqui deferent verba tua (te ignorante) ad eos, sicque improvise punieris ab eis. Sicque quod dicitur, Aves cœli, etc., est hyperbolica locutio, et tropicus sermo: quemadmodum Christus dixit ad Pharisæos, Si hi tacuerint, lapides clamabunt. Et Propheta: Lapis, inquit, de pariete clamabit. Et communiter dicimus: Parietes non celabunt.
paras.en: [[10:20|Detract not the king, no not in thy thought; and speak not evil of the rich man in thy private chamber|In cogitatione tua regi ne detrahas, et in secreto cubiculi tui ne maledixeris diviti]]: that is, beware so carefully of speaking against thy superiors, princes and prelates, and those more powerful than thou, that thou neither murmur against them in thy heart nor purpose to disparage them, nor do it in the most secret place, even though they be wicked; but commit them to the judgment of God, and to the superiors they have on earth, or to the supreme Pontiff, or to a general synod, where they can be accused in due order. Say, then, to thy thought: Behold, they are my judges, not I theirs. It is not for me to judge my superiors, whom (though they be froward[[1 Pet 2:18||]]) I must obey and be subject to with reverence, for the sake and love of him from whom is all power[[Rom 13:1||]], whose vicars they are. [[10:20|because even the birds of the air will carry thy voice, and he that hath wings will tell what thou hast said|Quia et aves cœli portabunt vocem tuam, et qui habet pennas annuntiabit sententiam]]: that is, in some way or other thy superiors themselves will come to know of thy detraction and cursing: for what thou hast often thought, thou wilt at last pour out, since [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|ex abundantia cordis os loquitur]]. And since many seek to please their betters, some will carry thy words to them (without thy knowing), and so thou wilt be punished by them unawares. And so the saying [[10:20|the birds of the air|Aves cœli]], etc., is a hyperbole and a figure of speech: as Christ said to the Pharisees: [[Luke 19:40|if these shall hold their peace, the stones will cry out|Si hi tacuerint, lapides clamabunt]]. And the Prophet says: [[Hab 2:11|the stone shall cry out of the wall|Lapis, inquit, de pariete clamabit]]. And we commonly say: Walls will not keep secrets.

paras.t: Possunt autem per aves cœli, intelligi homines leves, garruli, inconstantes, quemadmodum in Matthæo, per aves cœli, designantur dæmonia. Et, habens pennas, vocatur superior, potestate se erigens: qui contra detrahentem sibi proferet damnationis sententiam.
paras.en: By [[10:20|the birds of the air|aves cœli]], however, can be understood light, garrulous and inconstant men, as in Matthew the demons are signified by the birds of the air[[Matt 13:4||]][[Matt 13:19||]]. And [[10:20|he that hath wings|habens pennas]] is the name for a superior lifting himself up by his power, who will pronounce sentence of condemnation against the one who detracts him.

paras.t: Porro mystice, prohibemur obloqui, murmurare, maledicere Regi sæculorum omnipotenti, omnia intuenti, ne a dæmonibus accusemur apud eumdem.
paras.en: Further, mystically, we are forbidden to speak against, to murmur at, or to curse the almighty King of ages, who beholds all things, lest we be accused before him by the demons.

11.title: EXPLICATIO CAPITULI UNDECIMI : MITTE PANEM TUUM SUPER TRANSEUNTES AQUAS.
11.title_en: Explanation of the eleventh chapter: Cast thy bread upon the running waters

paras.t: Hic ad opera misericordiæ spiritualia ac corporalia admonemur. Mitte panem tuum, id est, corporalem ac spiritualem refectionem effunde, super transeuntes aquas, id est super pauperes mendicantes, atque domesticos inopes : qui instar aquarum multi sunt, et moventur hinc inde, ac pergunt ad ultimum finem. Unde et in Apocalypsi legitur : Aquæ multæ, populi multi. Hinc admonet Isaias : Frange esurienti panem tuum. Et iterum : Beati, inquit, qui seminatis super omnes aquas. Quia post multa tempora invenies illum, id est, fructum et præmium consequeris inde in die mortis atque judicii tui. Qui enim miseretur pauperis, fœneratur Domino. Propterea in Tobia asseritur : Quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors. Præmium enim bonum tibi thesaurizas in die necessitatis, quoniam eleemosyna ab omni peccato et a morte liberat, et non patietur animam ire in tenebras. Fiducia magna coram summo Deo, est eleemosyna omnibus facientibus eam. Hinc Christus in die judicii misericordibus dicet : Quamdiu uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis.
paras.en: Here we are exhorted to the works of mercy, spiritual and corporal. [[11:1|Cast thy bread|Mitte panem tuum]], that is, pour out bodily and spiritual refreshment, [[11:1|upon the running waters|super transeuntes aquas]], that is, upon the poor who beg, and the needy in their own homes: who like waters are many, and are moved hither and thither, and pass on to their last end. Hence in the Apocalypse too we read: Many waters, many peoples[[Apoc 17:15||]] [Denis gives the sense of the verse: The waters … are peoples]. Hence Isaias admonishes: [[Is 58:7|Deal thy bread to the hungry|Frange esurienti panem tuum]]. And again: [[Is 32:20|Blessed|Beati]], he says, [[Is 32:20|are ye that sow upon all waters|qui seminatis super omnes aquas]]. [[11:1|for after a long time thou shalt find it again|Quia post multa tempora invenies illum]]: that is, thou shalt obtain fruit and reward from it in the day of thy death and of thy judgment. For [[Prov 19:17|He that hath mercy on the poor, lendeth to the Lord|miseretur pauperis, fœneratur Domino]]. Therefore it is said in Tobias: [[Tob 4:8|According to thy ability be merciful.|Quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors]] [[Tob 4:10|For thus thou storest up to thyself a good reward for the day of necessity.|Præmium enim bonum tibi thesaurizas in die necessitatis]] [[Tob 4:11|For alms deliver from all sin, and from death, and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness.|quoniam eleemosyna ab omni peccato et a morte liberat, et non patietur animam ire in tenebras]] [[Tob 4:12|Alms shall be a great confidence before the most high God, to all them that give it.|Fiducia magna coram summo Deo, est eleemosyna omnibus facientibus eam]] Hence Christ will say to the merciful on the day of judgment: [[Matt 25:40|as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me|Quamdiu uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis]].

paras.t: Da partes septem, necnon et octo. Per hos duos numeros determinatos, designari videtur numerus indeterminatus : ad insinuandum, quod de omnibus quæ supersunt, copiose sit communicandum pauperibus, sicut ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus : Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe, divites fieri in bonis operibus, facile tribuere, communicare, thesaurizare sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum. Ideo tamen exprimit septenarium numerum et octonarium, quoniam opera misericordiæ septem sunt in genere, per quæ ad octo beatitudines pervenitur; vel quoniam septimus dies in lege celebris fuit, videlicet sabbatum (ut patet in Exodo), et die octavo fiebat circumcisio, juxta illud Genesis : Infans octo dierum circumcidetur in vobis. At vero, secundum expositores catholicos, ideo ait, Septem, et, Octo, ut innuat utriusque Testamenti Scripturam in debita veneratione habendam. Vetus enim Testamentum significatur per Septem, propter septimi diei celebritatem; et novum, per Octo, propter resurrectionis octavam. Quia ignoras quid futurum sit mali super terram, id est quæ tribulationes et angustiæ, quæ pestes et prælia, seu quando et qualiter morieris. Ideo indiges facere misericordiæ opera, ut tunc adjuveris ac eruaris : quia, ut ait Apostolus, pietas ad omnia utilis est, promissionem habens vitæ quæ nunc est, et futuræ. Nempe, ut ait Salvator, Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Ideo ait Psalmista : Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus.
paras.en: [[11:2|Give a portion to seven, and also to eight|Da partes septem, necnon et octo]] [Denis reads *partes*, "portions", in the plural]. By these two fixed numbers an unfixed number seems to be meant: to suggest that of all that one has over, one should share abundantly with the poor, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich of this world|Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe]] [[1 Tim 6:18|to be rich in good work, to give easily, to communicate to others|divites fieri in bonis operibus, facile tribuere, communicare]], [[1 Tim 6:19|To lay up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come|thesaurizare sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum]]. Yet he names the number seven and the number eight because the works of mercy are seven in kind, through which one comes to the eight beatitudes; or because the seventh day, namely the sabbath, was solemn in the Law (as is plain in Exodus), and on the eighth day circumcision was done, according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 17:12|An infant of eight days old shall be circumcised among you|Infans octo dierum circumcidetur in vobis]]. But according to the Catholic expositors he says *seven* and *eight* to intimate that the Scripture of both Testaments is to be held in due veneration. For the Old Testament is signified by seven, because of the solemnity of the seventh day; and the New by eight, because of the octave of the resurrection. [[11:2|for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth|Quia ignoras quid futurum sit mali super terram]]: that is, what tribulations and distresses, what plagues and battles, or when and how thou shalt die. Therefore thou needest to do the works of mercy, that then thou mayest be helped and delivered: for, as the Apostle says, [[1 Tim 4:8|godliness is profitable to all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come|pietas ad omnia utilis est, promissionem habens vitæ quæ nunc est, et futuræ]]. For indeed, as the Saviour says, [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.|Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]] Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 40:2|Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor: the Lord will deliver him in the evil day.|Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus]]

paras.t: Si repletæ fuerint nubes exhalationibus ac vaporibus humidis, imbrem, id est pluviam, super terram effundent : ita et tu, exemplo naturæ, de plenitudine tua impertire pauperibus.
paras.en: [[11:3|If the clouds be full|Si repletæ fuerint nubes]] of exhalations and moist vapours, [[11:3|they will pour out rain|imbrem]], that is, showers, [[11:3|upon the earth|super terram effundent]]: so thou too, after the example of nature, impart to the poor out of thy fullness.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, nubes sunt virtuosi prælati, contemplativique viri, et prædicatores sancti : qui instar nubium elevantur a terra, et ad cœlestia volant. Quæ quum fuerint rivis sapientiæ ac doctrinæ repletæ, et supernis charismatibus redundantes, verba sapientialia, instar stillarum, audientibus influunt, et corda eorum irrigant ac fecundant; luceque sapientiæ eis infusæ illuminant proximos, juxta illud in Job : Nubes spargunt lumen suum : quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit, ad omne quod præceperit illis super faciem orbis terrarum, sive in una tribu, sive in terra sua, sive in quocumque loco misericordiæ suæ eas jusserit inveniri. De quibus loquitur Isaias : Qui sunt isti, qui ut nubes volant? Quarum pluviam, id est doctrinam et prædicationem, Deus aufert ingratis, quemadmodum in Isaia testatur : Mandabo nubibus, ne pluant super eam imbrem. Unde et in Actibus Apostolorum sic legitur : Vetati sunt (Paulus et sui) a Spiritu Sancto, loqui verbum Dei in Asia; et non permisit eos Spiritus Jesu.
paras.en: Spiritually, the clouds are virtuous prelates, contemplative men and holy preachers, who like clouds are lifted up from the earth and fly to heavenly things. When these have been filled with streams of wisdom and doctrine, and overflow with heavenly gifts, they pour words of wisdom, like drops, into their hearers, and water their hearts and make them fruitful; and by the light of wisdom poured into them they enlighten their neighbours, according to that in Job: [[Job 37:11|the clouds spread their light|Nubes spargunt lumen suum]]: [[Job 37:12|Which go round about, whithersoever the will of him that governeth them shall lead them, to whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth|quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit, ad omne quod præceperit illis super faciem orbis terrarum]], [[Job 37:13|Whether in one tribe, or in his own land, or in what place soever of his mercy he shall command them to be found.|sive in una tribu, sive in terra sua, sive in quocumque loco misericordiæ suæ eas jusserit inveniri]] Of them Isaias speaks: [[Is 60:8|Who are these, that fly as clouds|Qui sunt isti, qui ut nubes volant?]]? Their rain, that is, doctrine and preaching, God takes away from the ungrateful, as he testifies in Isaias: [[Is 5:6|I will command the clouds to rain no rain upon it|Mandabo nubibus, ne pluant super eam imbrem]]. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles too we read thus: [[Acts 16:6|they were forbidden|Vetati sunt]] (Paul and his companions) [[Acts 16:6|by the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia|a Spiritu Sancto, loqui verbum Dei in Asia]]; [[Acts 16:7|and the Spirit of Jesus suffered them not|et non permisit eos Spiritus Jesu]].

paras.t: Consequenter insinuat, quam necessarium sit in præsenti vita operibus insistere virtuosis, quia in morte cessant tempus et status merendi ac demerendi. Si ceciderit lignum, id est, si homo per mortem corruerit, atque devenerit ad austrum, id est ad ardorem Solis justitiæ, ad numerum, partem atque consortium electorum, sive ad aquilonem, id est ad frigus iniquitatis, et ad caritatis omnimodam exstinctionem, et ad partem ac numerum reproborum. Unde Antisiodorensis in Summa sua, per austrum intelligit regionem Spiritus Sancti; per aquilonem, regionem diaboli. In quocumque loco ceciderit, id est, in qualicumque affectione dispositioneque cordis obierit, ibi erit, id est, in ea æternaliter et inconvertibiliter permanebit. Si enim recesserit anima a corpore in caritate et conversione ad Deum, inavertibiliter manebit ad ipsum in æternum conversa; si autem in aversione seu culpa mortali, inconvertibiliter et inflexibiliter manebit aversa a Deo.
paras.en: Next he suggests how necessary it is in the present life to apply oneself to virtuous works, since at death the time and the state of meriting and demeriting come to an end. [[11:3|If the tree fall|Si ceciderit lignum]], that is, if a man has fallen down by death and come [[11:3|to the south|ad austrum]], that is, to the heat of the Sun of justice, to the number, portion and fellowship of the elect, [[11:3|or to the north|sive ad aquilonem]], that is, to the cold of iniquity and the utter extinction of charity, and to the portion and number of the reprobate. Hence the Auxerrois [William of Auxerre, author of the *Summa aurea*] in his Summa understands by the south the region of the Holy Ghost, by the north the region of the devil. [[11:3|in what place soever it shall fall|In quocumque loco ceciderit]], that is, in whatever affection and disposition of heart he has died, [[11:3|there shall it be|ibi erit]], that is, he will remain in it eternally and unchangeably. For if the soul has left the body in charity and in conversion to God, it will remain turned towards him for ever, never to turn away; but if in aversion, that is, in mortal sin, it will remain turned away from God, never to turn back and never to bend.

paras.t: Ideo asserit Damascenus, libro secundo : Quod angelis fuit ruina, hoc hominibus est mors. Quemadmodum enim angeli tenebrarum immutabiliter manent in illa affectione et aversione, in qua erant peccando, et corruendo ex cœlo; ita et anima jugiter manet in dispositione et affectione qua recessit a corpore hora mortis. Nam tota hæc vita et tota ejus duratio, est via et peregrinatio ad futuram : cujus viæ terminus mors est. Idcirco post mortem non manet status aut duratio promerendi aut demerendi. Nec damnati unquam pœnitent de suis peccatis, in quantum fuerint offensiva inhonorativaque Dei; nec cupiunt esse cum Deo ex aliquo ejus amore, vel ad laudem et gloriam ejus. Imo summe et ineffabiliter odiunt Deum, et inæstimabiliter invident gloriæ ejus. Sed quantum in ipsis est, cuperent æternaliter frui rebus creatis caducis, quibus in hac vita finaliter inhæserunt, et in quarum libidinoso amore recesserunt a corpore. Verumtamen, in quantum esse cum Deo, esset damnatis evasio tormentorum suorum, forsitan vellent esse cum eo. Hinc quoque asserit Augustinus : In quo quemque invenerit suus novissimus dies, in hoc eum comprehendet mundi novissimus dies : quoniam qualis in die hoc moritur, talis in illo judicabitur. Et Psalmista : Non mortui laudabunt te, Domine, neque omnes qui descendunt in infernum. Et sanctus Job : Viam (inquit) per quam non revertar, ambulo.
paras.en: Therefore Damascene says, in the second book: What the fall was to the angels, death is to men. For just as the angels of darkness remain unchangeably in that affection and aversion in which they were when they sinned and fell from heaven, so the soul too remains for ever in the disposition and affection with which it left the body at the hour of death. For the whole of this life and all its duration is a way and a pilgrimage to the life to come, and the end of this way is death. Therefore after death there remains no state or duration of meriting or demeriting. Nor do the damned ever repent of their sins inasmuch as they were offensive and dishonouring to God; nor do they desire to be with God out of any love of him, or for his praise and glory. Rather they hate God supremely and unspeakably, and envy his glory beyond all reckoning. But, so far as in them lies, they would wish to enjoy for ever the perishable created things to which they clung to the end in this life, and in lustful love of which they left the body. Yet inasmuch as being with God would be for the damned an escape from their torments, perhaps they would wish to be with him. Hence Augustine too says: In whatever state his last day finds each man, in that the last day of the world will take him; since as a man is when he dies on this day, so will he be judged on that. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 113:25|The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord: nor any of them that go down to hell.|Non mortui laudabunt te, Domine, neque omnes qui descendunt in infernum]] [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 17, counting the second part of the psalm separately; in the Vulgate's numbering it is verse 25]. And holy Job: [[Job 16:23|I am walking in a path|Viam]] (he says) [[Job 16:23|by which I shall not return|per quam non revertar, ambulo]].

paras.t: Denique homo vocatur arbor seu lignum, juxta illud Evangelii : Jam securis ad radicem arboris posita est : omnis ergo arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur. Unde et Christus in passione : Si in viridi (inquit) ligno hæc faciunt, in arido quid fiet? Philosophi quoque dicunt hominem esse arborem eversam. Nam sicut in arbore radix est loco oris, attrahendo nutrimentum humoris, et est in parte inferiori : sic in homine os, quo sumitur alimentum, est in parte superiori, prout etiam secundo de Anima tangit Philosophus. Rursus, sicut arbor ramos suos extendit sursum, sic homo crura ac brachia sua veluti ramos extendit deorsum. Amplius, quoniam sole ad austrum ascendente, cuncta virescunt in terra, diesque prolongantur, et dies fit clarior, ardor quoque lucis solaris in terra augetur : recte per austrum, pars electorum et regio Spiritus Sancti, seu fervor exprimitur caritatis : per aquilonem vero, portio reproborum et regio inimici, quoniam sole illinc elongato, frigora oriuntur durissima, et venti inde perflant acerrimi. Unde Hieronymum sequens Albinus, fatetur quod auster in Scripturis communiter in bonam partem accipitur, aquilo autem in malam, juxta illud in Canticis : Surge, Aquilo (id est recede), et veni, Auster. Et in Jeremia : Ab aquilone pandetur omne malum super omnes habitatores terræ.
paras.en: Further, man is called a tree or wood, according to that of the Gospel: [[Matt 3:10|now the axe is laid to the root of the trees|Jam securis ad radicem arboris posita est]]: [[Matt 3:10|Every tree therefore that doth not yield good fruit, shall be cut down, and cast into the fire|omnis ergo arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur]]. Hence Christ too said in his Passion: [[Luke 23:31|if in the green wood|Si in viridi]] (he says) [[Luke 23:31|they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?|ligno hæc faciunt, in arido quid fiet?]] The philosophers too say that man is an inverted tree. For as in a tree the root takes the place of the mouth, drawing in moisture for nourishment, and is in the lower part, so in man the mouth, by which food is taken, is in the upper part, as the Philosopher also touches on in the second book On the Soul. Again, as a tree stretches its branches upward, so man stretches his legs and arms downward like branches. Moreover, since when the sun climbs towards the south all things grow green on the earth, the days lengthen and the day grows brighter, and the heat of the sun's light on the earth increases, the south rightly expresses the portion of the elect and the region of the Holy Ghost, or the fervour of charity; and the north the portion of the reprobate and the region of the enemy, since when the sun is far off from there the harshest colds arise, and the bitterest winds blow from there. Hence Albinus [that is, Alcuin], following Jerome, states that in the Scriptures the south is commonly taken in a good sense and the north in a bad, according to that in the Canticles: [[Cant 4:16|Arise, O north wind|Surge, Aquilo]] (that is, depart), [[Cant 4:16|and come, O south wind|et veni, Auster]]. And in Jeremias: [[Jer 1:14|From the north shall an evil break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land|Ab aquilone pandetur omne malum super omnes habitatores terræ]].
