paras.t: Qui observat ventum, non seminat; et qui considerat nubes, nunquam metet : id est, qui incerta pericula nimis anxie metuit, nunquam faciet opera bona tempore opportuno : sed differt ea ex timore eventus periculorum incertorum, et sic postea aptum non reperiet tempus. Per quod innuit, quod opera misericordiæ non sunt differenda ex timore futuræ caristiæ, præsertim dum signa probabilia non apparent, nec ex simili irrationabili excusatione. Similiter qui in ipsis pauperibus curiose discernit, an sint digni recipere, an vere indigeant, an nil mali intendant, sæpe falletur, et eis frequenter negabit quibus est dandum. Hinc docuit Christus sollicitudinem immoderatam abjicere, nec temere judicare, nec inordinate timere : imo in omni eventu sperare in Domino, nec de futuris immoderatam assumere conjecturam. Propterea ait et Seneca in libro de Quatuor virtutibus : Plura sunt quæ nos terrent, quam quæ premunt. Illud tibi præcipio, ne sis miser ante tempus, quum illa quæ imminere formidas, nunquam fortasse ventura sint. Primum respice, an certa sint argumenta mali futuri : plerumque suspicionibus laboramus. Nescio quomodo magis vana perturbant : vera enim modum suum habent. Verisimile est aliquid mali futurum ; non tamen statim est verum. Quam multa non expectata venerunt ! quam multa expectata nunquam comparuerunt ! Habet etiam mala fortuna levitatem. Satis cito dolebis, quum venerit : interim meliora confide. Hæc Seneca. Qui et in suis ait Proverbiis : Stultum est timere quod vitari non potest.
paras.en: [[11:4|He that observeth the wind, shall not sow|Qui observat ventum, non seminat]]: [[11:4|and he that considereth the clouds, shall never reap|et qui considerat nubes, nunquam metet]]: that is, he who fears uncertain dangers too anxiously will never do good works at the fitting time, but puts them off for fear that uncertain dangers may come about, and so afterwards will find no suitable time. By this he intimates that the works of mercy are not to be put off for fear of a coming dearth, especially when no likely signs of it appear, nor on any like unreasonable excuse. Likewise he who examines the poor themselves too curiously, whether they are worthy to receive, whether they are truly in need, whether they intend no harm, will often be deceived, and will often refuse those to whom he ought to give. Hence Christ taught us to cast off immoderate solicitude[[Matt 6:25||]] [the margin gives Matt. vi, 25–34], not to judge rashly[[John 7:24||]], not to fear inordinately[[Matt 10:31||]], but rather in every event to hope in the Lord, and not to make immoderate guesses about the future. Therefore Seneca too says, in the book On the Four Virtues [the margin corrects this: in the Letters, the first of book II, that is, Letter 13]: There are more things that frighten us than that crush us. This I charge thee: be not wretched before the time, since the things thou dreadest as imminent may perhaps never come. First consider whether there are sure proofs of the coming evil: for the most part we are troubled by suspicions. Somehow empty things disturb us more: for true ones have their own measure. It is likely that some evil will come; yet it is not therefore at once true. How many things have come that were not expected! How many that were expected have never appeared! Even ill fortune is fickle. Thou wilt grieve soon enough when it comes: meanwhile trust in better things. So far Seneca. He also says in his Proverbs: It is foolish to fear what cannot be avoided.

paras.t: Quomodo ignoras quæ sit via spiritus, id est, quæ sit operatio animæ, an scilicet procedat ex caritate, an non ; vel qualiter anima sit producta, et de non esse ad esse deducta, corporisque infusa. Quamvis enim sciamus quod anima creando infunditur, et infundendo creatur ; tamen ipsam creationem comprehendere non valemus, qualiter solo divinæ voluntatis imperio quid esse incipiat, quod prorsus non fuit. Et qua ratione, id est qua manerie, quo processu, influxu et ordine, ossa infantuli compingantur, id est, formentur et invicem connectantur, in ventre prægnantis : et venarum ac ossium varietatem ignoras, quomodo ex immundo et modico semine formetur corpus humanum in diversos artus et lineamenta atque effigies, ac de eodem semine aliud quidem mollescat in carnibus, aliud induratur in ossibus, aliud in venis palpitet, aliudque ligetur in nervis ; sic nescis opera Dei occulta, qui fabricator est omnium. Nam sicut faber per instrumenta diversa, ex una materia efficit aliud sic, aliud aliter ; sic Deus omnipotens per ministeria corporum cœlestium et motorum motuumque eorum, producit inferiora hæc mixta ex elementis. Omnia tamen originaliter fecit ex nihilo. Et juxta hunc modum loquitur Plato in primo Timæi : Dicendum (inquiens) cur conditor fabricatorque universi, omne hoc instituendum putaverit. Itaque opera Dei ignoras, imo et nescis quando et qualiter seu qua via spiritus tuus exibit de corpore tuo. Non ergo omittas aut differas misericordiæ opera, spe vitæ longævæ in sæculo, quasi personaliter indigens bonis tuis in posterum.
paras.en: [[11:5|As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit|Quomodo ignoras quæ sit via spiritus]], that is, what is the working of the soul, namely whether it proceeds from charity or not; or how the soul is produced, brought from not being into being, and infused into the body. For although we know that the soul is infused by being created and created by being infused, yet we cannot comprehend that creation itself: how, by the sole command of the divine will, something begins to be which was not at all. [[11:5|nor how|Et qua ratione]], that is, in what manner, by what process, influence and order, [[11:5|the bones are joined together|ossa infantuli compingantur]], that is, are formed and connected one to another, [[11:5|in the womb of her that is with child|in ventre prægnantis]]: and thou knowest not the variety of the veins and bones [Denis's text of the verse adds these words, and *infantuli*, "of the little infant", after *ossa*, "bones"; neither is in the Vulgate], how from an unclean and slight seed the human body is formed into its diverse limbs, features and shapes, and how of the same seed one part softens into flesh, another hardens into bone, another throbs in the veins, and another is bound into sinews; [[11:5|so thou knowest not the works of God|sic nescis opera Dei]] [Denis reads *opera Dei occulta*, "the hidden works of God"], [[11:5|who is the maker of all|qui fabricator est omnium]]. For as a smith with different tools makes of one material one thing in this way and another in that, so God almighty, through the ministry of the heavenly bodies and of their movers and motions [that is, the spiritual movers of the heavenly spheres], produces these lower things mixed from the elements. Yet he made all things in the beginning out of nothing. And in this way Plato speaks in the first part of the Timæus: It must be said (he says) why the founder and maker of the universe thought fit to establish all this. And so thou knowest not the works of God; nay, thou knowest not either when or how, or by what way, thy spirit will go out of thy body. Do not, then, omit or put off the works of mercy in the hope of a long life in the world, as though thou wouldst need thy goods for thyself hereafter.

paras.t: His consonat quod secundo Machabæorum, virilis et sancta ac venerandissima illa septem filiorum martyrum mater, legitur ad illos in martyrio constitutos, dixisse : Nescio qualiter in utero meo apparuistis ; neque enim ego spiritum et animam donavi vobis, et singulorum membra non ego compegi, sed creator mundi, qui omnium invenit originem.
paras.en: With this agrees what we read in the second book of Machabees: that that manly, holy and most venerable mother of the seven martyred sons said to them as they stood in their martyrdom: [[2 Mach 7:22|I know not how you were formed in my womb|Nescio qualiter in utero meo apparuistis]]; [[2 Mach 7:22|for I neither gave you breath, nor soul|neque enim ego spiritum et animam donavi vobis]], [[2 Mach 7:22|neither did I frame the limbs of every one of you|et singulorum membra non ego compegi]]. [[2 Mach 7:23|But the Creator of the world|sed creator mundi]], [[2 Mach 7:23|that found out the origin of all|qui omnium invenit originem]].

paras.t: Mane semina semen tuum : id est, cito et sine dilatione, moxque in irradiatione lucis gratiæ super te, opera bona exerce, agrum cordis tui fecunda, verbum Dei annuntia, ita ut mentem tuam in primis a sentibus, spinis, ac tribulis passionum ac vitiorum emundes. Hinc in Osee scriptum est : Seminate vobis in justitia, et metite in ore misericordiæ; ac in Jeremia, Novate vobis novale, et nolite serere super spinas. Et vespere ne cesset manus tua : id est, assidue actibus virtuosis insiste, ut nullam temporis tui partem, nullamque durationis tuæ ætatem infructuose expendas, sed in pueritia, adolescentia, juventute, ac senio adhæreas, obsequarisque Domino ; quia nescis quid magis oriatur, id est, in qua temporis parte, vel in qua ætate migrabis a corpore, seu quid amplius Deo complaceat de te, hoc, an illud; et si utrumque simul oriatur, seu placeat Creatori, melius erit, id est, multo plus apud Deum erit meritorium, si ei serviveris in utroque, seu qualibet tua ætate, et tam mane quam vespere. Quasi dicat : Dato quod diu victurus sis, non tamen nocebit tibi, sed proderit, quod cito et mane incepisti ei servire : imo gratissimum ei est, si quis juventutis et adolescentiæ suæ florem, vigorem, et vivacitatem sibi obtulerit, et in sua sancta servitute expenderit.
paras.en: [[11:6|In the morning sow thy seed|Mane semina semen tuum]]: that is, quickly and without delay, as soon as the light of grace shines upon thee, practise good works, make the field of thy heart fruitful, proclaim the word of God; yet so that thou first cleanse thy mind of the briars, thorns and thistles of the passions and vices. Hence it is written in Osee: [[Osee 10:12|Sow for yourselves in justice, and reap in the mouth of mercy|Seminate vobis in justitia, et metite in ore misericordiæ]]; and in Jeremias: [[Jer 4:3|Break up anew your fallow ground, and sow not upon thorns|Novate vobis novale, et nolite serere super spinas]]. [[11:6|and in the evening let not thy hand cease|Et vespere ne cesset manus tua]]: that is, apply thyself constantly to virtuous acts, so as to spend no part of thy time and no age of thy life without fruit, but cleave to the Lord and serve him in childhood, youth, manhood and old age; [[11:6|for thou knowest not which may rather spring up|quia nescis quid magis oriatur]], that is, in what part of time or at what age thou wilt depart from the body, or what in thee may please God more, [[11:6|this or that|hoc, an illud]]: [[11:6|and if both together|et si utrumque simul]] spring up, or please the Creator, [[11:6|it shall be the better|melius erit]], that is, it will be far more meritorious with God if thou hast served him in both, that is, at every age of thine, and in the morning as well as in the evening. As if he said: Granted that thou art to live long, yet it will not harm thee but profit thee that thou didst begin early, in the morning, to serve him: nay, it is most pleasing to him if anyone offers him the flower, vigour and liveliness of his youth and manhood, and spends them in his holy service.

paras.t: Dulce lumen, et delectabile est oculis, videre solem. Potest hoc superficialiter accipi, quod lumen istud sensibile sit amicum naturæ, et perfectio quædam visus exterioris, ideoque suave hominibus. Similiter vita præsens, quæ luminis nomine designatur, dulcis appetibilisque consistit, et delectabile est oculis videre solem. Propter quod dixit Tobias : Quale mihi gaudium est, qui in tenebris sedeo, et lumen cœli non video?
paras.en: [[11:7|The light is sweet, and it is delightful for the eyes to see the sun.|Dulce lumen, et delectabile est oculis, videre solem]] This can be taken at the surface: that this light of the senses is friendly to nature and a certain perfection of the outward sight, and therefore pleasant to men. Likewise the present life, which is meant by the name of light, is sweet and desirable, and [[11:7|it is delightful for the eyes to see the sun|delectabile est oculis videre solem]]. For which reason Tobias said: [[Tob 5:12|What manner of joy shall be to me, who sit in darkness and see not the light of heaven?|Quale mihi gaudium est, qui in tenebris sedeo, et lumen cœli non video?]]

paras.t: Melius autem exponuntur hæc de lumine increato, ita quod Salomon tangit hic breviter præmium actuum misericordiæ, omniumque virtutum, quo inflammari debemus ad bene agendum. Dulce lumen, id est, Deus qui est lux increata, immensa, superpurissima, vere et incomparabiliter dulcis est in se ipso et universis perfruentibus eo : in cujus clara facialique visione beatitudo nostra est sita, sicut in Joanne ait Salvator : Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum. De quo subditur : et delectabile est oculis interioribus plene purgatis, videre clare per speciem solem justitiæ, unigenitum Filium Dei. De quo Pater per Malachiam loquitur, dicens : Orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ. Unde et Sapientiæ quinto impii sero pœnitentes, fatentur : Justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et Sol sapientiæ non est ortus nobis. Qui Sol suam intuitionem promittit pro præmio, dicendo : Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo ; et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum. Denique, quum delectatio consurgat ex unione potentiæ cum convenienti objecto, ipseque intellectus sit nobilissima vis animæ, et objectum hoc æternum ac increatum sit infinitæ omnino amœnitatis ac convenientiæ; delectabilissimum plane est, ipsum fruitive conspicere. Ideo de electis ait Psalmista Deo : Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos : quoniam apud te est fons vitæ, et in lumine tuo videbimus lumen. Tantæ igitur beatitudinis spe et amore, simus semper bonis ferventer intenti; et timore separationis ab ea, studeamus semper ad mortem esse parati.
paras.en: But these words are better expounded of the uncreated light, so that Solomon here touches briefly on the reward of the works of mercy and of all the virtues, by which we ought to be fired to do well. [[11:7|The light is sweet|Dulce lumen]], that is, God, who is light uncreated, immense, more than most pure, is truly and incomparably sweet in himself and to all who enjoy him: in the clear vision of whom, face to face, our beatitude lies, as the Saviour says in John: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum]]. Of whom it is added: [[11:7|and it is delightful for the eyes|et delectabile est oculis]] within, fully cleansed, [[11:7|to see|videre]] clearly, by open sight [*per speciem*, as opposed to by faith], [[11:7|the sun|solem]] of justice, the only-begotten Son of God. Of him the Father speaks through Malachias, saying: [[Mal 4:2|unto you that fear my name, the Sun of justice shall arise|Orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ]]. Hence also in the fifth chapter of Wisdom the wicked, repenting too late, confess: [[Wis 5:6|the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et Sol sapientiæ non est ortus nobis]] [Denis reads *Sol sapientiæ*, "the sun of wisdom"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *intelligentiæ*, "of understanding"]. This Sun promises the sight of himself as a reward, saying: [[John 14:21|he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him and will manifest myself to him|Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo ; et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum]]. Further, since delight arises from the union of a power with its fitting object, and the intellect is the noblest power of the soul, and this object, eternal and uncreated, is of altogether infinite loveliness and fittingness, it is plainly most delightful to behold it in enjoyment. Therefore the Psalmist says to God of the elect: [[Ps 35:9|They shall be inebriated with the plenty of thy house; and thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure.|Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos]] [[Ps 35:10|For with thee is the fountain of life; and in thy light we shall see light.|quoniam apud te est fons vitæ, et in lumine tuo videbimus lumen]] In the hope and love, then, of so great a beatitude, let us always be fervently intent on good works; and in fear of being parted from it, let us strive always to be ready for death.

paras.t: Propterea subditur : Si annis multis, id est, quantumcumque diu, vixerit homo, et in his omnibus lætus fuerit, id est, prospera habens, et gaudens in bonis, meminisse debet temporis tenebrosi, id est horæ mortis, sibi indesinenter appropinquantis : quæ ob suam amaritudinem ac terribilitatem, nox et tenebrosa vocatur ; et dierum multorum, id est durationis futuri sæculi, quæ fine carebit. Hinc in Ecclesiastico legitur : In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum. Et Gregorius : Sic agenda est præsentis vitæ lætitia, ut amaritudo mortis, ac districtio sequentis judicii, nunquam recedant a memoria. Hinc Seneca dixit : Omnis dies velut ultimus ordinandus est. Qui quum venerint, vanitatis arguentur præterita, id est, in futuro sæculo, et statim post mortem fiet uniuscujusque particulare judicium, et mala quæ gessit ostendentur vana fuisse, et reprehendentur, damnabuntur ac punientur.
paras.en: Therefore it is added: [[11:8|If a man live many years|Si annis multis]], that is, however long [[11:8|a man live|vixerit homo]], [[11:8|and have rejoiced in them all|et in his omnibus lætus fuerit]], that is, having prosperity and rejoicing in good things, [[11:8|he must remember the darksome time|meminisse debet temporis tenebrosi]], that is, the hour of death, drawing ever nearer to him, which because of its bitterness and terror is called night and darksome; [[11:8|and the many days|et dierum multorum]], that is, the duration of the world to come, which will have no end. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:27|In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils|In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum]]. And Gregory: The gladness of the present life is to be so used that the bitterness of death and the strictness of the judgment that follows never leave the memory. Hence Seneca said: Every day is to be ordered as though it were the last. [[11:8|which when they shall come, the things past shall be accused of vanity|Qui quum venerint, vanitatis arguentur præterita]], that is, in the world to come; and straightway after death the particular judgment of each one will take place, and the evil things he has done will be shown to have been vain, and will be rebuked, condemned and punished.

paras.t: Lætare ergo, juvenis, in adolescentia tua, et in bono sit cor tuum in diebus juventutis tuæ, et ambula in viis cordis tui, et in intuitu oculorum tuorum. Secundum superficiem litteræ, videtur hic Salomon admonere ad vivendum voluptuose, juxta desideria cordis et concupiscentiam oculorum. Et si littera ita sumatur, dicunt expositores, quod dicat hæc verba ironice. Nam statim subjungit : et scito quod pro omnibus his adducet te Deus in judicium. Vel in persona carnalium dixit hæc. Quasi dicat : Quum tot mala sint et adversa, interim voluptatibus fruere.
paras.en: [[11:9|Rejoice therefore, O young man, in thy youth, and let thy heart be in that which is good in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart, and in the sight of thy eyes|Lætare ergo, juvenis, in adolescentia tua, et in bono sit cor tuum in diebus juventutis tuæ, et ambula in viis cordis tui, et in intuitu oculorum tuorum]]. By the surface of the letter Solomon seems here to exhort us to live for pleasure, after the desires of the heart and the concupiscence of the eyes. And if the letter is taken so, the expositors say that he says these words in irony. For he at once adds: [[11:9|and know that for all these God will bring thee into judgment|et scito quod pro omnibus his adducet te Deus in judicium]]. Or he said these things in the person of carnal men; as if he said: Since there are so many evils and adversities, meanwhile enjoy thy pleasures.

paras.t: Nihilo minus textus potest exponi in sensu salubri. Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua, id est, a tempore adolescentiæ Deo servi in lætitia : sicut ait Apostolus ad Philippenses, Gaudete in Domino semper; et Psalmista, Servite Domino in lætitia. Et in bono honesto, id est actu virtutum, sit cor tuum jugiter occupatum in diebus juventutis tuæ. Nam et mores hominis meliores sunt in juventute, quam in adolescentia vel senectute, prout in libro Politicorum docet Philosophus. In adolescentia namque sanguine fervente, passiones sunt fortiores, quibus ratio offuscatur; in senectute vero natura declinat, et ratio incipit debilitari communiter. Et ambula in viis cordis tui, id est exercitiis internis ac bonis, quibus mens tendit in Deum, et in intuitu oculorum tuorum, id est secundum dictamen et judicium oculorum interiorum, et conscientiæ atque synderesis; et scito quod pro omnibus his adducet te Deus in judicium, id est, copiosam dabit mercedem, quum approbaverit sua judiciali sententia hujusmodi vitam tuam. Unde et Apostolus Corinthios exhortatur : Stabiles estote, abundantes in opere Domini semper, scientes quod labor vester non est inanis in Domino.
paras.en: Nevertheless the text can be expounded in a wholesome sense. [[11:9|Rejoice therefore, O young man, in thy youth|Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua]], that is, from the time of thy youth serve God in gladness: as the Apostle says to the Philippians, [[Phil 4:4|Rejoice in the Lord always|Gaudete in Domino semper]]; and the Psalmist, [[Ps 99:2|serve ye the Lord with gladness|Servite Domino in lætitia]]. And [[11:9|in that which is good|in bono]] and honest, that is, in the practice of the virtues, [[11:9|let thy heart be|sit cor tuum]] constantly occupied [[11:9|in the days of thy youth|in diebus juventutis tuæ]]. For a man's ways are better in manhood than in youth or old age, as the Philosopher teaches in the book of the Politics [Denis distinguishes *adolescentia*, youth, from *juventus*, the prime of life that follows it; the Douay-Rheims renders both "youth"]. For in youth, when the blood is hot, the passions are stronger, and reason is darkened by them; but in old age nature declines, and reason commonly begins to weaken. [[11:9|and walk in the ways of thy heart|Et ambula in viis cordis tui]], that is, in good inward exercises, by which the mind tends to God, [[11:9|and in the sight of thy eyes|et in intuitu oculorum tuorum]], that is, according to the dictate and judgment of the inward eyes, of conscience and synderesis [that is, the natural habit of the mind by which it holds the first principles of right conduct]; [[11:9|and know that for all these God will bring thee into judgment|et scito quod pro omnibus his adducet te Deus in judicium]], that is, he will give an abundant reward when he has approved such a life of thine by his judicial sentence. Hence the Apostle too exhorts the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 15:58|be ye steadfast|Stabiles estote]], [[1 Cor 15:58|always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord|abundantes in opere Domini semper, scientes quod labor vester non est inanis in Domino]].

paras.t: Aufer iram per vitium a corde tuo, id est, appetitum vindictæ refrena, et cito indulge, quatenus Deus in suo judicio tibi indulgeat : qui in Evangelio protestatur, Si non remiseritis unusquisque fratri suo de cordibus vestris, nec Pater vester cœlestis dimittet vobis peccata vestra. Unde et in Levitico jussum est : Non quæras ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. In Genesi quoque Joseph fratribus suis legitur injunxisse : Ne irascamini in via. Et in Job præcipitur : Non te superet ira, ut aliquem opprimas. Et amove malitiam, id est adulterium et omnem luxuriam, a carne tua. Qui enim fornicatur, peccat in corpus suum; et se ipsum in Baptismate Deo consecratum, facit diaboli servum ac membrum. Adolescentia enim et voluptas, vana sunt : quia a summo et incommutabili bono avertunt, impediunt, et elongant. Adolescentia tamen, prout est pars ætatis, non est vitiosa in se; sed in ea incitatur homo potissime ad inania ac lasciva. Voluptas vero illegitimæ copulæ est iniqua.
paras.en: [[11:10|Remove anger|Aufer iram]] that comes of vice [Denis's text adds *per vitium*, "through vice", that is, sinful anger] [[11:10|from thy heart|a corde tuo]], that is, curb the desire for revenge and forgive quickly, so that God may forgive thee in his judgment; who declares in the Gospel: [[Matt 18:35|if you forgive not every one his brother from your hearts|Si non remiseritis unusquisque fratri suo de cordibus vestris]], [[Matt 6:15|neither will your Father forgive you your offences|nec Pater vester cœlestis dimittet vobis peccata vestra]] [Denis joins the end of Matt 18:35 to Matt 6:15, adding *cœlestis*, "heavenly"]. Hence it was commanded in Leviticus too: [[Lev 19:18|Seek not revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|Non quæras ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. In Genesis too Joseph is read to have charged his brethren: [[Gen 45:24|Be not angry in the way|Ne irascamini in via]]. And in Job it is commanded: [[Job 36:18|let not anger overcome thee to oppress any man|Non te superet ira, ut aliquem opprimas]]. [[11:10|and put away evil|Et amove malitiam]], that is, adultery and all lust, [[11:10|from thy flesh|a carne tua]]. For [[1 Cor 6:18|he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body|Qui enim fornicatur, peccat in corpus suum]]; and he makes himself, who was consecrated to God in Baptism, a servant and member of the devil. [[11:10|For youth and pleasure are vain|Adolescentia enim et voluptas, vana sunt]]: because they turn us away from the highest and unchangeable good, hinder us and draw us far from it. Yet youth, as a part of life, is not vicious in itself; but in it a man is most of all incited to empty and wanton things. But the pleasure of unlawful intercourse is wicked.

paras.t: Postremo, circa illud, Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua, posset quis quærere, qualiter possit juvenis in adolescentia sua lætari, quum juventus et adolescentia sint distinctæ partes ætatis, ita quod tempore juventutis, adolescentia jam defluxit : nisi forsan dicatur juvenis delectari in ea secundum esse quod habet in apprehensione. Et respondendum, quod juventus quandoque, sicut et hic, extense accipitur, prout ad adolescentiam se extendit. Et sæpe pro eodem sumuntur.
paras.en: Lastly, concerning the words [[11:9|Rejoice therefore, O young man, in thy youth|Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua]], someone might ask how a young man [*juvenis*, one in the prime of life] can rejoice in his youth [*adolescentia*], since the prime of life and youth are distinct parts of life, so that by the time of the prime of life youth has already slipped away: unless perhaps it be said that the young man delights in it according to the being it has in his apprehension [that is, as it is held in memory]. And the answer is that *juventus* is sometimes, as here, taken in a wider sense, as stretching back to cover youth. And they are often used for the same thing.

12.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI DUODECIMI : MEMENTO CREATORIS TUI IN DIEBUS JUVENTUTIS TUÆ.
12.title_en: Exposition of the twelfth chapter: Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth

paras.t: Hortatur jam Salomon ad virtuose agendum celeriter, ex consideratione brevitatis vitæ præsentis, et corruptionis assiduæ corporis nostri, imminentisque mortis. Et loquitur in isto capitulo multum metaphorice et obscure; sed ex verbis quæ tandem subjungit, dat occasionem intelligendi quid dicere velit.
paras.en: Solomon now exhorts us to act virtuously and quickly, from the consideration of the shortness of the present life, of the constant decay of our body, and of impending death. And in this chapter he speaks very much in metaphors and obscurely; but by the words he adds at the end he gives us the means of understanding what he wishes to say.

paras.t: Memento Creatoris tui, non superficiali, rara, informi, sed cordiali, assidua, et formata recordatione : ita ut ejus majestatem toto posse honores, ejus bonitatem super omnia fervide diligas, ejus justitiam expavescas, infinitam excellentiam ejus jugiter laudes, veritatem et sapientiam ejus reverenter ac limpide contempleris, beneficia et promissa ipsius attendas, et gratus esse totis viribus semper coneris. Sic igitur Dei præsentiam incessabiliter penses in diebus juventutis tuæ, id est statim ab exordio ætatis adultæ, hæc aliqualiter incipiendo. Et quanto plus creveris ætate, ad pueritiam adolescentiamque perveniendo; tanto perfectius impleas jam prædicta. Itemque juventus hic sumitur, prout contra senectutem distinguitur, et totum tempus adultæ includit ætatis. Denique, protestante S. Hilario, id potissime Deo tenemur, ut sicut totum quod sumus, possumus et habemus, ab ipso accepimus; sic nos ipsos et omne quod valemus ac possidemus, ejus obsequio mancipemus, atque ad ejus ordinemus amorem et cultum. Sicque ratione beneficentiæ nobis ab ipso exhibitæ, debemus nos totos dilectioni et honorificentiæ ejus : et multo plus, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos; et maxime propter infinitam dignitatem ac honorabilitatem ipsius, sed et propter liberalissima ejus promissa. Nequaquam ergo obliviscamur ipsius, sed in omni ejus obsequio pensemus majestatem ipsius, quatenus eum ingenti reverentia eum exoremus, laudemus, colamus, et veneremur in omnibus. In omni quoque tentatione reminiscamur suæ gloriosæ et supervenerandæ præsentiæ, ut erubescamus, vereamur, et omittamus in ejus præsentia ipsum offendere, et viliter nos habere.
paras.en: [[12:1|Remember thy Creator|Memento Creatoris tui]], not with a superficial, rare and unformed remembrance, but with one that is heartfelt, constant and formed [that is, quickened by charity, as "formed faith" is faith living by charity]: so that thou honour his majesty with all thy power, love his goodness fervently above all things, dread his justice, praise his infinite excellence continually, contemplate his truth and wisdom reverently and clearly, attend to his benefits and promises, and strive always with all thy strength to be grateful. Thus, then, ponder unceasingly the presence of God [[12:1|in the days of thy youth|in diebus juventutis tuæ]], that is, straight from the beginning of the grown age [*ætas adulta*: here evidently the first years of discretion, since boyhood and adolescence come after it], making some beginning of these things; and the more thou growest in age, coming on to boyhood and adolescence, the more perfectly fulfil what has been said. Youth is also taken here as it is distinguished over against old age, and so it includes the whole time of grown age. Lastly, as St. Hilary declares, we are bound to God above all in this: that as we have received from him all that we are, can do and have, so we should devote ourselves and all that we are capable of and possess to his service, and order them to his love and worship. And so, by reason of the benefits he has shown us, we owe ourselves wholly to loving and honouring him; and much more so [[1 John 4:10|because he hath first loved us|quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos]][[1 John 4:19||]]; and most of all on account of his infinite dignity and worthiness of honour, and also on account of his most generous promises. Let us therefore by no means forget him, but in all our service of him let us ponder his majesty, so that with great reverence we may beseech, praise, worship and venerate him in all things. In every temptation also let us remember his glorious and most venerable presence, so that we may blush, fear, and forbear to offend him in his presence and to behave basely.

paras.t: Antequam veniat tempus afflictionis tuæ, id est angustiæ, adversitatis, et senectutis : in quibus Deo servire, et ad ipsum confugere, est quodammodo necessitatis, nec ex mera libertate puraque caritate videtur procedere, ideo Deo minus acceptum est ; et appropinquent anni de quibus dicas : Non mihi placent. Isti sunt anni ætatis decrepitæ et mortis amaræ, imo et quotidianæ : quia, ut beatus asserit Augustinus, quando ætas vergit ad occasum, senex plenus est querelis et nullis gaudiis. Et rursus testatur : Quum homines cupiunt senectutem, quid aliud optant, nisi longam infirmitatem? Sanctus quoque Gregorius : Ipse (inquit) defectus corruptionis, quid est, nisi quædam prolixitas mortis?
paras.en: [[12:1|before the time of affliction come|Antequam veniat tempus afflictionis tuæ]] [Denis reads *afflictionis tuæ*, "of thy affliction"], that is, of distress, adversity and old age: in which to serve God and to flee to him is in a manner of necessity, and does not seem to proceed from mere freedom and pure charity, and therefore it is less acceptable to God; [[12:1|and the years draw nigh of which thou shalt say: They please me not|et appropinquent anni de quibus dicas : Non mihi placent]]. These are the years of decrepit age and of bitter death, nay, of daily death: for, as blessed Augustine asserts, when age declines towards its setting, the old man is full of complaints and of no joys. And again he testifies: When men desire old age, what else do they wish for but a long infirmity? St. Gregory too: This very failing of corruption (he says), what is it but a kind of drawing out of death?

paras.t: Antequam tenebrescant sol et lumen et stellæ et luna. Quemadmodum Rabbi Moyses ille Ægyptius, magnus philosophus atque theologus, fassus est, consuetudo Scripturæ est, ut luminaria cœli et orbes cœlestes, propter homines condita, dicantur obtenebrari, mœrere, et quasi in deterius variari, dum homines in præcipuas labuntur adversitates, calamitates et mortes. Unde in Ezechiele Dominus loquitur regi Ægypti : Operiam, quum exstinctus fueris, cœlos, et nigrescere faciam stellas ejus; solem nube tegam, et luna non dabit lumen suum; omnia luminaria cœli mœrere faciam super te. Similiter in Isaia, quum dixisset Scriptura, Interfecit eos, etc., mox adjecit : et complicabuntur sicut liber cœli, et omnis militia eorum defluet. Itaque juxta hunc modum loquendi potest intelligi, quod homine in angustiis senii constituto, et propinquante ad mortem sol lumenque ejus, luna ac sidera tenebrescunt, quia non fulgent homini tali ad ejus solatium. Verumtamen expositores, per solem et lunam, communiter intelligunt oculos corporales : qui omnibus membris lucent, ducatumque præbent per lumen visuale et vim visivam, quæ connata sunt oculis ac residet in pupilla, senectutisque tempore, præsertim in morte, per debilitationem obtenebrescunt. Per stellas vero, alii sensus intelliguntur : qui ornant caput sicut sidera cœlum, et illuminant aliqualiter hominem, quemadmodum astra mundum, quia cognitio nostra intellectiva, a sensitiva sumit exordium, atque per sensuum apprehensionem dirigitur homo in agendis ac evitandis.
paras.en: [[12:2|Before the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars be darkened|Antequam tenebrescant sol et lumen et stellæ et luna]]. As Rabbi Moyses the Egyptian, a great philosopher and theologian, has acknowledged [that is, Moses Maimonides], it is the custom of Scripture that the lights of heaven and the heavenly spheres, which were made for men's sake, are said to be darkened, to mourn, and as it were to change for the worse, when men fall into great adversities, calamities and deaths. Hence in Ezechiel the Lord says to the king of Egypt: [[Ezech 32:7|I will cover the heavens, when thou shalt be put out, and I will make the stars thereof dark: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light|Operiam, quum exstinctus fueris, cœlos, et nigrescere faciam stellas ejus; solem nube tegam, et luna non dabit lumen suum]]; [[Ezech 32:8|I will make all the lights of heaven to mourn over thee|omnia luminaria cœli mœrere faciam super te]]. Likewise in Isaias, when Scripture had said, [[Is 34:2|he hath killed them|Interfecit eos]], etc., it soon added: [[Is 34:4|and the heavens shall be folded together as a book|et complicabuntur sicut liber cœli]]: [[Is 34:4|and all their host shall fall down|et omnis militia eorum defluet]]. So, according to this manner of speaking, it can be understood that when a man is set in the straits of old age and draws near to death, his sun and its light, the moon and the stars grow dark, because they do not shine on such a man for his comfort. Yet the expositors commonly understand by the sun and the moon the bodily eyes, which give light to all the members and guide them by the visual light and the power of sight, which are inborn in the eyes and reside in the pupil, and which in the time of old age, and above all in death, grow dark through weakening. By the stars, however, the other senses are understood, which adorn the head as the stars adorn the sky, and in some measure enlighten man as the stars do the world; for our intellectual knowledge takes its beginning from the knowledge of the senses, and through what the senses apprehend man is directed in what he is to do and to avoid.

paras.t: Et revertantur nubes post pluviam. Per aquas et flumina ac nubes, in Scripturis quandoque significantur gratiarum fluenta, divinorum charismatum dona, et rivi sapientiæ atque scientiæ. De quibus in Joanne loquitur Christus : Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ; et in Apocalypse, Qui vult, accipiat aquam vitæ gratis; et in Isaia, Miserator eorum reget eos, et ad fontes aquarum potabit eos; itemque in Psalmo, Fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei. Interdum per ista, in Scriptura exprimitur tribulatio magna, et impetus angustiæ copiosæ : sicut in Psalmo, Elevaverunt flumina, Domine, elevaverunt flumina vocem suam; et rursus, Salvum me fac, Domine, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam; atque in Isaia, Adducet Dominus super eos aquas multas et fortes, regem Assyriorum. Et ita hoc loco per nubes, insinuantur caligines inundationesque afflictionum, quibus agonizantes copiosissime ac mœstissime involvuntur in corpore et anima, in singulis membris ac viribus: quibus tanquam nubibus densis ac tempestuosis operiuntur. Quæ nubes tunc revertuntur post pluvias, id est post præcedentes tribulationes, timores, pressuras.
paras.en: [[12:2|and the clouds return after the rain|Et revertantur nubes post pluviam]]. By waters, rivers and clouds the Scriptures sometimes signify the streams of graces, the gifts of divine charisms, and the rivers of wisdom and knowledge. Of these Christ speaks in John: [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me|Qui credit in me]], [[John 7:38|Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]; and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:17|he that will, let him take the water of life, freely|Qui vult, accipiat aquam vitæ gratis]]; and in Isaias: [[Is 49:10|he that is merciful to them, shall be their shepherd, and at the fountains of waters he shall give them drink|Miserator eorum reget eos, et ad fontes aquarum potabit eos]]; and again in the Psalm: [[Ps 45:5|The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful|Fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei]]. At times, on the other hand, great tribulation and the onrush of abundant distress are expressed by these in Scripture: as in the Psalm, [[Ps 92:3|The floods have lifted up, O Lord: the floods have lifted up their voice|Elevaverunt flumina, Domine, elevaverunt flumina vocem suam]]; and again, [[Ps 68:2|Save me, O God: for the waters are come in even unto my soul|Salvum me fac, Domine, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam]]; and in Isaias, [[Is 8:7|the Lord will bring upon them the waters of the river strong and many, the king of the Assyrians|Adducet Dominus super eos aquas multas et fortes, regem Assyriorum]]. And so in this place the clouds suggest the darknesses and floods of afflictions in which the dying are wrapped most abundantly and most sorrowfully, in body and soul, in each of their members and powers, and by which they are covered as by dense and stormy clouds. These clouds return then after the rains, that is, after the tribulations, fears and oppressions that went before.

paras.t: Quando commovebuntur custodes domus, id est costæ: quibus intestina vallantur, et tota ventris mollities conservatur, ne intra se corruens comprimatur. Possunt quoque custodes domus, intelligi sensus exteriores: per quos custoditur domus, id est corpus, quod est animæ habitaculum, a diversis periculis. Rursus, custodes domus, id est hominis, in quo Deus per gratiam commoratur, vel diabolus residens dominatur, sunt intellectus et voluntas; qui imperant inferioribus viribus, et ab adversis multis custodiunt hominem; sed morte instante, multiplici concutiuntur horrore. Custodes quoque habitaculi, in quo agonizans jacet, tunc commoventur compassione, terrore et angustia. Et mutabuntur viri fortissimi, id est, crura ac tibiæ, quæ totius corporis sustentant ac deferunt pondus, præ infirmitate vacillabunt ac titubabunt. Quæ dicuntur viri fortissimi, quia robustissime præ ceteris quæ in homine sunt, consolidant teneritudinem carnis. Vel : Viri fortissimi, id est, qui antea robustissimi erant, tunc præ ægritudine nutant. Et otiosæ erunt molentes, id est, dentes, qui instar molæ comminuunt cibos, tunc ab officio suo deficient, non valentes conterere cibum, imminuto numero : quia tunc solent excidere, et numero minorari in senectute; et tenebrescent videntes per foramina, id est, oculi caligabunt : qui per organa sua in capite sita ac profundata, tanquam per foramina cernunt. Unde in Genesi leguntur suis oculis Isaac et Jacob præ senectute non potuisse clare videre.
paras.en: [[12:3|When the keepers of the house shall tremble|Quando commovebuntur custodes domus]], that is, the ribs, by which the bowels are walled in and the whole softness of the belly is preserved, lest it collapse upon itself and be crushed. The keepers of the house can also be understood as the outward senses, by which the house, that is, the body, which is the dwelling of the soul, is guarded from various dangers. Again, the keepers of the house, that is, of the man in whom God dwells by grace or the devil abides and rules, are the intellect and the will, which command the lower powers and guard the man from many adversities; but when death is at hand they are shaken with manifold horror. The keepers too of the dwelling in which the dying man lies are then moved with compassion, terror and anguish. [[12:3|and the strong men shall stagger|Et mutabuntur viri fortissimi]] [Denis's text reads *mutabuntur*, "shall be changed", where the Vulgate has *nutabunt*, "shall stagger"], that is, the legs and shins, which hold up and carry the weight of the whole body, will waver and totter for weakness. They are called the strongest men because, more sturdily than anything else in man, they make firm the tenderness of the flesh. Or: the strongest men, that is, those who were formerly most robust, then totter through sickness. [[12:3|and the grinders shall be idle|Et otiosæ erunt molentes]], that is, the teeth, which grind food like a mill, will then fail in their office, not being able to crush the food, [[12:3|in a small number|imminuto numero]] [Denis reads *imminuto numero*, "their number being lessened"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *in minuto numero*]: for then they usually fall out and grow fewer in number in old age; [[12:3|and they that look through the holes shall be darkened|et tenebrescent videntes per foramina]], that is, the eyes will grow dim, which see as it were through holes, through their organs set deep in the head. Hence we read in Genesis that Isaac[[Gen 27:1||]] and Jacob[[Gen 48:10||]] could not see clearly with their eyes for old age.

paras.t: Et claudent ostia in platea, in humilitate vocis molentis. Ostia hominis sunt, os ejus et labia, ac cetera viæ seu aperturæ, per quas ejiciuntur superfluitates naturæ. Unde orat Propheta : Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis meis. In Ecclesiastico quoque habetur, Ori tuo facito ostia : id est, labia tua ab illicita locutione refrena. Hæc ostia, morte instante, clauduntur, dum loqui non prævalent, et præ angustia afflictionum invicem comprimuntur. Ideo additur : In humilitate, id est exilitate et dejectione, vocis molentis, id est aerem confringentis : quia tunc vix loqui possunt exiliter ac depresse. Hoc ostium positum est in platea, id est in planitie ac latitudine vultus. Vel, Claudent ostia in plateis : quoniam senes ægrotantes ac agonizantes, faciunt januas domus suæ claudi; nec egredi queunt, nec ludentium jocis alludunt.
paras.en: [[12:4|And they shall shut the doors in the street|Et claudent ostia in platea]], [[12:4|when the grinder's voice shall be low|in humilitate vocis molentis]]. A man's doors are his mouth and lips, and the other ways or openings through which the superfluities of nature are cast out. Hence the Prophet prays: [[Ps 140:3|Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth: and a door round about my lips.|Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis meis]] [the margin's Ps. cxi, 3 is a misreading of Ps. cxl, 3]. In Ecclesiasticus too we have: [[Ecclus 28:28|make doors and bars to thy mouth|Ori tuo facito ostia]] [Denis quotes only "make doors to thy mouth"]: that is, rein in thy lips from unlawful speech. These doors are shut when death is at hand, when they can no longer speak, and they are pressed together by the anguish of their afflictions. Therefore it is added: [[12:4|when the grinder's voice shall be low|In humilitate, id est exilitate et dejectione, vocis molentis]]: low, that is, thin and downcast; the grinder's, that is, the voice that breaks up the air [*molens*, "grinding"]: for then they can hardly speak, and only thinly and in an undertone. This door is set [[12:4|in the street|in platea]], that is, in the flat and broad surface of the face. Or: [[12:4|they shall shut the doors in the street|Claudent ostia in plateis]], because old men who are sick and dying have the doors of their house shut; they cannot go out, nor do they join in the jests of those at play.

paras.t: Et consurgent ad vocem volucris, id est, in galli cantu evigilabunt ac surgent, vel necessitudine urinandi, a qua diu nequeunt abstinere, vel quia diu in uno latere non valent jacere. Nempe frigescente jam sanguine, et siccato humore, quibus materia alitur somni, ad levem evigilant sonum ; deficiente quoque vigore naturæ, non possunt diu tenere urinam. Et obsurdescent omnes filiæ carminis, id est aures : quæ in melodiis et cantibus delectantur, propter quod filiæ carminis nuncupantur.
paras.en: [[12:4|and they shall rise up at the voice of the bird|Et consurgent ad vocem volucris]], that is, they will wake and rise at cockcrow, either from the need to pass water, from which they cannot long hold back, or because they cannot lie long on one side. For now that the blood is growing cold and the moisture is dried up, by which the matter of sleep is fed, they wake at a slight sound; and since the vigour of nature is failing, they cannot hold their water long. [[12:4|and all the daughters of music shall grow deaf|Et obsurdescent omnes filiæ carminis]], that is, the ears, which delight in melodies and songs, and are therefore called the daughters of music.

paras.t: Excelsa quoque timebunt, et formidabunt in via : id est, ipsi infirmi senes et morti appropinquantes, verebuntur secreta et alta judicia Dei, atque ignotam ingredi metuent regionem. Vel : Excelsa, id est supremæ vires animæ, scilicet intellectus et voluntas, expavescent mortis discrimen, et viam universæ contremient carnis. Vel, lapsis poplitibus ac tremiscente vestigio, etiam in plano fluctuantes itinere, defectum ac offendicula gressuum formidabunt.
paras.en: [[12:5|And they shall fear high things, and they shall be afraid in the way|Excelsa quoque timebunt, et formidabunt in via]]: that is, the infirm old men themselves, drawing near to death, will dread the secret and lofty judgments of God, and will fear to enter an unknown country. Or: [[12:5|high things|Excelsa]], that is, the highest powers of the soul, namely the intellect and the will, will be terrified at the peril of death and will tremble at the way of all flesh. Or: with their knees giving way and their step trembling, wavering even on a level road, they will fear the failing and the stumbling of their steps.

paras.t: Florebit amygdalus, impinguabitur locusta, et dissipabitur capparis. Hæc tria, puta amygdalus, locusta, et capparis, per metaphoram seni conveniunt : amygdalus, ratione canitiei; locusta, propter crurum dolorem, ac pedum tumorem. Locusta quippe est animal breve et parvum, in cruribus debile : cujus proles est bruchus, qui quum alatus fuerit, et volare inceperit, locusta vocatur, ut dictum est super illud Joelis : Residuum erucæ, comedit locusta. Capparis, propter libidinis infrigidationem. Florebit ergo in sene amygdalus, id est, caput capillorum canitie quasi floribus suis operietur ; impinguabitur locusta, id est, crura dolebunt, et pedes indigestis humoribus tumidi fient ac gravabuntur, ac tibiæ intumescent. Aliqui tamen per locustam teneram, intelligunt mollem ventrem, qui tempore senii, incoctis solet impinguari humoribus, deficiente calore ad consumendum. Et dissipabitur capparis, id est, libido frigescet, et concupiscentia exstinguetur : quæ nomine capparis designatur, eo quod capparis herba sit excitans luxum, et renibus valet, in quibus libido viget. Propter quod ait Salvator : Sint lumbi vestri præcincti. Porro (ut legitur) capparis est genus fruteti conforme lentisco, habens in summitatibus seminis sui rotunda capitula, nascens in aridis locis, et petræ adhærens; et super omnia medicamina juvat. Semen ejus sali compositum, cibis est aptum; ventrem mollit, provocatque urinam. Radix ejus potata, paralyticis mirifice prodest, menstruis imperat. Semen ejus cum aceto coctum, et ore retentum, dolorem dentium mitigat. Radix ejus si masticetur, dolorem eumdem compescit.
paras.en: [[12:5|the almond tree shall flourish, the locust shall be made fat, and the caper tree shall be destroyed|Florebit amygdalus, impinguabitur locusta, et dissipabitur capparis]]. These three, the almond tree, the locust and the caper, fit an old man by way of metaphor: the almond tree by reason of white hair; the locust because of the pain in the legs and the swelling of the feet. For the locust is a short and small creature, weak in the legs, whose offspring is the bruchus, which, when it has grown wings and begun to fly, is called a locust, as was said on that verse of Joel: [[Joel 1:4|That which the palmerworm hath left, the locust hath eaten|Residuum erucæ, comedit locusta]]. The caper, because of the cooling of lust. So then, in the old man, [[12:5|the almond tree shall flourish|Florebit ergo in sene amygdalus]], that is, his head will be covered with white hair as with its flowers; [[12:5|the locust shall be made fat|impinguabitur locusta]], that is, the legs will ache, and the feet will become swollen and heavy with undigested humours, and the shins will swell. Some, however, understand by the tender locust the soft belly, which in the time of old age is usually fattened with unconcocted humours, since the heat to consume them is failing. [[12:5|and the caper tree shall be destroyed|Et dissipabitur capparis]], that is, lust will grow cold and concupiscence will be extinguished. It is signified by the name of the caper because the caper is a plant that excites lust and is good for the reins, in which lust thrives. For which reason the Saviour says: [[Luke 12:35|Let your loins be girt|Sint lumbi vestri præcincti]]. Further (as we read), the caper is a kind of shrub like the mastic tree, having round little heads at the tops of its seed, growing in dry places and clinging to the rock; and it helps more than any medicine. Its seed mixed with salt is good with food; it softens the belly and provokes urine. Its root, taken as a drink, is wonderfully good for paralytics and governs the menses. Its seed boiled with vinegar and held in the mouth eases toothache. Its root, if chewed, checks the same pain.

paras.t: Quando ibit homo in domum æternitatis suæ, id est statum et mansionem futuri sæculi, cujus duratio finem non habet, et circuibunt in platea plangentes, id est propinqui et amici, defunctum ad tumulum deferentes, ejusque mortem in via deflentes.
paras.en: [[12:5|because man shall go into the house of his eternity|Quando ibit homo in domum æternitatis suæ]] [Denis reads *Quando*, "when"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *Quoniam*, "because"], that is, into the state and dwelling of the world to come, whose duration has no end; [[12:5|and the mourners shall go round about in the street|et circuibunt in platea plangentes]], that is, relatives and friends, carrying the dead man to the tomb and bewailing his death on the way.

paras.t: Antequam rumpatur funis argenteus. In omnibus his repetendum est illud : Memento Creatoris tui. Itaque reminiscere Dei tui indesinenter, antequam rumpatur funis argenteus, id est splendida vita ista, instar funiculi diu protracta, seu elementorum commixtio, instar funiculi in tuo corpore colligata : hoc est, antequam dissolvatur complexionis tuæ harmonia. Et recurrat vitta aurea, vel, ut aliqui legunt, Vita aurea. Per vittam auream, quidam intelligunt animam pretiosam, variis viribus proprietatibusque intextam. Et auream vitam, quidam accipiunt vitam futuram justis promissam, et vitiis perditam : quæ ita se habet ad vitam præsentem, sicut aurum ad argentum. Potest quoque per vittam auream, significari nobilissima illa harmonia, quæ in resurrectione futura tribuetur electis, et aliqualiter fuit ante lapsum in primis parentibus. Itaque antequam anima recurrat ad suum conditorem, et antequam vita beata reddatur, memor sis Dei.
paras.en: [[12:6|Before the silver cord be broken|Antequam rumpatur funis argenteus]]. In all these we must repeat that phrase: [[12:1|Remember thy Creator|Memento Creatoris tui]]. Remember thy God, then, unceasingly, [[12:6|before the silver cord be broken|antequam rumpatur funis argenteus]], that is, this bright life, drawn out long like a cord; or the mingling of the elements, bound together in thy body like a cord: that is, before the harmony of thy complexion is dissolved [the complexion is the balanced mixture of humours that makes up the body's constitution]. [[12:6|and the golden fillet shrink back|Et recurrat vitta aurea]], or, as some read, the golden life [*vita aurea* for *vitta aurea*, "golden fillet": the two words differ by one letter]. By the golden fillet some understand the precious soul, interwoven with various powers and properties. And by the golden life some take the life to come, promised to the just and lost through vices, which stands to the present life as gold to silver. The golden fillet can also signify that most noble harmony which will be given to the elect in the resurrection to come, and which in some measure existed in our first parents before the fall. So then, before the soul runs back [*recurrat*, the verb of the verse] to its Maker, and before the life of bliss is given back, be mindful of God.

paras.t: Et conteratur hydria super fontem, id est, vesica humorum aquaticorum contentiva, destruatur ad stomachum : ex quo, velut ex fonte, suscipit talem humorem. Ut enim ait Cyrillus in suis Proverbiis, quatuor digestionibus cibus percoquitur, ut deinde membris purior atque veracior tribuatur. Omnis etenim cibus, antequam substantiæ carnis incorporetur, quatuor digestionibus expurgatur. Primo vadit ad stomachum, et ibi digeritur, et sequestratur purum ab impuro, et impurum emittitur per secessum. Deinde purum relictum ad hepar emittitur, ac ibi digeritur; fitque sanguis, et sequestratur purum ab impuro : impurum emittitur per urinam, ac purum relictum, a venis attrahitur. Et ibi tertio digeritur, sequestraturque purum ab impuro : et impurum emittitur per sudorem et sputum; deinde purum relictum, per membra spargitur. Et in membris quarto digeritur, sequestraturque purum ab impuro : et illud impurum, quod quasi purum est, servatur in vasis spermaticis, et in generatione emittitur; purissimum autem relictum, convertitur in membrorum substantiam, factum vivum, atque substantia vitæ.
paras.en: [[12:6|and the pitcher be crushed at the fountain|Et conteratur hydria super fontem]], that is, the bladder, which holds the watery humours, is destroyed at the stomach, from which, as from a fountain, it receives that humour. For as Cyril says in his Proverbs, food is cooked through by four digestions, so that it may then be given to the members purer and truer. For all food, before it is incorporated into the substance of the flesh, is purged by four digestions. First it goes to the stomach and is digested there, and the pure is separated from the impure, and the impure is sent out by the bowel. Then the pure that remains is sent to the liver and digested there; and it becomes blood, and the pure is separated from the impure: the impure is sent out in the urine, and the pure that remains is drawn in by the veins. And there it is digested a third time, and the pure is separated from the impure: the impure is sent out in sweat and spittle; then the pure that remains is spread through the members. And in the members it is digested a fourth time, and the pure is separated from the impure: and that impure part which is almost pure is kept in the seminal vessels and emitted in generation; but the purest that remains is turned into the substance of the members, made living, and the substance of life.

paras.t: Et conteratur rota super cisternam, id est caput, instar rotæ rotundum, superpositum cordi, quod est fons caloris ac vitalium origo spirituum.
paras.en: [[12:6|and the wheel be broken upon the cistern|Et conteratur rota super cisternam]] [Denis reads *conteratur*, "be crushed"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *confringatur*], that is, the head, round like a wheel, set above the heart [the cistern], which is the fountain of heat and the source of the vital spirits.

paras.t: Et revertatur pulvis in terram suam unde erat, id est, caro resolvatur in terram : quæ, quantum ad materiam, prædominatur in corpore; et spiritus redeat ad eum qui dedit illum, id est ad Creatorem, ut judicetur et remuneretur. Qua auctoritate confunduntur Apollinaris et sui sequaces, dicentes animas cum corporibus propagari, descindi, ac seminari, non ab extra infundi; et quidam philosophi ac Sadducæi, qui dixerunt animas hominum mori cum corpore.
paras.en: [[12:7|And the dust return into its earth, from whence it was|Et revertatur pulvis in terram suam unde erat]], that is, let the flesh be resolved into earth, which, as regards matter, predominates in the body; [[12:7|and the spirit return to God, who gave it|et spiritus redeat ad eum qui dedit illum]] [Denis reads *ad eum*, "to him"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *ad Deum*], that is, to the Creator, to be judged and rewarded. By this authority Apollinaris and his followers are confounded, who say that souls are propagated with bodies, cut off and sown, not poured in from without [that is, that the soul is handed on by the parents in generation, not created by God]; and also certain philosophers and the Sadducees, who said that men's souls die with the body.

paras.t: His metaphorice ac parabolice dictis, ad principium redit hujus voluminis : Vanitas, inquiens, vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes, et omnia vanitas : sicut in primo capitulo expositum est. Tanquam dicat : Quum omnis homo ad finem istum venturus sit, ut corpus redigatur in pulverem, et anima revertatur ad Creatorem; vanissimum est, in rebus caducis, in deliciis et mundi honoribus occupari, beatitudinem quærere, et constituere finem in talibus.
paras.en: Having said these things in metaphor and parable, he returns to the beginning of this book: [[12:8|Vanity|Vanitas]], he says, [[12:8|of vanities, said Ecclesiastes, and all things are vanity|vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes, et omnia vanitas]], as was explained in the first chapter. As if to say: Since every man is to come to this end, that his body is brought back to dust and his soul returns to the Creator, it is the height of vanity to be taken up with perishable things, with pleasures and the honours of the world, to seek happiness in such things and to set one's end in them.

paras.t: Quumque esset sapientissimus Ecclesiastes : prout tertio Regum et secundo Paralipomenon, supra quoque expositum est. Loquitur autem de se ipso, quasi de alio, ut moris est auctoribus Scripturarum in propriis loqui libris. Se quoque commendat, non ad propriam laudem, sed ad Dei honorem et nostram ædificationem, ut certius ei credamus, ejusque verba attentius contemplemur. Docuit populum Israeliticum sibi commissum, præsertim domesticos suos, ac alios ad ipsum pro informatione accedentes, sicut reginam Saba; et enarravit quæ fecerat: ut patuit supra secundo capitulo. Et investigans veritatem de singulis, prout supra fuit expositum, composuit parabolas multas, videlicet tria millia, ut legitur tertio Regum. Quæ tamen non sunt omnes descriptæ, ut dictum est in expositione libri Proverbiorum.
paras.en: [[12:9|And whereas Ecclesiastes was very wise|Quumque esset sapientissimus Ecclesiastes]]: as is set forth in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 4:29||]] [the margin gives III Reg. iv, 29–34] and the second of Paralipomenon[[2 Par 9:23||]], and as was also explained above[[Eccles 1:16||]]. He speaks of himself as of another, as is the custom of the authors of the Scriptures when they speak in their own books. He commends himself too, not for his own praise but for the honour of God and our edification, so that we may believe him more surely and consider his words more attentively. [[12:9|he taught the people|Docuit populum]] of Israel committed to him, especially those of his household, and others who came to him for instruction, like the queen of Saba; [[12:9|and declared the things that he had done|et enarravit quæ fecerat]], as appeared above in the second chapter[[Eccles 2:1||]] [the margin gives Eccle. ii, passim, that is, throughout the chapter]. [[12:9|and seeking out|Et investigans]] the truth about each thing, as was explained above[[Eccles 1:13||]], [[12:9|he set forth many parables|composuit parabolas multas]], namely three thousand, as we read in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 4:32||]]. Not all of these, however, were written down, as was said in the exposition of the book of Proverbs.

paras.t: Quæsivit verba utilia ad salutem, et conscripsit, per se vel per alios, sermones rectissimos, id est ab omni falsitate et injustitia alienos, ac veritate plenos : quantum ad ea quæ dixit ex ratione et absoluta assertione, non autem quantum ad ea quæ in isto protulit libro in persona carnalium : unde est illud, Nihil habet homo amplius jumento, etc.
paras.en: [[12:10|He sought profitable words|Quæsivit verba utilia]] for salvation, [[12:10|and wrote|et conscripsit]], by himself or by others, [[12:10|words most right|sermones rectissimos]], that is, free from all falsehood and injustice, [[12:10|and full of truth|ac veritate plenos]]: as regards what he said from reason and as an absolute assertion, but not as regards what he set down in this book in the person of carnal men, such as that saying: [[Eccles 3:19|man hath nothing more than beast|Nihil habet homo amplius jumento]], etc.

paras.t: Verba sapientium, qui libros sacræ ediderunt Scripturæ, et aliorum veraciter sapientium, sunt sicut stimuli : quoniam pungunt et excitant tardos, negligentes ac somnolentos; et quasi clavi in altum defixi, id est, firma et immobiliter vera, sicut clavi profunde incussi manent firmissime suo in loco, vel tam sublimiter fixi, quod nequeunt attingi aut extrahi. Altum autem, pro profundo frequenter accipitur : sicut in Psalmo, Veni in altitudinem maris; atque in Joanne, Puteus altus est. Sunt etiam quasi clavi, quia acuta ad increpandum, penetrativa ad inflammandum, efficacia ad interimendum omne peccatum. Unde in Jeremia Dominus loquitur : Nonne verba mea sunt quasi ignis, et quasi malleus conterens petram? Per Isaiam quoque Christus testatur : Posuit me quasi sagittam electam, et posuit os meum quasi gladium acutum. Quæ verba sapientium, per magistrorum consilium data sunt a pastore uno : id est, a Deo provisore universorum, et fidelium suorum summo pastore, data sunt per Moysen et Prophetas, qui consuluerunt et docuerunt hæc observari. Quasi dicat : Non per me solum aut principaliter data sunt. Deinde in novo Testamento per Apostolos et Evangelistas a Christo donata sunt, qui est princeps pastorum, et dixit : Unus est magister vester, Christus.
paras.en: [[12:11|The words of the wise|Verba sapientium]], who produced the books of sacred Scripture, and of others who are truly wise, are [[12:11|as goads|sicut stimuli]]: because they prick and rouse the slow, the negligent and the sleepy; [[12:11|and as nails deeply fastened in|et quasi clavi in altum defixi]], that is, firm and immovably true, as nails driven deep remain most firmly in their place; or fixed so high that they cannot be reached or pulled out. Now *altum* ["high"] is often taken for "deep" [*in altum*, rendered "deeply" in the Douay-Rheims]: as in the Psalm, [[Ps 68:3|I am come into the depth of the sea|Veni in altitudinem maris]]; and in John, [[John 4:11|the well is deep|Puteus altus est]]. They are also like nails because they are sharp for rebuking, piercing for inflaming, and effective for slaying every sin. Hence the Lord says in Jeremias: [[Jer 23:29|Are not my words as a fire|Nonne verba mea sunt quasi ignis]], [[Jer 23:29|and as a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?|et quasi malleus conterens petram]] Through Isaias, too, Christ testifies: He [[Is 49:2|hath made me as a chosen arrow|Posuit me quasi sagittam electam]], and [[Is 49:2|he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword|posuit os meum quasi gladium acutum]]. These [[12:11|words of the wise|verba sapientium]], [[12:11|which by the counsel of masters are given from one shepherd|per magistrorum consilium data sunt a pastore uno]]: that is, by God, the provider of all things and the chief shepherd of his faithful, they were given through Moses and the Prophets, who counselled and taught that these things be kept. As if to say: they were not given through me alone, nor chiefly through me. Then in the New Testament they were given by Christ through the Apostles and Evangelists; for he is the prince of pastors, and he said: [[Matt 23:10|one is your master, Christ|Unus est magister vester, Christus]][[Matt 23:8||]].

paras.t: His amplius, fili mi, ne requiras, id est nil quod non contineatur aliquo modo in Scripturis. Faciendi plures libros nullus est finis: quia ex una consideratione oritur alia, et jugiter novæ considerationes occurrunt. Et qui cessare proposuit atque quiescere uno quocumque libro completo, antequam illum compleverit, ex considerationibus interim sibi occurrentibus incitatur ad alios componendos. Frequensque meditatio, id est diligens consideratio, assidue necessaria ad libros componendos, carnis afflictio est, id est, corpus molestat, caput debilitat, et interiores exagitat sensus, qui rationi subserviunt, et similitudines atque phantasmata repræsentant : sicque (ut Commentator fatetur) vere fortiterque laborant. Talis quoque meditatio est sæpe laboriosa spiritui, cui difficile est quædam difficilia intelligere, de quibus vult scribere. Sed et corpus corruptibile aggravat animam, et terrena habitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem.
paras.en: [[12:12|More than these, my son, require not|His amplius, fili mi, ne requiras]], that is, nothing that is not contained in some way in the Scriptures. [[12:12|Of making many books there is no end|Faciendi plures libros nullus est finis]]: because from one consideration another arises, and new considerations continually present themselves. And one who has resolved to stop and rest when some one book is finished is spurred on, before he has finished it, to compose others, by the considerations that occur to him in the meantime. [[12:12|and much study|Frequensque meditatio]], that is, the diligent consideration that is constantly needed for composing books, [[12:12|is an affliction of the flesh|carnis afflictio est]]: that is, it troubles the body, weakens the head, and harasses the inner senses, which serve the reason and present likenesses and images [*phantasmata*: the pictures formed by the imagination, from which the intellect draws its concepts]; and so (as the Commentator acknowledges) they labour truly and hard. Such meditation is often laborious for the spirit too, which finds it hard to understand certain difficult things about which it wishes to write. And besides, [[Wis 9:15|the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|corpus corruptibile aggravat animam, et terrena habitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem]].

paras.t: Finem loquendi pariter omnes audiamus, id est summam omnium Scripturarum, saluberrimumque compendium, in cujus adimpletione tota pendet Scriptura. Deum time filiali timore, et mandata ejus, tam negativa, quibus vitia prohibentur, quam affirmativa, quibus virtutum actus præcipiuntur, et præsertim præcepta caritatis Dei ac proximorum, observa, perseverando usque in finem. Hoc est enim omnis homo : id est, ad hoc conditi sunt homines universi, et in hoc consistit eorum salus atque perfectio maxima, in plena observatione præcepti caritatis divinæ.
paras.en: [[12:13|Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse|Finem loquendi pariter omnes audiamus]], that is, the sum of all the Scriptures and their most wholesome compendium, on the fulfilling of which the whole of Scripture hangs. [[12:13|Fear God|Deum time]] with filial fear [that is, the fear of a son who dreads to offend his father, as distinct from servile fear, the fear of punishment], [[12:13|and keep his commandments|et mandata ejus]], both the negative ones, by which vices are forbidden, and the affirmative, by which acts of virtue are commanded, and above all the precepts of charity towards God and our neighbours: [[12:13|keep|observa]] them, persevering to the end. [[12:13|for this is all man|Hoc est enim omnis homo]]: that is, for this all men were made, and in this consists their salvation and greatest perfection, in the full keeping of the precept of divine charity.

paras.t: Cuncta quæ fiunt, adducet Deus in judicium : id est, omnium hominum actus interiores et exteriores judicabit Omnipotens, imo et bonorum actuum omissiones; pro omni errato, id est, ad puniendum quidquid erronee et inique est commissum, et omnem errorem fidei sanctæ contrarium. Sive bonum, sive malum sit. Hoc refertur ad illud, Cuncta quæ fiunt : ut sit sensus, Omnia judicabit tam bona quam mala. Vel si refertur ad illud, Pro omni errato, sensus est, quod omne erratum dijudicabit et puniet, sive sit bonum ex genere, sed perversa factum intentione, ut ire ad ecclesiam ob laudem humanam; sive sit malum ex propria ratione. Hinc ait Apostolus : Omnes nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi, ut referat unusquisque prout gessit in corpore, sive bonum, sive malum.
paras.en: [[12:14|And all things that are done, God will bring into judgment|Cuncta quæ fiunt, adducet Deus in judicium]]: that is, the Almighty will judge the inward and outward acts of all men, and even their omissions of good acts; [[12:14|for every error|pro omni errato]], that is, to punish whatever has been committed erroneously and wickedly, and every error contrary to the holy faith. [[12:14|whether it be good or evil|Sive bonum, sive malum sit]]. This refers to the words [[12:14|all things that are done|Cuncta quæ fiunt]], so that the sense is: he will judge all things, good as well as bad. Or if it refers to the words [[12:14|for every error|Pro omni errato]], the sense is that he will judge and punish every error, whether it be good in its kind [*bonum ex genere*: good by the kind of act it is, apart from the intention] but done with a perverse intention, like going to church for the praise of men, or evil by its very nature. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:10|we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive|Omnes nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi, ut referat unusquisque]] [[2 Cor 5:10|according as he hath done|prout gessit]] in the body, [[2 Cor 5:10|whether it be good or evil|sive bonum, sive malum]].

paras.t: Dicunt Hebræi, quod propter hanc ultimam auctoritatem, liber hic Salomonis receptus sit in sanctarum canone Scripturarum. In aliis enim videbatur sæpius deviasse; hic vero Omnipotentis justitiam declaravit, et qualiter serviendum sit ei, qui est super omnia Deus sublimis et benedictus. Amen.
paras.en: The Hebrews say that it was on account of this last sentence that this book of Solomon was received into the canon of the holy Scriptures. For in the other parts he seemed often to have gone astray; but here he declared the justice of the Almighty, and how we must serve him who is God, exalted and blessed above all things. Amen.
